# The Problem of Suffering and the Goodness of God: An Honest Reckoning

There is a kind of honesty required when speaking about suffering in the presence of God's goodness. It is the honesty that refuses easy answers, that sits with the widow in her silence before offering words, that acknowledges that the problem of evil is not primarily an intellectual puzzle to be solved but a wound that runs through human experience. Yet it is also an honesty that does not surrender the possibility that God is good—that somehow, in ways we may not fully comprehend, divine goodness and human suffering coexist in the same universe.

The problem is real. A child dies of leukemia. A woman is trafficked into slavery. A man loses everything to addiction, dragging his family into darkness with him. Innocent people suffer catastrophically while the guilty often prosper. And if God is all-powerful, He could prevent these things. If He is all-good, He would want to. Yet they happen. This is not a problem that yields to clever wordplay or dismissive gestures toward the inscrutability of God's ways. It is the problem that has turned believers into skeptics and skeptics into bitter certainty that no benevolent God exists.

Any serious theological response must begin by acknowledging the force of this objection. The suffering is not hypothetical. The injustice is not abstract. And the stakes are not merely intellectual—they are the stakes of whether faith itself remains possible in a world of genuine evil.

## The Free Will Defense

One enduring response to the problem of suffering locates the source of much evil in human freedom. God, the argument goes, created human beings with genuine liberty—the ability to choose good or evil. A world in which humans cannot genuinely choose evil is not a world in which they can genuinely choose good. Love, virtue, and moral goodness become possible only where the alternative—hatred, vice, and moral evil—is genuinely available. To create beings capable of authentic moral agency is to accept the risk that they will use that freedom to harm themselves and others.

This defense has considerable power. Much suffering is indeed traceable to human choice: war, exploitation, cruelty, negligence, addiction. If God had created a world where we could not hurt each other, He would have created a world where we could not freely love each other. The sacrifice of that freedom seems too high a price for safety. There is something deeply human in the desire to choose, even at the cost of danger, rather than to be safe automatons.

Yet the defense faces a real limitation: it accounts for moral evil but not natural evil. It explains suffering caused by human choice but not the suffering caused by disease, earthquake, hurricane, and the simple fact of bodily vulnerability. A child born with a painful genetic disorder has not chosen this suffering, nor has anyone else chosen it for her. The same applies to countless natural disasters and illnesses. The free will defense, while illuminating an important truth about the relationship between freedom and goodness, cannot bear the full weight of explaining why God permits a world in which nature itself inflicts agony on the innocent.

Moreover, even within the domain of moral evil, the defense leaves questions unanswered. God could have created beings with free will but with greater natural inclination toward good, or with limits on the magnitude of harm they can inflict. The fact that He did not do so suggests that either He could not (which would limit His power) or He chose not to (which raises the question of why). The free will defense illuminates one dimension of the problem but does not fully resolve it.

## Soul-Making and Spiritual Growth

Another response, sometimes called the soul-making theodicy, suggests that suffering serves a developmental purpose in the formation of human character and spiritual maturity. The argument draws on the observation that some of our most important virtues—courage, compassion, perseverance, humility—can be developed only in the context of difficulty and resistance. A world without suffering might be a world without genuine growth, without the possibility of becoming the kind of person capable of deep love and meaningful achievement.

This theodicy resonates with Scripture in important ways. The Letter of James begins by urging readers to "consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance" (James 1:2-3). The author is not suggesting that suffering is good in itself, but that God can work through it to develop spiritual maturity. Similarly, the Psalms repeatedly move from lament to trust, suggesting that the experience of suffering, when brought before God, can deepen faith rather than destroy it. And Paul writes that he "rejoices in [his] sufferings for you, and fills up in [his] flesh what is still lacking in regard to Christ's afflictions" (Colossians 1:24), suggesting that suffering can be redemptive and transformative.

Yet this response too has limits that must be acknowledged with pastoral sensitivity. Not all suffering produces growth; some destroys. Trauma can shatter a person rather than strengthen them. Prolonged illness can deplete rather than develop. And even if we grant that some suffering can be redemptive, it does not follow that all the suffering in the world is necessary for human development. A God of infinite wisdom and power could presumably achieve human maturation through less devastating means. The fact that He does not suggests either that He cannot, or that something else is at stake in His permission of suffering.

Moreover, it is deeply troubling to suggest to someone in acute agony that their suffering is "for their spiritual growth." Such words, offered in the presence of real pain, can sound like cruelty dressed in theological language. The soul-making theodicy may offer some consolation in retrospect, when growth has actually occurred, but it is a poor comfort in the moment of suffering itself.

## The God Who Suffers

Perhaps the most distinctive Christian response to the problem of suffering does not attempt to explain why God permits it, but rather insists that God does not stand outside suffering, dispensing it from a safe distance. Instead, in the Incarnation and the Cross, God enters into human suffering, experiencing it from within.

The Gospels present Jesus not as a detached problem-solver but as one who weeps at the tomb of Lazarus, who sweats blood in Gethsemane, who cries out in abandonment on the cross. The crucifixion is not a solution to the problem of suffering—it does not explain why suffering exists—but it is a radical statement about God's relationship to it. God does not merely permit suffering; God suffers. The infinite enters into the finite, the eternal into time, the divine into pain.

This response does not satisfy the demand for explanation, and it should not pretend to. It does not tell us why children die or why injustice flourishes. But it offers something that may be more important: it offers solidarity. The God revealed in Christ is not a distant architect indifferent to human agony. He is Emmanuel, God with us, present in the darkness, bearing the weight of human suffering in His own flesh.

The Apostle Paul writes that "the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with wordless groans" (Romans 8:26). Even prayer itself becomes an expression of shared suffering, the Spirit groaning with us when words fail. This is not an explanation; it is a companionship.

## The Limits of Understanding

What must be said, finally, is that the problem of suffering may not have a complete answer available to us. This is not a cop-out but a statement of intellectual humility. We are finite creatures attempting to comprehend the purposes of an infinite God. We see through a glass darkly. Our understanding of divine justice may be as limited as a child's understanding of parental discipline—we may lack the conceptual framework to fully grasp why God permits what He permits.

This does not mean that faith is irrational or that the problem is unimportant. It means that faith, at its deepest, is not primarily about having satisfying explanations. It is about trust in the character of God despite the absence of complete understanding. It is what Job expresses when, after his anguished questioning receives no direct answer, he says: "I know that my redeemer lives... And after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God" (Job 19:25-26). Job does not receive an explanation for his suffering. Instead, he receives an encounter with God, and in that encounter, his need for explanation becomes secondary to his need for relationship.

## A Measured Conclusion

The goodness of God and the reality of suffering remain in tension. The free will defense illuminates one dimension of that tension. The soul-making theodicy suggests that suffering can serve purposes beyond mere punishment or randomness. The Cross testifies that God does not stand apart from human agony but enters into it. Yet none of these responses fully resolves the problem. The suffering of the innocent remains troubling, the existence of natural evil remains mysterious, and the magnitude of human pain often seems disproportionate to any conceivable good it might produce.

What remains is not a solution but a posture: the posture of one who continues to trust in God's goodness while refusing to minimize the reality of suffering, who seeks to understand while accepting the limits of understanding, who brings both lament and hope before God, knowing that the God who hears the cry of the suffering is Himself present in that cry. This is not a satisfying answer to the problem of evil. But it may be the most honest answer available to those who have encountered both the reality of suffering and the presence of God.

# The Question God Refuses to Dismiss: Suffering and the Goodness of God

The problem of suffering remains the most serious intellectual challenge to Christian faith—not because Christians lack sophisticated responses, but because no response can fully dissolve the ache of it. A child dies of leukemia. A woman is brutalized by someone she trusted. A man's mind deteriorates into dementia while his body lingers. In these moments, arguments about divine omnipotence and benevolence feel like philosophy papers scattered on a hospital bed. Yet the problem persists not as mere abstraction but as the lived tension between what we claim to believe about God and what we actually experience in a world shot through with suffering that seems gratuitous, senseless, and cruel.

We do well to begin by stating the problem with precision rather than dismissing it. The logical problem of evil, classically formulated, runs like this: If God is omnipotent, he can prevent all suffering. If God is good, he would want to prevent all suffering. Yet suffering exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, or he is not good, or he does not exist. This formulation has teeth. It is not merely emotional complaint but a genuine logical tension that demands serious engagement. The modern atheist objection to Christianity is not primarily that suffering exists—suffering's reality is not in dispute—but that the existence of apparently unnecessary suffering sits uneasily with the claim that an all-powerful, all-good God governs the world.

To dismiss this objection as faithless is to refuse the very intellectual honesty that faith requires. The medieval theologian Thomas Aquinas, no lightweight in matters of doctrine, acknowledged that suffering presents a genuine problem requiring genuine explanation. The biblical book of Job refuses to minimize the weight of the question. Job's friends initially attempt theodicy—explaining why Job's suffering must serve some divine purpose—and God himself rejects their explanations as inadequate. "You have not spoken of me what is right," God tells them. The text suggests that some suffering resists neat theological packaging.

Yet the Christian tradition has developed several responses that, while not eliminating the tension, do illuminate it in ways worth serious consideration.

## The Free Will Defence

One of the most enduring responses appeals to human freedom. An omnipotent God, this argument suggests, faces a genuine logical constraint: he cannot create beings with libertarian free will and simultaneously guarantee that they will never choose evil. To create free creatures is to accept the risk that they will abuse their freedom. Much human suffering—perhaps most of the suffering we inflict on one another—results from human choices made in exercise of genuine freedom. God could have created a world of puppets, but such a world would contain no moral agency, no genuine love, no authentic virtue. A world with free creatures and the suffering that sometimes follows from their choices is, arguably, better than a world of determined automatons.

This response has considerable force. It explains a significant portion of human suffering: war, abuse, betrayal, cruelty. It preserves human dignity by treating us as genuine agents rather than divine marionettes. And it has biblical resonance. The Genesis account of humanity created in God's image includes the capacity to choose, to rebel, to turn away. The epistles repeatedly exhort believers to choose righteousness, a rhetoric that makes sense only if genuine choice exists. Paul's wrestling with predestination and human responsibility in Romans 9-11 suggests the tradition recognized this tension without resolving it into neat determinism.

Yet the free will defence does not fully explain suffering. It accounts well for the suffering we inflict on one another, but what of natural suffering? The free will defence struggles to explain why God permits earthquakes that bury children, diseases that ravage the innocent, the random cruelties of nature. A child born with a painful genetic disorder has not chosen anything; the suffering she endures cannot be attributed to anyone's free choice. The theodicy that works well for moral evil—suffering caused by human choice—proves inadequate for natural evil, the suffering that springs from the structure of the physical world itself.

## Soul-Making and Spiritual Growth

A second response, sometimes called soul-making theodicy, suggests that suffering serves a formative purpose in human spiritual development. This view, developed by theologians like Irenaeus and more recently by John Hick, proposes that God permits suffering not as punishment for sin but as the context within which spiritual maturation occurs. Courage cannot develop without danger. Compassion cannot deepen without exposure to others' pain. Faith cannot be tested and strengthened without trial. A world without suffering would be a world without the possibility of genuine moral and spiritual growth.

This response has genuine psychological and spiritual insight. Anyone who has emerged from significant suffering often testifies to unexpected growth: deeper wisdom, greater compassion, more authentic faith. The apostle Paul writes of rejoicing in his sufferings because they produce endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope. The image of God refining faith like gold in fire appears throughout Scripture. These are not pious platitudes but genuine observations about how suffering can reshape us.

Yet here too we must be honest about limits. This theodicy works better for some suffering than others. A person who survives cancer and emerges with deepened faith has experienced soul-making. But what of the person who dies of cancer at thirty? What spiritual growth justifies the suffering of someone who never experiences the supposed benefit? And we must resist the temptation to impose meaning on suffering retroactively, assuring the grieving that their loss will "make them stronger" or "teach them something valuable." This can feel like adding insult to injury, as if the suffering itself were justified by whatever growth might emerge. Some suffering seems simply destructive, diminishing rather than developing the soul.

Moreover, the soul-making theodicy risks making suffering itself the point, when the Christian tradition has long recognized suffering as an intrusion, a disorder in God's creation, something to be resisted and healed rather than welcomed as pedagogical opportunity. Jesus healed the sick; he did not tell them their illnesses were spiritually beneficial. The resurrection promises not the eternal continuation of suffering but its ultimate abolition. A theodicy that makes suffering itself the goal seems to undercut this fundamental Christian hope.

## The Cross as God's Participation

A third response, less a logical argument than a theological reorientation, points to the cross as God's answer to suffering. This response does not explain suffering so much as transform our relationship to it by insisting that God does not remain aloof from human pain but enters into it. In Jesus, God experiences suffering from within. God does not explain suffering from a distance but suffers alongside us, bearing the weight of the world's pain in his own body.

This response carries profound spiritual and theological significance. It means that when we suffer, we are not abandoned by God but joined by him. The cross becomes the revelation not of God's explanation for suffering but of God's solidarity with those who suffer. This is not theodicy in the classical sense—it does not answer the question "Why does God permit suffering?"—but it transforms the question itself. The cross suggests that the question is not primarily about divine explanation but about divine presence.

The Psalms reflect this dynamic. The psalmists do not typically receive explanations for their suffering; instead, they encounter God's presence within their suffering. "The Lord is near to the brokenhearted," the psalmist declares, not explaining why hearts break but affirming that God draws near to those who are broken. The cross fulfills and deepens this promise. God does not answer the problem of suffering with a theodicy but with a presence.

Yet we must be careful not to sentimentalize the cross. The cross was not redemptive because suffering itself is redemptive; it was redemptive because God transformed it. Jesus did not embrace suffering as good but as something to be endured and overcome. The resurrection is not a gentle spiritual comfort but a radical contradiction of death, a promise that suffering will not have the final word.

## The Limits of Understanding

In the end, we must acknowledge what honest reflection reveals: no theodicy fully satisfies. The free will defence explains moral evil but not natural evil. Soul-making theodicy illuminates some suffering but not all. The cross assures us of God's presence but does not explain why God permits suffering in the first place. Each response captures something true, yet none closes the gap completely.

This is not a failure of theology but a recognition of reality. We are finite creatures attempting to comprehend the ways of an infinite God. The book of Job ends not with explanation but with encounter. God does not answer Job's questions about why he suffers; instead, God overwhelms Job with the sheer reality of divine wisdom and power expressed in creation. Job's response—"I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you"—suggests that the deepest answer to suffering is not intellectual but relational: knowing God more fully, encountering his character more deeply.

This does not mean we should abandon the intellectual task. Honest wrestling with the problem of evil is itself a form of faith, a refusal to accept easy answers or to pretend that suffering is less serious than it is. But it means recognizing that faith ultimately rests not on solved problems but on trust in a God whose character we have come to know through Scripture, through tradition, through the testimony of countless believers, and through our own encounter with divine grace.

The suffering in our world remains a genuine problem, one that demands our continued thought and our deepest compassion. Yet the Christian claim is not that we have solved the problem but that we have met the God who suffers with us and promises ultimately to end suffering. In that promise, and in the presence of the God who makes it, we find not explanation but hope.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a version of this essay that begins with a tidy philosophical syllogism and ends with a reassuring conclusion. This is not that essay. Not because the philosophical questions don't matter — they do, enormously — but because the problem of suffering is not first encountered in a seminar room. It is encountered in a hospital corridor at 2 a.m., in the aftermath of a diagnosis, in the quiet of a house that used to hold a child's laughter. Any honest engagement with this question must begin by acknowledging that it is asked, most often, through tears.

The formal problem is well known. If God is omnipotent, He has the power to prevent suffering. If God is perfectly good, He has the desire to prevent suffering. Suffering exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, not perfectly good, or not real. This is not a frivolous objection. It is, as the philosopher J.L. Mackie argued, a genuine logical tension at the heart of theistic belief — not merely an emotional difficulty but an intellectual one. Dismissing it as a failure of faith does no one any favors. The objection deserves to be met on its own terms, with honesty about what can and cannot be said in response.

What makes the problem particularly acute for Christians is that the tradition does not merely claim that God exists, but that God is love — that the fundamental character of ultimate reality is self-giving goodness. A distant deity, an indifferent first cause, would not generate the same tension. It is precisely because Christians make such extraordinary claims about divine goodness that the existence of extraordinary suffering demands an account.

## The Freedom That Costs

One of the most enduring responses is the free will defense, articulated with particular rigor by Alvin Plantinga. The argument holds that God, in creating beings capable of genuine love and moral agency, necessarily created beings capable of choosing evil. A world of automata — creatures programmed to always do good — would not be a world containing real love, real courage, or real virtue. These goods require the possibility of their opposites. God does not will the evil that free creatures commit, but He permits the conditions under which evil becomes possible because those same conditions make possible the highest goods.

This response carries real force. It accounts for a vast amount of the suffering in the world — the cruelties of war, the devastation of injustice, the quiet destructions of selfishness and neglect. And it takes seriously the biblical narrative's insistence that human beings are genuine agents, not puppets. When Genesis describes the primal act of disobedience, it does not portray God as the author of the choice but as the one who grieves it. The story insists: this was not what was intended. Something has gone wrong, and the wrongness traces back to creaturely freedom.

But the free will defense, taken alone, is incomplete. It struggles with what philosophers call natural evil — the suffering caused not by human choices but by earthquakes, cancers, genetic disorders, the predatory structure of the natural world. A child born with a devastating illness has not been harmed by anyone's free choice in any obvious sense. The tectonic plate does not choose to shift. To attribute all natural evil to some downstream consequence of a primordial human fall, as some theological traditions have attempted, raises as many questions as it answers and risks turning the doctrine of the fall into a mechanism it was never meant to be.

## The Furnace and the Formation

A second major response — the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern form by John Hick — takes a different approach. Rather than focusing on the origin of suffering, it focuses on its potential purpose. On this view, the world is not meant to be a paradise but a place of formation. Suffering, struggle, and even tragedy are the conditions under which virtues like compassion, perseverance, and sacrificial love can develop. A world without difficulty would be a world without growth. Human beings are not created as finished products but as creatures in the process of becoming — and that process requires resistance, challenge, even pain.

There is something genuinely illuminating here. Anyone who has suffered and come through it knows that certain kinds of depth, empathy, and wisdom are forged nowhere else. The apostle Paul, writing to the church in Rome, speaks of suffering producing endurance, endurance producing character, and character producing hope — and he is clearly drawing on lived experience, not abstract theory. James makes a similar move, urging his readers to count trials as occasions for the development of steadfastness. These are not glib sentiments. They come from communities that knew persecution, poverty, and loss.

But the soul-making theodicy, pressed too far, becomes monstrous. It works reasonably well for moderate suffering — the hardships that build resilience, the failures that teach humility. It becomes obscene when applied to extreme cases. To tell the parent of a dying child that this suffering is for their spiritual development is not theology; it is cruelty. To suggest that the Holocaust was a soul-making exercise is to lose all moral seriousness. The theodicy is useful as a partial account, but it must not be made to carry more weight than it can bear. Some suffering is so excessive, so disproportionate to any conceivable good that could come from it, that invoking growth or character formation feels like an insult to the sufferer.

This is where intellectual honesty demands a pause. Both responses — free will and soul-making — illuminate genuine aspects of the problem. Neither resolves it entirely. And any theologian or philosopher who claims to have a complete answer to why God permits the specific sufferings that exist in this world is claiming more than any human being can know.

## The God Who Enters the Wreckage

But Christianity does not offer only philosophical arguments. It offers a story — and at the center of that story is something that no other major theological tradition provides: a God who suffers.

The cross of Christ is not, in the first instance, an explanation of suffering. It is something stranger and, I think, more profound. It is God's entry into suffering from the inside. The incarnation means that God does not observe human pain from a safe distance. In Jesus, God experiences hunger, exhaustion, betrayal, abandonment, torture, and death. The cry from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — is a direct quotation of Psalm 22, and it is perhaps the most disorienting sentence in all of Scripture. God, addressing God, asking *why*.

This does not solve the intellectual problem in any neat sense. But it fundamentally changes its character. The question is no longer simply "Why does God allow suffering?" but "What kind of God enters into it willingly?" The cross reveals a God who does not stand above the anguish of the world but bears it. And the resurrection that follows is not a negation of the suffering — the risen Christ still bears the wounds — but a declaration that suffering does not have the final word.

The book of Job is instructive here precisely because of what it does *not* do. Job's friends offer him theodicies — you must have sinned, God is teaching you something, justice will be restored. The text systematically dismantles every one of these explanations. When God finally speaks from the whirlwind, He does not give Job an answer. He gives Job *Himself*. "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" is not a rebuke so much as an invitation into a larger frame of reference — one that Job cannot fully comprehend but that he can trust, because he has encountered the One who inhabits it. Job's response is not "Now I understand" but "Now I have seen you." The resolution is relational, not intellectual.

This is not a cop-out, though it can be made into one. To say "we cannot fully understand" is honest only if it is paired with a genuine willingness to sit in the darkness rather than paper over it with false comfort. The biblical tradition, remarkably, makes room for this. The psalms of lament — nearly a third of the Psalter — are not failures of faith. They are acts of faith, directed at a God who is trusted enough to be accused. "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" That question is canonical Scripture. The tradition itself authorizes the protest.

## Living Without a Final Answer

Where does this leave us? Not with a solution, but perhaps with something more livable than a solution. We have partial answers that illuminate without resolving. We have a God who, according to the central claim of the Christian faith, does not exempt Himself from the suffering He permits. We have a biblical tradition that holds together trust and anguish without requiring that one silence the other. And we have the honest acknowledgment that we see, as Paul puts it, through a glass darkly.

What we do not have — and what I think we should stop pretending to have — is a comprehensive explanation that makes suffering make sense. The danger of theodicy is that it can become a way of domesticating evil, of explaining it so thoroughly that we lose our capacity to be appalled by it. The proper Christian response to suffering includes both the intellectual work of thinking carefully about God's purposes and the moral refusal to declare that everything is fine. Everything is not fine. The Christian hope is not that everything is fine but that everything will be redeemed — that the God who entered the tomb will, in the end, wipe every tear from every eye.

Until then, the most faithful posture may be the one modeled by the biblical writers themselves: holding together an unshakable conviction that God is good with an unflinching recognition that the world is broken, and refusing to let go of either truth. This is not comfortable. It is not meant to be. But it has the virtue of being honest — honest about the weight of suffering, honest about the limits of understanding, and honest about the stubborn, persistent hope that the darkness, however deep, is not the end of the story.

But Christianity does not offer only philosophical arguments. It offers a narrative — and at the center of that narrative is something no other major theological tradition provides in quite the same way: a God who does not remain untouched by the world's pain.

The cross of Christ is not, in the first instance, an explanation of suffering. It is something stranger. In Jesus, God experiences hunger, exhaustion, betrayal, torture, and death. The cry from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — is a direct quotation of Psalm 22, and it is perhaps the most disorienting sentence in all of Scripture. God, addressing God, asking *why*.

A note of theological honesty is required here. The claim that God "suffers" is not uncontested. The classical tradition — Aquinas, the Cappadocians, much of Reformed orthodoxy — insists that God does not suffer in the divine nature, and that Christ's suffering is real precisely *in his human nature*. Moltmann's *The Crucified God* presses in the other direction, arguing that the cross reveals suffering within the life of the Trinity itself. This essay cannot resolve that debate. But even the most classical account must reckon with the fact that the incarnation means God has united himself to a suffering human life in the most intimate way possible. However one parses the metaphysics, the cross is not the act of a spectator.

The Psalm 22 citation deserves closer attention. The psalm as a whole moves from desolation to vindication — from "why have you forsaken me?" to "all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord." Some scholars argue that Jesus, in quoting the opening line, invokes the entire psalm, including its resolution. Others insist that the cry of dereliction should be taken at face value: a moment of genuine divine abandonment. The tension between these readings may itself be the point. The cross holds together absence and presence, forsakenness and faithfulness, in a way that resists tidy resolution.

The tradition itself authorizes the protest.

We have a biblical tradition that holds together trust and anguish without requiring that one silence the other.

What we do not have — and what we should stop pretending to have — is a comprehensive explanation that makes suffering make sense. # The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a version of this essay that begins with a tidy philosophical syllogism and ends with a reassuring conclusion. This is not that essay. Not because the philosophical questions don't matter — they do, enormously — but because the problem of suffering is not first encountered in a seminar room. It is encountered in a hospital corridor at 2 a.m., in the aftermath of a diagnosis, in the quiet of a house that used to hold a child's laughter. Any honest engagement with this question must begin by acknowledging that it is asked, most often, through tears.

The formal problem is well known. If God is omnipotent, He has the power to prevent suffering. If God is perfectly good, He has the desire to prevent suffering. Suffering exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, not perfectly good, or not real. This is not a frivolous objection. It is, as the philosopher J.L. Mackie argued, a genuine logical tension at the heart of theistic belief — not merely an emotional difficulty but an intellectual one. Dismissing it as a failure of faith does no one any favors. The objection deserves to be met on its own terms, with honesty about what can and cannot be said in response.

What makes the problem particularly acute for Christians is that the tradition does not merely claim that God exists, but that God is love — that the fundamental character of ultimate reality is self-giving goodness. A distant deity, an indifferent first cause, would not generate the same tension. It is precisely because Christians make such extraordinary claims about divine goodness that the existence of extraordinary suffering demands an account.

## The Freedom That Costs

One of the most enduring responses is the free will defense, articulated with particular rigor by Alvin Plantinga. The argument holds that God, in creating beings capable of genuine love and moral agency, necessarily created beings capable of choosing evil. A world of automata — creatures programmed to always do good — would not be a world containing real love, real courage, or real virtue. These goods require the possibility of their opposites. God does not will the evil that free creatures commit, but He permits the conditions under which evil becomes possible because those same conditions make possible the highest goods.

This response carries real force. It accounts for a vast amount of the suffering in the world — the cruelties of war, the devastation of injustice, the quiet destructions of selfishness and neglect. And it takes seriously the biblical narrative's insistence that human beings are genuine agents, not puppets. When Genesis describes the primal act of disobedience, it does not portray God as the author of the choice but as the one who grieves it. The story insists: this was not what was intended. Something has gone wrong, and the wrongness traces back to creaturely freedom.

But the free will defense, taken alone, is incomplete. It struggles with what philosophers call natural evil — the suffering caused not by human choices but by earthquakes, cancers, genetic disorders, the predatory structure of the natural world. A child born with a devastating illness has not been harmed by anyone's free choice in any obvious sense. The tectonic plate does not choose to shift. To attribute all natural evil to some downstream consequence of a primordial human fall, as some theological traditions have attempted, raises as many questions as it answers and risks turning the doctrine of the fall into a mechanism it was never meant to be.

## The Furnace and the Formation

A second major response — the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern form by John Hick — takes a different approach. Rather than focusing on the origin of suffering, it focuses on its potential purpose. On this view, the world is not meant to be a paradise but a place of formation. Suffering, struggle, and even tragedy are the conditions under which virtues like compassion, perseverance, and sacrificial love can develop. A world without difficulty would be a world without growth. Human beings are not created as finished products but as creatures in the process of becoming — and that process requires resistance, challenge, even pain.

There is something genuinely illuminating here. Anyone who has suffered and come through it knows that certain kinds of depth, empathy, and wisdom are forged nowhere else. The apostle Paul, writing to the church in Rome, speaks of suffering producing endurance, endurance producing character, and character producing hope — and he is clearly drawing on lived experience, not abstract theory. James makes a similar move, urging his readers to count trials as occasions for the development of steadfastness. These are not glib sentiments. They come from communities that knew persecution, poverty, and loss.

But the soul-making theodicy, pressed too far, becomes monstrous. It works reasonably well for moderate suffering — the hardships that build resilience, the failures that teach humility. It becomes obscene when applied to extreme cases. To tell the parent of a dying child that this suffering is for their spiritual development is not theology; it is cruelty. To suggest that the Holocaust was a soul-making exercise is to lose all moral seriousness. The theodicy is useful as a partial account, but it must not be made to carry more weight than it can bear. Some suffering is so excessive, so disproportionate to any conceivable good that could come from it, that invoking growth or character formation feels like an insult to the sufferer.

This is where intellectual honesty demands a pause. Both responses — free will and soul-making — illuminate genuine aspects of the problem. Neither resolves it entirely. And any theologian or philosopher who claims to have a complete answer to why God permits the specific sufferings that exist in this world is claiming more than any human being can know.

## The God Who Enters the Wreckage

But Christianity does not offer only philosophical arguments. It offers a story — and at the center of that story is something that no other major theological tradition provides: a God who suffers. This approach, sometimes called a cruciform theodicy, shifts the ground of the discussion entirely. Where the free will defense and the soul-making theodicy attempt to explain suffering from above — to offer reasons why a good God might permit it — the theology of the cross approaches the question from below, from inside the wreckage itself.

The cross of Christ is not, in the first instance, an explanation of suffering. It is something stranger and, I think, more profound. It is God's entry into suffering from the inside. The incarnation means that God does not observe human pain from a safe distance. In Jesus, God experiences hunger, exhaustion, betrayal, abandonment, torture, and death. The cry from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — is a direct quotation of Psalm 22, and it is perhaps the most disorienting sentence in all of Scripture. God, addressing God, asking *why*.

This does not solve the intellectual problem in any neat sense. But it fundamentally changes its character. The question is no longer simply "Why does God allow suffering?" but "What kind of God enters into it willingly?" The cross reveals a God who does not stand above the anguish of the world but bears it. And the resurrection that follows is not a negation of the suffering — the risen Christ still bears the wounds — but a declaration that suffering does not have the final word.

The cruciform approach also makes room for something the other theodicies tend to suppress: protest. The book of Job is instructive here precisely because of what it does *not* do. Job's friends offer him theodicies — you must have sinned, God is teaching you something, justice will be restored. The text systematically dismantles every one of these explanations. When God finally speaks from the whirlwind, He does not give Job an answer. He gives Job *Himself*. "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" is not a rebuke so much as an invitation into a larger frame of reference — one that Job cannot fully comprehend but that he can trust, because he has encountered the One who inhabits it. Job's response is not "Now I understand" but "Now I have seen you." The resolution is relational, not intellectual.

This is not a cop-out, though it can be made into one. To say "we cannot fully understand" is honest only if it is paired with a genuine willingness to sit in the darkness rather than paper over it with false comfort. The biblical tradition, remarkably, makes room for this. The psalms of lament — nearly a third of the Psalter — are not failures of faith. They are acts of faith, directed at a God who is trusted enough to be accused. "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" That question is canonical Scripture. The tradition itself authorizes the protest. What some theologians have called a protest theodicy finds its roots not in modern skepticism but in the oldest layers of Israel's worship — the insistence that the world is not as it should be, spoken directly into the face of the God who made it.

## Living Without a Final Answer

Where does this leave us? Not with a solution, but perhaps with something more livable than a solution. We have partial answers that illuminate without resolving. We have a God who, according to the central claim of the Christian faith, does not exempt Himself from the suffering He permits. We have a biblical tradition that holds together trust and anguish without requiring that one silence the other. And we have the honest acknowledgment that we see, as Paul puts it, through a glass darkly.

What we do not have — and what I think we should stop pretending to have — is a comprehensive explanation that makes suffering make sense. Everything is not fine. The Christian hope is not that everything is fine but that everything will be redeemed — that the God who entered the tomb will, in the end, wipe every tear from every eye.

Until then, the most faithful posture may be the one modeled by the biblical writers themselves: holding together an unshakable conviction that God is good with an unflinching recognition that the world is broken, and refusing to let go of either truth. This is the posture of a people who have seen the wounds on the risen body — who know that the God they trust has scars, and that those scars are not erased but transfigured. It is not comfortable. It is not meant to be. But it has the virtue of being honest — and of placing its hope not in an explanation that resolves the tension, but in the scarred hands of the One who has promised to.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a moment in Dostoevsky's *The Brothers Karamazov* when Ivan Karenin describes, in meticulous and unbearable detail, the suffering of children — a girl locked in a freezing outhouse by her parents, a boy torn apart by hunting dogs before his mother's eyes. Then he turns to his brother Alyosha, the young monk, and says: "It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return him the ticket."

Ivan does not argue that God does not exist. He argues that no final harmony, no eschatological resolution, could ever justify the tears of one tortured child. And he is raising the question that every honest theology must face without flinching: If God is good, and God is sovereign, then what do we make of the world as it actually is?

This is not merely an academic puzzle. It is the question whispered in hospital corridors, screamed at gravesides, and carried silently by people who have stopped praying because they cannot reconcile what they were told about God with what they have experienced of life. Any response that does not begin by honoring the weight of that experience is not worth offering.

## The Problem, Stated Plainly

The logical problem of evil, in its classical formulation, runs something like this: If God is omnipotent, He could prevent suffering. If God is omnibenevolent, He would want to prevent suffering. Suffering exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, not good, or not there at all.

The force of this argument is not merely logical. It is existential. It is one thing to discuss the problem of evil in a seminar room. It is another to hold it in your hands when the diagnosis comes back, when the child does not survive, when the earthquake buries a village, when systemic cruelty grinds on for generations without apparent divine interruption. The sheer scale and distribution of suffering — its randomness, its disproportionate weight on the vulnerable, its apparent indifference to innocence — presses against every claim that the universe is governed by a loving will.

Philosophers have rightly noted that the logical form of the problem can be addressed: there is no strict contradiction between God's existence and the existence of evil if God might have morally sufficient reasons for permitting it. But this observation, while technically important, can feel thin in the face of actual suffering. The question is not only whether God *could* have reasons, but whether any reasons could be adequate — whether the math of justification even applies to a child's pain. Ivan's protest is precisely that the calculus itself is obscene.

We must hold this tension honestly. The moment theodicy becomes glib, it has failed.

## The Free Will Defense: Love and Its Costs

One of the most enduring responses to the problem of evil is the free will defense, articulated with particular rigor by Alvin Plantinga but rooted in a tradition stretching back through Augustine. The argument holds that God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, relationship, and moral action, necessarily created beings capable of choosing cruelty, selfishness, and destruction. A world of automata who could only do good would not be a world containing love in any meaningful sense. Love requires freedom, and freedom entails the real possibility of its misuse.

There is genuine depth here. The biblical narrative itself seems to take human freedom with radical seriousness. The opening chapters of Genesis do not present evil as something God designed into the system but as something that enters through choice — through the mysterious but real capacity of creatures to turn away from the source of their life. The narrative of Scripture, from the garden to the exile to the cross, is shaped by the interplay between divine purpose and human agency, and God is consistently portrayed as one who woos, warns, grieves, and waits rather than overrides.

Yet the free will defense has real limits, and we should name them. It addresses moral evil — the suffering humans inflict on one another — with some plausibility. It is far less adequate to natural evil: the earthquake, the childhood leukemia, the parasitic wasp. No human choice caused the tectonic plate to shift. And even within the domain of moral evil, the defense raises hard questions about proportion. Does the freedom of one person to choose violence justify the suffering of their victim? The defense explains why evil is *possible*; it does not fully explain why God permits *this much* of it, or why the innocent bear its heaviest cost.

## Soul-Making: Suffering as Formation

A second significant response comes from what John Hick called the "soul-making" theodicy, drawing on the thought of Irenaeus. On this view, the world is not meant to be a paradise but a place of becoming — an environment in which moral and spiritual growth is possible precisely because it contains challenge, difficulty, and even pain. Virtues like courage, compassion, patience, and sacrificial love are not qualities that can exist in a vacuum; they require resistance, struggle, and the real possibility of failure. A world without suffering would be a world without the conditions for the deepest forms of human goodness.

There is something to this. Scripture does not treat suffering as simply meaningless. The letter of James opens with the striking instruction to "consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of various kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance" (James 1:2-3). Paul, writing from prison, speaks of a mysterious process by which "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3-4). The Psalms of lament — and there are many — do not resolve into silence but into a deepened, harder-won trust. The biblical witness repeatedly suggests that God does something *in* suffering, even when He does not remove it.

But the soul-making theodicy, pressed too far, becomes cruel. It works tolerably well for moderate suffering that a person survives and integrates. It becomes grotesque when applied to the Holocaust, to the trafficking of children, to the infant who dies before any "soul-making" could conceivably occur. To tell a mother that her child's death was for her spiritual formation is not theology; it is violence dressed in religious language. Hick himself acknowledged that the theodicy requires an eschatological horizon — a life beyond this one in which the process is completed and the suffering redeemed — but even this does not fully answer Ivan's challenge. The question remains: Could a good God not have found a less devastating curriculum?

We must be honest: these theodicies illuminate corners of the problem, but neither of them resolves it. They are partial lights, not full explanations. And perhaps this is itself significant.

## The Cross: God Inside the Suffering

There is a third movement in Christian thought that is not, strictly speaking, a theodicy at all — it does not explain *why* God permits suffering — but it makes a claim that, if true, changes the nature of the question entirely. It is the claim that in Jesus Christ, God has entered into suffering from the inside.

The crucifixion is not, in Christian theology, merely an unfortunate event that happened to a good teacher. It is the moment when God, in the person of the Son, submitted to the worst that human evil and natural mortality could inflict. The cry of dereliction from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34) — is not a decorative quotation. It is the voice of God experiencing abandonment. The one who is supposed to be the answer to suffering is himself consumed by it.

This does not solve the problem of evil in any philosophical sense. But it reframes it. The God revealed in the cross is not a distant deity who permits suffering from a safe distance while offering explanations. He is a God who has, in some profound and mysterious way, taken the suffering into Himself. Jürgen Moltmann, writing in *The Crucified God*, argued that the cross means God suffers *with* and *in* the victims of history — that the pain of the world is not external to the divine life but is borne within it.

This matters pastorally in ways that abstract theodicy often does not. When the psalmist cries out, "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1), the Christian claim is that this cry is not met with a syllogism but with a presence — the presence of One who has Himself cried out in the same darkness. The letter to the Hebrews insists that we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who "has been tempted in every way, just as we are" (Hebrews 4:15). The comfort offered is not comprehension but companionship — and, beyond that, the promise of resurrection, the insistence that suffering does not have the final word.

## Living With the Question

I want to be careful here not to present the mystery of God's purposes as a rhetorical escape hatch — the theological equivalent of a shrug. "We can't understand God's ways" is true, but it can function as a way of avoiding the question rather than honoring it. The book of Job is instructive precisely because it refuses both options. Job's friends offer tidy theodicies — you must have sinned, God is teaching you something, the wicked always get what they deserve — and God explicitly rebukes them. But God does not give Job an explanation either. He gives Job *Himself* — the overwhelming, irreducible presence of the Creator, who speaks from the whirlwind not to answer Job's questions but to reframe them within a reality so vast that Job's categories cannot contain it.

This is not a cop-out if — and only if — the God who refuses to explain is also the God who shows up. The biblical pattern is not explanation but presence, not a theory of suffering but a promise of faithfulness. "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you" (Isaiah 43:2). Not: I will explain the waters. Not: I will prevent the waters. I will be *with you*.

For those in the midst of suffering, this may not feel like enough. And we should have the honesty to say so. There are seasons when the silence of God is deafening, when the promises feel like words on a page and nothing more, when the darkness does not lift. The lament psalms exist because the people of God have always known this experience. Faith is not the absence of this anguish; sometimes faith is the decision to keep speaking to a God who seems not to answer.

The problem of suffering is not one we solve. It is one we inhabit — with whatever courage, honesty, and trembling hope we can muster. The Christian claim is not that we have a satisfying explanation, but that we have a God who is not afraid of the dark, because He has already been there, and that the dawn He promises is not a theory but a person, and a future, and a world made new where every tear — every last one — is wiped away.

Until then, we walk by faith, which is to say, we walk in partial darkness, holding to a hand we cannot always feel, trusting a goodness we cannot always see, and carrying one another's grief as best we can. It is not a complete answer. But it may be the truest one we have.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a moment in Dostoevsky's *The Brothers Karamazov* when Ivan Karamazov describes, in meticulous and unbearable detail, the suffering of children — a girl locked in a freezing outhouse by her parents, a boy torn apart by hunting dogs before his mother's eyes. Then he turns to his brother Alyosha, the young monk, and says: "It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return him the ticket."

Ivan does not argue that God does not exist. He argues that no final harmony, no eschatological resolution, could ever justify the tears of one tortured child. And he is raising the question that every honest theology must face without flinching: If God is good, and God is sovereign, then what do we make of the world as it actually is?

This is not merely an academic puzzle. It is the question whispered in hospital corridors, screamed at gravesides, and carried silently by people who have stopped praying because they cannot reconcile what they were told about God with what they have experienced of life. Any response that does not begin by honoring the weight of that experience is not worth offering.

## The Problem, Stated Plainly

The logical problem of evil, in its classical formulation, runs something like this: If God is omnipotent, He could prevent suffering. If God is omnibenevolent, He would want to prevent suffering. Suffering exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, not good, or not there at all.

The force of this argument is not merely logical. It is existential. It is one thing to discuss the problem of evil in a seminar room. It is another to hold it in your hands when the diagnosis comes back, when the child does not survive, when the earthquake buries a village, when systemic cruelty grinds on for generations without apparent divine interruption. The sheer scale and distribution of suffering — its randomness, its disproportionate weight on the vulnerable, its apparent indifference to innocence — presses against every claim that the universe is governed by a loving will.

Philosophers have rightly noted that the strict logical contradiction can be addressed: there is no formal inconsistency between God's existence and the existence of evil if God might have morally sufficient reasons for permitting it. But this observation, while technically important, does not dissolve the deeper challenge. Even if we grant that some suffering might serve a greater purpose, the problem of *gratuitous* evil remains — the suffering that appears utterly pointless, excessive, unredeemed by any discernible good. The three-year-old who dies of bone cancer. The village swept away in a mudslide while its inhabitants sleep. The centuries of chattel slavery. The sheer surplus of agony in the world presses the question: even if some suffering is explicable, is there not an enormous residue that defies every justification? Ivan's protest is precisely that the calculus itself is obscene — that the very attempt to weigh a child's tears against some cosmic benefit degrades both the child and the God who supposedly permits it.

We must hold this tension honestly. The moment theodicy becomes glib, it has failed.

## The Free Will Defense: Love and Its Costs

One of the most enduring responses to the problem of evil is the free will defense, articulated with particular rigor by Alvin Plantinga but rooted in a tradition stretching back through Augustine. The argument holds that God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, relationship, and moral action, necessarily created beings capable of choosing cruelty, selfishness, and destruction. A world of automata who could only do good would not be a world containing love in any meaningful sense. Love requires freedom, and freedom entails the real possibility of its misuse.

There is genuine depth here. The biblical narrative itself takes human freedom with radical seriousness. The opening chapters of Genesis do not present evil as something God designed into the system but as something that enters through choice — through the mysterious but real capacity of creatures to turn away from the source of their life. And the text presses further than we sometimes notice: the consequences of that turning ripple outward beyond the human agents themselves. The ground is cursed "because of you," God tells Adam; thorns and thistles, pain and death enter the fabric of the world (Genesis 3:17–19). The narrative suggests a deep entanglement between human rebellion and the disorder of creation itself — a connection Paul later develops when he writes that "the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth" (Romans 8:22). This does not amount to a neat causal explanation, but it complicates the clean separation we often draw between moral evil and natural evil, suggesting that in the biblical imagination, the brokenness of the world is of a piece.

Yet the free will defense has real limits, and we should name them. Even granting this cosmic entanglement, it strains credulity to draw a straight line from human sin to childhood leukemia or the parasitic wasp. And within the domain of moral evil, the defense raises hard questions about proportion. Does the freedom of one person to choose violence justify the suffering of their victim? The defense explains why evil is *possible*; it does not fully explain why God permits *this much* of it, or why the innocent bear its heaviest cost.

## Soul-Making: Suffering as Formation

A second significant response comes from what John Hick called the "soul-making" theodicy, drawing on the thought of Irenaeus. On this view, the world is not meant to be a paradise but a place of becoming — an environment in which moral and spiritual growth is possible precisely because it contains challenge, difficulty, and even pain. Virtues like courage, compassion, patience, and sacrificial love are not qualities that can exist in a vacuum; they require resistance, struggle, and the real possibility of failure. A world without suffering would be a world without the conditions for the deepest forms of human goodness.

There is something to this. Scripture does not treat suffering as simply meaningless. The letter of James opens with the striking instruction to "consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of various kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance" (James 1:2–3). Paul, writing from prison, speaks of a mysterious process by which "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3–4). The Psalms of lament — and there are many — do not resolve into silence but into a deepened, harder-won trust. The biblical witness repeatedly suggests that God does something *in* suffering, even when He does not remove it.

But the soul-making theodicy, pressed too far, becomes cruel. It works tolerably well for moderate suffering that a person survives and integrates. It becomes grotesque when applied to the Holocaust, to the trafficking of children, to the infant who dies before any "soul-making" could conceivably occur. To tell a mother that her child's death was for her spiritual formation is not theology; it is violence dressed in religious language. Hick himself acknowledged that the theodicy requires an eschatological horizon — a life beyond this one in which the process is completed and the suffering redeemed — but even this does not fully answer Ivan's challenge. The question remains: Could a good God not have found a less devastating curriculum?

The defense explains why evil is *possible*; it does not fully explain why God permits *this much* of it, or why the innocent bear its heaviest cost.

## Soul-Making: Suffering as Formation

While the free will defense addresses the *origin* of moral evil, a second significant response focuses less on the source of suffering and more on its potential *purpose*. John Hick called this the "soul-making" theodicy, drawing on the thought of Irenaeus. On this view, the world is not meant to be a paradise but a place of becoming — an environment in which moral and spiritual growth is possible precisely because it contains challenge, difficulty, and even pain. Virtues like courage, compassion, patience, and sacrificial love are not qualities that can exist in a vacuum; they require resistance, struggle, and the real possibility of failure. A world without suffering would be a world without the conditions for the deepest forms of human goodness.

There is something to this. Scripture does not treat suffering as simply meaningless. The letter of James opens with the striking instruction to "consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of various kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance" (James 1:2–3). The Psalms of lament — and there are many — do not resolve into silence but into a deepened, harder-won trust. The biblical witness repeatedly suggests that God does something *in* suffering, even when He does not remove it.

I want to be careful here not to present the mystery of God's purposes as a rhetorical escape hatch — the theological equivalent of a shrug. But God does not give Job an explanation either. He gives Job *Himself* — the overwhelming, irreducible presence of the Creator, who speaks from the whirlwind not to answer Job's questions but to reframe them within a reality so vast that Job's categories cannot contain it.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a moment in Dostoevsky's *The Brothers Karamazov* when Ivan describes, in meticulous and unbearable detail, the suffering of children — a girl locked in a freezing outhouse by her parents, a boy torn apart by hunting dogs before his mother's eyes. Then he turns to his brother Alyosha, the young monk, and says: "It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return him the ticket."

Ivan does not argue that God does not exist. He argues that no final harmony, no eschatological resolution, could ever justify the tears of one tortured child. And he is raising the question that every honest theology must face without flinching: If God is good, and God is sovereign, then what do we make of the world as it actually is?

This is not merely an academic puzzle. It is the question whispered in hospital corridors, screamed at gravesides, and carried silently by people who have stopped praying because they cannot reconcile what they were told about God with what they have experienced of life. Any response that does not begin by honoring the weight of that experience is not worth offering.

What follows tests three families of Christian response against the full weight of real suffering: the free will defense, the soul-making theodicy, and the theology of the cross as God's solidarity with sufferers. Each illuminates something genuine. Each faces serious limits. Together they point not toward a satisfying explanation but toward a posture of trust, lament, and faithful presence in the pain of others — which may be the truest response available to us.

## The Problem, Stated Plainly

The logical problem of evil, in its classical formulation, runs something like this: If God is omnipotent, He could prevent suffering. If God is omnibenevolent, He would want to prevent suffering. Suffering exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, not good, or not there at all.

The force of this argument is not merely logical. It is existential. It is one thing to discuss the problem of evil in a seminar room. It is another to hold it in your hands when the diagnosis comes back, when the child does not survive, when the earthquake buries a village, when systemic cruelty grinds on for generations without apparent divine interruption. The sheer scale and distribution of suffering — its randomness, its disproportionate weight on the vulnerable, its apparent indifference to innocence — presses against every claim that the universe is governed by a loving will.

Philosophers have rightly noted that the logical form of the problem can be addressed: there is no strict contradiction between God's existence and the existence of evil if God might have morally sufficient reasons for permitting it. But this observation, while technically important, can feel thin in the face of actual suffering. The question is not only whether God *could* have reasons, but whether any reasons could be adequate — whether the calculus of justification even applies to a child's pain. Ivan's protest is precisely that the calculus itself is obscene.

We must hold this tension honestly. The moment theodicy becomes glib, it has failed.

## The Free Will Defense: Love and Its Costs

The free will defense foregrounds love's authenticity but leaves natural evil and the suffering of the innocent as stubborn counterexamples. Articulated with particular rigor by Alvin Plantinga and rooted in a tradition stretching back through Augustine, the argument holds that God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, relationship, and moral action, necessarily created beings capable of choosing cruelty, selfishness, and destruction. A world of automata who could only do good would not be a world containing love in any meaningful sense. Love requires freedom, and freedom entails the real possibility of its misuse.

The biblical narrative takes human freedom with radical seriousness. The opening chapters of Genesis do not present evil as something God designed into the system but as something that enters through choice — through the mysterious but real capacity of creatures to turn away from the source of their life. Crucially, Genesis 3 is not a philosophical treatise; it is a narrative about relationship ruptured, about trust broken between creatures and Creator, and its consequences rippling outward into violence, exile, and death. The story of Scripture from the garden to the exile to the cross is shaped by the interplay between divine purpose and human agency, with God consistently portrayed as one who woos, warns, grieves, and waits rather than overrides.

Yet the free will defense has real limits. It addresses moral evil — the suffering humans inflict on one another — with some plausibility. It is far less adequate to natural evil: the earthquake, the childhood leukemia, the parasitic wasp. No human choice caused the tectonic plate to shift. Some defenders extend the argument by positing that natural evil results from the freedom of a fallen creation or from demonic agency, but these moves require significant metaphysical commitments that not all Christian traditions share. Augustine's alternative — that evil is a *privation*, an absence of good rather than a created thing — offers a different route, locating evil's origin not in any positive force but in the turning away from Being itself. This is philosophically elegant, but it can feel abstract to the point of irrelevance when applied to concrete horrors. Even within the domain of moral evil, the defense raises hard questions about proportion. Does the freedom of one person to choose violence justify the suffering of their victim? The defense explains why evil is *possible*; it does not fully explain why God permits *this much* of it, or why the innocent bear its heaviest cost.

If free will accounts for moral evil but strains under the weight of natural evil, the soul-making theodicy attempts to address both — by reframing suffering itself as purposeful.

## Soul-Making: Suffering as Formation

John Hick, drawing on the theology of Irenaeus, proposed that the world is not meant to be a paradise but a place of becoming — an environment in which moral and spiritual growth is possible precisely because it contains challenge, difficulty, and pain. Virtues like courage, compassion, patience, and sacrificial love require resistance, struggle, and the real possibility of failure. A world without suffering would be a world without the conditions for the deepest forms of human goodness.

Scripture does not treat suffering as simply meaningless. James opens his letter with the striking instruction to "consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of various kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance" (James 1:2–3). This is not a universal algorithm for all pain; James is writing to a community under pressure, offering a framework for *communal* endurance, not a private explanation for every tragedy. Similarly, Paul writes from prison that "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3–4) — but this sequence is bounded by the eschatological hope Paul has just described, the hope that "does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts" (5:5). The logic is inward and spiritual, not a claim that every instance of suffering has a discernible pedagogical purpose.

But the soul-making theodicy, pressed too far, becomes cruel. It works tolerably well for moderate suffering that a person survives and integrates. It becomes grotesque when applied to the Holocaust, to the trafficking of children, to the infant who dies before any "soul-making" could conceivably occur. To tell a mother that her child's death was for her spiritual formation is not theology; it is violence dressed in religious language. Some suffering appears genuinely gratuitous — disproportionate to any plausible growth it might produce. Hick himself acknowledged that the theodicy requires an eschatological horizon — a life beyond this one in which the process is completed — but eschatology is precisely what is contested. The question remains: Could a good God not have found a less devastating curriculum?

We must be honest: these theodicies illuminate corners of the problem, but neither resolves it. They are partial lights, not full explanations. And perhaps this is itself significant — perhaps the Christian tradition's deepest response to suffering is not a theory at all but a person.

## The Cross: God Inside the Suffering

There is a third movement in Christian thought that is not, strictly speaking, a theodicy — it does not explain *why* God permits suffering — but it makes a claim that, if true, changes the nature of the question entirely. In Jesus Christ, God has entered into suffering from the inside.

The crucifixion is not merely an unfortunate event that happened to a good teacher. It is the moment when God, in the person of the Son, submitted to the worst that human evil and natural mortality could inflict. The cry of dereliction — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34) — is a quotation of Psalm 22, a psalm that begins in anguish but moves toward trust and cosmic praise. Jesus's use of it is not decorative. It places his suffering within Israel's long tradition of lament — the tradition of crying out to God *from within* the experience of God's apparent absence. The theological claim is staggering: the one who is supposed to be the answer to suffering has himself been consumed by it, and in doing so has taken the full weight of human abandonment into the divine life.

Jürgen Moltmann, in *The Crucified God*, argued that the cross means God suffers *with* and *in* the victims of history — that the pain of the world is not external to the divine life but is borne within it. This must be stated carefully: it does not mean God *caused* suffering in order to experience it, nor does it automatically answer why suffering exists in the first place. What it does is reframe the question. The God revealed in the cross is not a distant deity who permits suffering from a safe distance while offering explanations. He is a God who has entered the darkness and who, in the resurrection, has inaugurated a future in which suffering will not have the final word.

This matters pastorally in ways that abstract theodicy often does not. The letter to the Hebrews insists that we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who "has been tempted in every way, just as we are" (Hebrews 4:15). The Greek word translated "sympathize" — *sympathēsai* — carries the sense not merely of feeling sorry for, but of suffering *alongside*, of a solidarity rooted in shared experience. The comfort offered is not comprehension but companionship — the presence of One who has himself cried out in the same darkness.

If God in Christ does not spare us from pain but holds it with us, what does that mean for our communities as we walk with the grieving, the frightened, and the broken?

## Living With the Question

The book of Job is instructive precisely because it refuses tidy resolution. Job's friends offer confident theodicies — you must have sinned, God is teaching you something, the wicked always get what they deserve — and God explicitly rebukes them. But God does not give Job an explanation either. He speaks from the whirlwind, not to answer Job's questions but to reframe them within a reality so vast that Job's categories cannot contain it. "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" (Job 38:4). This is not a power play. It is an invitation into humility before a creation whose depths Job has not fathomed — and, crucially, it is accompanied by *presence*. God shows up. The one who refused to explain did not refuse to appear.

I want to be careful not to present mystery as a rhetorical escape hatch. "We can't understand God's ways" is true, but it can function as a way of silencing legitimate grief rather than honoring it. Mystery is trustworthy only if the God who withholds explanation also gives himself. The biblical pattern is not explanation but presence, not a theory of suffering but a promise of faithfulness. "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you" (Isaiah 43:2). Not: I will explain the waters. Not: I will prevent the waters. *I will be with you.*

For those in the midst of suffering, this may not feel like enough. We should have the honesty to say so. There are seasons when the silence of God is deafening, when the promises feel like words on a page and nothing more, when faith goes numb for months or years. The lament psalms exist because the people of God have always known this experience. Faith is not the absence of this anguish; sometimes faith is the decision to keep speaking to a God who seems not to answer.

What this means practically — in churches, in homes, at bedsides — is that our first calling is not to explain but to be present. To sit with the grieving without rushing to interpretation. To pray prayers of lament that name the darkness honestly, as the psalms do, without demanding premature resolution. To build communities where doubt is not punished, where questions are held, where acts of mercy and justice bear witness to God's goodness even when we cannot articulate it. The theology of the cross finds its embodiment not only in doctrine but in the congregation that shows up, that stays, that carries one another's grief as a form of worship.

The problem of suffering is not one we solve. It is one we inhabit. The Christian claim is not that we possess a satisfying explanation, but that we know a God who is not afraid of the dark — because he has already been there. And that the dawn he promises is not a theory but a person, and a future, and a world made new where "he will wipe every tear from their eyes" and "death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4).

Until then, we walk by faith, which is to say, we walk in partial darkness, holding to a hand we cannot always feel, trusting a goodness we cannot always see, and bearing one another's pain as best we can. It is not a complete answer. But it may be the truest one we have.
