The lynching tree and the cross are, for Cone, the same event — and any theology of the cross that cannot see that has domesticated the scandal into something manageable. Cone's reading does not dissolve the problem of suffering. But it insists that theodicy is not only a philosophical puzzle; it is a question whose shape is determined by social location, by who is suffering and who is watching. The God who hangs on the cross is not the God of the comfortable asking why suffering exists. He is the God of the condemned, present in the place where God appears most absent.

What this tradition offers is not an explanation but a refusal: the refusal of the picture of a God who watches from a safe distance. It answers the question "Does God care?" not with a proposition but with a wound.

The resurrection, in this light, is not the cancellation of the cross but its vindication — the claim that suffering and death do not have the final word. Paul writes not that suffering is good, but that "neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39). That is a confession of trust, not a solution to a puzzle.

---

## The Limits of Understanding — and Honest Lament

Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that we do not fully understand why a good God permits the suffering that exists. But before reaching for that acknowledgment, it is worth pausing at Psalm 88 — the darkest psalm in the Psalter. Unlike most lament psalms, it does not turn. It does not arrive at praise or renewed confidence. It ends in the word "darkness." It is a prayer that receives no recorded answer, and its presence in the canon is itself a theological statement: unresolved lament is legitimate speech before God. The Bible does not only contain the stories of those whose wrestling led somewhere. It contains this one too.

The book of Job ends not with an explanation but with a theophany — God speaking from the whirlwind, asking Job where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid. This is sometimes read as divine bullying, God silencing the sufferer with a display of power. But read more generously, it is an invitation to a different kind of knowing: to recognize that we are creatures with limited vantage points, that the moral logic of the universe may be more complex than our categories can contain. This is not a cop-out if it is held alongside genuine engagement rather than instead of it. The responses above are worth making — they illuminate real dimensions of the problem. But they are not complete.

And sometimes, the wrestling does not end in faith. Some people lose their faith because of suffering and do not recover it, and they are not lesser for that. The tradition that insists on honest wrestling also has to make room for the silence that follows when no answer comes. To pretend otherwise — to imply that genuine engagement with this question always curves back toward belief — would be its own kind of evasion.

What can be said is this: the problem of suffering is real, the question is legitimate, and faith that has not wrestled with it is probably not faith but comfort. The God of Scripture is not threatened by the question — Job asked it, the Psalmist of Psalm 88 asked it, Jesus asked it from the cross. What that tradition suggests is that honest wrestling is itself a form of faithfulness. And the God who meets us in the whirlwind, who enters the tomb, who is present in the place of execution — that God is not one who owes us an answer so much as one who has promised not to abandon us in the asking.

That is not everything. But it is not nothing.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a kind of argument that arrives not as philosophy but as grief. A parent sits beside a hospital bed. A village is buried under rubble. A child is born into a body that will betray her before she learns to speak. In these moments, the question of God's goodness does not present itself as an intellectual puzzle to be solved over coffee. It arrives as an accusation, raw and reasonable: if God is both perfectly good and all-powerful, why does this exist? Why does *any* of this exist?

The honest answer is that no response fully satisfies. But that is not the same as saying no response is worth making. The problem of suffering deserves to be taken seriously — seriously enough to resist both the cold comfort of clever argument and the warm evasion of easy reassurance.

---

## The Problem, Stated Fairly

The classical formulation, associated with Epicurus and sharpened by David Hume, runs something like this: if God is omnipotent, he could prevent suffering. If God is omnibenevolent, he would want to prevent suffering. Suffering exists. Therefore, either God lacks the power, lacks the will, or does not exist. The argument is not a trick. It draws on genuine moral intuition — that gratuitous pain is bad, that a good being with the means to stop it would do so, and that the scale of human and animal suffering across billions of years of natural history is not a minor footnote but an overwhelming fact.

What makes the problem especially acute is not just its logical form but its texture. The suffering that strains faith is rarely abstract. It is the specific: the child who suffers not because of any choice she made, the earthquake that swallows the just and unjust alike, the cancer that takes a father of young children while the cruel live long. Philosopher William Rowe called these "gratuitous evils" — instances of suffering that appear to serve no greater good, that could have been prevented without moral cost. His challenge is not merely that evil exists, but that *some* evil appears genuinely pointless. And that is harder to dismiss. The question is not only whether a good God could permit suffering in principle, but whether a good God could permit *this much* of it, distributed *this arbitrarily*, for no apparent redemptive purpose.

Any theological response that does not sit with this weight before it speaks has already failed.

---

## The Free Will Defence

One of the most enduring responses to the problem of moral evil — suffering caused by human choices — is the free will defence, developed with particular care by Alvin Plantinga. The argument holds that genuine freedom is a good of such significance that even God, in creating free beings, accepts the possibility that they will choose wrongly. A world with free creatures who can love, create, and choose the good is, on this account, more valuable than a world of moral automatons who never cause harm because they never truly choose anything.

There is something right here. The biblical narrative takes human freedom with extraordinary seriousness. The story of Eden is not merely about disobedience; it is about the terrifying weight of genuine agency. The Christian theological tradition has long understood the Fall not simply as a moment of rule-breaking but as the fracturing of a right relationship between humanity, creation, and God — a rupture with consequences that extend into the structure of human society and, some traditions have argued, into the natural order itself. When the prophets indict Israel for injustice — "they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals" (Amos 2:6) — they are not describing mechanical failure but moral betrayal. The same freedom that enables covenant faithfulness enables covenant rupture. Scripture seems to insist that God did not want puppets.

Yet the free will defence has limits that its proponents sometimes understate. It accounts poorly for natural evil — the tsunami, the plague, the genetic disorder. No human freedom caused the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 that killed tens of thousands, an event that famously shook Voltaire's faith in providence. And even within moral evil, the defence can feel inadequate to scale: could not an omnipotent God have arranged the world so that freedom was preserved but its worst consequences were mitigated? The defence is not without merit, but it is not a solution. It is a partial illumination.

---

## Soul-Making and the Pedagogy of Suffering

A second tradition, rooted in Irenaeus and developed in modern form by John Hick, proposes that suffering is not an anomaly within God's good creation but a necessary feature of a world designed for moral and spiritual formation. Human beings, on this account, are not created perfect and then corrupted; they are created with the *potential* for perfection and are meant to grow into it. A world without suffering, without resistance, without the possibility of failure and loss, would be a world in which certain virtues — courage, compassion, perseverance, solidarity with the broken — could not exist at all. You cannot learn to be brave in a world where nothing frightens you. You cannot learn mercy in a world where no one suffers.

There is genuine biblical resonance here. The letter to the Romans does not pretend that suffering is pleasant, but it does suggest that suffering "produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3-4). The book of Job, read carefully, is not primarily about why Job suffers but about what suffering does to a person — and what it reveals about the nature of genuine faith. Job's friends, with their tidy explanations, are ultimately rebuked. The man who refuses easy answers and wrestles honestly with God is the one whom God vindicates.

But this theodicy has a breaking point, and intellectual honesty demands we name it plainly. The soul-making argument works tolerably well for suffering that is proportionate, temporary, and educative. It strains badly when applied to the suffering of infants who die before they can form a self, or to the extinction of species across geological time. And there is a further problem the argument tends to obscure: if the goal is human formation, the sheer redundancy of suffering becomes difficult to justify. Could not the same virtues have been cultivated at a fraction of the cost? The question is not only whether suffering can sometimes produce good, but whether *this* suffering — this scale, this distribution, this apparent randomness — is remotely proportionate to any educational end. To say that Auschwitz was a school for the human soul is not a theological insight — it is an obscenity. Hick himself acknowledged this, and his later work became increasingly eschatological, depending on a cosmic redemption beyond death to justify suffering's cost. That move may be right, but it is a faith claim, not a proof.

---

## The Cross as God's Answer

There is a third response that is less a philosophical argument than a theological gesture — and perhaps, for that reason, more honest about what kind of problem suffering actually is. It is the claim that God's answer to suffering is not primarily an explanation but a presence: the incarnation and crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth.

This is not a comfortable claim, and it should not be made too quickly. But it deserves serious attention. The New Testament does not offer a systematic theodicy. What it offers is a story: that the God who created the world entered it, lived in it as a vulnerable human being, was betrayed, tortured, and executed, and descended into what the Apostles' Creed calls "hell" — the place of absolute abandonment. The cry from the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46), is not a moment of weakness that the resurrection subsequently erases. It is the moment when God, in Christ, stands inside the very desolation that suffering creates. Significantly, that cry is the opening line of Psalm 22 — meaning Jesus dies with the language of lament on his lips, reaching back into Israel's long tradition of bringing anguish honestly before God.

What this means is not that suffering is explained but that it is not suffered alone. The theologian Jürgen Moltmann, writing in the shadow of the Holocaust, argued that the cross reveals a God who is not impassible and remote but who takes human pain into the divine life itself. This is not a solution to the problem of evil in the logical sense. It does not tell us why God permitted the suffering in the first place. But it refuses the picture of a God who watches from a safe distance, and it offers something that philosophical argument cannot: solidarity. It answers the question "Does God care?" not with a proposition but with a wound.

The resurrection, in this light, is not the cancellation of the cross but its vindication — the claim that suffering and death do not have the final word, that the story is not yet finished. Paul writes to the Romans not that suffering is good, but that "neither death nor life... nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:38-39). That is a confession of trust, not a solution to a puzzle.

---

## The Limits of Understanding — and Why That's Not a Cop-Out

At some point, intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that we do not fully understand why a good God permits the suffering that exists. The book of Job ends not with an explanation but with a theophany — God speaking from the whirlwind, asking Job where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid. This is sometimes read as divine bullying, God silencing the sufferer with a display of power. But read more generously, it is an invitation to a different kind of knowing: to recognize that we are creatures with limited vantage points, that the moral logic of the universe may be more complex than our categories can contain.

This is not a cop-out if it is held alongside genuine engagement rather than instead of it. The difference between "we cannot know" as intellectual humility and "we cannot know" as intellectual laziness is whether we have done the hard work first. The responses above are worth making — they illuminate real dimensions of the problem. But they are not complete.

What can be said, finally, is this: the God of Scripture is not threatened by the question. Job asked it. The Psalmists asked it with startling directness — "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" cries Psalm 13; Psalm 88 ends without resolution, in darkness, with no dawn breaking. Jesus asked it from the cross. This is not incidental. It suggests that honest protest is not the opposite of faith but one of its most ancient expressions — that bringing anguish before God, refusing to pretend, is itself a form of faithfulness. The tradition does not ask us to have answers. It asks us to keep the conversation open.

The problem of suffering is real, the question is legitimate, and faith that has not wrestled with it is probably not faith but comfort. What the biblical witness suggests is that the God who meets us in the whirlwind, who enters the tomb, is not one who owes us an answer so much as one who has promised not to abandon us in the asking.

That is not everything. But it is not nothing.

The solidarity of the cross does not always feel like sufficient answer, and the church's task includes bearing witness to that inadequacy without abandoning those who feel it. Some people's faith has not survived their suffering, and that is not simply a failure of understanding. It may be the most honest response available to them. Any theology that cannot look that fact in the face has not yet looked suffering in the face.

---

At some point, intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that we do not fully understand why a good God permits the suffering that exists. And perhaps the hardest case is one that the foregoing responses have not adequately addressed: the suffering of animals across billions of years of evolutionary history, predation and extinction and pain in a world where no human freedom is implicated and no soul is being formed. The cross's solidarity, if it is to mean anything here, must be understood cosmically — Paul's image of "the whole creation groaning" (Romans 8:22) gestures toward this, but it does not explain it. The Psalms know this territory. Psalm 88 — perhaps the darkest in the entire collection — ends not in praise but in darkness: "darkness is my closest friend." There is no turn, no resolution, no morning after the night. It is a prayer that does not arrive anywhere, and the fact that it is in the canon at all suggests that Scripture regards this kind of faithful accusation as legitimate, perhaps even necessary. # The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a moment in grief when theology feels like an insult. When a parent sits beside a hospital bed watching a child struggle to breathe, or when a community buries its young after an act of senseless violence, the carefully arranged sentences of systematic theology can seem not merely inadequate but obscene. This is not a reason to abandon the question. It is a reason to approach it with the seriousness it deserves.

The problem of suffering is among the most ancient and most honest challenges to belief in a good God. It is not, at its core, a trick question designed to embarrass the faithful. It arises from within human experience itself, from the collision between what we believe about God and what we actually live through. Stated plainly, the argument runs something like this: if God is omnipotent, he can prevent suffering; if God is omnibenevolent, he desires to prevent suffering; yet suffering exists — and not merely in small doses, but in staggering, overwhelming, apparently indiscriminate quantities. Therefore, either God lacks the power to prevent it, lacks the will to prevent it, or does not exist at all. The philosopher David Hume framed this as a dilemma borrowed from Epicurus: "Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? Then he is impotent. Is he able, but not willing? Then he is malevolent. Is he both able and willing? Whence then is evil?"

This is not a straw man. It is a genuine and searching objection, and it deserves a genuine and searching response — not a response designed to win an argument, but one capable of sustaining a life.

---

**The Free Will Defence**

One of the most enduring responses to the problem of suffering distinguishes between what philosophers call *moral evil* — the suffering caused by human choices — and *natural evil* — the suffering caused by earthquakes, disease, and flood. The free will defence addresses the former. Its logic is straightforward: God created human beings as genuinely free agents, not as puppets or automatons. A world in which love is possible is a world in which rejection is possible. A world in which courage exists is a world in which cowardice exists. A world in which genuine moral agency operates is a world in which genuine moral failure occurs. The philosopher Alvin Plantinga argued that even an omnipotent God cannot create free creatures who always choose rightly — not because God is limited, but because the concept itself is contradictory. A freedom that is guaranteed is not freedom at all.

This response has real force. It preserves the dignity of human agency and explains a substantial portion of human suffering — war, exploitation, cruelty, injustice. The suffering that humans inflict on one another is not a flaw in God's design but a consequence of the design's most serious feature.

Yet the free will defence has limits, and honest engagement requires acknowledging them. It does not adequately account for natural evil. The child who dies of a brain tumour has not been harmed by anyone's free choice. The village swallowed by a tsunami did not suffer because of human wickedness. If God is the architect of the natural order, then the natural order's capacity for devastation raises questions that free will alone cannot answer. Furthermore, even within the domain of moral evil, the defence can feel abstract in the face of specific atrocities. That God permitted Auschwitz to preserve human freedom is a sentence that many survivors and their descendants find not merely insufficient but morally repugnant. The philosopher Emmanuel Levinas, himself a survivor of the Nazi camps, suggested that after the Holocaust, easy theodicies — explanations that make suffering fit neatly into a larger scheme — become a form of cruelty to the victim.

This is a serious objection, and it should not be deflected.

---

**The Soul-Making Theodicy**

A second major response, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern form by the philosopher John Hick, approaches the question from a different angle. Hick argued that the Genesis narrative does not depict humanity as created perfect and then fallen, but as created immature and intended to grow. Human beings are made in the *image* of God, but they are called toward the *likeness* of God — a distinction that implies a journey, a process of formation. On this reading, the world is not a pleasure garden designed for human comfort but a vale of soul-making, a place where character is forged precisely through difficulty, resistance, and suffering.

This is not a frivolous idea. There is something recognizable in it. We know, in ordinary experience, that compassion is often born from pain, that courage cannot exist without danger, that patience is developed through frustration, that depth of character tends to come from those who have suffered and endured. C.S. Lewis, writing in *The Problem of Pain*, observed that God's love is not the indulgent affection of a permissive parent but the demanding love of a sculptor, a surgeon, a trainer — the love that is willing to cause temporary pain in pursuit of permanent flourishing.

And yet this theodicy, too, has its limits — limits that Lewis himself eventually confronted. When his wife Joy died of cancer, he wrote in *A Grief Observed* that God, in his grief, seemed like a cosmic sadist, a door slammed in his face. The soul-making argument can feel, in the depths of acute suffering, like a justification for cruelty. More seriously, it struggles to account for suffering that is not formative — suffering that simply destroys, that leaves its victims not refined but shattered, that ends not in growth but in death. The child who dies at four years old has not had the opportunity for soul-making. The man who loses his mind to dementia in his final years is not being shaped toward greater likeness to God. At some point, the argument requires us to posit that the full accounting will be made in eternity — a move that is not necessarily wrong, but which must be made carefully, without using future hope to dismiss present anguish.

---

**The Cross as God's Answer**

What Christian theology offers that purely philosophical theodicy cannot is not primarily an argument but an event. The cross is not an explanation of suffering; it is God's entrance into it.

The Letter to the Hebrews describes Jesus as one who was "made perfect through suffering" — a phrase that is startling when applied to the Son of God, and which suggests that even the divine life, made flesh, was not exempt from the crucible of human pain. In Gethsemane, Jesus prays that the cup might pass from him — a prayer that is not answered in the way he asks. On the cross, he quotes Psalm 22: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" This is not a moment of polished theology. It is a cry of dereliction, the voice of abandonment. Christians have sometimes been too quick to rush past this moment toward the resurrection. But the cry itself is Scripture, and it is in the canon for a reason. It means that the experience of God's absence in the midst of suffering is not a sign of faithlessness. It is, in some sense, a participation in Christ.

The cross does not answer the philosophical problem of evil in the sense of providing a logical solution. It does something different and, arguably, something more important. It refuses the idea that God observes suffering from a safe distance. It places God inside the suffering, not as a spectator but as a victim — and, Christians believe, as one who transforms the suffering from within. The resurrection does not cancel the cross; it passes through it. The risen Christ still bears wounds.

This is not a theodicy in the classical sense. It does not explain why God permits suffering. But it addresses the deeper pastoral question that lies beneath the philosophical one: *Is God with us in this?* The cross answers yes — not with a syllogism but with a body.

---

**The Limits of Understanding**

The Book of Job is perhaps the most honest theological text in the Bible precisely because it refuses to resolve the problem of suffering into a tidy answer. Job's friends offer theodicies — suffering is punishment, suffering is discipline, God's ways are inscrutable — and God rebukes them. Job protests, rails, demands an audience, and is not rebuked but answered. The answer from the whirlwind is not an explanation of Job's suffering. It is an encounter with the vastness of God. "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" It is a question designed not to humiliate Job but to reframe what kind of question he has been asking.

To acknowledge the limits of human understanding is not a cop-out. It is an honest recognition of what finite creatures can and cannot know. The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old, incomprehensibly vast, and operating according to complexities that exceed our comprehension. The claim that we can fully assess God's reasons for permitting suffering from within our particular vantage point is, at minimum, epistemically ambitious. What we can say is that the absence of a complete explanation is not the same as the absence of an explanation. Our inability to see does not settle the question either way.

What it does require is that we hold the tension honestly — neither pretending that suffering is not a serious challenge to faith, nor pretending that faith has nothing to say in response.

---

**A Final Word**

The problem of suffering will not be solved in an essay. It will not be solved in a library. It is lived with, prayed through, wept over. The most faithful response to it is not a more sophisticated argument but a more attentive presence — to those who suffer, to the God who entered suffering, and to the hope that the last word has not yet been spoken.

What Christian faith ultimately offers is not an explanation but a promise: that suffering is not the final reality, that the God who was crucified is the God who rose, and that the tears which are shed in this life are being, somehow, kept. "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes." That sentence does not answer every question. But it is addressed to people who are weeping, and it does not tell them to stop.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a particular kind of silence that falls in a hospital room when the news is bad. It is not the silence of peace. It is the silence of a world that has stopped making sense. In that silence, the ancient question reasserts itself with a force no philosophy seminar can quite prepare you for: if God is good, and God is powerful, why is this happening?

This is not a question to be answered quickly. It deserves the respect of being stated clearly first.

---

## The Problem, Honestly Stated

The logical problem of evil, as David Hume framed it and Epicurus before him, is deceptively simple. If God is omnipotent, he can prevent suffering. If God is omnibenevolent, he wants to prevent suffering. Yet suffering exists — in staggering, often grotesque abundance. Therefore, either God lacks the power, or God lacks the goodness, or God does not exist at all. The argument has a clean, cold elegance.

But the problem runs deeper than logic. There is what philosophers call the *evidential* problem: even if we could imagine some theoretical justification for some suffering, the sheer scale and distribution of it seems to resist any tidy accounting. A child dying of a brain tumour before she has had the chance to form a single memory. The Holocaust. Tsunamis that swallow fishing villages whole. These are not abstract data points. They are particular events, particular bodies, particular screams. The philosopher William Rowe asked us to consider a fawn dying slowly in a forest fire, suffering alone, its death witnessed by no one and serving no discernible purpose. What possible good, he asked, could justify that?

And then there is the existential problem — the one that does not arrive as an argument but as a weight. Suffering does not merely challenge the coherence of theism. It challenges the *livability* of faith. To believe that God is good while burying your child is not an intellectual exercise. It is an act of extraordinary, sometimes agonising, will.

Anyone who approaches this question without feeling its full gravity is not really engaging with it.

---

## The Free Will Defence

The oldest and most persistent response to the problem of moral evil — suffering caused by human choices — is the free will defence, most rigorously developed in modern form by Alvin Plantinga. The argument holds that a world containing free creatures capable of genuine love and genuine virtue is more valuable than a world of perfectly obedient automatons. But genuine freedom entails the genuine possibility of its misuse. God could not, even in principle, create free beings who were also guaranteed never to choose evil. That would be a contradiction — not a limitation of God's power, but a logical impossibility, like asking for a square circle.

There is real weight here. The biblical narrative does not present human freedom as a theological footnote. It is load-bearing. The entire arc of Scripture — from the garden to the cross to the new creation — presupposes that human beings are genuine moral agents whose choices matter, whose love can be real, whose rebellion can be real. A God who overrode human freedom at every point of potential harm would not be a God in relationship with persons; he would be a programmer running a simulation.

But the free will defence, as far as it goes, does not go far enough. It addresses the evil that human beings do to one another. It says nothing about the fawn in the forest. It says nothing about the earthquake, the cancer, the flood. Natural evil — suffering that arises not from human choice but from the structure of the physical world — requires a different kind of reckoning. And even within moral evil, the defence can feel thin when the suffering is so asymmetric: the perpetrators often flourish while the innocent bear the cost of freedom they never asked to have exercised against them.

---

## Soul-Making Theodicy

John Hick, drawing on the early church father Irenaeus, proposed a different framework. Rather than imagining humanity as created perfect and then fallen, Hick suggested we understand human beings as created immature — made in the image of God, but not yet in the likeness. We are, on this reading, unfinished creatures in a world designed not for our comfort but for our formation. Suffering, resistance, moral struggle — these are not bugs in the system. They are, in some sense, the system itself, the conditions under which genuine virtue, courage, compassion, and love become possible.

C.S. Lewis made a similar point in *The Problem of Pain*: "God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world." The metaphor is deliberately uncomfortable. It implies that God uses suffering instrumentally, as a tool of transformation. And something in this rings true to experience. We recognise, often in retrospect, that our deepest growth has come through our hardest seasons. The person who has never suffered is rarely the person of deepest character.

And yet. The soul-making theodicy faces a serious objection that must not be evaded. It works reasonably well for *survivable* suffering — the kind that can be looked back on, integrated, learned from. It breaks down badly in the face of suffering that simply destroys. The child who dies before she can be formed by her suffering. The man whose trauma does not make him wise but only damaged. The suffering that does not build a soul but dismantles one. Hick's framework can begin to sound like a justification for abuse — the claim that what does not kill you makes you stronger, offered to someone it has in fact killed. Real theodicy must reckon with the suffering that does not redeem in any visible way.

---

## The Cross as God's Answer

There is a response to suffering that is not, strictly speaking, a theodicy at all — it does not explain why suffering exists, but it does something different. It asks us to look at what God has done in the midst of it.

The cross is the centre of Christian faith, and it is, among other things, a statement about suffering. The God of Christian theology is not an unmoved observer of human pain, issuing explanations from a safe distance. He is, in the person of Jesus of Nazareth, a participant in it. The cry from the cross — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — is not a rhetorical device. It is the sound of genuine dereliction, of a person experiencing abandonment so complete that the usual language of divine presence has failed. Jesus quotes Psalm 22, a psalm that begins in anguish and ends in vindication, but in the moment of crucifixion, he is in the anguish, not yet at the vindication.

This matters enormously. The Christian God is not the God of Aristotle — the Unmoved Mover, serene and untouched. The Christian God is the one who has, in the words of Jürgen Moltmann, entered the "godforsaken" places of human experience and been present there. The resurrection does not erase the crucifixion. It does not explain it away or retroactively justify it as merely instrumental. It transforms it. It declares that death and suffering do not have the final word — but it does not pretend they are not real, or that they do not matter, or that the cry from the cross was not genuine.

This is not a logical refutation of the problem of evil. It does not tell us why the fawn suffered in the forest. But it offers something that logic alone cannot: a God who can be trusted *in* the darkness, not merely explained *from* the light. The pastoral reality of faith is that people in extremis rarely need a syllogism. They need to know whether God is with them. The cross says: yes, and at cost.

---

## The Limits of Understanding — and Why They Matter

It would be dishonest to end here without acknowledging what remains genuinely unresolved. The responses above are not solutions. They are partial illuminations — real, but incomplete. The free will defence does not account for natural evil. Soul-making theodicy does not account for unredemptive suffering. The cross is a profound answer but not a comprehensive explanation. And the honest theologian must say: we do not know why God permits this particular suffering, in this particular form, at this particular cost.

The book of Job is instructive here. Job's friends offer theodicy — elaborate explanations for why Job's suffering must be deserved, must fit within a coherent moral framework. God rebukes them. Job, who has done nothing but protest and demand an answer, is vindicated. The lesson is not that questions are wrong. It is that tidy explanations that domesticate suffering into a system are a kind of falsehood. The whirlwind speech of God in Job 38-41 does not answer Job's questions. It expands his vision — it places him within a cosmos so vast and complex that his accounting of it was always going to be partial. This is not a cop-out. It is an invitation to a different kind of knowing: relational, not merely propositional.

Paul, writing from prison, does not offer a theodicy either. He offers something stranger and more demanding: "I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content" (Philippians 4:11). *Learned* — it is a word of process, of formation, of hard-won orientation. Not explanation, but trust forged in the furnace.

---

## A Final Word

The problem of suffering is real, and it is not going away. It has ended faith for some people, and it has deepened faith for others, and it has left still others in a long, honest suspension between the two. None of those responses should be met with contempt.

What Christian theology offers is not a clean answer but a particular story — of a God who does not watch from outside, who enters the suffering, who absorbs the worst of it, and who promises that the last word has not yet been spoken. That promise is either true or it is not. But it is not nothing. In the silence of the hospital room, it is, for many people, the only thing that holds.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a question that refuses to be answered neatly, that rises unbidden from hospital rooms and gravesites and the aftermath of disasters both natural and human-made. It is not primarily a philosopher's question, though philosophers have wrestled with it for centuries. It is the question of a parent watching a child suffer, of a survivor standing in the rubble of what used to be a life. The question is simple and devastating: if God is good, and if God is powerful, why does this happen?

We should begin by taking the objection seriously, because it deserves seriousness. The logical form is well-known: if God is omnipotent, he could prevent suffering; if God is omnibenevolent, he would want to prevent suffering; yet suffering exists in staggering quantities and with apparent randomness and cruelty. Therefore, either God lacks the power, lacks the goodness, or does not exist at all. This is not a trick argument. It carries genuine weight. The sheer volume of suffering in the world — not merely inconvenience or difficulty, but the bone-deep suffering of innocents, the suffering that seems to serve no conceivable purpose — presses hard against any easy confidence in a loving Creator. David Hume put it bluntly: is God willing to prevent evil but not able? Then he is impotent. Is he able but not willing? Then he is malevolent. The argument has not lost its force with age.

And yet many thoughtful people, including those who have suffered greatly, have found reasons to maintain faith. Not because the problem disappears, but because other considerations complicate the picture in ways that deserve honest examination.

---

## The Free Will Defence

The most familiar response to the problem of suffering is the free will defence, associated in its modern philosophical form with Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs roughly as follows: a world containing genuinely free creatures who choose to love and do good is more valuable than a world of moral automatons, even if that freedom makes evil possible. God could have created beings who always chose rightly, but only by making them incapable of genuine choice — which is to say, by not creating free beings at all. The existence of moral evil, then, is the shadow side of a genuine good: human freedom.

This response has real strength. The biblical narrative takes human freedom with extraordinary seriousness. The drama of Genesis is not the story of a puppeteer whose creation malfunctioned; it is the story of creatures given genuine agency, genuine responsibility, and a genuine capacity for betrayal. The prophets thunder against Israel not because Israel was determined to fail but because Israel chose to fail — chose idolatry, chose injustice, chose to oppress the widow and the orphan — when another path was available. Freedom, in the biblical imagination, is not incidental to human dignity; it is constitutive of it.

But the free will defence has limits, and intellectual honesty requires acknowledging them. It addresses moral evil — the suffering caused by human choices — with some plausibility. It struggles considerably with what philosophers call natural evil: earthquakes, tsunamis, childhood cancers, the long catalogue of suffering that has nothing to do with human freedom. The child born with a degenerative disease has not been wronged by anyone's free choice. The village buried by a landslide is not the victim of human wickedness. Here the free will defence, taken alone, falls short. We need other resources.

---

## Soul-Making and the Irenaean Tradition

A second response, developed in different forms by Irenaeus in the early church and by the modern theologian John Hick, begins from a different premise about what human beings are. Rather than viewing humanity as created perfect and fallen, this tradition understands human beings as created immature — as creatures with the potential for moral and spiritual depth, but who must grow into that depth through genuine experience, including the experience of struggle and suffering.

On this view, a world without suffering would not be a paradise; it would be a nursery that never allowed its children to grow up. Virtues like courage, compassion, patience, and resilience are not possible in a world without adversity. They are not merely tested by difficulty; they are formed by it. A person who has never faced genuine loss cannot truly comfort another who is grieving. A person who has never struggled cannot truly understand what it means to persevere. The world, on this account, is not a pleasure-garden but a vale of soul-making — a phrase borrowed from the poet Keats, who was not writing theology but who grasped something real.

There is genuine biblical resonance here. The letter to the Romans speaks of suffering producing endurance, endurance producing character, and character producing hope — not as a glib formula, but as a hard-won observation about how human beings are actually shaped (Romans 5:3-4). The book of Job, which we will return to, shows a man whose encounter with suffering produces not a simpler faith but a deeper one, stripped of easy assumptions and forced into genuine encounter with the divine. The psalms of lament — and there are more of them than psalms of praise — document a faith that is not destroyed by anguish but refined by it, a faith that dares to say "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" and somehow finds that the question itself is a form of address.

Yet this response also has limits that must be named. The soul-making theodicy risks becoming a kind of cosmic utilitarianism, in which individual suffering is justified by the character it builds — either in the sufferer or in those who witness it. But this is cold comfort to the child who dies before she has had the chance to be shaped by anything. It risks treating persons as means rather than ends. And it does not obviously account for the sheer excess of suffering in the world — the quantities that seem far beyond what any pedagogical purpose would require. If the world is a school, it is a school with a curriculum that seems, at times, grotesquely disproportionate to the lesson.

---

## The Cross as God's Answer

There is a third response that operates differently from the first two, because it does not primarily offer an explanation. It offers a location.

The Christian claim is not merely that God sympathizes with human suffering from a safe distance, or that God has arranged suffering for our benefit while remaining untouched by it. The Christian claim is that God entered suffering. The incarnation is not a footnote to Christian theology; it is the center. And the cross is not a transaction conducted in the abstract; it is the death of a particular person, in a particular way, at a particular time — a death involving abandonment, physical agony, and the cry of dereliction: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). Jesus does not quote Psalm 22 as a proof-text. He prays it. He inhabits it.

This is what Jürgen Moltmann, writing out of the shadow of the Holocaust, called the crucified God — the recognition that the question of suffering cannot be answered from outside the human condition, because God has not remained outside it. Whatever else the cross means, it means that God is not the remote architect of a system in which suffering occurs. God is present within the suffering. The question "Where is God when I suffer?" receives, in Christian theology, the most unexpected of answers: here. Here, in the darkness. Here, in the abandonment. Here, in the place where no explanation comes.

This does not dissolve the problem. It would be dishonest to pretend it does. The suffering does not become less real because God shares it. The grief does not lift because the cross happened. But it changes the character of the question. It means that faith in a good God is not faith in a God who has arranged things from a comfortable distance, but faith in a God who has been where we are — and who, in the resurrection, claims that this is not the final word.

---

## What We Cannot Know, and Why That Matters

Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that these responses do not add up to a complete answer. They are not meant to. The book of Job is instructive here precisely because of how it ends. God does not explain the suffering to Job. God asks questions: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" (Job 38:4). This is not God bullying Job into silence. It is God pointing to the vast asymmetry between divine perspective and human perspective — not to dismiss Job's questions, but to locate them within a context that Job cannot fully see. Remarkably, God commends Job for his honest wrestling and rebukes Job's friends for their tidy explanations (Job 42:7). The lesson seems to be that honest anguish is more faithful than false comfort.

There is a difference between saying "we cannot fully understand" as a way of ending the conversation and saying it as a way of remaining honest within the conversation. The former is evasion; the latter is intellectual integrity. We are finite creatures reasoning about an infinite God, creatures embedded in time reasoning about a being who encompasses time. Some degree of epistemic humility is not a retreat — it is simply accurate.

But epistemic humility is not the same as indifference. The problem of suffering is not merely a puzzle to be solved; it is a reality to be inhabited alongside those who suffer. Theology that cannot sit with a grieving parent without reaching for an explanation has missed something essential. The most faithful response to suffering is often not an argument but a presence — the willingness to remain, to mourn, to refuse the comfort of easy answers.

The question of suffering and the goodness of God remains open. It is not a question that admits of a final, satisfying closure on this side of whatever lies ahead. But it is a question that can be held — honestly, painfully, and with a faith that has looked at the cross and found there not an answer, exactly, but a companion in the dark.

# The Weight of the World and the Goodness of God

There is a particular kind of silence that falls in a hospital room after bad news has been delivered. The doctor has left. The chart is closed. And the person in the bed, or the person standing beside it, is left alone with a question that no amount of medical training can answer: *Why?* Not why in the biochemical sense — why this cell mutated, why this vessel burst — but why in the deeper sense, the sense that has occupied human beings since at least the writing of the book of Job. Why does a world governed by a good and omnipotent God contain this much suffering?

This is not a question that deserves a quick answer. It deserves, first of all, to be heard.

---

## The Problem Stated Honestly

The philosophical problem of evil is usually expressed in the form of a trilemma. If God is all-powerful, he could prevent suffering. If God is all-good, he would want to prevent it. Yet suffering exists, in quantities and qualities that can only be described as staggering. Therefore, either God lacks the power to prevent suffering, or God lacks the will, or God does not exist at all. The argument has been stated most sharply by philosophers like J.L. Mackie and David Hume, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than deflected with piety.

But the problem is not merely philosophical. It is personal and visceral. It is the Holocaust. It is a child dying of a disease she did nothing to contract. It is the earthquake that buries a village in rubble on an ordinary Tuesday morning. It is the slow, grinding suffering of depression or chronic pain — suffering that does not announce itself as dramatic or meaningful, but simply continues. The abstract argument is hard enough; the actual weight of human suffering is something else entirely. Anyone who addresses this question while remaining unmoved by it has not fully understood the question.

We should also be honest about what the problem rules out as insufficient. "God works in mysterious ways" is true, but if deployed too quickly it functions as a conversation-stopper rather than an answer. "Everything happens for a reason" can be a genuine theological conviction, but in the mouth of a person who has never lost a child, it sounds like an insult. The question demands more than these formulas, and the people asking it deserve more.

---

## The Free Will Defence

One of the oldest and most carefully developed responses to the problem of suffering is the free will defence, associated in its modern philosophical form with Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs roughly as follows: genuine love and genuine goodness require freedom. A world in which human beings were compelled to do good would not be a world of genuine moral agents but a world of sophisticated automatons. God, in creating beings capable of love, necessarily created beings capable of its opposite. The suffering caused by human cruelty — war, abuse, oppression, exploitation — is the shadow cast by the light of human freedom.

This argument has real force. There is something deeply right about the intuition that a world of programmed virtue would be morally impoverished, that the capacity for heroism and sacrifice requires the capacity for cowardice and cruelty. The cross itself, on this reading, is the supreme instance: the freedom of human beings to reject and crucify the Son of God is also the freedom that makes their redemption meaningful rather than mechanical.

But the free will defence, taken alone, has significant limits. It handles moral evil — suffering caused by human choices — with some plausibility. It handles natural evil — earthquakes, cancer, tsunamis — much less well. The child who contracts leukemia has not been harmed by anyone's free choice. The village buried by an earthquake is not the victim of human cruelty. To say that natural suffering is also somehow a consequence of the fall, as some theologians have argued, is possible, but it requires metaphysical commitments that are not self-evidently true and that press hard against our scientific understanding of a universe in which predation and extinction predate human beings by hundreds of millions of years. The free will defence is an important piece of the answer. It is not the whole answer.

---

## Soul-Making and the Purposes of Suffering

A second major response comes from the tradition associated with Irenaeus and developed in the twentieth century by John Hick: what is sometimes called the soul-making theodicy. On this account, human beings are not created perfect and then corrupted; they are created with the *potential* for moral and spiritual maturity, and that maturity can only be achieved through struggle. A world without resistance, without difficulty, without the possibility of genuine loss, would be a world in which certain virtues — courage, compassion, perseverance, faith — could not develop. Suffering, on this view, is not simply a problem to be explained away but a condition for the possibility of human growth.

There is something here that resonates with genuine human experience. The people who have been most deeply formed — who carry a kind of gravity and grace that others seem to lack — are very often people who have suffered. Not because suffering is automatically ennobling (it can just as easily destroy), but because it creates the conditions in which character can be forged or broken. Paul's letter to the Romans touches this when he writes that "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3-4). This is not a triumphalist claim. It is a careful, sequential account of how something good might emerge from something terrible.

And yet. The soul-making theodicy, too, runs into hard cases. How much suffering is required to make a soul? The Holocaust produced not only survivors of profound moral depth but also, in many cases, the destruction of faith altogether. The suffering of infants, of those with severe cognitive disabilities, of those who die before they can integrate any experience at all — these cases press hard against the idea that suffering is primarily pedagogical. There is something almost obscene about explaining a child's death as a lesson for someone else's spiritual development. The theodicy risks making victims into instruments, which is its own kind of moral failure.

---

## The Cross as God's Answer

There is a third way of approaching this question that is less a philosophical argument and more a theological claim — one that does not so much solve the problem of suffering as transform the context in which it is held. It is the claim that in Jesus of Nazareth, God entered the suffering of the world rather than remaining insulated from it.

The Gospel accounts of the crucifixion are not comfortable texts. Jesus dies in agony, abandoned by his friends, mocked by bystanders, and — most strikingly — crying out in the words of Psalm 22: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" This is not the cry of someone who has a theodicy worked out. It is the cry of desolation, of felt abandonment, of genuine darkness. Christian theology has always insisted that this cry is not merely performative — that something real is happening in the God-forsakenness of the cross, that the Son of God genuinely enters into the experience of suffering and abandonment that human beings know.

What this means for the problem of suffering is not that the problem is solved but that it is shared. God is not the distant architect of a world gone wrong, watching from outside. God is the one who has gone into the darkness. The resurrection does not cancel the cross; it vindicates the one who died on it, and it opens the possibility of hope without requiring that suffering be explained away. Paul does not say that suffering is good; he says that suffering cannot separate us from the love of God (Romans 8:38-39). That is a different claim, and a more honest one.

This response has been developed in what some call protest theodicy — associated with thinkers like Elie Wiesel and Jürgen Moltmann — which insists that the proper response to unjust suffering is not explanation but lament, and that lament addressed to God is itself a form of faith. The Psalms are full of this. "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1) is not a failure of trust; it is trust pushed to its limits and still holding on. Job does not receive a philosophical answer to his suffering; he receives a theophany — an encounter with the living God — and it is enough, not because his questions are answered but because the relationship is restored.

---

## Living with What We Cannot Resolve

It would be dishonest to end this essay by claiming that these responses fully dissolve the problem of suffering. They do not. There is a remainder — a residue of cases, a weight of accumulated grief, that no theodicy fully accounts for. The intellectual humility to acknowledge this is not a retreat from faith; it is a condition of intellectual integrity.

What we can say is this: the problem of suffering is not a problem that faith ignores. The Bible does not ignore it. Job does not ignore it. The Psalms do not ignore it. Jesus on the cross does not ignore it. The tradition of Christian thought has wrestled with it seriously for two thousand years, and the wrestling has produced not resolution but something perhaps more valuable: the resources to keep faith alive in the dark, to lament without despair, to hope without pretending that hope is easy.

For the person sitting in that hospital room, none of this may be immediately useful. Theodicy is not pastoral care. What that person may need first is not an argument but a presence — someone willing to sit in the silence without rushing to fill it with answers. But eventually, when the silence has been honored, the questions will return. And they deserve more than platitudes.

The goodness of God and the reality of suffering remain in tension. That tension is not something to be resolved cheaply. It is something to be inhabited, honestly, with whatever faith we can muster — which is, perhaps, what faith has always been.

# The Weight of the World and the Goodness of God

There is a question that does not wait for philosophy seminars. It arrives at three in the morning, in hospital waiting rooms, at gravesides in the rain. It is asked by parents holding children who will not recover, by survivors of violence who cannot understand why no one intervened, by ordinary people whose lives have been quietly destroyed by illness or loss or cruelty. The question is old and it is simple: if God is good, and if God is powerful, why is there so much suffering?

This is not a question we should rush past. The philosopher's version — the logical problem of evil — puts it with cold precision: an omnipotent being could prevent suffering; an omniscient being would know how; an omnibenevolent being would want to. Yet suffering exists, abundantly and grotesquely. Therefore, the argument goes, no such being exists. This is not a cheap objection. It deserves to be taken seriously, not least because the people asking it are often not asking it from an armchair. They are asking it from inside the wreckage of their lives.

## The Honest Weight of the Problem

Let us not minimize what we are dealing with. The suffering of the world is not merely inconvenient or uncomfortable. Children die of cancer. Genocides happen. Tsunamis swallow villages. People are tortured. The natural world operates on a logic of predation and decay that seems indifferent to any moral order. And much of this suffering falls on people who, by any ordinary reckoning, have done nothing to deserve it. The book of Job knows this. Job is described at the outset as "blameless and upright," and yet everything is taken from him — his children, his health, his dignity. His friends arrive with explanations, and the explanations are not merely inadequate; they are, the text eventually tells us, wrong. God rebukes them for it.

Any theological account of suffering that cannot look at the worst cases — at Auschwitz, at pediatric oncology wards, at mass graves — without flinching has already failed. The question is whether there are responses that are honest enough to deserve serious consideration, not whether there is a response that makes the problem disappear. The problem does not disappear. But some responses go deeper than others.

## The Free Will Defence

The most familiar philosophical response is the free will defence, developed with particular rigor by Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs roughly like this: a world containing creatures capable of genuine moral choice — creatures who can love, sacrifice, create, and commit — is more valuable than a world of morally determined automatons. But genuine freedom, by definition, includes the freedom to choose wrongly. God cannot create free beings and simultaneously guarantee that they will always choose rightly; that would be a contradiction. Therefore, a significant portion of human suffering — suffering caused by human cruelty, injustice, and negligence — is the necessary cost of a world in which genuine love and moral agency are possible.

This is a serious argument, and it carries real weight. The capacity for love and the capacity for cruelty are not separable options that God could simply have distributed differently. A world in which evil was impossible would also be a world in which goodness was meaningless — not chosen, not costly, not real in any morally significant sense. When Paul writes to the Romans about love that "endures all things," he is describing something that only has content because it operates against resistance, because it costs something, because it is chosen in the face of alternatives.

But the free will defence has acknowledged limits, and intellectual honesty requires naming them. It accounts for moral evil — the suffering caused by human choices — but it does not obviously account for natural evil: earthquakes, childhood leukemia, the slow cruelty of degenerative disease. These do not seem to be the consequences of human freedom. A child born with a fatal genetic condition has not been harmed by anyone's choice. The free will defence, taken alone, leaves this category of suffering largely unaddressed.

## Soul-Making and the Purposes of Suffering

A second major tradition of response comes from what is sometimes called the soul-making theodicy, associated most prominently with the theologian John Hick, drawing on earlier threads in Irenaeus. The central insight is that human beings are not created complete. We are created, in Hick's language, not in the finished image of God but as beings with the potential to grow toward that image. Moral and spiritual maturity — courage, compassion, patience, wisdom — cannot be given ready-made. They can only be developed through struggle, resistance, and difficulty.

On this view, the world is not primarily a place of comfort but a place of formation. Suffering, while not good in itself, can function as the condition under which certain essential human qualities come into being. C.S. Lewis, who arrived at this territory through grief rather than argument, put it in *The Problem of Pain* by noting that God "whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world." Lewis himself later complicated this view considerably in *A Grief Observed*, written after his wife's death, where he confronts the possibility that the God he thought he knew might be something far more troubling. The honesty of that later book is part of its theological value.

The soul-making theodicy has genuine explanatory power, particularly for suffering that genuinely does form and deepen human character. There is something true in the observation that certain kinds of wisdom are simply not available to people who have never suffered. The Psalms of lament — Psalm 22, Psalm 88, the depths of Lamentations — were not written by people who had been sheltered from pain. They carry authority precisely because they were written from inside darkness.

But this theodicy, too, has limits that must be acknowledged. Not all suffering forms. Some suffering merely destroys. A child who dies at two years old has not had the opportunity to be formed by her suffering. A person broken by trauma into dissociation and despair has not been refined; they have been shattered. The soul-making framework can become, if we are not careful, a way of aestheticizing suffering at a safe distance — finding meaning in other people's pain without sitting with them in it. When it functions that way, it becomes another version of Job's friends, and deserves the same rebuke.

## The Cross as God's Answer

There is a third response — less a philosophical argument than a theological claim — that operates differently from the previous two. It is the claim that in the cross of Jesus Christ, God does not explain suffering from outside but enters into it from within.

This is the move that distinguishes Christian theology from more abstract theism. The God of the philosophers may be omnipotent and omniscient, but the God of the New Testament is also the one who, in the person of Jesus, cries out from a cross: *"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"* This is a quotation from Psalm 22, a psalm of desolation that ends in vindication but does not rush there — it lingers, for most of its length, in the experience of abandonment. Jesus, on the cross, is not a philosopher observing suffering. He is a man dying in agony, experiencing the full weight of human darkness and God-forsakenness.

This does not resolve the intellectual problem. It does not explain why the child is sick or why the earthquake happened. But it does something that intellectual resolution cannot do: it refuses to let God stand at a comfortable distance from the world's pain. The Christian claim is that God is not the unmoved mover watching suffering from outside the system. God has, in some sense that strains language to its limits, suffered. The cross is not a solution to the problem of suffering; it is a solidarity with it. And the resurrection is not a denial of the darkness of Good Friday but its transformation — not the erasure of the wounds (Thomas still finds them in the risen body) but the declaration that death and suffering do not have the final word.

Jürgen Moltmann, writing in *The Crucified God*, argued that any God who could not suffer would be less than the God of the cross — a God of power without love. The suffering God is not a God diminished but a God revealed.

## Living with the Unanswered

None of these responses constitutes a full solution. The honest theologian does not have a full solution. What we have are partial lights in a large darkness, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. The book of Job ends not with an explanation but with a theophany — God speaks out of the whirlwind, and the questions multiply rather than resolve, and somehow this is enough for Job. Not because the questions are answered but because the one he was questioning shows up. This is not an intellectual maneuver. It is something stranger and more difficult: the claim that presence matters when explanation fails.

What this means pastorally — for those of us who sit with people in their suffering — is that we should be slow to explain and quick to remain. The theodicies have their place, and honest theological reflection is not a luxury but a necessity. But the person in the hospital room does not first need an argument. They need someone willing to stay. The God of the cross, at least, seems to understand this.

The problem of suffering is real. The goodness of God is claimed. The tension between them is not dissolved by clever argument, and any account that pretends otherwise has not understood either the suffering or the God. What faith offers is not resolution but company — the long, costly, sometimes agonizing companionship of a God who, according to the Christian story, knows what it is to cry out into the dark and hear nothing, and who did not stop there.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a kind of argument that arrives not in lecture halls but in hospital rooms. It does not come dressed in philosophical language. It comes in the form of a parent watching a child die, or a person of faith discovering that prayer has not moved the illness, or a survivor of atrocity wondering what kind of God could have watched and done nothing. The problem of suffering is not primarily an intellectual puzzle. It is a wound in human experience that has been asking the same question for as long as human beings have believed in anything at all: *How can this be, if God is good?*

Any serious engagement with this question must begin by taking that wound seriously.

---

## The Problem, Stated Honestly

The philosophical formulation is old and blunt. If God is omnipotent, God could prevent suffering. If God is omniscient, God knows it is occurring. If God is perfectly good, God would want to prevent it. Yet suffering exists — not merely inconvenient suffering, but the kind that seems to serve no purpose: the suffering of children, the suffering of the innocent, the slow extinction of entire peoples, the casual cruelty of disease. Therefore, the argument concludes, either God lacks the power, lacks the knowledge, lacks the goodness, or does not exist at all.

This is not a weak argument. Philosophers like David Hume and J.L. Mackie pressed it with rigor, and Mackie in particular insisted that the existence of evil is not merely in tension with theism but logically incompatible with it. More recently, the *evidential* form of the problem — advanced by William Rowe — does not claim logical contradiction but asks why, if God exists, there is so much gratuitous suffering: pain that seems to accomplish nothing, that builds nothing, that redeems no one. A fawn dying slowly in a forest fire, observed by no one, serving no apparent purpose — what theodicy accounts for that?

To answer this question too quickly is a kind of pastoral and intellectual failure. The person who has lost a child does not need a syllogism. And the philosopher who has posed the question deserves more than a slogan. Both deserve honesty about what can and cannot be said.

---

## The Free Will Defence

The oldest and most durable theological response is the free will defence, most rigorously developed in the twentieth century by Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs roughly as follows: genuine love and genuine moral goodness require freedom. A God who created beings capable of love but incapable of choosing otherwise would have created something less than persons — automatons performing the appearance of virtue. To create beings capable of real relationship, real love, real moral agency, God had to create beings who could also choose cruelty, indifference, and destruction. The suffering that flows from human choice is therefore not evidence against God's goodness but a consequence of it.

This response has genuine force. Much of the world's worst suffering is traceable to human decision: war, exploitation, genocide, the structures of injustice that grind the poor to nothing. When we ask why God did not stop the Holocaust, we are also asking why God did not override the freedom of millions of human beings who participated in it, enabled it, or looked away. The free will defence insists that a world containing genuine human freedom — even at this cost — may be more valuable than a world of determined goodness.

But the defence has limits, and they must be acknowledged. It accounts for *moral* evil — suffering caused by human choice — but it struggles with *natural* evil: the earthquake, the cancer cell, the flood that drowns the innocent. No human freedom explains a child born with a degenerative disease. And even within the realm of moral evil, one might ask whether the freedom to commit genocide is worth the genocide. Plantinga's response — that God could not create free beings who always freely choose rightly without contradicting the meaning of freedom itself — is philosophically sophisticated, but it does not dissolve the anguish. It clarifies the logic without healing the wound.

---

## Soul-Making and the Suffering That Forms

A second major tradition of theodicy is associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern form by the philosopher John Hick. Rather than treating human beings as created perfect and fallen, this view sees humanity as created immature and destined for growth. We are made in the image of God, but the *likeness* of God — the full moral and spiritual development that resembles divine character — is something we must grow into. And growth, by its nature, requires resistance.

On this account, a world without suffering would be a world without the conditions for genuine virtue. Courage requires danger. Compassion requires the existence of those who suffer. Patience, resilience, self-sacrifice — none of these can be developed in a frictionless world. C.S. Lewis, though not an Irenaean in the technical sense, captured something of this when he wrote that God whispers to us in our pleasures but shouts in our pain, calling it "his megaphone to rouse a deaf world." The idea is not that God inflicts suffering sadistically, but that suffering, in a fallen and developing world, can become the medium through which character is formed and depth of soul is achieved.

There is something genuinely true here. It is a recognizable human experience that great suffering, when it does not destroy, often deepens. People who have walked through grief often speak of a tenderness and seriousness that was not there before. The pastoral literature of every tradition is full of this testimony.

But the soul-making theodicy also has a shadow side that must be named. It can slide, almost without noticing, into a kind of cosmic utilitarianism that treats individual suffering as raw material for someone else's development. The child who dies of cancer does not obviously benefit from her own death. The soul being made may be someone else's. And there is something morally troubling about a theodicy that treats persons as instruments for a larger educational project. Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov, perhaps the most powerful literary critic of theodicy, makes exactly this point: he refuses to accept any harmony that is purchased at the price of a single child's tear. The argument is not easily dismissed.

---

## The Cross as God's Answer

There is a third response that is not strictly a theodicy — it does not explain why suffering exists — but it may be the most theologically serious answer the Christian tradition offers. It is the claim that in Jesus of Nazareth, God did not remain at a distance from suffering but entered it.

The Gospel accounts of the crucifixion are not triumphalist. They are stark. Jesus dies in agony, abandoned by his disciples, mocked by those watching, and — in the most devastating line in the New Testament — crying out with the words of Psalm 22: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* Whatever else is happening in that moment, the Gospel writers refuse to soften it. This is not a man who dies peacefully, assured of divine comfort. This is a man who dies in the experience of desolation.

Psalm 22 itself is instructive. It is a psalm that begins in abandonment and ends in vindication — but it does not skip the middle. The psalmist does not resolve the anguish quickly. He sits in it, names it, cries it to God. The tradition of lament in Scripture is broader than many Christians recognize. Job refuses to offer false comfort to himself or to God. The book of Lamentations contains almost no resolution — it ends in something close to silence. The Psalms are full of voices that accuse God of sleeping, of hiding, of forgetting. This is not faithlessness. It is a kind of fierce fidelity — the refusal to pretend that everything is fine when it is not.

The cross does not explain suffering. But it does something perhaps more important: it refuses to leave God outside of it. The Christian claim is not that God watches suffering from a safe distance and will eventually explain it all. The claim is that God has been there — in the dirt, in the pain, in the cry of dereliction. Jürgen Moltmann, writing in the shadow of the Holocaust, argued in *The Crucified God* that the only God who can speak to Auschwitz is a God who has suffered, not a God of impassive power. Whether or not one accepts every aspect of Moltmann's theology, the instinct is right: the cross relocates the question. It does not answer *why* God permits suffering, but it answers *where* God is when suffering occurs.

---

## What Cannot Be Said, and Why That Matters

It would be dishonest to claim that these responses dissolve the problem. They don't. The free will defence does not account for natural evil. The soul-making theodicy risks instrumentalizing persons. The theology of the cross answers a different question than the one the skeptic is asking. And the intellectual humility that acknowledges the limits of human understanding — while genuine and necessary — must not become a way of avoiding the force of the objection.

What can be said is this: the problem of suffering is real, the objection is serious, and the person who cannot believe in God because of it is not being foolish. They may be being more honest than the person who resolves the tension too quickly.

What can also be said is that the Christian tradition, at its most serious, has never promised that suffering will be explained. It has promised something stranger and more demanding: that suffering will be redeemed, that the last word is not spoken by death, and that the God who was present in the cry of dereliction on a Friday afternoon was not defeated by it.

That is not a proof. It is a confession. And in the presence of real suffering, confession — honest, undefensive, made in full acknowledgment of what it cannot answer — may be the most truthful thing that can be offered.
