What does it mean to say that God is good when suffering persists in the world? This is not a question posed once and settled, but a persistent, living tension that presses on believers in every season of pain—in hospital rooms, in the grief of losing a child, in the ache of chronic illness, in the quiet despair of long waitings and unanswerable questions. If goodness is the measure by which we judge reality, how do we read a world in which good seems intermittently mocked by the presence of suffering? The task, then, is not to paper over distress with pious slogans, but to think clearly, theologically, and pastorally about the problem in light of God’s revealed character, and to name what human beings can and cannot know.

Presenting the problem fairly begins with distinguishing types of evil and acknowledging the breadth of experience. Moral evil arises where human beings act—the cruelty of a massacre, the cruelty of exploitation, the vices that deform communities. Natural evil includes the suffering caused by earthquakes, cancers, droughts, and degenerative illnesses—events not directly caused by human malice, yet devastating in their consequences. It would be a straw man to treat the problem as one-dimensional: sincere questions about moral guilt and collective culpability, on the one hand, and the sorry mercy of a broken, fragile creation, on the other. The objection is not merely about the existence of pain in general, but about the compatibility of credible accounts of God’s goodness with the persistence of such pain—especially when pain seems random, gratuitous, or prolonged beyond plausible explanations.

To engage seriously with the problem, we should listen to two levels of response: intellectual defenses that try to preserve coherence between belief in a benevolent God and the presence of evil, and the more narrative, experiential theologies that locate meaning, purpose, and even transformation within suffering itself. The main lines of thought I want to draw on are: the free will defense (and its corollaries for moral evil), the soul-making or character-formation theodicy, and the cruciform understanding of God’s own suffering in the cross. A fourth, more contemporary angle—often called a protest theodicy—will be referenced as a way of noticing the way suffering exposes God’s presence with the oppressed. These are not mutually exclusive; in a lived faith, they participate in a larger discernment that resists reduction.

First, the free will defense. The claim is straightforward: moral evil arises from creatures endowed with genuine freedom to choose, and such freedom is intrinsically valuable. If we are to be truly human—capable of love, courage, fidelity, and justice—then we must be free to choose against God as well as for God. A world with morally meaningful goods demands a landscape in which persons can freely harm one another—otherwise virtue would be a mirage, and love would be compulsory sentiment rather than a robust, voluntary response. A benevolent creator might, in theory, create beings who always do right, but as soon as you do that, the very depths of moral value—courage under temptation, mercy toward the guilty, self-sacrificial love—lose their meaning. The price of such a world, the defense goes, is the possibility of devastating choices, which includes suffering caused by others’ malice and injustice.

But the free will defense faces real challenges. It has to explain not only the existence of moral evil but the pervasive scale of suffering that seems gratuitous, even when people do not intend to harm. Natural evils—diseases, earthquakes, famines—are especially resistant to the idea that they are required by human freedom. If God’s governance of the cosmos relies on freedom alone, why should innocent creatures bear the consequences? And why does suffering so often appear to be random, disproportionate, or unmerited? The defense, when pressed, typically appeals to larger goods—humility, solidarity, the growth of virtue, the flourishing of justice that can only emerge in the crucible of difficulty. It is not a proof, but a plausible account that tries to show that moral order and love require a landscape where freedom is real.

Second, the soul-making theodicy (often associated with Irenaeus and later developed by John Hick). The argument here is that suffering is not a glitch to be excised but a tool for spiritual and moral formation. Creation, in this view, is a growing process toward the likeness of God, and the present world is a school in which character is formed through trial, disappointment, and dependence on grace. Suffering tests our motives, strengthens perseverance, disciplines vanity, and opens us to the needs of others. To be formed in virtue—patience, empathy, faithfulness—requires resistance; the rough edges of real life rub us into a sturdier pattern. The cross, in this reading, becomes not an exception to the rule but the revelation of how God works through weakness. The Son of God suffers, and in that self-giving, the invitation is issued to creatures to participate in God’s redemptive purposes.

Yet the soul-making story must reckon with hard questions. Why should innocents, especially the very young or those with no capacity to understand or resist, be subjected to the crucible of growth? If suffering is primarily for our formation, what of the children who die before they can form anything at all? The critique is pointed: virtuous outcomes do not automatically justify present pain, and not every life yields recognizable moral fruit from suffering. A robust soul-making theodicy can be persuasive for many on a journey of faith, but it cannot pretend that pain’s justification is always evident, or that all suffering serves a clear end in this life. It must be honest about limits and the possibility that some forms of pain may exceed what even a wise and loving creator would permit if all we could see were the present moment.

A third course, the cross as God’s answer. The Christian claim is not merely that God uses suffering for some broader purpose, but that God himself enters into suffering in Jesus Christ and, in so doing, reveals a divine solidarity with human pain. The cross discloses that God is not a distant legislator who remains untouched by the condition of the world; God is profoundly present in the pain of the world. In Jesus, God bears what humans bear, takes on the consequences of sin, and defeats suffering not merely by explanation but by solidarity and final victory. The resurrection then becomes the reference point for interpretation: even the most devastating events—death, betrayal, abandonment—are reframed in light of a future that cannot be extinguished. Suffering is not rewarded with automatic justification, but it is given a meaning that transcends it; it is joined to the redemptive purpose that culminates in new creation.

The cross-oriented reading also resists sentimental solutions. It does not pretend that pain is simply permitted for some unknown good; it is linked to a love that bears the pain with us, accompanies us in lament, and invites us toward fidelity and hope. The biblical narrative continually returns to a paradox: God’s ultimate act of power, in the crucified Christ, is inseparable from weakness and vulnerability. This is not a rejection of rational accounts of evil; it is a claim about the shape of divine action in history. If God could endure the worst that human beings can do and still pursue life for the world, then our response is not to demand that God explain every pain away but to trust that God’s love remains active in redeeming and transforming even the most afflicted circumstances. The cross, then, is both a critique of suffering (it reveals its depth) and a beacon for hope (it reveals the possibility of deliverance and reconciliation).

A fourth, more provocatively pastoral angle is the protest theodicy—the claim that suffering and oppression are not simply obstacles to God’s plan but a lacerating exposure of the world’s brokenness that God does not ignore. In this reading, God’s presence with the afflicted is not merely remedial; it is prophetic. Suffering makes visible the inviolable dignity of the image of God in every person and often becomes the arena in which the community discovers its own complicity in hurt and its obligation to act for justice. The biblical corpus abounds with laments, cries of the oppressed, and promises of divine vindication—psalms and prophetic books that teach us to bear witness to pain while insisting that God’s kingdom comes with justice. This approach does not provide a neat algorithm for ending pain, but it refuses to let suffering be a mute testimony. It calls the church to stand with the weak, to work against structures that perpetuate harm, and to hold onto God’s covenant faithfulness when all human assurances fail.

What holds these perspectives together is not a single, fixed explanation but a shared conviction that God’s goodness is not threatened by suffering, even when suffering resists comprehension. Scripture models a hermeneutic of wrestling rather than a catechism of neat answers. The biblical story—Job’s honest complaint, the psalms of lament, the prophets who name suffering while insisting on God’s sovereignty, the passion and resurrection of Christ—refuses to reduce God to a mere theorem about causes and purposes. Instead, it presents God as the one who enters the story, who hears the cries, and who carries the weight of pain into new possibilities. The text invites us to trust in a God who is with us in the fire, not to pretend that the flames do not hurt.

Scriptural engagement for this discussion stays concrete without becoming proof-texting. We learn, for example, from Job that suffering is not always the consequence of hidden sin, nor is it easily explainable by “greater goods” that exist beyond our sight. We learn from the Psalms that lamenting is not faith’s betrayal but its honest articulation before God, an expression that both questions and worships. We learn from Romans that creation itself longs for liberation and that the Spirit intercedes when words fail. We learn from the cross that God’s power is made perfect in weakness and that love can redefine the meaning of victory. None of these texts function as a brute answer to a survey question; together they form a framework for navigating a world in which pain speaks with enormous force.

Acknowledging the limits of human understanding remains essential. Theologians talk candidly about mystery, but mystery is not license to retreat into evasive silence. Rather, it humbles us to hold our beliefs with humility, while continuing to seek and learn. We can acknowledge that our vantage point is finite: we inhabit time-and-space in a cosmos that bears the mark of sin’s corruption and the impact of human and natural evils. Yet we are not released from reasoning. We can observe patterns—how communities that live with compassion and justice often emerge more resilient, how acts of mercy can elevate the dignity of the suffering, how communities that lament together may also glimpse a future beyond despair. These observations do not solve the mystery, but they illuminate a way forward that remains faithful to God’s character as good and loving.

In pastoral practice, the problem of suffering must translate into faithful accompaniment. The church’s vocation is not to file away pain as a philosophical nuisance but to sit with the broken-hearted, to weep with those who weep, and to offer practical and spiritual nourishment. Lament is not a failure of faith but a form of trust that refuses to let suffering be the final word. Prayer is not an escape from reality but a courageous petition that God would act with mercy and transforming power. Community matters: patients and carers, families and neighbors, pastors and friends—these relationships become the tangible answer to the problem of suffering in the moment. Regimens of care, humane policies, social justice, and medical advances all belong to the broad enterprise of the church’s response to pain. Yet even when cures seem slow or impossible, the church can point to the cross and the resurrection as the ultimate horizon: not a denial of pain, but a declaration that pain is not the final term in God’s good world.

And here, the theological imagination is anchored in a hopeful realism. God is good, and God is with us; good does not always negate suffering, but it can redeem it in unexpected ways. The gospel does not reduce life to a problem-solution equation; it proclaims that God’s love, revealed in Jesus, is the stage upon which human pain is not dismissed but transfigured. The future God promises—restoration, justice, a new creation—gives the present moment a direction. That direction is not sentimentality but a stubborn fidelity: to witness, to bear one another’s burdens, to care for the vulnerable, to hope in the face of despair. The problem remains hard, but it is not void of light. The cross shows that God would rather bear the pain with us than remove us from the world’s fragility by any shortcut. The resurrection assures us that sorrow, while real, is not sovereign.

In closing, to speak of suffering in light of God’s goodness is to tell a story that does not pretend to resolve every tension but to hold it with integrity. The problem of evil will always press into the mystery of God, because God’s ways are not ours, and his thoughts are not ours. Yet the Christian tradition insists that goodness—God’s goodness—must be read in association with God’s self-revelation in the crucified and risen Christ. The best of Christian thinking is not a clever rebuttal to every objection but a proclamation of a God who enters into our pain, who shares our sorrow, who works toward a future where pain and death are no more. The truth of this claim does not erase the ache of now, but it invites us to walk through the ache with a companionship that is costly, faithful, and real.

Thus, the problem of suffering is not an elimination of faith but a crucible for it: an invitation to trust more deeply in a God who is good, who is with us in the valley, and who, in a yet unseen consummation, will bring all things to their intended end. In the meantime, the church’s testimony—robustly intellectual, honestly humble, and pastorally attentive—seeks to bear witness to that goodness in concrete acts of love, in the lament that gives voice to pain, in the courage to pursue justice, and in the steady proclamation that forgiveness, mercy, and renewal are not mere ideas but realities announced in the person of Jesus Christ. If pain tests faith, faith, grounded in the cruciform God, can also empower a patient, enduring hope that does not vanish when the lights go down. That is the gift of a robust, honest theology to a world that suffers—and yet remains, by grace, not without hope.

G2RPNO0_GqcIf8CYOVy-P.text:
Suffering presses on us as a hard ordinary fact of life and, for many, as a piercing test of faith. When we ask, “If God is good, why does this hurt so badly?” we are not seeking a clever rationalization to soothe the ache. We want to remain honest about the pain, brave in naming it, and faithful in listening for a word that could sustain us. The problem of evil is not a trivia question for theologians; it is a burden carried by parents who lose a child, by the chronically ill, by victims of injustice, by refugees who carry the weight of shattered homes, by those who watch a world they love unravel week after week. And yet, to speak about the goodness of God amid suffering is not to pretend the ache away but to illuminate its shape so that hope, not despair, has room to breathe.

Presenting the problem fairly

The classical problem can be framed briefly but not simplistically. If God is all-knowing, all-powerful, and wholly good, then two kinds of observations seem to resist easy reconciliation with divine benevolence. First, the sheer amount and variety of suffering—moral evils inflicted by one person upon another, and natural evils arising without any human malice—appear to be either gratuitous or at least difficult to justify. Second, the problem is not merely theoretical: suffering is particular, concrete, and personal. It has a face, a duration, a texture, and sometimes a backstory of trauma and loss. The question becomes not only, “Why evil exists in the universe?” but, “Why do certain evils persist in a world governed by a good Creator who could, in principle, prevent them?”

Two strands of the problem are often distinguished: the moral evil produced by human choices and the natural evils that seem to arise from the order of creation itself. A fair approach does not straw-man the objections: it acknowledges that some people suffer through systems of oppression that appear to mock a good Creator, while others suffer through impersonal forces—disease, disasters, accidental harm—that raise the question of whether the created order could be otherwise. The evidential burden is heavy, even if the logical burden is not airtight: how could a world with genuine freedom and meaningful goods also be free from gratuitous, disproportionately severe suffering? And if God could prevent pain without violating freedom or destroying meaningful goods, why does He not intervene more often, more decisively, or more transparently?

Within this terrain, several moves have been offered, each honest in its own way and each limited in its own way. The two I want to explore here are not exhaustive, but they illuminate the kinds of answers Scripture and tradition have pressed into the open space between God’s goodness and human agony.

Free will defense: moral evil as the price of genuine love

One time-honored response centers on human freedom. If love is a true love, it presupposes liberty; coercion would undermine virtue just as surely as falsehood undermines trust. The argument is not that evil is a good thing but that moral evil—ensuing from human choices—has a price tag attached to it: freedom costs. The world with genuine liberty would permit persons to align with or against the good, and the misuses of liberty can multiply into many forms of harm. In this view, moral evils become understandable as the price we pay for a world in which love can be real, even if such a world entails pain and error.

This defense is strong where the problem is most acute: it addresses the intentional harms that arise from human agents—tyranny, exploitation, hatred, violence. It preserves the possibility that creatures can grow in virtue through freely chosen responses to God and neighbor and that love’s risks are inseparable from love’s value. Yet the defense is not a full testament to the problem’s enormity. It sagely notes that not all suffering arises from human choice, and some harms are inexplicable as mere consequences of a willful choice. Natural evils—diseases, earthquakes, genetic vulnerability—do not fit neatly inside a free-willed calculus. Moreover, even with moral evil, the scale and pattern of suffering sometimes appear disproportionate to the deficit of freedom they seem to justify. If the price of freedom is a world of such persistent heartbreak, why is the price so high and so unevenly distributed? The defense, while clarifying the worth of liberty, is not a comprehensive answer to the lament of the innocent who suffer without a clear agent to blame.

Soul-making theodicy: suffering as the rough road to maturity

Another persistent line of thought, most associated with Irenaeus and later sharpened by John Hick, pictures the world as a training ground in which character is formed through challenges, opposition, and the cruciform tests of endurance. Suffering, in this view, is not a glitch to be excised but a medium through which moral and spiritual virtues are cultivated. Courage, perseverance, compassion, humility, steadfast trust—these are not given at birth but discovered under pressure. The world, with its hardships, becomes a workshop in which beings first come to resemble their Creator through the disciplined development of virtue. The ultimate telos is not a sanitized world free of pain but a mature humanity capable of loving rightly in a universe that demands resilience.

There is something compelling about this account. It recognizes that life’s trials are not meaningless; they can yield a greater goods such as steadfast faith and deeper solidarity with others who suffer. It also helps explain why God might allow pain without relinquishing sovereignty: He is shaping beings who can bear and channel goodness in worlds that demand virtue under pressure. Yet this approach faces hard questions of scale and fairness. It can seem to justify severe or prolonged evil by appealing to a larger telos that people in crisis cannot reasonably glimpse. When a child suffers without perceivable improvement or when systemic evils persist for generations, the soul-making hope can feel distant, even evasive. And if the most horrific evils are not mere missteps but part of the training program, how does one reconcile the depth of suffering with the compassion one would expect from a benevolent Creator? The soul-making theodicy must be careful not to reduce pain to a mere instrument or to insinuate that the cosmos must be evil in order to become good.

The cross as God’s answer: cruciform theodicy

A third and urgently relational response centers on the specific act of God in Jesus Christ. In the Christian witness, God is not distant from suffering but decisively present in it. The cross is not merely a demonstration of divine compassion; it is a claim about the nature of divine love: God does not coerce or annihilate, but enters into the deepest vulnerability of human existence. In this sense, suffering becomes the stage upon which God’s love is most clearly displayed and most deeply felt. The cruciform pattern—where God chooses solidarity with the broken, where weakness is the path to strength, where pain is transformed into a source of ultimate victory—offers a reframing of the problem. If God has chosen to bear pain in order to redeem it, then the seriousness of suffering is not denied, but its meaning is transfigured. The Risen Christ, whom believers name as alive and present, stands as the pledge that pain is not the final word; the world’s history is moving toward a new creation where mourning gives way to comfort and tears to joy.

A cruciform reading does not erase the questions; it reframes them. It invites trust in a God who has suffered with us, who has not outsourced compassion to others but has bound Himself to the suffering of humanity. It also invites courage to imitate a God who does not avert pain but bears it with us, and to work, with that same spirit, toward justice, mercy, and healing in the present age. Yet even the cross leaves us with questions about the origin and ordering of suffering. If God is able to prevent needless pain without compromising freedom or the possibility of genuine goods, why permit certain evils to persist? How do we read the innocent’s pain in a world where God’s self-giving love has already been displayed? The cross offers a powerful answer to the problem of meaning and the orientation of hope, but it does not entirely remove the philosophical tension. It invites—dare we say, it commands—a posture of trust that is not mere resignation but active hope: in Christ, God is with us; in the Spirit, God accompanies our teams of care; in the coming age, God intends a world where pain and death are ultimately undone.

Scripture’s witness: narratives of lament, trust, and hope

Scripture offers a robust, not simplistic, conversation with the problem of suffering. It is not a single, neat solution but a chorus of voices that wrestle with pain while insisting on God’s sovereignty and goodness. The Book of Job is a patient, raw testimony to the reality that the innocent suffer, that the reasons are not readily present to human perception, and that no tidy syllogism can finally settle the cry of the heart. Job’s friends provide conventional explanations that fall short; Job himself insists on honesty before God, not a clever defense. The book’s arc moves toward a divine encounter that does not supply a full catalog of reasons for every pain, but it does insist that God’s governance cannot be reduced to a mere mechanism of cause and effect. In the literature of Israel, lament and protest are never mere complaints; they are acts of faith that demand God’s presence and justice.

The prophets do not offer a painless panacea; they speak of judgment and mercy, deliverance and restoration, often under the image of suffering servants and wounded redeemers. The servant songs in Isaiah portray a figure who bears suffering in solidarity with others and whose wounds become a source of healing for many. The New Testament relocates this pattern in the crucified and risen Jesus, the one who embodies God’s solidarity with the afflicted and who inaugurates a new creation in which the old order’s pain is no more. Creation’s groaning—Paul’s language for the world under the weight of sin—points to a future hope where the created order itself participates in God’s healing. The apostle’s insistence that all things work together for good for those who love God is not a blanket claim that every particular pain has a neatly explicable purpose but a promise that God’s redemptive purposes reach even through suffering to bring about a larger, gracious good.

The limits of human understanding, rightly acknowledged

All three strands—the free will defense, the soul-making reading, and cruciform interpretation—offer ways to think about suffering that are faithful to biblical witness and to a robust sense of God’s goodness. Yet each also bears a limit. Human beings are finite; our vantage points are partial. We inhabit histories of pain that resist quick resolution. A fair theodicy should acknowledge this epistemic humility without slipping into cynicism or sentimentality. We can say with honesty that there are mysteries about God’s purposes that we do not, cannot, fully fathom. We can speak about God’s goodness as reliable and trustworthy in the pattern of love revealed in Christ, while admitting that we may not understand every particular instance of pain under heaven.

That humility, however, should not become a posture of quietism or escape. There are things we can know, and our knowing comes with moral responsibility. We can discern, in Scripture and in experience, that God’s goodness is not demonstrated by the absence of suffering but by the presence of grace amid it, by a pattern of consolation that exists for those who suffer, and by a compelling vision of justice that invites human work for a more merciful world. The limits of our understanding do not absolve us of the obligation to care, to pursue justice, to comfort the afflicted, to practice lament when required, and to bear witness to a hope that is not naïve but robustly grounded in the person of Jesus.

A pastoral habit of hopeful realism

To be pastorally aware is to hold intention with those who suffer: to listen with patience, to name pain with accuracy, to accompany people in the long night without offering a pat answer, and to invite them toward a future shaped by God’s promises. In practice, this means several commitments. First, to lament well: to voice honest questions before God, to acknowledge anger and fear, and to refuse a hasty move to spiritualize away the hurt. Lament is not a defeatist confession; it is a form of faithful petition that keeps the heart open to God’s presence in the bottom of the valley. Second, to bear one another’s burdens: to practice practical care, to stay present, to help with the tasks that pain often makes hard—meal preparation, financial strain, childcare, medical decisions, grief rituals. Community is not a distraction from theology; it is a concrete enactment of the love that God manifests in Christ. Third, to hold to hope—an informed hope that looks with honesty at pain while leaning toward the future’s promises. The gospel does not flatten sorrow into a gloss; it reframes sorrow within the contour of God’s coming reign, where “the former things” pass away and “the dwelling of God is with humanity” in a renewed creation. In this hopeful realism, faith becomes not a denial of pain but a robust response to it.

Toward a synthesis: living with paradox, or a faithful posture

What, then, can be said that faithfully honors both the seriousness of suffering and the goodness of God? Perhaps the most honest stance is not to choose one solution over the others but to live with a disciplined synthesis that keeps these strands in tension. God’s love is not proven by the absence of pain; God’s love is proven by the willingness to bear pain with, for, and for the sake of others. Freedom matters because it makes possible real love; pain enters the world as a consequence of that freedom, yet God’s redemptive purposes move through pain toward a future where evil is undone. The world’s testing of character may be painful, but the cosmic drama is not reduced to a tale of unmerited suffering; it is a drama of redemption in which suffering becomes the very arena in which God’s power is made known in weakness.

In the end, the problem of suffering cannot be solved in a single stroke of philosophical reasoning or in a single line of doctrinal formula. It must be inhabited—in life, in worship, in care for the vulnerable, in the patient work of healing and reconciliation. The Christian imagination, informed by Scripture and shaped by the cross, offers a way to hold onto both honesty and hope: honesty about the real weight of pain, and hope sustained by the conviction that God’s goodness remains reliable, not because pain has been fully explained, but because Jesus has entered into the deepest places of pain and emerged bearing the promise of a new creation.

If there is a final word, let it be this: the God who is good is not indifferent to our wounds. The God who is sovereign is not distant from our night. The God who acts in Jesus Christ is not content with a world where the strong prevail and the weak are crushed; He is the God who bears our griefs and carries our sorrows, who offers a path through death to life. To follow such a God in a world of pain is to practice a patient courage—to name, to lament, to resist evil where one can, to comfort where one is able, and to persevere in hope because the cross, and ultimately the resurrection, testifies that love will not be defeated.

For those who suffer, this is not a theoretical consolation. It is a call to faithful companionship: to listen, to stand with, to advocate for justice, to attend to the sick, to refuse cynicism and despair, and to hold fast to the conviction that goodness has a name, and that name is Jesus. If the world’s wounds tell a grim and urgent story, the church’s witness proclaims a counter-story—a story of a God who enters into the world’s suffering, who refuses to abandon His creatures to the dark, and who invites all to a future where pain is healed, sorrow is turned to joy, and the Creator’s work is finished in a new creation where love is our final and enduring reality.

GPjyp8l5zC_Ss0UwSmeec.text:
Pain presses on the question of God’s goodness with a stubborn stubbornness. It arrives not only as a historical problem for philosophers but as a daily, intimate ache for people who live with loss, illness, injustice, or the slow erosions of meaningful relationships. If God is love and if God is all-powerful, why does suffering persist, and sometimes flourish, in a world God calls "very good"? The problem is not a mere academic puzzle; it is the ground on which lives are lived and faith is tested. Any honest Christian reflection must name the problem bravely, listen to Scripture with careful attention, and weigh the explanations that have been offered—two or three in particular, each with its own insights and its own challenges.

The problem, stated plainly, has two strands. First, there is the logical or evidential problem: if God is all-wise and all-good, the existence of evil and immense human misery seems incompatible with such a God. Second, there is the more experiential, pastoral problem: even if there is a theodicy that could in theory reconcile God’s goodness and power with suffering, it must still sit with real people who have endured real pain, sometimes for a long season, and who need to know that their suffering matters to God and to the people who claim to follow him. This is not a call to window-dressing, but a demand that philosophy and theology not drift into abstraction while the world bleeds. The God we worship has shown himself to be not distant but near; the task for doctrine is to honor both the mystery and the mercy.

To begin, it helps to distinguish the kinds of evil we face. Human beings do harm; moral evil arises from choices that fracture love—abuse, exploitation, cruelty, indifference. But nature—storms, disease, natural disasters, genetic fragility—also inflicts suffering even when no human agent stands behind it. The biblical writers do not pretend this distinction dissolves the problem; they constantly hold together a world in which the good creation is marred by human rebellion and in which the material world itself groans, waiting for redemption. The challenge for theology is to account for both, and to do so in a way that remains faithful to the witness of Scripture and to the experience of people who bear the weight of pain.

Two major lines of response have shaped Christian thought in the last two millennia. The first is the free will defense, which emphasizes the moral texture of creation. The second, often called a version of the soul-making theodicy, emphasizes growth, formation, and the character of the human person in a world that presses toward maturity through trial. A third approach, which I will treat toward the end, reads the problem through the cruciform center of Christian faith—the cross as the locus where God’s goodness is most clearly disclosed and most profoundly enacted, not apart from suffering but through it.

1) The free will defense: freedom as the precondition of love (and the risk it entails)

The free will line of thought begins with a simple, stubborn insight: authentic love and genuine responsibility require freedom. Love that is coerced is not love at all; it is obedience under duress or manipulation. If God made beings with real powers to choose the good, then the possibility of choosing evil must accompany the possibility of choosing good. In this frame, much of the suffering that accompanies moral evil is the tragic by-product of creatures who violate the order of love. Violence, cruelty, oppression—these are the malignant fruits of freedom misused.

Suffering may thus be explained as the necessary environment in which love takes shape. The capacity to choose rightly requires the possibility to choose wrongly; without that possibility, moral agents would be less than fully responsible, and so would be less truly human. The world would be a stage for scripted virtue rather than a field for genuinely formed character. The freedom to love also entails the possibility of turning away from love, sometimes with consequences that ripple through others’ lives.

There are, however, difficult questions to hold here. First, why should natural evils be part of this account? If freedom alone generates much suffering, why do storms and disease persist even when human agency seems minimal? The defense typically argues that natural laws operate with reliability and predictability in ways that enable moral agents to flourish. A world with consistent natural law might be the kind of world where relationships, institutions, and communities can endure long enough to cultivate virtues such as patience, forgiveness, courage, and hope. But this sounds to many like a mere stratagem for avoiding the heart of the problem, especially when we encounter innocent sufferers—infants, the chronically ill, those who cannot alter their circumstances by choice. Critics push back: if natural evils exist in a world designed for moral realism, why are some instances of suffering so gratuitous, disproportionate, or seemingly arbitrary?

Defenders reply that gratuitous suffering is precisely the kind of thing we cannot infer from our limited vantage point. Skeptical theists argue that human beings, with our bounded perspectives, cannot discern the full range of purposes God might pursue through suffering. What seems gratuitous to us might be a faint and partial view of a larger, even cosmic, design—one that yields goods we cannot presently perceive, goods such as the deeper roots of trust, solidarity, mercy, or reverence. The moral dimension remains alive in this account: suffering tests love, purifies pride, and invites communities to bear one another’s burdens. In this sense, the free will defense does not pretend to remove pain; it reframes its place by insisting that the freedom to choose love is supremely worth the risk of moral evil.

Yet the free will defense does not solve the problem for everyone. It does not eliminate the heartache of a child’s illness, the tearing apart of families by violence, or the ache of a community ravaged by disaster. It also risks implying that those who suffer are, in some sense, participating in a divine economy of virtue-building that they did not choose or consent to. And so the defense must be held in a way that is deeply pastoral: it should not become a philosophical cocoon that excuses suffering or uses freedom as a cover for neglect or injustice. It calls Christians to cultivate a community where freedom is guarded not only as a right but as a vocation to love, to weep with those who weep, and to work against structures that deform freedom into domination.

2) Soul-making theodicy: growth through testing, formation toward likeness to God

A second line of response shifts attention from freedom to formation. The soul-making theodicy, associated most famously with John Hick and rooted in the earlier thought of Irenaeus, understands suffering as the arena in which the human person is formed into a likeness of Christ. The world, with its trials and its ever-present possibility of failure, functions as a kind of school for virtue. The storms of life are not merely punishments or accidents; they are raw material for the becoming person—people who develop courage, compassion, humility, perseverance, and hope.

In this view, God’s purposes are not primarily to maximize comfort or pain-free happiness but to cultivate a character capable of loving rightly in a world that resists such love. Pain acts as a co-educator with grace, shaping dispositions that mere ease cannot form. The resurrection then becomes not merely a future event but the horizon that puts present hardship in a larger frame: the end of the story glitters with the promise of transformation and vindication.

Critics of soul-making request a more exact accounting for what suffers and why; they ask why some harms seem so gratuitous—especially in cases of infant suffering or congenital disabilities. If the world is a moral classroom, why are some students left with permanent impairment, or why do some learn more slowly than others? The critique presses the claim that a virtue-centered pedagogy should yield meaningful moral outcomes with proportional pains; when suffering feels arbitrary, the pedagogy appears evasive.

Proponents respond in two ways. First, they insist that the pain of loss or deviation does not negate the possibility of genuine growth; second, they claim that God’s plan is not a mere arithmetic of goods and evils but a drama in which ultimate fulfillment—God’s presence, justice, and mercy—unfolds in time. The biblical witness often nods toward that future horizon: the present sufferings anticipate a more glorious future, a restoration in which the created order is redeemed from the distortions of sin. Yet, this is not a promise that pain will be superfluous to the story; it is the claim that pain, rightly endured, can contribute to a character that participates more fully in God’s life.

As with the free will defense, the soul-making theodicy requires patient, humble engagement. It asks not for a pat explanation of every sorrow but for a framework in which God’s purposes against the grain of hurt can be discerned with honest-wrestle hope. What makes this approach pastorally viable is its insistence that suffering is not ultimately for nothing: it can, if received in faith and with community, refine us, reorient our loves, and render the end more glorious than the beginning.

3) The cross as God’s answer: cruciform wisdom for a suffering world

A third approach turns the cruciform core of Christianity into a decisive corrective to mere speculative apologetics. The cross, we may say, is not a footnote in the narrative of God’s goodness but the decisive revelation of God’s posture toward suffering. In the crucified Jesus, God does not stand at a distance while humanity suffers; God enters into suffering, bears the injury of evil, and defeats sin and death through self-giving love. The cross is not a theological puzzle solved by clever arguments; it is the dramatic display that God’s goodness is not absent in pain but steady within it, not triumphant over suffering by bypassing it but by transforming its meaning through love.

In biblical language, this is the cruciform logic: God’s power is perfected in weakness; God reconciles the world to himself not through triumphalist domination but through costly, self-giving love. The Gospels present Jesus as the manifestation of God’s solidarity with the suffering: he weeps with those who weep; he bears pain for others’ sake; he accepts abandonment and torture to redeem. The apostolic witness makes the same move: in Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection, God does not explain away suffering but reveals how it is to be endured with trust. The cross becomes the lens through which we interpret all other suffering: it may not remove pain immediately, but it discloses God’s purposes in and through pain—purity of motive, solidarity with the weak, and a path toward ultimate vindication and life.

The cruciform view does not silence the questions that pain raises; it reframes them. If God is love, the depth and cost of divine love are seen most clearly on the cross. If God is sovereign, the cross does not erase the mystery of providence; it grounds the claim that God’s plan is not to suppress freedom or to annihilate creation’s fragility but to redeem it through redeeming love. The resurrection then anchors hope: the end of suffering is not an illusion but a real, future reality in which all things are made new. In this light, suffering does not exhaust meaning; it can be transformed into witness, into a testimony to the power of love that binds all things together.

Scripture, not merely philosophy, keeps these threads together. The biblical story begins with a creation deemed good and ends with a creation reconciled. Between those bookends, the biblical writers tell of lament and praise, of perplexity and assurance. Job’s questions, expressed in raw honesty, meet God’s sovereignty expressed in a whirlwind: the Lord does not fully explain why the righteous suffer, yet he asserts that his wisdom and governance are trustworthy. The psalms of lament give voice to disorientation, then pivot toward trust, because the God who heeds the cry of the afflicted is also the God who hears and acts in history. The apostolic letters insist that present sufferings cannot finally separate us from the love of God in Christ, because what God has accomplished in the cross and what God has promised in the resurrection are more powerful than the forces that crush or confuse. In short, Scripture holds a cruciform claim: God’s goodness is displayed most clearly in willingness to bear evil in solidarity with the wounded, and God’s victory becomes visible not by eliminating all pain now but by ensuring that no pain is final and that love can prevail.

A shared space: biblical imagination and human limitation

In engaging these responses—free will, soul-making, and cruciform theodicy—we should be careful not to obscure the limits of human understanding. We will not finally “solve” the problem of suffering for every case, nor should we pretend that we can. Skeptical theism rightly guards against simplistic theodicies that pretend to know why each particular suffering occurs. Yet faith does not surrender to mystery as an excuse for indifference; it leans into mystery with a posture of trust and a willingness to act justly in light of what we do know. We can say with humility that God’s ways are higher than ours, and we can still insist that God’s character remains good, and that God is present with us in the deepest valleys.

A pastoral mode of engagement keeps these ideas honest. The church does not need only to offer explanations; it must offer presence. When a family mourns the loss of a child, when a community endures the blast of violence, when a person endures long illness, the church’s response should be concrete: sit with the bereaved in their grief, advocate for the vulnerable, refuse easy answers that belittle pain, and enact mercy in tangible ways. Theology, finally, exists to illuminate worship, increase courage for compassion, and enable communities to bear one another’s burdens in the name of Christ.

A short, pastoral synthesis

Taken together, these perspectives offer a composite approach to the problem of suffering that remains faithful to the biblical portrayal of God’s goodness and to the real pain that people endure.

- The free will defense preserves the dignity of moral responsibility and love, while acknowledging that the freedom that enables good also carries risk. It invites communities to cultivate virtue and to confront evil in systems and structures that deform freedom into domination.

- The soul-making (or formational) approach reframes pain as a context for character and grace—an invitation to grow toward wholeness and Christlikeness, even when the path is jagged and the outcomes are not guaranteed in this life.

- The cruciform or cross-centered perspective grounds out the best answer in the heart of the gospel: God enters into suffering, bears its weight with us, invites us to participate in his life, and promises a future in which pain is dissolved and all things are made new. The cross does not erase mystery, but it reveals God’s solidarity and ultimate victory.

Scripture underwrites this triad. Creation is good; the fall distorts creation and invites suffering; Christ’s life, death, and resurrection redeem that brokenness; the Spirit sustains the church as it lives in hope and works toward justice. The believer is called to lament honestly, to trust deeply, and to act mercifully. The Christian life is not a refusal to name sorrow; it is a hopeful engagement with sorrow in light of divine love that has entered into the world.

On limits and honesty: what we can and cannot claim

We must acknowledge, with honesty, that some questions remain unanswerable in this life. There are instances that defy neat rationalization, where even the most probable explanations feel inadequate in the face of a particular tragedy. Skeptical theism refers to such moments to remind us that our cognitive horizon is narrow; it should not tempt us to dismiss God or to abandon compassion. But acknowledging limits is not a refusal of discourse. We can (and should) sharpen our theological tools: we can defend the dignity of free will, propose a formative purpose to suffering, and insist that God’s ultimate answer to evil is found in the crucified and risen Christ who bears our pain and bears it through to its decisive conclusion.

In the end, the goodness of God is not demonstrated by the absence of suffering but by the presence of God within suffering. If we search the biblical narrative for where God’s goodness shines most clearly, we do not reach a list of explanations as much as a person: Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, who bears our grief, who conquers through weakness, who invites us to trust even when the path is dark, and who promises that justice and mercy will prevail. The cross, then, becomes both the hinge and the horizon: a moment when God’s love is provenologically real at the cost of suffering, and a horizon toward which all creation moves, when God’s justice and mercy fill the earth as the waters cover the sea.

Thus, we walk forward with both honesty and hope. We acknowledge the realities of pain and the genuine perplexity it can provoke. We listen to those who cry out in lament and sit with them in silence when words fail. We hold fast to the claims of Scripture about God’s love, sovereignty, and faithfulness, and we attend to the church’s vocation to be a healing presence in the world. If the problem of suffering tests the mind and wounds the heart, the Christian faith offers a posture of faithful endurance: a willingness to wrestle with difficult questions, a readiness to be formed through trial, and a steadfast confidence that the God who speaks peace into chaos has not abandoned us but is with us, even now, as the one who suffered with us and, in the end, makes all things new.

The ache that suffering leaves in the body and the soul is not easily disarmed by syllogisms or polished pieties. It arrives as a knock in the night, a question in a hospital waiting room, a tear on the cheek of a child who has just learned that life will demand more from them than they can yet give. To speak of the goodness of God in light of such real pain is not to dodge the question or to offer a pious gloss. It is to enter into a conversation that has forged believers and their neighbors for two millennia: the problem of evil in the light of a God who is both good and powerful. What follows here is an attempt to name the problem honestly, to examine a few coherent Christian responses, and to do so with Scripture not as a talisman of proof-texts but as a living conversation partner. It is also an invitation to live in the tension—humble, hopeful, and pastorally attentive to real people who suffer.

The problem, stated plainly, is this: if God is all-good, God would not desire or allow harm; if God is all-powerful, God could prevent harm; yet harm exists in the world in ways that are intimate and indiscriminate, both moral and natural. The objection is not merely that pain exists but that the existence of pain seems to conflict with the character of God as generous, just, and loving. The objection is sharpened by two facts that Scripture itself does not shy away from naming. First, human beings exercise agency in ways that hurt others—greed, pride, cruelty, indifference. Moral evil, then, is not an accidental byproduct of a broken system but often the result of deliberate choices. Second, the creation itself bears marks of a world out of alignment—natural disasters, disease, decay, misfortune—that do not look like the orderly, good purpose one might expect from a Creator who calls all things “very good.” The problem, in short, asks whether the logic of a perfectly good and sovereign God can accommodate both the moral agency of creatures and the presence of pain that seems almost gratuitous.

Two broad lines of response—each with theological depth and real philosophical ballast—have organized Christian thinking across centuries. They are not mutually exclusive; many people find strength in an integrated account that draws from more than one.

1) Free will and the authenticity of creaturely order
A long-standing defense centers on freedom. If real love, goodness, and moral value require that creatures act in ways that are genuinely their own, then freedom becomes a necessary condition for any meaningful relationship with God and with one another. Evil, in this view, arises when free beings misuse their liberty. The world is not a closed system of automatic consequences but a stage on which love must sometimes risk injury for the sake of genuine choice. In this framework, God creates a world with real possibilities: acts of mercy that heal, and acts of cruelty that wound—but these latter possibilities arise because God would not crush the potential for love by enforcing a rigid, painless determinism.

This “free will defense” helps with moral evil. It makes space for human accountability and moral growth. It also offers a partial reconciliation with natural evil: if you grant that a world in which creatures exercise meaningful freedom is likely to be accompanied by the possibility of others’ harm—not as God’s desire but as a corollary of genuine moral agency—then some portion of suffering can be understood as the unintended, though not purposeless, consequence of freedom in a morally serious cosmos.

Yet this defense does not solve all puzzles. It struggles with natural evil—earthquakes, tsunamis, cancer—that are not the direct result of human choice. It also leaves the scale and gravity of certain evils hard to bear: why should innocent children experience the worst misfortunes? It can feel abstract when faced with guardian-figures, neighbors, or refugees who suffer not from their own clear malice but from a chain of circumstances that seems to escape human control. In short, the free will defense preserves a meaningful place for human responsibility and genuine relationship, but it does not by itself provide a complete account of suffering’s breadth and depth.

2) Soul-making, formation, and a world as apprenticeship
A second line of thought envisions suffering as part of a divinely ordered process of character formation. Rooted in the thought of early Christian writers and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick, the soul-making theodicy contends that a world with resisting circumstances—privation, challenge, trial, and even pain—is a necessary environment for virtues such as courage, compassion, patience, and faith. A cosmos without any friction might preclude the growth of serious moral and spiritual goods. In that sense, the world is less a stage for effortless bliss and more a workshop for becoming—how to love without dissolving into sentimentality, how to endure without becoming bitter, how to trust in the unseen while walking through the visible storm.

This approach can feel intuitively generous: suffering is not gratuitous punishment but training wheels for the person God intends us to become. It also speaks to communities that bear the burden of long-suffering—the caregivers who endure exhaustion in clinics, the families who labor to keep hope alive in disaster zones, the millions who learn to rely on mercy in ways they never anticipated.

But the soul-making story also encounters hard questions. If the world is crafted for our growth, why is the growth so uneven? Why do some fare better than others under similar pressures? Why does the scale and texture of suffering sometimes seem arbitrary or unmitigated by any apparent virtue in the sufferer? And if character formation is the goal, is it plausible to frame all pain as a necessary instrument toward that end? The critique here is not that the idea is false, but that it requires a more capacious answer about the nature of goodness, the character of God, and the purposes by which a suffering-filled world might be judged as ultimately good.

A biblically informed reader will hear echoes of this approach in the biblical witness itself. The Psalms teach us to address God honestly with lament while still clinging to trust. The prophets speak of testing and refinement that purifies the people. The apostolic writers insist that present sufferings, though real and painful, are not the final word, because God’s redemptive work in Christ is aimed toward the renewal of all things. The soul-making impulse, then, gains shape not by offering a clever riddle about why pain exists but by inviting a patient narrative in which pain is endured, meaning is sought, and hope for transformation persists.

3) The cross as God’s answer: solidarity, love, and the unveiling of ultimate meaning
If one gathers the biblical witness around a central claim, it may be this: God is not distant from suffering but has entered into it in the most vulnerable way imaginable. The Christian story does not pretend that suffering is only a problem to be solved by abstract logic; it invites us to consider that God’s answer to suffering is not primarily a proof-text or explanation but a person—Jesus Christ. In the incarnate Word, God joins the human condition in its deepest depths and, in doing so, redefines what counts as victory and meaning.

The cross is not merely a demonstration of divine power subdued by a cruel event; it is a revelation of divine love that binds suffering to redemptive ends. In Jesus, God bears pain with the wounded rather than tolerating it from a distance. The crucified one embodies the paradox that in God’s economy vulnerability can be powerfully transformative. The resurrection that follows offers not a denial of suffering but a claim that God’s final word is life, liberation, and the renewal of all things. The cross becomes a lens through which to view the entire drama: suffering is not exempt from God’s attention; rather, it is the arena in which God’s fidelity is most clearly shown and God’s purpose for creation is decisively enacted.

This approach intersects with several biblical motifs. The prophets and the psalms present honest grappling with pain, the question of “why?” and “how long?” Yet they also press toward trust that God is for life, that mercy remains possible even in the midst of injustice, and that God’s plan will prevail in the end. The apostolic testimony emphasizes that Jesus’ own suffering qualifies him to help others who are tempted or overwhelmed by adversity. Creation itself—groaning in travail—anticipates liberation, not annihilation. In this sense, the cross is not merely an argument for how God relates to pain; it is the most reliable sign that God’s goodness is not a thesis about avoiding pain but a present reality in which pain can be redefined, forgiven, and translated into compassionate action.

To say the cross is God’s answer does not erase the mystery of suffering. It refrains from offering every personal consolation and refuses to pretend that pain can be categorized into a neat, fully satisfying explanation. Yet it provides a narrative framework in which the most dreadful events are not the final note. God’s solidarity with us in Christ, and God’s power to redeem through that solidarity, invites believers to bear one another’s burdens, to pursue justice, and to trust that God’s purposes extend beyond the visible horizon.

Scripture as a living conversation
To engage with Scripture in this discussion, one does not simply collect proof-texts to win an argument; one enters into a conversation in which human pain and divine mercy are wrestled with in real time. The biblical narrative gives us a spectrum of voices: the raw honesty of lament that raises questions to God; the patient persistence of faith that refuses to abandon trust; the sober proclamations of hope that look toward a new creation. Consider these threads.

- In Genesis, suffering enters the world as a consequence of human choice and the brokenness that follows. Yet even here the story keeps moving toward a gracious promise, a trajectory toward restoration that God will pursue across the ages.

- Job and his friends stage a dramatic dialogue about justice, innocence, and the limits of human grievance. Job’s refusal to reduce his pain to an easy philosophical answer is itself a faithful witness; the divine response—sovereignty articulated not as a taxonomic explanation but a demand that Job recognize the vastness and goodness of God beyond human categories—points us toward humility before mystery while affirming God’s ultimate goodness.

- The Psalms model the practice of lament as a spiritual art: to name the pain honestly, to question, to grieve, and yet to anchor trust in God’s steadfast love. Lament is not a denial of faith; it is a fortification of faith under pressure.

- In Romans, creation groans and believers groan, yet all of it is encompassed by a larger purpose: God’s Spirit intercedes, and nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of Christ. This moves the discussion beyond mere arguments into a posture of trust that reinterprets suffering through the lens of grace and eschatological hope.

- The late chapters of Revelation cast a final word of cosmic renewal: pain and sorrow will be removed, the former things will pass away, and God will dwell with his people in a world re-created for life. The Christian hope is not a denial of hardship but an insistence that hardship will be reconciled to a reality where mercy, justice, and peace reign.

The limits of human understanding, and the humility that follows
No honest theological account can pretend to exhaust the mystery of suffering. There are genuine limits to what human reason, even when illuminated by Scripture and tradition, can fully articulate. Yet acknowledging limitation is not the same as capitulating to cynicism or giving up on reason. We can, and must, press into the question with both careful analysis and faithful hope. The goal is not to produce a silver-bullet explanation that perfectly accounts for every particular pain but to offer a coherent shape to reality in which life can bear weight, sorrow can be shared, and a genuinely good God can be trusted with the whole of existence.

Toward a pastorally responsible posture
If God is good and God is powerful, the Christian response to suffering is not an abstract algorithm but a set of faithful practices that accompany people who bear pain.

- Lament and trust. The church should cultivate spaces where people can voice questions without fear of repudiation. Lament keeps the heart tender toward God while naming the realities of pain. It also guards against a premature triumphalism that would demand a speedy, tidy answer to every cry.

- Solidarity with the vulnerable. Suffering calls forth practical compassion—shelter for the homeless, care for the sick, advocacy for the marginalized, and the patient presence that listens long. The Christian claim that God is with us in suffering obligates us to be with others in their sorrow.

- Hope that looks beyond the present. The Christian life is lived in the tension between the now and the not-yet. We work for justice and healing now, while trusting that God’s final verdict on suffering will be enacted in the renewed creation. This hope does not belittle pain; it dignifies it by promising purpose, repair, and ultimate reconciliation.

- Mercy that transforms rather than merely explains. We should avoid offering pat theologies as if they were sufficient to discharge all pain. Instead, we can point to the Cross as the event that reveals God’s solidarity and love, and to the church as the people who bear one another’s burdens in the light of that revelation.

A hopeful, honest conclusion
The problem of suffering is not a problem we can finally solve by argument alone, nor a problem we can dismiss by sentiment. It is, instead, a reality we inhabit with the Creator who spoke the world into being, who entered the world as a sufferer in the person of Jesus, and who will finally heal and renew all things. The goodness of God is not demonstrated by the absence of pain but by the way God holds pain within a larger work of mercy. The cross is the clearest and most piercing sign of that mercy: in it, God disarms despair, redefines victory, and gathers a broken world into a future where every tear will be wiped away.

To live within this stance is not to pretend that every sorrow has a neat, sufficient explanation. It is to trust that the God who is good and who loves us enough to bear our pain can be trusted with the whole of reality, including the deepest dark moments. It is to join a people who lament without despair, who press toward justice without cynicism, and who, on a daily basis, offer tangible acts of mercy in a world that often feels as if it teeters on the edge of meaning. If we must name our questions and hold them up to the light of faith, may we also name our loves and hold them up to witness to a God who remains present, who does not abandon the broken, and whose ultimate justice and mercy are sure.

In the end, the problem of suffering is not resolved by a single answer but embraced within a narrative: creation’s longing for redress, humanity’s call to respond with courage and compassion, and the cross’s claim that God himself has not abandoned us but chosen to be with us in the darkness. If goodness is the nature of God—and if God’s goodness is proven most vividly in the grace shown at the cross and the promise of new life—then suffering, terrible as it is, cannot be the last word. The last word, we believe, is a future in which God makes all things new, a present reality in which we are invited to cooperate with mercy, and a patient hope that clings to the character of God even when the reasons for present pain remain beyond our grasp.

Suffering presses on every life with a loud insistence, and the question it raises is not only logical but deeply pastoral. If God is good and all-powerful, why does pain exist? Why do the innocent suffer, the faithful falter, and the world seem to bend toward decay even as prayers rise for mercy? A thoughtful faith cannot paper over the ache with platitudes, nor can it let the problem collapse into cynicism. The task, then, is to hold together the conviction of God’s goodness with a sober accounting of human and natural evil, while listening for what Scripture and the best philosophical reflection can offer toward discernment and comfort.

The problem, honestly stated, has both moral and natural dimensions. Moral evil arises from the actions of free creatures. People lie, betray, murder, and inflict harm; societies legislate injustice; and the very capacities that make us morally admirable—freedom, love, courage, fidelity—also carry the danger of choosing what is cruel or selfish. Natural evil includes disease, natural disasters, genetic misfortune, and the harsh rightness of a world governed by cause and effect. The problem deepens when we notice what seems gratuitous: suffering that appears purposeless, prolonged, or borne by those least able to bear it—the child with a rare illness, a family crushed by famine, the vulnerable left to languish in poverty while systems of power remain unmoved. These are not side effects of a hidden plan but the face of a world where harm persists even as we seek to do good.

In presenting the objection, a fair account must distinguish the different forms of the challenge. The classic logical formulation asks how an all-powerful, all-loving God could allow evil at all. If God can do anything, and wants the best for creatures he loves, how can needless pain persist? The evidential or probabilistic version shifts the question: given the amount, magnitude, and seeming randomness of suffering, how compatible is such reality with divine goodness and sovereignty? And a pastoral reframing asks not only whether God could prevent every evil, but whether God’s purposes in suffering might be deeper than relief from pain, perhaps shaping character, forming hope, or pointing communities toward justice. Each axis deserves serious attention, and none should be dismissed with a glib shrug.

Two broad lines of response have shaped Christian reflection in helpful, sometimes hopeful, and sometimes contested ways. The first is the free will defense. The second is the idea that suffering serves some form of character formation or soul-making. A third, emotionally and theologically formative for many, is the claim that the cross—God’s self-giving in Jesus—reframes suffering as God’s own solidarity with the world's pain and as the decisive revelation of divine love and ultimate victory. None of these explanations, on their own, solves every dimension of the problem; each has strengths and limits. Taken together, they offer a more textured witness to the mystery and the mercy of God.

The free will defense rests on a sturdy moral intuition: to love well, beings must be free. If moral goodness is meaningful only where freedom exists, then some degrees of evil become a plausible cost of genuine love. A world in which creatures never choose wrong would inevitably lack the depth of relationship love requires. In this reading, God creates trustworthy beings who freely choose to love, forgive, and do justice; in the same breath, God permits the possibility that those same beings will misuse their freedom in ways that wound others and fracture creation. Evil, then, is not simply God’s will but the byproduct of free agents who bend the will away from the good.

This defense elegantly addresses moral evil and, to some degree, natural evil by appealing to a larger logic of freedom that surpasses human manipulation. It also invites hope: the possibility that love, not coercion, is the shape of reality. Yet the defense does not resolve all difficulties. First, it is hard to account for the most gratuitous natural evils—floods, earthquakes, cancers—without appealing to agents who act outside themselves, or to a world where even “natural” events are permitted within a fallen order. Second, it is not clear that freedom alone suffices to justify the deep, long-lasting, and sometimes intergenerational suffering that seems disproportionate or random. And third, there are questions about why an all-wise God would allow the conditions that make horror more likely than sweetness (for example, the vulnerability of children to harm). The free will defense, therefore, must be complemented by other considerations if it is to dignify rather than simply explain away suffering.

A second line of reflection is the soul-making theodicy, associated most closely with the philosopher-teacher John Hick. The argument is not that God causes suffering to punish or to demand a price for sin, but that such trials are necessary for the development of character and virtue in a world where not all growth comes through ease. In a realm where moral and spiritual maturity require persistence, humility, courage, and perseverance, struggle becomes the soil in which virtues take root. Suffering exposes fragility, shines a light on injustice, and invites reliance on God who alone can sustain in the furnace. To this end, affliction becomes a tutor: not an end in itself, but a means through which souls are disciplined toward a more robust, more compassionate form of humanity.

There is something helpful about imagining a God who uses human pain to refine rather than to ruin. Yet the soul-making account must face serious challenges. The most pointed is the ethics of severity: do the ends ever justify the severity of the means, especially when the protagonists include children who lack the capacity to contribute to their own “growth”? If a God of love would not want to cause unnecessary suffering, is much of the world’s pain truly necessary for character formation? And if the cosmos aims for soul-making at all, why should it require such disproportionate and often unmerited tribulation? The critique is not that the idea is evil in itself; it is that it risks making the divine love seem instrumental, even indifferent to the immediate harm of those who suffer.

A third, biblically grounded angle presses more insistently on God’s own participation in suffering. The cross of Christ stands, in this view, not as a mere demonstration of God’s patience with a wayward world but as the decisive answer to the problem of suffering. If God becomes incarnate, lives among us, suffers at our hands, and dies on a Roman cross, then pain is not a signal that God is absent or cold but a place where God is most fully present—grieving with the broken, absorbing harm, and bearing it toward redemption. The cross embodies a paradox: the loving power of God is revealed most clearly not in the absence of pain but in the willingness to be pierced by it for the sake of others. Then the resurrection points beyond the crucifixion: pain is not the last word; God’s purposes prevail in a future reversal of sorrow, a new creation where tears are wiped away and every form of injustice is undone.

This “cross as answer” or “protest-theodicy” is not a neat solution to every dimension of the problem, but it adds a powerful pastorally resonant claim: God’s goodness does not spare God from the world’s distress; rather, God enters into it with us, transforms it by love, and redefines what victory looks like. The biblical witness supports this stance in multiple directions. The Old Testament’s lament literature voices not a resigned fatalism but an active wrestling with God—honest questions, unblinking cries, and a trust that survives the dark night. The suffering Servant of Isaiah 53 bears not his own transgressions but the sins of others, suffering in solidarity with the broken. The Gospels present Jesus as the pivot of human history, not a distant deity who averts pain but a God who bears pain, prays, surrenders, dies, and rises. The apostolic writings then insist that creation groans in travail, awaiting the redemption that comes through Christ; the present age is not abandoned, but it is not yet perfected. In this sense, the cross reframes the problem: God’s goodness is not measured by the absence of pain but by the promise that pain has a limit and purpose within a larger drama of healing and restoration.

None of these responses, taken alone, settles every case or silences every ache. The free will defense helps explain moral evil but struggles with natural evil and gratuitous cruelty. Soul-making offers a hopeful anthropology of suffering but risks making a cold calculus in the faces of innocent pain. The cross-and-resurrection perspective anchors the problem in God’s own self-gift and future glory, yet it must be read with pastoral sensitivity to present distress, lest believers learn to endure at the expense of justice or consolation. What is essential is not a single panacea but a coherent, humbly held mosaic: God is good; God is sovereign; and human beings live in a world of both structural brokenness and personal vulnerability in which God promises presence, meaning, and ultimate redemption.

Scripture offers a linguistically rich and emotionally honest map for navigating the mystery without surrendering to nihilism or passive piety. Job refuses simplistic answers as his friends insist on cause-and-effect explanations; Job’s own integrity and lament become a catalyst for a larger divine dialogue about sovereignty and wisdom. The Psalms model a posture of honest complaint and confident trust, a rhythm of lament followed by reaffirmation of God’s steadfast love. The Wisdom literature—Proverbs and Ecclesiastes—reminds us that life often operates under patterns we do not fully perceive and that wisdom includes recognizing the limits of our knowledge. In the New Testament, the cross reframes suffering: what looks like a defeat is part of a paradoxical victory, a way by which God’s love defeats death. The narrative arc—sentiment, trial, repentance, hope—invites believers to hold their pain in the same hands that hold the promises of God.

Acknowledging limits is crucial here, but it must not become an excuse for passive resignation. Human beings do not, and cannot, plumb the depths of God’s purposes in every instance. Yet we are not left without guidance. The Christian conviction that God is good, that God is just, and that God has acted decisively in Jesus Christ provides a stabilizing center for moral imagination and pastoral care. In the here-and-now, that means practice: we cultivate communities of presence (sitting with the afflicted, offering practical help), we nurture a liturgy of lament (prayer that names pain, questions, and longing), and we pursue justice in the world (addressing poverty, hunger, oppression) because to do so is to participate in the ongoing work of God’s kingdom. The biblical pattern invites a spirituality of both honesty and hope: to name sorrow truthfully, to confess our confusion where we must, and to trust that God’s good purposes are bigger than our understanding and deeper than our hurt.

To hold these strands together in pastoral life means paying attention to the particularities of real suffering. Some people bear wounds that require more than theological reflection: chronic illness, the loss of a child, the collapse of a marriage, persecution, or the daily grind of poverty. In such cases, the response of faith communities matters as much as the content of doctrinal argument. A faithful response is not a pat reassurance but a steady presence: listening without defensiveness, naming the pain without racing to pat answers, reframing the question toward what is most practically and morally essential in the moment—care for the vulnerable, restoration where possible, and the cultivation of hope that feels real even when it is tempered by sorrow.

If I may offer a concluding reflection, it would be this: the goodness of God is not a guarantee of painless living, but it is a guarantee of hospitality toward pain, a promise that God is with us in the deepest trials, and a pledge that a time is coming when suffering itself will be swallowed up in a broader renewal. The cross makes sense not as an escape from suffering but as a redefinition of it—God’s self-gift, God’s solidarity, God’s power that unshackles life from ultimate fear. In the present, we walk with sufferers, we name the wounds, we study the world’s brokenness with tear-streaked earnestness, and we lean into the hope that God’s purposes for creation include the making of all things new. Our theology must be sturdy enough to withstand the questions and gentle enough to cradle the fainting, the lonely, and the grieving.

In the end, belief in a good God who allows suffering does not erase the ache; it reframes the ache within a larger story. The problem remains real, but so does the hope—an eschatological horizon where justice, mercy, and peace kiss at last and where tears are wiped away. The goodness of God, proclaimed in word and enacted in love, invites believers to live with integrity in the tension: to wrestle with the mystery, to lament with honesty, to pursue justice, to cling to Christ who bore the cross and rose again, and to trust that a world reconciled to God is not a dream but the sure destination toward which the Spirit now moves us and the Son now leads us.
