To speak about suffering “in light of the goodness of God” is to stand at a crossroads where logic, faith, and lived experience all demand to be heard. The question is not merely theoretical. It rises in hospital waiting rooms and at gravesides; it appears in the aftermath of betrayal, abuse, famine, war, and quiet depression. For many, it is less a puzzle to be solved than a wound that won’t close: If God is good, and God is powerful, why is the world like this? And what does it mean to trust such a God?

Any honest exploration must begin by granting the force of the problem. The biblical writers themselves do not treat suffering as an illusion or a trivial inconvenience. They describe the world as a place where creation “groans” (Romans 8), where the righteous are sometimes crushed and the wicked sometimes flourish (Psalm 73), where prayers feel unanswered (Psalm 13), and where even the faithful can be bewildered by divine silence (Job 30). The problem of suffering is not only that pain exists, but that it often seems random, excessive, and morally scandalous.

Philosophers sometimes frame the issue as a logical tension: if God is all-good, God would want to eliminate evil; if God is all-powerful, God could; yet evil persists—so is God not good, not powerful, or not real? Even if one concedes that the strict “logical problem” may not be airtight (perhaps God could have reasons beyond our grasp), the “evidential problem” remains: the sheer quantity and kinds of suffering—especially apparently pointless suffering—make God’s goodness feel improbable. A child dies slowly of cancer. A community is wiped out by an earthquake. An animal is torn apart in the wild. A person is violated and then lives with the consequences for decades. In such cases, it is not enough to say, “God can bring good out of it.” The question presses harder: Why allow it at all, especially when the victims did not choose it?

Christian faith cannot meet this challenge by minimizing pain, blaming sufferers, or offering neat answers that fit on a greeting card. Many religious explanations fail precisely because they protect a tidy picture of God at the expense of truth and compassion. The Bible resists that impulse. It contains fierce protests and prayers that sound, at times, like accusations. It gives us saints who argue with God, and it does not rush to silence them.

### I. The Bible’s refusal to sanitize suffering

Consider Job, not as a morality tale with an easy lesson, but as a sustained confrontation with undeserved suffering. Job is introduced as righteous, and his calamities are not portrayed as punishment. The most chilling aspect of the book is not simply Job’s losses but the inadequacy of the explanations offered by his friends. They defend a world in which suffering reliably corresponds to personal sin, because such a world feels morally intelligible: God rewards the good and punishes the bad. Job rejects that framework, not because he denies human sinfulness in general, but because it fails to tell the truth about his situation. The book refuses simplistic equations: righteous people can suffer terribly, and their suffering is not always traceable to a specific fault.

At the end, when God speaks from the whirlwind, the “answer” is not a step-by-step justification of every sorrow. God confronts Job with the vastness and wildness of creation—realities that exceed Job’s capacity to manage or fully comprehend. This is not a divine shrug, nor is it a rebuke of lament itself. In fact, God says Job has spoken rightly in comparison with the friends, who offered polished theology but lacked truth and tenderness. The message is subtle: God does not condemn honest protest; God condemns confident misrepresentation.

The Psalms likewise refuse to hurry past grief. They give language to bewilderment (“How long, O Lord?”), to anger (“Why do you hide your face?”), and to exhausted trust that hangs on by its fingernails. Lament is not faith’s opposite; it is one form faith takes when the world is unbearable.

Then, in the Gospels, suffering is neither denied nor romantically glorified. Jesus heals the sick and feeds the hungry, treating suffering as an enemy to be resisted, not a “gift” to be cherished. Yet he also rejects easy causal attributions. When asked about a man born blind—who sinned, this man or his parents?—Jesus refuses the premise that his disability is a moral scorecard (John 9). When told of a tragic massacre and a tower collapse, he does not claim the victims were worse than others (Luke 13). He acknowledges the reality of tragedy without turning it into a moral spectacle.

This scriptural honesty sets the tone: Christians are not invited to become experts at explaining suffering from a safe distance. We are invited to tell the truth about it before God, and to seek a way of faithfulness that does not require denying the darkness.

With that groundwork, we can consider theological responses that attempt to make sense of suffering while keeping God’s goodness intact. No response eliminates all mystery; each has strengths and limits. But taken together, they may illuminate different aspects of a problem too large for a single lens.

### II. Free will and the gravity of love

One classic response is the free will defense: much suffering is the result of human choices, and a world with genuine freedom is a world where evil is possible. Love, on this account, cannot be coerced. If God aims not merely for creatures who behave correctly but for persons capable of real relationship—trust, self-giving, courage, fidelity—then God must allow room for refusal. The same human capacity that makes compassion possible also makes cruelty possible.

This response has moral and pastoral resonance because it takes evil seriously. It refuses to treat atrocities as mere “parts of a plan,” and it recognizes the dignity of human agency. Scripture consistently depicts human beings as responsible actors whose decisions matter. The biblical story is filled with choices that harm and choices that heal, and God’s commands assume that obedience and disobedience are meaningful. The prophets denounce exploitation precisely because it could have been otherwise. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem not as a scripted inevitability but as a tragic refusal: “How often would I have gathered your children… and you were not willing” (Matthew 23:37).

The free will framework also makes sense of why some suffering feels morally direct: betrayal wounds because trust was real; oppression is evil because humans possess real power over one another. If we were automatons, “sin” would be a category mistake, and moral growth would be meaningless.

Yet this approach does not solve everything. First, not all suffering is a direct consequence of human wrongdoing. Natural disasters, genetic diseases, and the predation and decay woven into the biological world are harder to attribute to free choices. Second, even when suffering is caused by human evil, it can still seem disproportionate. Why should one person’s freedom be allowed to devastate another’s life? A world with freedom need not be a world with maximal harm. One could imagine guardrails built into reality—limits that preserve agency while preventing extreme atrocities.

Christians sometimes respond by expanding the picture: freedom may include not only human freedom but a creation granted its own integrity—an ordered world with stable patterns that make meaningful life possible, even though those same patterns sometimes yield tragedy. A world where fire reliably warms can also burn; tectonic plates sustain life yet can quake. Still, this too raises questions. Why create a world where the same stability that enables flourishing also permits devastation? We can sketch possible reasons, but we cannot prove them.

The free will defense, then, is not a total answer. It is, however, a significant partial illumination: it helps us see that at least some suffering is not “sent” by God as punishment or instruction but is the genuine cost of a world where love can be real and evil can be named as evil.

### III. Soul-making and the possibility of deepened humanity

A second response, often called the “soul-making” theodicy (associated with Irenaeus and later John Hick), suggests that some suffering functions as a context for the formation of mature character. Certain virtues—courage, patience, compassion, forgiveness, hope—are not downloadable into a creature like software. They must be forged, and forging typically involves hardship. On this view, God’s goal is not merely to create beings in a finished state but to bring persons to maturity through a journey.

Scripture contains hints of this pattern, though it does not flatten suffering into mere self-improvement. Paul can speak of suffering producing endurance, character, and hope (Romans 5), and James can speak of trials producing steadfastness (James 1). These are not commands to enjoy pain; they are testimonies that God can work in and through hardship without being the author of evil. The Bible is realistic that courage grows in danger, that compassion grows when we draw near to the afflicted, and that certain forms of wisdom are learned only in the valley.

This framework can be pastorally helpful when it validates the possibility that suffering might not be wasted. Many people can testify that they emerged from grief with a deeper tenderness, a clarified sense of what matters, or a capacity to accompany others in pain. The Christian tradition also speaks of saints whose faith was refined under pressure, not because pain is good, but because God is able to meet people in it.

But here again, the limits are crucial. Soul-making can easily become cruel if it is used to justify another person’s suffering: “This is happening to build your character.” Some suffering does not seem “formative” so much as deformative—trauma that fractures trust, violence that destroys, chronic pain that erodes personality. And what about suffering that ends in death before any visible growth occurs? What about infants, or those with severe cognitive disabilities, or victims whose lives are cut short? If suffering is for “development,” it can seem like an unacceptable means, as though God were using people as instruments for a project.

The best versions of soul-making theology avoid treating suffering as inherently good or intrinsically intended. Instead, they emphasize God’s redemptive capacity: not that God needs suffering to form virtue, but that in a broken world God is able to bring depth even from what should not have happened. This is closer to the biblical pattern, where God does not call evil good, yet repeatedly brings good from evil—most dramatically in the crucifixion.

Still, “redemption” is not the same as “explanation.” To say God can bring growth out of suffering is not to say we can always see why a particular suffering was permitted. That gap must be faced honestly, not papered over.

### IV. Protest, lament, and the dignity of unanswered questions

A third approach, sometimes called “protest theodicy,” does not try to justify God’s ways so much as to insist that the faithful are permitted—indeed sometimes obligated—to protest evil in God’s presence. The heart of this view is that lament is not unbelief; it is a form of covenant relationship. If God is truly good, then we can appeal to God’s own character against the world’s horrors. We can say, with the psalmists, “This is not how it should be,” and direct that cry toward the One we believe made the world for more than this.

Scripture validates this posture. Abraham argues for justice over Sodom; Moses pleads for mercy after Israel’s sin; the prophets accuse Israel (and by implication, the world) of betraying God’s intent for the vulnerable. Even Jesus takes the words of Psalm 22 on his lips: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The Gospels do not present that cry as a failure of faith but as the faithful Son entering fully into the abyss of human desolation.

Protest theology is pastorally vital because it gives sufferers permission to tell the truth without being scolded into silence. It also guards against a dangerous temptation: defending God in a way that harms the wounded. Sometimes the most “pious” thing to do is to refuse premature closure, to sit in the ash heap with Job rather than becoming one more voice explaining his pain.

Yet protest alone cannot be the whole story. If lament is all we have, we are left with a God who hears complaints but offers no hope. Biblical lament, however, often moves—sometimes slowly, sometimes not at all in a given psalm—toward a stubborn clinging to God’s goodness. It is precisely because God is believed to be good that protest has meaning. Lament is the language of people who refuse to let go of God, even when God feels absent.

### V. The cross: not an explanation, but an unveiling

At the center of Christianity is not a philosophical argument but an event: the crucifixion of Jesus. If we ask what Christianity most decisively says about suffering, it is not that God stands at a safe distance offering reasons. It is that God enters into suffering.

The New Testament does not treat the cross as an unfortunate detour. It is portrayed as the place where God’s love is most fully revealed. Jesus is not simply a martyr showing courage; he is Emmanuel—God with us—bearing betrayal, injustice, humiliation, physical agony, and the apparent silence of heaven. The cross does not answer every “why,” but it changes the question of “where is God?” In Christian faith, God is found not only in the heights of triumph but in the depths of abandonment.

This matters because one of the most corrosive dimensions of suffering is loneliness: the sense that one is unseen, unheard, or discarded by the universe. The cross does not remove pain, but it denies that God is indifferent. It suggests that God’s goodness is not the goodness of a distant manager optimizing outcomes, but the goodness of a Father who, in the Son and by the Spirit, takes suffering into God’s own life and overcomes it from within.

The resurrection then functions as God’s “yes” to Jesus and God’s “no” to death—not a denial of suffering but a promise that suffering will not have the final word. Paul’s language in Romans 8 is not of easy victory but of groaning, waiting, and hope: creation is subjected to futility, yet it is destined for liberation; believers groan, yet the Spirit intercedes with “groanings too deep for words.” Hope here is not optimism; it is trust that God’s future is real even when the present is brutal.

Still, we must be careful. The cross is not a neat solution that makes atrocities acceptable. It does not imply that every tragedy is secretly good because God can redeem. Rather, it reveals that God’s response to evil is not merely to permit it for a time but to judge it, absorb it, and ultimately defeat it. The cross dignifies sufferers: the crucified Christ stands in solidarity with victims, not with victors.

### VI. The limits of understanding—and the responsibility of love

To acknowledge limits is not to evade. It is to be truthful about the size of the question. The book of Job does not end with a tidy rationale for each loss; it ends with encounter, humility, and a kind of restored life that does not erase the scars. Likewise, Christians should be wary of claiming to see the whole tapestry from a single thread. Some suffering may have discernible causes; much will not. Some goods may arise from pain; many pains remain simply grievous.

Yet the admission of mystery must not become a way to protect ourselves from compassion. When people suffer, the immediate Christian calling is not to explain but to love: to feed, visit, protect, advocate, mourn, and pray. Scripture repeatedly ties faithfulness to practical mercy. Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan does not end with the victim learning a lesson; it ends with someone binding wounds and paying costs. Whatever intellectual account one adopts, it should never make us less responsive to suffering in front of us.

Christianity ultimately holds together two truths that are hard to keep in the same hands: God is good, and the world is genuinely horrific at times. The Bible does not force a choice between them. It teaches us to protest evil, to resist it, to confess when we cause it, to endure when we cannot escape it, and to hope—often with tears—that God’s goodness is not a theory but a reality that has stepped into history and will one day set things right.

For some, that hope will still feel fragile. Faith does not eliminate the scream of “why?” It gives the scream an адресsee. It dares to say that the universe is not morally blank, that our outrage at suffering is not merely chemical disappointment but a signpost to a deeper standard of goodness. It trusts, without pretending to see everything, that God is not the enemy of the suffering but its ultimate healer and judge.

In the end, the Christian response to suffering is not a single argument but a posture: honest lament, responsible freedom, costly compassion, and a hope anchored in the crucified and risen Christ. It is measured enough to admit what we do not know, and tender enough to sit with those who hurt. If God is good, then suffering is not “normal,” even if it is common. It is an intruder. And the Christian gospel insists that God has not made peace with that intruder—that God has entered the battlefield, and that the story is not finished.

It rises in hospital waiting rooms and at gravesides; it appears in the aftermath of betrayal, abuse, famine, war, and quiet depression. For many, it is less a puzzle to be solved than a wound that will not close: If God is good, and God is powerful, why is the world like this? And what does it mean to trust such a God?

Any honest exploration must begin by granting the force of the problem. The biblical writers themselves do not treat suffering as an illusion or a trivial inconvenience. They describe creation as a place that “groans” (Romans 8), where the righteous are sometimes crushed and the wicked sometimes flourish (Psalm 73), where prayers feel unanswered (Psalm 13), and where even the faithful can be bewildered by divine silence (Job 30). The problem of suffering is not only that pain exists, but that its distribution often seems random, its intensity excessive, and its occurrence morally scandalous.

Philosophers sometimes frame the issue as a logical tension: if God is all-good, God would want to eliminate evil; if God is all-powerful, God could; yet evil persists—so is God not good, not powerful, or not real? Even if one concedes that the strict “logical problem” may not be airtight (perhaps God could have reasons beyond our grasp), the “evidential problem” remains: the sheer quantity and kinds of suffering—especially apparently pointless suffering—make God’s goodness feel improbable. A child dies slowly of cancer. A community is wiped out by an earthquake. An animal is torn apart in the wild. A person is violated and then lives with the consequences for decades. In such cases, it is not enough to say, “God can bring good out of it.” The question presses harder: Why allow it at all, especially when the victims did not choose it?

Christian faith cannot meet this challenge by minimizing pain, blaming sufferers, or offering neat answers that fit on a greeting card. Many religious explanations fail precisely because they protect a tidy picture of God at the expense of truth and compassion. The Bible resists that impulse. It contains fierce protests and prayers that sound, at times, like accusations. It gives us saints who argue with God, and it does not rush to silence them.

### I. The Bible’s refusal to sanitize suffering

Consider Job—not as a morality tale with an easy lesson, but as a sustained confrontation with undeserved suffering. Job is introduced as righteous, and his calamities are not portrayed as punishment. The most chilling aspect of the book is not simply Job’s losses but the inadequacy of the explanations offered by his friends. They defend a world in which suffering reliably corresponds to personal sin, because such a world feels morally intelligible: God rewards the good and punishes the bad. Job rejects that framework, not because he denies human sinfulness in general, but because it fails to tell the truth about his situation. The book refuses simplistic equations: righteous people can suffer terribly, and their suffering is not always traceable to a specific fault.

At the end, when God speaks from the whirlwind, the “answer” is not a step-by-step justification of every sorrow. God confronts Job with the vastness and wildness of creation—realities that exceed Job’s capacity to manage or fully comprehend. This is not a divine shrug, nor is it a rebuke of lament itself. In fact, God says Job has spoken rightly in comparison with the friends, who offered polished theology but lacked truth and tenderness. The message is subtle: God does not condemn honest protest; God condemns confident misrepresentation.

The Psalms likewise refuse to hurry past grief. They give language to bewilderment (“How long, O Lord?”), to anger (“Why do you hide your face?”), and to exhausted trust that hangs on by its fingernails. Lament is not faith’s opposite; it is one form faith takes when the world is unbearable.

Then, in the Gospels, suffering is neither denied nor romantically glorified. Jesus heals the sick and feeds the hungry, treating suffering as an enemy to be resisted, not a “gift” to be cherished. Yet he also rejects easy causal attributions. When asked about a man born blind—who sinned, this man or his parents?—Jesus refuses the premise that his disability is a moral scorecard (John 9). This scriptural honesty sets the tone: Christians are not invited to become experts at explaining suffering from a safe distance. We are invited to tell the truth about it before God, and to seek a way of faithfulness that does not require denying the darkness.

In this spirit of truthful engagement, various theological traditions have proposed ways of *thinking with* the problem—not of solving it. Some of these are **theodicies** proper: attempts (always partial, always contested) to justify God’s ways in the face of evil. Others are better described as **theological responses**: postures, practices, and convictions that shape how believers live, pray, and love amid suffering even when justification remains incomplete. We begin with two classic justificatory attempts, and then turn to responses that refuse to let explanation become the price of faithfulness.

### II. Free will and the gravity of love

One well-known response is the free will defense: much suffering is the result of human choices, and a world with genuine freedom is a world where evil is possible. Love, on this account, cannot be coerced. If God aims not merely for creatures who behave correctly but for persons capable of real relationship—trust, self-giving, courage, fidelity—then God must allow room for refusal. The same human capacity that makes compassion possible also makes cruelty possible.

This response has moral and pastoral resonance because it takes evil seriously. It refuses to treat atrocities as mere “parts of a plan,” and it recognizes the dignity of human agency. Scripture consistently depicts human beings as responsible actors whose decisions matter. The biblical story is filled with choices that harm and choices that heal, and God’s commands assume that obedience and disobedience are meaningful. The prophets denounce exploitation precisely because it could have been otherwise. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem not as a scripted inevitability but as a tragic refusal: “How often would I have gathered your children… and you were not willing” (Matthew 23:37). That grief suggests not a God delighted by inevitable outcomes, but a God who honors human agency enough to be rejected—and who names that rejection as genuinely tragic.

The free will framework also clarifies why some suffering feels morally direct: betrayal wounds because trust was real; oppression is evil because humans possess real power over one another. If we were automatons, “sin” would be a category mistake, and moral growth would be meaningless. In that sense, freedom is not a small add-on to the world; it is part of what makes humans capable of love—and thus capable of doing real harm.

Yet this approach does not solve everything. First, not all suffering is a direct consequence of human wrongdoing. Natural disasters, genetic diseases, and the predation and decay woven into the biological world are harder to attribute to free choices. Second, even when suffering is caused by human evil, it can still seem disproportionate. Why should one person’s freedom be allowed to devastate another’s life? One might ask why a good God did not create a world with such “guardrails”—limits that preserve genuine agency while constraining the capacity for extreme, irreversible harm.

Christians sometimes respond by widening the picture: perhaps freedom includes not only human freedom but a creation granted its own integrity—an ordered world with stable patterns that make meaningful life possible, even though those same patterns sometimes yield tragedy. A world where fire reliably warms can also burn; tectonic plates sustain life yet can quake. A world with consistent natural laws may be a precondition for rational creatures to act responsibly at all. Still, this too raises questions. Why create a world where the same stability that enables flourishing also permits devastation? We can sketch possible reasons, but we cannot prove them.

They emphasize God’s redemptive capacity: not that God needs suffering to form virtue, but that in a broken world God is able to bring depth even from what should not have happened. We can say, with the psalmists, “This is not how it should be,” and direct that cry toward the One we believe made the world for more than this.

And even Jesus takes the words of Psalm 22 on his lips: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The Gospels do not present that cry as a failure of faith but as the faithful Son entering fully into the abyss of human desolation.

At the center of Christianity is not a philosophical argument but an event: the crucifixion of Jesus. If we ask what Christianity most decisively says about suffering, it is not that God stands at a safe distance offering reasons. It is that God enters into suffering.

Christianity ultimately holds together two truths that are hard to keep in the same hands: God is good, and the world is genuinely horrific at times. The Bible does not force a choice between them. It dares to say that the universe is not morally blank, that our outrage at suffering is not merely chemical disappointment but a signpost to a deeper standard of goodness. It trusts, without pretending to see everything, that God is not the enemy of the suffering but its ultimate healer and judge.

It is measured enough to admit what we do not know, and tender enough to sit with those who hurt. If God is good, then suffering is not “normal,” even if it is common. It is an intruder. Here, too, we must be careful. The cross is not a neat solution that makes atrocities acceptable. It does not imply that every tragedy is secretly good because God can redeem. Rather, it reveals that God’s response to evil is not merely to permit it for a time but to judge it, absorb it, and ultimately defeat it. The cross dignifies sufferers: the crucified Christ stands in solidarity with victims, not with victors.

### VI. The limits of understanding—and the responsibility of love

To acknowledge limits is not to evade. It is to be truthful about the size of the question. The book of Job does not end with a tidy rationale for each loss; it ends with encounter, humility, and a kind of restored life that does not erase the scars. Some goods may arise from pain; many pains remain simply grievous.

It teaches us to protest evil, to resist it, to confess when we cause it, to endure when we cannot escape it, and to hope—often with tears—that God’s goodness is not a theory but a reality that has stepped into history and will one day set things right.

For some, that hope will still feel fragile. Faith does not eliminate the scream of “why?” It gives the scream an addressee. It dares to say that the universe is not morally blank, that our outrage at suffering is not merely chemical disappointment but a signpost to a deeper standard of goodness. It trusts, without pretending to see everything, that God is not the enemy of the suffering but its ultimate healer and judge.

In the end, the Christian response to suffering is not a single argument but a posture: honest lament, responsible freedom, costly compassion, and a hope anchored in the crucified and risen Christ. It is measured enough to admit what we do not know, and tender enough to sit with those who hurt. If God is good, then suffering is not “normal,” even if it is common. It is an intruder. And the Christian gospel insists that God has not made peace with that intruder. Instead, God has entered the battlefield, taking the full weight of suffering upon the cross, and rising in resurrection as the pledge that the story is not finished—and that the final word belongs not to the scream of “why,” but to the promise of new creation.

When the earth opened beneath the Philippine village of Guinsaugon in 2006, swallowing an elementary school full of children while their parents watched from higher ground, the cameras lingered on a mother who kept brushing mud from her face long after the mud had dried.  Her gesture said what most observers felt but could not yet voice: something here is irreconcilably wrong.  Theologians call it the problem of evil; she called it the absence of her little boy.  Both statements point to the same wound: if the One who made galaxies is both good and able, why does the mud still take children?

1.  Stating the wound honestly  
The objection is not that pain exists—anyone can imagine a world with paper cuts and even death at ninety.  The scandal is the quantity, texture, and distribution of agony: tsunamis that erase generations, toddlers with bone cancer, pervasive psychological cruelty that leaves no external scar yet hollows a person for decades.  The data are cumulative and, crucially, apparently gratuitous.  A single case of “horrendous evil” (Marilyn Adams’s phrase) would suffice; the world serves up millions.  The logical version of the problem— “God and evil are contradictory” —has been trimmed back by analytic philosophers, but the evidential or “probabilistic” version survives every seminar: given the scope of misery, God’s existence seems unlikely, perhaps very unlikely.  No straw man is required; the argument is articulated daily in hospice wards, refugee camps, and in the quiet apostasy of a teenager who watches her father metastasise.  Any response that will not stand in that mud with that mother is, by definition, no response at all.

2.  The freedom defence: love and the shadow it casts  
Augustine located evil’s origin in the will of rational creatures; Plantinga sharpened the claim into a “defence” rather than a theodicy: it is possible that a world containing significantly free persons who can choose the good is more valuable than a world of affectionate automata, even if that freedom is systematically abused.  The gift of genuine love entails the possibility of genuine rape, genuine gas chambers.  God’s omnipotence, on this view, is not the power to do nonsense—such as “create a free creature who cannot choose”—but the power to bring good out of decisions that are not His.

The intuition is strong.  We praise the parent who, at great risk, allows an adolescent to make catastrophic choices so that the young adult who emerges is morally her own.  Yet three edges remain sharp.  First, the quantity of “natural” evil—tectonic plates, parasites, supernovae—seems unrelated to anyone’s freedom.  Second, even when suffering is humanly authored, the victims are often those least able to bear it.  The freedom that produced Dachau did not respect the autonomy of the toddlers tossed into fire.  Third, Scripture itself suggests that God sometimes intervenes to restrain freedom (Gen 20:6; 2 Kings 19:35), raising the question why such restraint is selective.  The defence is therefore best taken as a partial explanation, a way of saying that love’s grammar may require a risky stage.  It does not by itself balance the ledger.

3.  Soul-making and the furnace of identity  
Irenaeus pictured humanity as created immature, destined for a “second blessing” that requires the resistance of a hostile environment.  John Hick modernised the motif: pain is the chisel that sculpts soul.  Personality is forged, the argument runs, only where there is real pressure, real failure, real forgiveness.  A world without tears would produce moral infants.  The theodicy gains traction when we notice how shallow untested virtue often is, and how depth of character correlates—though not universally—with endured adversity.  The Epistle of James seems to endorse the scheme: “Consider it pure joy…when you face trials…so that you may be mature and complete” (1:2-4).  The same writer, however, immediately commands the church to relieve, not romanticise, the widows’ distress (1:27), reminding us that the furnace is judged by what it makes, not by the heat for its own sake.

Critics reply that many lives are broken, not built, by the furnace.  Severe abuse can arrest moral growth altogether; some children drown, literally, before they acquire the neural hardware for virtue.  Soul-making must therefore appeal to a longer narrative—perhaps an afterlife in which the半成品 (half-finished) self is completed.  Without that post-mortem chapter the theory feels like a teacher who burns the lesson plan along with the student.  Yet the intuition persists: when we meet someone whose compassion has the grain of weathered oak, we usually discover a history of weather.  The question is whether the finished sculpture justifies the shavings, especially the shavings that end up in graves.

4.  The cross as God’s answer, not God’s explanation  
Christianity’s most radical move is not to defend God by theory but to insist that God has entered the contradiction.  In the crucified Jew from Nazareth, the tradition claims, the One who authorises galaxies authorises vulnerability: spittled, stripped, god-forsaken.  Jürgen Moltmann argues that here the Deity does not merely sympathise from altitude; the Son experiences the godforsakenness that human beings inflict and endure.  Thus the cross is not a theodicy in the sense of an explanatory account; it is, rather, a theophany—God’s self-disclosure in the place where explanations run out.  The same night that cameras filmed the mud-soaked mother, a relief worker told me he could still pray because “the silhouette of the crucified hangs between me and every scream.”  The image does not solve the logical puzzle, but it refuses to let the puzzle be abstract.

Scripture underwrites the strangeness.  The Psalms accuse God to His face—“You have put me in the lowest pit, in the darkest depths” (Ps 88:6)—yet do not thereby sever covenant.  Lamentations structures entire chapters around alphabetic acrostics of grief, as if to say: every letter we possess is borrowed to stammer pain.  Yet the New Testament dares to place the resurrection on the far side of the accusation, not as cancellation but as vindication of the God who bleeds.  Rowan Williams notes that the risen Jesus still carries scars; they are not erased but transfigured.  The promise, then, is not that suffering makes sense, but that sense-making is not the final human need.  The final need is presence, and presence is offered even—especially—where sense collapses.

5.  The limits of sight and the ethics of waiting  
Any intellectually honest discussion must concede massive epistemic limitation.  I do not know why this child and not that one, why 8.0 on the Richter scale at 2 a.m.  I also do not know why the same physical laws that produce plate tectonics also produce stable continents on which love can evolve.  The concession, however, must never be deployed as a conversational stop sign.  “God’s ways are mysterious” is true; uttered too quickly it becomes a sanctified shrug, a refusal to sit Shiva with the universe.  The proper posture is the one modelled by Job: a willingness to live inside the questions while refusing to relinquish either the data of pain or the data of hope.  After forty chapters of dialogue the Whirlwind does not answer Job’s forensic questions; it relocates his imagination within a cosmos too large to be surveyed, yet not indifferent to the sparrow’s fall.

Meanwhile the church is commanded to act as an embodied protest against the structure it cannot yet explain.  Every cup of cold water, every antibiotic, every visit to a dementia ward is a small but real eschatological sign: the story does not end in the mud.  Thus the limits of understanding do not paralyse; they delegate.  If I cannot calculate the calculus of global pain, I can at least reduce the numerator in my neighbour’s equation.  The ethics of waiting—lament, solidarity, practical mercy—becomes the corollary of intellectual humility.

6.  Pastoral postscript: what can be said at the grave  
I once stood at the graveside of a seventeen-year-old who had hung himself in the family garage.  The father, a philosopher, asked me afterward whether any argument could “make this rational.”  I heard myself say something I had not planned: “No argument can, but perhaps a story can carry it.”  I told him the story of Joseph, whose brothers’ malice became the hidden road to survival for thousands (Gen 50:20).  The narrative does not glorify the brothers’ sin; it insists that God’s creativity is wider than human perversity without thereby justifying the perversity.  The father wept, not because the tale solved the logic but because it gave him a place to stand while the logic remained unsolved.  That, I think, is the most any theology can offer this side of resurrection: not a ledger that balances but a location—within the ongoing, costly, scarred life of God—where the ledger can be held, questioned, and ultimately re-negotiated in the presence of the One who, Christians dare to say, will not let the mud have the final word.

In the end the problem of suffering is not an intellectual sudoku to be cracked but a wound in the body of the world, and therefore in the body of God.  We are invited to become, in Paul’s phrase, “fellow workers with God” in the slow, often invisible knitting of that body.  Some days the only credible apologetic is a shared silence and a bowl of soup.  On other days we may glimpse, in the face of a forgiven enemy or a cancer patient who still blesses, fragments of a larger redemptive plot.  Neither the silence nor the glimpse erases the scream, yet neither does the scream erase the glimpse.  The two are held in tensive, unfinished coexistence—what Karl Barth called “the time between the times.”  To live honestly inside that tension, refusing premature closure either by despair or by explanation, is perhaps the only “answer” that remains credible while the mud is still wet.

1.  Naming the wound without euphemism  
The evidential problem can be stated in a single sentence: the scale, intensity, and apparent randomness of pain make the existence of an all-powerful, perfectly good God seem unlikely.  It is not the fact of death that offends; it is the density of agony—tsunamis that vacuum whole kindergarten classes, parasites that blind infants, psychological cruelty that hollows a person for decades while leaving the skin unmarked.  One case of what Marilyn Adams calls “horrendous evil” would suffice; the world files them by the million.  Philosophers call this the “probabilistic” version of the problem: given the data, God’s existence is not logically impossible, but it is—so the argument runs—improbable.  No straw man is required; the objection is whispered every night in hospice wards and shouted outside abortion-clinic bombings.  Any response that cannot be spoken aloud in those rooms is, by definition, no response at all.

2.  Freedom and the shadow it casts  
Augustine located evil’s origin in the will of rational creatures; Alvin Plantinga formalised the intuition into a “defence” rather than a full theodicy.  The claim is that a world containing significantly free persons who can choose the good is more valuable than a world of affectionate automata, even if that freedom is routinely weaponised.  The gas chamber, on this view, is the price of genuine love.

Second, even when evil is humanly authored, the victims are often those least able to bear it: the freedom that produced Dachau did not respect the autonomy of the toddlers tossed into fire.  Third, Scripture itself shows God sometimes restraining freedom—Genesis 20:6 (“I kept you from sinning against me”), 2 Kings 19:35 (an angel decimates an army overnight)—which raises the obvious question why such restraint is selective. Irenaeus pictured humanity as created immature, destined for a second blessing that needs the resistance of a hostile environment.  John Hick updated the motif: pain is the chisel that sculpts soul.  The intuition is recognizable—virtue untested often is virtue unformed—James 1:2-4 sounds as if it agrees: “Consider it pure joy…when you face trials…so that you may be mature and complete.”  Yet the same writer immediately commands the church to relieve, not romanticise, the widows’ distress (1:27), reminding us that the furnace is judged by what it makes, not by the heat for its own sake.

A parent stands beside a hospital bed; a refugee watches the sea swallow her child; a teenager wakes to the smell of smoke and the sound of sirens inside his own skull. The cry that rises is not “Why does this happen?” but “Why does this happen to me?”—a cry so intimate that any answer sounds like betrayal.  

Christian faith announces, Sunday after Sunday, that God is good, that “his mercy endures forever,” that in Jesus “all things hold together.” Then comes the Monday news, and the creed collides with the carnage. The problem is not abstract: a syllogism does not bleed. Yet the intellectual shape of the clash is sharp enough to cut faith to the bone:

1. God is omnipotent.  
2. God is perfectly good.  
3. Evil and suffering exist.  

The three cannot simultaneously be true; at least one must give. Honest doubters say, “Then either God is weak, or God is wicked, or God is absent.” Honest believers feel the same sting. Any apologetics that begins by softening the third premise—“Well, evil is only apparent”—has already failed, because it has not sat in the room with the mother who must choose which arm of her toddler gets the chemotherapy port.  

I. The protest and the silence  

Job is the patron saint of this territory. His friends offer tidy theodicies; he offers raw lawsuit. “Let the Almighty answer me!” (Job 31:35). And when the Voice does come, it is not the expected brief for the defense but a tour of cosmos and behemoth, a whirlwind of wonder that never mentions the dead children whose absence started the whole debate. The book’s final verdict, startlingly, is not that Job finally understands, but that God “approved” the honest rage and disapproved the religious smoothing-over. Scripture itself, then, canonizes protest. Silence in the face of suffering is not always pious; sometimes it is diabolic.  

Yet the same Bible dares to speak of a “good” God. The tension is not resolved by one chapter’s turning of the page; it is stretched across the whole story. Any Christian response must therefore hold two convictions in dialectical embrace: the moral rightness of lament and the metaphysical claim that, in the end, love and not chaos sits on the throne.  

II. The freedom defense: love and the possibility of hell  

One classical exit from the trilemma is the Free-Will Defense, refined by Augustine, polished by C. S. Lewis, formalized by Alvin Plantinga. Moral evil—Auschwitz, trafficking, the cruelties of small bullies—springs from the will of creatures. To create beings capable of loving, God must create beings capable of fingering the trigger. A world of robots, always choosing the right, might be safe, but it would be loveless; and loveless goodness is not the summum bonum.  

The argument has weight. Most parents intuit it: you do not digitally spy on your adolescent every minute, not because you do not care but because love that cannot say no is not love. The cross itself, in one reading, is the dramatic culmination of this risk: the Son hands himself over to human verdict, and the human verdict is “Crucify.” God endures the cost of the very freedom he gave.  

Yet the defense limps when confronted with natural evil—tsunamis, parasites, dementia. Earthquakes do not choose; they simply shake. One can reply that fallen human will affects the whole cosmos (“the whole creation groans,” Romans 8), but this stretches the causal chain into speculation and does little for the parent whose three-year-old is devoured by a brain-eating amoeba. The free-will defense answers some of the problem; it does not answer all of it.  

III. The soul-making wager: crucibles and companionship  

John Keats called the world “the vale of soul-making.” Irenaeus, not knowing Keats, said the same: humans are created immature, in the image, destined by grace toward the likeness. Suffering, in this scheme, is not the intrusion but the gymnasium. Muscles grow by resistance; compassion grows by the fractures that let the heart expand.  

Scriptural imagination is rich here. Joseph’s bones carry the memory of a pit and a prison; the grain dreams that save Egypt could come no other way. Jesus himself “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), a sentence so strange it can only mean that the eternal Son, in time, deepened his human capacity to trust through the very process of pain. The church is a body whose members, in Paul’s astounding phrase, “fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ” (Colossians 1:24). Lacking—not in atonement, but perhaps in manifestation: the Messiah’s suffering continues in mine, so that the world can see what redemption looks like in a voice like mine.  

Yet the soul-making theodicy, too, has its critics. Dostoevsky’s Ivan will not accept any future harmony built on the tears of one tortured child. Nor can we quantify the dosage: how much chemotherapy of the spirit is enough? Some lives appear to be only crucible, never gold. To tell the bereaved mother that her child’s death is “character-building” is pastoral malpractice unless one is willing to be the first character built by it.  

IV. The cross as refusal of anesthesia  

Christianity’s most audacious claim is not that it explains suffering but that God enters it. The crucified man is not a symbol appended to deity; he is the Eternal himself, “slain from the foundation of the world” (Revelation 13:8). Every other theodicy risks what Simone Weil called “the distance of the dentist”: God observes the drill, patient endures it. At Golgotha the dentist lies in the chair.  

This is not an answer in the sense of a syllogism; it is an answer in the sense of a presence. The cross does not tell us why the world hurts; it shows us who is there when it does. The resurrection then adds the wild, impertinent claim that the story does not end in the emergency room. But the empty tomb is only credible if the reader has not skipped chapter 15 of Luke; the hands still carry the holes. Glory is not amnesia.  

Thus the Christian vision refuses both the Stoic’s “Grin and bear it” and the secular “Fix it or forget it.” Instead it offers the more difficult path of lament and loyalty: I will accuse the night, and I will stay with the Maker of the morning. The psalms rehearse this grammar: seventy percent of them are complaint, yet every one is prayed to the God whose “steadfast love” is sung at the end. Faith is not the denial of scream; it is the scream’s direction.  

V. The limits of the ladder  

All our theodicies are attic stairs thrown against infinity. We climb, and the rungs snap. The most honest theological sentence may be Paul’s “Now I know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9), spoken after apostolic visions, thorn-in-the-flesh, and three missionary journeys. “In part” is not a modest preface to future omniscience; it is the permanent condition of creatures. The same chapter insists that love, not knowledge, is what finally remains.  

Yet “I don’t know” is not the same as “There is no answer.” To acknowledge the ocean’s depth is not to assert that no bottom exists; it is to admit that my rope is short. The limitation is in me, not necessarily in the reality. Humility is not a cop-out unless it becomes a cul-de-sac. The church is commanded to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15) before it is authorized to speak anything else.  

VI. Pastoral postures: the first five minutes  

In hospital rooms I have learned that the first five minutes belong to silence, eye contact, and, if permitted, touch. Anything that starts with “God must have a reason…” violates the protocol. Later, if trust grows, larger sentences can be risked. Even then, the best service theology offers is to keep the sufferer from the twin abysses of despair and denial.  

Communion, not explanation, is the primary gift the church carries. When the woman hemorrhaging for twelve years touches the hem of Jesus’ robe, he does not give a lecture on immunology; he says, “Daughter.” Identity precedes insight. Only after she is re-named does he pronounce peace. Every theodicy must pass through that narrative sieve: does it help a wounded person hear “Daughter,” “Son,” “Beloved”? If not, it is straw.  

VII. The long look  

Still, the intellectual question remains, because humans are destined to think as well as to weep. Here the eschatological horizon is indispensable. The New Testament’s final images are not of immortal souls floating upward but of a new earth, no sea, no night, no temple because the whole city is temple. Whatever that means, it means at least that history matters, that every act of love and every bullet alike are notes in a score that will be played again, transposed, judged, healed. God pledges to “wipe away every tear,” not to explain every tear. The promise is not retrospective justification but prospective restoration: the tear becomes part of the music, not deleted but transformed.  

That future is not yet. Faith lives, therefore, in the interval called Advent: the King has come, the King is coming, the kingdom is inaugurated yet contested. Suffering is the birth pang, Paul says, but birth pangs still hurt like death. To live in the overlap is to accept that the answer to the problem of evil is a story, not a sound bite, and we are on page 873 of a 1,200-page novel.  

VIII. Conclusion: the risk of trust  

The problem of evil is not finally a puzzle to solve but a crisis to survive. It asks of the believer not a theorem but a person: will you keep company with the hidden God when every signal says absence? The risk is enormous; the alternative is a cynicism that protects the heart by freezing it.  

Christianity gambles on the character of this God, attested by a crucified Jew whose followers insist they met him breakfasting on a beach three days after state terror did its worst. If that testimony is true, then the goodness of God is not the goodness of a spectator but of a co-sufferer who invites me into an unfinished drama. My role is to lament the evil, to fight the evil, and—impossibly—to trust that the Author who entered the play will write the final chapter in a mode I cannot now imagine.  

That trust is not a leap across an intellectual chasm; it is more like staying in the marriage when the scans come back malignant. It is learned slowly, in the dark, with no guarantee that my particular nightmare will end happily this side of death. The only immediate guarantee is the presence of the One whose own story passed through tomb and garden, who therefore knows the way and walks it with me.  

The scream remains. Sometimes it is my scream. Yet in the echo I have heard, not an explanation, but a name. The name does not solve the problem; it carries it, with me, toward the day when the problem and I shall both be transformed. Until then, honesty and hope are braided together, a cord not easily broken, strong enough to keep a fractured heart from bleeding out, fragile enough to keep it tender.

The scream is always the same.  
A parent stands beside a hospital bed; a refugee watches the sea swallow her child; a teenager wakes to the smell of smoke and the sound of sirens inside his own skull. The cry that rises is not “Why does this happen?” but “Why does this happen to me?”—a cry so intimate that any answer sounds like betrayal.  

Christian faith announces, Sunday after Sunday, that God is good, that “his mercy endures forever,” that in Jesus “all things hold together.” Then comes the Monday news, and the creed collides with the carnage. The problem is not abstract: a syllogism does not bleed. Yet the intellectual shape of the clash is sharp enough to cut faith to the bone:

1. God is omnipotent.  
2. God is perfectly good.  
3. Evil and suffering exist.  

The three cannot simultaneously be true; at least one must give. Honest doubters say, “Then either God is weak, or God is wicked, or God is absent.” Honest believers feel the same sting. Any apologetics that begins by softening the third premise—“Well, evil is only apparent”—has already failed, because it has not sat in the room with the mother who must choose which arm of her toddler gets the chemotherapy port.  

I. The protest and the silence  

Job is the patron saint of this territory. His friends offer tidy theodicies; he offers raw lawsuit. “Let the Almighty answer me!” (Job 31:35). And when the Voice does come, it is not the expected brief for the defense but a tour of cosmos and behemoth, a whirlwind of wonder that never mentions the dead children whose absence started the whole debate. The book’s final verdict, startlingly, is not that Job finally understands, but that God “approved” the honest rage and disapproved the religious smoothing-over. Scripture itself, then, canonizes protest. Silence in the face of suffering is not always pious; sometimes it is diabolic.  

Yet the same Bible dares to speak of a “good” God. The tension is not resolved by one chapter’s turning of the page; it is stretched across the whole story. Any Christian response must therefore hold two convictions in dialectical embrace: the moral rightness of lament and the metaphysical claim that, in the end, love and not chaos sits on the throne.  

II. The freedom defense: love and the possibility of hell  

One classical exit from the trilemma is the Free-Will Defense, refined by Augustine, polished by C. S. Lewis, formalized by Alvin Plantinga. Moral evil—Auschwitz, trafficking, the cruelties of small bullies—springs from the will of creatures. To create beings capable of loving, God must create beings capable of fingering the trigger. A world of robots, always choosing the right, might be safe, but it would be loveless; and loveless goodness is not the summum bonum.  

The argument has weight. Most parents intuit it: you do not digitally spy on your adolescent every minute, not because you do not care but because love that cannot say no is not love. The cross itself, in one reading, is the dramatic culmination of this risk: the Son hands himself over to human verdict, and the human verdict is “Crucify.” God endures the cost of the very freedom he gave.  

Yet the defense limps when confronted with natural evil—tsunamis, parasites, dementia. Earthquakes do not choose; they simply shake. One can reply that fallen human will affects the whole cosmos (“the whole creation groans,” Romans 8), or appeal to the traditional idea of an angelic or demonic fall introducing cosmic disorder. Still, these moves stretch the causal chain into speculation and do little for the parent whose three-year-old is devoured by a brain-eating amoeba. The free-will defense answers some of the problem; it does not answer all of it.  

III. The soul-making wager: crucibles and companionship  

John Keats called the world “the vale of soul-making.” Irenaeus, not knowing Keats, said the same: humans are created immature, in the image, destined by grace toward the likeness. Suffering, in this scheme, is not the intrusion but the gymnasium. Muscles grow by resistance; compassion grows by the fractures that let the heart expand.  

Scriptural imagination is rich here. Joseph’s bones carry the memory of a pit and a prison; the grain dreams that save Egypt could come no other way. Jesus himself “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), a sentence so strange it can only mean that the eternal Son, in time, deepened his human capacity to trust through the very process of pain. The church is a body whose members, in Paul’s astounding phrase, “fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ” (Colossians 1:24). Lacking—not in the sufficiency of his atonement, but in the ongoing manifestation of redemptive suffering, so that the world can see what redemption looks like in a voice like mine.  

Yet the soul-making theodicy, too, has its critics. Dostoevsky’s Ivan will not accept any future harmony built on the tears of one tortured child. Nor can we quantify the dosage: how much chemotherapy of the spirit is enough? Some lives appear to be only crucible, never gold. To tell the bereaved mother that her child’s death is “character-building” is pastoral malpractice unless one is willing to be the first character built by it.  

IV. The cross: where explanation collapses and presence begins  

The Free-Will and Soul-Making defenses offer necessary but insufficient frameworks. They attempt to explain the world’s structure, but they cannot bear the weight of its cruelty. Christianity’s most audacious claim is not that it explains suffering but that God enters it.  

The crucified man is not a symbol appended to deity; he is the Eternal himself, “slain from the foundation of the world” (Revelation 13:8). Every other theodicy risks what Simone Weil called “the distance of the dentist”: God observes the drill, patient endures it. At Golgotha the dentist lies in the chair.  

This is not an answer in the sense of a syllogism; it is an answer in the sense of a presence. The cross does not tell us why the world hurts; it shows us who is there when it does. The resurrection then adds the wild, impertinent claim that the story does not end in the emergency room. But the empty tomb is only credible if the reader has not skipped chapter 15 of Luke; the hands still carry the holes. Glory is not amnesia.  

Thus the Christian vision refuses both the Stoic’s “Grin and bear it” and the secular “Fix it or forget it.” Instead it offers the more difficult path of lament and loyalty: I will accuse the night, and I will stay with the Maker of the morning. The psalms rehearse this grammar: seventy percent of them are complaint, yet every one is prayed to the God whose “steadfast love” is sung at the end. Faith is not the denial of scream; it is the scream’s direction.  

V. The limits of the ladder  

All our theodicies are attic stairs thrown against infinity. We climb, and the rungs snap—not because the bottom is necessarily missing, but because our rope is short and our arms tired. The most honest theological sentence may be Paul’s “Now I know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9), spoken after apostolic visions, thorn-in-the-flesh, and three missionary journeys. “In part” is not a modest preface to future omniscience; it is the permanent condition of creatures. The same chapter insists that love, not knowledge, is what finally remains.  

Yet “I don’t know” is not the same as “There is no answer.” To acknowledge the ocean’s depth is not to assert that no bottom exists; it is to admit that my rope is short. Humility is not a cop-out unless it becomes a cul-de-sac. The church is commanded to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15) before it is authorized to speak anything else.  

VI. Pastoral postures: the first five minutes  

In hospital rooms I have learned that the first five minutes belong to silence, eye contact, and, if permitted, touch. Anything that starts with “God must have a reason…” violates the protocol. Later, if trust grows, larger sentences can be risked. Even then, the best service theology offers is to keep the sufferer from the twin abysses of despair and denial.  

Communion, not explanation, is the primary gift the church carries. When the woman hemorrhaging for twelve years touches the hem of Jesus’ robe, he does not give a lecture on immunology; he says, “Daughter.” Identity precedes insight. Only after she is re-named does he pronounce peace. Every theodicy must pass through that narrative sieve: does it help a wounded person hear “Daughter,” “Son,” “Beloved”? If not, it is straw.  

VII. The long look  

Still, the intellectual question remains, because humans are destined to think as well as to weep. Here the eschatological horizon is indispensable. The New Testament’s final images are not of immortal souls floating upward but of a new earth, no sea, no night, no temple because the whole city is temple. Whatever that means, it means at least that history matters, that every act of love and every bullet alike are notes in a score that will be played again, transposed, judged, healed. God pledges to “wipe away every tear,” not to explain every tear. The promise is not retrospective justification but prospective restoration: the tear becomes part of the music, not deleted but transformed.  

That future is not yet. Faith lives, therefore, in the interval called Advent: the King has come, the King is coming, the kingdom is inaugurated yet contested. Suffering is the birth pang, Paul says, but birth pangs still hurt like death. To live in the overlap is to accept that the answer to the problem of evil is a story, not a sound bite, and we are on page 873 of a 1,200-page novel.  

VIII. Conclusion: the risk of trust  

The problem of evil is not finally a puzzle to solve but a crisis to survive. It asks of the believer not a theorem but a person: will you keep company with the hidden God when every signal says absence? The risk is enormous; the alternative is a cynicism that protects the heart by freezing it.  

Christianity gambles on the character of this God, attested by a crucified Jew whose followers insist they met him breakfasting on a beach three days after state terror did its worst. If that testimony is true, then the goodness of God is not the goodness of a spectator but of a co-sufferer who invites me into an unfinished drama. My role is to lament the evil, to fight the evil, and—impossibly—to trust that the Author who entered the play will write the final chapter in a mode I cannot now imagine.  

That trust is not a leap across an intellectual chasm; it is more like staying in the marriage when the scans come back malignant. It is learned slowly, in the dark, with no guarantee that my particular nightmare will end happily this side of death. The only immediate guarantee is the presence of the One whose own story passed through tomb and garden, who therefore knows the way and walks it with me.  

The scream remains. Sometimes it is my scream. Yet in the echo of that scream I have heard, not an explanation, but a name—the name of the One who screamed first, and who carries the sound, with me, toward the day when the problem and I shall both be transformed. Until then, honesty and hope are braided together, a cord not easily broken, strong enough to keep a fractured heart from bleeding out, fragile enough to keep it tender.

Christian faith announces, Sunday after Sunday, that God is good, that “his mercy endures forever,” that in Jesus “all things hold together.” Then comes the Monday news, and the creed collides with the carnage. The problem is not abstract: a syllogism does not bleed. Yet the intellectual shape of the clash is sharp enough to cut faith to the bone:

1. God is omnipotent.  
2. God is perfectly good.  
3. Evil and suffering exist.  

The three cannot simultaneously be true; at least one must give. Honest doubters say, “Then either God is weak, or God is wicked, or God is absent.” Honest believers feel the same sting. Any apologetics that begins by softening the third premise—“Well, evil is only apparent”—has already failed, because it has not sat in the room with the mother who must choose which arm of her toddler gets the chemotherapy port.  

I. The protest and the silence  

Job is the patron saint of this territory. His friends offer tidy theodicies; he offers raw lawsuit. “Let the Almighty answer me!” (Job 31:35). And when the Voice does come, it is not the expected brief for the defense but a tour of cosmos and behemoth, a whirlwind of wonder that never mentions the dead children whose absence started the whole debate. The book’s final verdict, startlingly, is not that Job finally understands, but that God “approved” the honest rage and disapproved the religious smoothing-over. Scripture itself, then, canonizes protest. Silence in the face of suffering is not always pious; sometimes it is diabolic.  

Yet the same Bible dares to speak of a “good” God. The tension is not resolved by one chapter’s turning of the page; it is stretched across the whole story. Any Christian response must therefore hold two convictions in dialectical embrace: the moral rightness of lament and the metaphysical claim that, in the end, love and not chaos sits on the throne.  

II. The freedom defense: love and the possibility of hell  

One classical exit from the trilemma is the Free-Will Defense, refined by Augustine, polished by C. S. Lewis, formalized by Alvin Plantinga. Moral evil—Auschwitz, trafficking, the cruelties of small bullies—springs from the will of creatures. To create beings capable of loving, God must create beings capable of fingering the trigger. A world of robots, always choosing the right, might be safe, but it would be loveless; and loveless goodness is not the summum bonum.  

The argument has weight. Most parents intuit it: you do not digitally spy on your adolescent every minute, not because you do not care but because love that cannot say no is not love. The cross itself, in one reading, is the dramatic culmination of this risk: the Son hands himself over to human verdict, and the human verdict is “Crucify.” God endures the cost of the very freedom he gave.  

Yet the defense limps when confronted by natural evil—tsunamis, parasites, dementia. Earthquakes do not choose; they simply shake. One can reply that fallen human will fractured the entire cosmos (“the whole creation groans,” Romans 8), so that tectonic plates and immune systems now misfire like bent gears. Even if this Augustinian thread is granted, it stretches the causal chain into speculation and does little for the parent whose three-year-old is devoured by a brain-eating amoeba. The free-will defense answers some of the problem; it does not answer all of it.  

III. The soul-making wager: crucibles and companionship  

John Keats called the world “the vale of soul-making.” Irenaeus, not knowing Keats, said the same: humans are created immature, in the image, destined by grace toward the likeness. Suffering, in this scheme, is not the intrusion but the gymnasium. Muscles grow by resistance; compassion grows by the fractures that let the heart expand.

But the empty tomb is only credible if the reader has not skipped chapter 15 of Luke; the hands still carry the holes. Glory is not amnesia.  

Thus the Christian vision refuses both the Stoic’s “Grin and bear it” and the secular “Fix it or forget it.” Instead it offers the more difficult path of lament and loyalty: I will accuse the night, and I will stay with the Maker of the morning. The psalms rehearse this grammar: one third of them are complaint, yet every one is prayed to the God whose “steadfast love” is sung at the end. Faith is not the denial of scream; it is the scream’s direction.  

VII. The limits of the ladder  

All our theodicies are attic stairs thrown against infinity. We climb, and the rungs snap. The most honest theological sentence may be Paul’s “Now I know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9), spoken after apostolic visions, thorn-in-the-flesh, and three missionary journeys. “In part” is not a modest preface to future omniscience; it is the permanent condition of creatures. The same chapter insists that love, not knowledge, is what finally remains.  

Yet “I don’t know” is not the same as “There is no answer.” To acknowledge the ocean’s depth is not to assert that no bottom exists; it is to admit that my rope is short. The limitation is in me, not necessarily in the reality. Humility is not a cop-out unless it becomes a cul-de-sac. The church is commanded to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15) before it is authorized to speak anything else.  

VIII. Pastoral postures: the first five minutes  

In hospital rooms I have learned that the first five minutes belong to silence, eye contact, and, if permitted, touch. Anything that starts with “God must have a reason…” violates the protocol. Later, if trust grows, larger sentences can be risked. Even then, the best service theology offers is to keep the sufferer from the twin abysses of despair and denial.  

Communion, not explanation, is the primary gift the church carries. When the woman hemorrhaging for twelve years touches the hem of Jesus’ robe, he does not give a lecture on immunology; he says, “Daughter.” Identity precedes insight. Only after she is re-named does he pronounce peace. Every theodicy must pass through that narrative sieve: does it help a wounded person hear “Daughter,” “Son,” “Beloved”? If not, it is straw.  

IX. A word to the one who screams now  

*If you are reading this between hospital shifts, or after the funeral director has left, you do not need to finish the essay. Go outside. Yell at the sky. Know that the One who keeps the stars alive has heard worse, and is still listening.*  

X. The long look  

Still, the intellectual question remains, because humans are destined to think as well as to weep. Here the eschatological horizon is indispensable. The New Testament’s final images are not of immortal souls floating upward but of a new earth, no sea, no night, no temple because the whole city is temple. Whatever that means, it means at least that history matters, that every act of love and every bullet alike are notes in a score that will be played again, transposed, judged, healed. God pledges to “wipe away every tear,” not to explain every tear. The promise is not retrospective justification but prospective restoration: the tear becomes part of the music, not deleted but transformed.  

That future is not yet. Faith lives, therefore, in the interval called Advent: the King has come, the King is coming, the kingdom is inaugurated yet contested. Suffering is the birth pang, Paul says, but birth pangs still hurt like death. To live in the overlap is to accept that the answer to the problem of evil is a story, not a sound bite, and we are somewhere around page 859 of a novel whose final chapter is sealed.  

XI. The risk of trust  

The problem of evil is not finally a puzzle to solve but a crisis to survive. It asks of the believer not a theorem but a person: will you keep company with the hidden God when every signal says absence? The risk is enormous; the alternative is a cynicism that protects the heart by freezing it.  

Christianity gambles on the character of this God, attested by a crucified Jew whose followers insist they met him breakfasting on a beach three days after state terror did its worst. If that testimony is true, then the goodness of God is not the goodness of a spectator but of a co-sufferer who invites me into an unfinished drama. My role is to lament the evil, to fight the evil, and—impossibly—to trust that the Author who entered the play will write the final chapter in a mode I cannot now imagine.  

That trust is not a leap across an intellectual chasm; it is more like staying in the marriage when the scans come back malignant. It is learned slowly, in the dark, with no guarantee that my particular nightmare will end happily this side of death. The only immediate guarantee is the presence of the One whose own story passed through tomb and garden, who therefore knows the way and walks it with me.  

The scream remains. Sometimes it is my scream. Yet in the echo I have heard, not an explanation, but a name. The name does not solve the problem; it carries it, with me, toward the day when the problem and I shall both be transformed. Until then, honesty and hope are braided together, a cord not easily broken, strong enough to keep a fractured heart from bleeding out, fragile enough to keep it tender.
