The Problem That Won’t Go Away

The question arrives uninvited. It comes at 3 a.m. to the parent keeping vigil beside a hospital bed, to the refugee who has just learned their family did not survive the crossing, to the child who cannot understand why the abuse keeps happening. It is whispered in chemotherapy wards, shouted in war zones, and carried silently by those whose depression feels like a cage with no key. If God is good, why this? Why now? Why me?

This is not an abstract puzzle for theologians to solve in comfortable libraries. It is the most persistent and personal challenge to faith, the rock upon which many believers have shipwrecked. The problem of suffering refuses theoretical resolution because it is always embodied, always particular. We are not discussing "evil" in general but *this* evil—this specific, unthinkable, irrevocable harm that has shattered a life. Any response that fails to honor that particularity has already missed the point.

**The Unflinching Problem**

The classical formulation is deceptively simple: If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good, then suffering should not exist. Since suffering clearly does exist, one of these attributes must be compromised. Perhaps God is not strong enough to stop it. Perhaps God does not know it’s happening. Or perhaps—and this is the one that chills us—God is not good.

The force of this argument lies not in its logic but in its emotional and moral weight. We can see the problem most clearly in the suffering of children. A two-year-old with terminal cancer has not chosen this. No human free will is exercised in the mutation of her cells. No soul-making seems possible when the soul in question is still learning what "mama" means. The tsunami that drowns thousands, the earthquake that buries villages, the genetic disorder that twists a body—these are "natural evils" that cannot be blamed on human agency. They simply *are*, and they mock any easy talk of divine providence.

Even moral evil—the violence, betrayal, and cruelty humans inflict on one another—raises the stakes. If God values free will so highly that God will not intervene to stop a rape or a genocide, what does that say about the victims whose will is being utterly violated? The freedom of the perpetrator seems to matter more than the freedom of the victim. The math doesn’t work.

These are not straw-man objections. They are the lived experience of millions, and they demand more than theological hand-waving. The Bible itself seems to understand this. The psalmists do not offer polite complaints but raw, howling protests: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?" (Psalm 22:1). The book of Job gives us forty chapters of anguished dialogue, with Job demanding an answer from heaven and his friends offering precisely the kind of pious explanations we are tempted to give. God’s final verdict? "My servant Job has spoken of me what is right"—not the friends with their tidy theodicies, but Job with his unanswered questions and his righteous rage.

**The God Who Suffers**

One Christian response begins not with an explanation but with a location: the cross. The claim is startling: God does not remain distant from suffering but enters directly into its heart. In Jesus, Christians believe, God becomes a particular man in a particular time, subject to particular suffering. He weeps at a friend’s tomb (John 11:35). He agonizes in a garden, sweating blood (Luke 22:44). He dies a criminal’s death, executed by the state, abandoned by his friends, crying out the opening line of Psalm 22: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).

This is not a God who explains suffering from the safety of heaven. This is a God who drinks it to the dregs. The cross does not solve the problem of evil in philosophical terms; it refuses to treat suffering as a problem to be solved at all. Instead, it reveals that God’s answer to human anguish is not a theory but a presence. The crucified God stands with the victim, not the executioner. The God who suffers is not aloof from our pain but immersed in it.

The apostle Paul picks up this theme, writing that "in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself" (2 Corinthians 5:19). Notice the direction: God moves toward the world, toward the mess, toward the pain. The cross reorients the question. We are no longer asking why an omnipotent God permits suffering, but how a suffering God might transform it from within. This is not a defense of God’s power but a revelation of God’s character. Power, it turns out, is not the ability to prevent all harm, but the capacity to enter the harm and bear it, transform it, ultimately redeem it.

Yet we must be honest: this response can feel insufficient to the one in agony. The mother whose child is dying does not want a God who suffers alongside her; she wants a God who heals. The survivor of torture does not find immediate comfort in the theological claim that God was present in their pain. The cross may be profound, but it is not a quick fix. Its power is revealed not in the moment of crucifixion but in the empty tomb that follows—an eschatological promise that death does not have the final word. For those still in the middle of their own Friday, Sunday can feel very far away.

**The Long Road of Soul-Making**

A second theological tradition, often called the "soul-making" theodicy, suggests that suffering serves a pedagogical purpose. Drawing on the early church father Irenaeus and developed by thinkers like John Hick, this view argues that God created humans immature, not finished, and that suffering is the furnace in which character is forged. We become who we are meant to be not despite suffering but through it. The virtues—courage, compassion, patience, love—require resistance to develop. A world without struggle would be a world without growth.

Scripture offers some support for this view. The book of James, in a passage that can sound callous to grieving ears, writes: "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness" (James 1:2-3). The apostle Paul, who knew suffering intimately—beatings, shipwrecks, imprisonment—writes that "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3-4). The hope, he insists, does not disappoint.

Yet we must handle this carefully, or it becomes cruelty dressed up as theology. To tell a grieving parent that their child’s death is a "soul-making" opportunity is obscene. To suggest that genocide builds character is grotesque. The soul-making theodicy works, if it works at all, only eschatologically—looking back from a redeemed future where all things have been made new. In the present, it can function as a justification for complacency: why work to end suffering if it serves a divine purpose?

The strength of this view is not in explaining particular instances of evil but in suggesting a framework for how God might work redemption within a broken world. It does not claim that suffering is good, but that God is so committed to human freedom and growth that God will not override the natural consequences of living in a world where choices matter. Gravity can be used to dance or to kill. The same world that allows for the development of love allows for the possibility of its violation.

What this view cannot do is account for suffering that exceeds any possible pedagogical value. Some pain is simply gratuitous, pointless, destructive. The soul-making theodicy must be held in tension with the cross, where God does not justify suffering but bears it. Together, they suggest that while God may bring good *from* evil, God does not *cause* evil for the sake of good. The distinction matters.

**The Limits of Our Seeing**

The book of Job concludes not with an explanation but with a divine appearance. God speaks from a whirlwind, not to answer Job’s questions, but to overwhelm him with the vastness of creation. "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" God asks (Job 38:4). It is a speech that could sound like a divine brush-off, a cosmic version of "might makes right." But read more carefully, it is something else: an invitation to trust the character of God even when we cannot see the plan.

Job’s problem was not that he lacked information but that he lacked perspective. He could not see the cosmic drama of which his suffering was a part. He could not know that his faithfulness was part of a larger story about the nature of righteousness and the character of God. The divine speech does not give him answers; it gives him presence. God shows up. And somehow, mysteriously, that is enough. Job can live with the questions because he has encountered the God who dwells in the questions.

This is the limit of human understanding, but it is not a cop-out. It is an honest acknowledgment that we are finite creatures trying to comprehend an infinite reality. We see "in a mirror dimly," Paul writes (1 Corinthians 13:12). We do not have God’s vantage point. This does not mean we should stop asking, stop protesting, stop working to alleviate suffering. The limit of our vision does not absolve us of our responsibility to act. But it does mean we must hold our theological explanations lightly, recognizing that they are maps, not the territory.

The danger of theodicy is that it can become a way of managing God, of making suffering safe for faith. But suffering is not safe, and God cannot be managed. The most honest theological response may be to sit with Job in the ash heap, to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), and to admit that some wounds will not heal in this life. The Christian hope is not that we will receive a satisfactory explanation, but that we will be given a new creation where every tear is wiped away (Revelation 21:4). That hope is eschatological—it looks forward to a future we cannot yet see.

**When Theodicies Fail**

All theological responses to suffering have a point at which they break. The free will defense cannot fully justify the suffering of the innocent. The soul-making theodicy cannot explain pointless pain. The cross, while profound, does not remove the sting of death in the present. This breaking point is not a failure of faith but its necessary condition. Faith that can only exist where there are answers is not faith but certainty. Real faith, the kind that sustains through the valley of the shadow of death, lives with unanswerable questions.

This is where pastoral awareness must shape our theology. The person in crisis does not need a lecture on the metaphysics of free will. They need presence. They need someone to hold their hand, to listen to their rage, to not rush in with explanations that serve more to comfort the explainer than the sufferer. The church’s first response to suffering must not be a theodicy but a casserole, a shoulder to cry on, a commitment to walk alongside. Words come later, if at all.

Jesus modeled this at Lazarus’s tomb. He did not say, "This is for the greater good." He wept. He entered the grief before he offered the resurrection. Our theology must follow that same path: incarnation before explanation, presence before answers.

**A Way Forward**

So where does this leave us? Not with a tidy solution, certainly. The problem of suffering does not have an answer that fits in a logical syllogism. But perhaps it has a direction. The Christian story suggests that suffering is not the final word, but it is a real word, a word God takes seriously enough to enter into it bodily.

The way forward is not to stop asking why, but to ask a different question as well: how? How can I bear this? How can we prevent future suffering? How can we create communities of care that embody the presence of Christ to those who are broken? The "why" may remain unanswered, but the "how" calls us to action.

We are invited to become part of God’s answer to suffering. When we feed the hungry, visit the prisoner, shelter the abused, we are God’s presence in a hurting world. We do not explain the pain away; we enter it, as Christ did. We become, in our small and flawed ways, the hands and feet of the God who suffers with us.

This does not make the problem go away. It does not satisfy the demand for an explanation. But it does suggest that the deepest response to suffering is not a theory but a life—a life shaped by the conviction that love is stronger than death, that presence is more powerful than absence, and that the God who wept at a tomb will one day wipe every tear from every eye.

Until that day, we live in the tension: honest about the horror, committed to the fight against it, and trusting that the One who hung on a cross knows our pain and will not abandon us to it. The problem remains. But so does God. And perhaps, in the end, that is enough.

### The Wound of the World: Suffering and the Silence of God

The question arrives not in seminary classrooms but in hospital waiting rooms, not in philosophical treatises but at gravesides. It comes from the mother who has just buried her child, from the refugee who has watched his village burn, from the woman who has lived with abuse whispered behind closed doors. "Where is God?" is not first an intellectual puzzle; it is a cry from a throat raw with screaming. The problem of suffering is not a problem to be solved but a wound to be acknowledged.

And yet, it is also a profound philosophical challenge. If God is all-good, all-knowing, and all-powerful, then the existence of horrendous evil appears to be a contradiction. A God who could prevent the rape of a child but does not is either not good, not powerful, or not there. This is not a straw man erected for easy demolition; it is the stark logic of human anguish. Theologians call it the *problem of evil*, but for those in its grip, it is simply the problem of *life*. We cannot dismiss it with platitudes about "mysterious ways" without betraying those whose suffering has become their identity.

#### The Freedom of the Fallen

One of the most enduring responses to this dilemma is the free will defense, articulated most powerfully by Augustine and refined by thinkers like Alvin Plantinga. Its premise is elegant: genuine love requires genuine freedom. God desires a world where creatures can choose the good, which necessitates the possibility of choosing evil. Moral evil—cruelty, violence, oppression—is the price of freedom. God does not stand aloof as a puppet master but has created beings capable of real relationship, which means they are capable of real betrayal.

There is truth here. We intuitively rebel against the idea that we are merely programmed automatons. The Holocaust was not a natural disaster; it was a series of human choices, made by people who could have chosen otherwise. The same freedom that allows a person to cradle a dying stranger in compassion enables another to wield a machete in hatred. God has given us the terrible dignity of causality.

But this defense, for all its value, begins to fray at the edges. It explains human cruelty adequately enough, perhaps, but what of the child with leukemia? What of the tsunami that drowns thousands? Natural evil—disease, disaster, decay—cannot be laid at the feet of human freedom. Some theologians extend the free will defense to spiritual beings, blaming demonic forces or a fallen creation, but this risks becoming a metaphysical shell game. The sufferer does not care whether cancer comes from a demon or a chromosome; they care that it *comes*. And more troublingly, the free will defense can sound like a justification that protects God at the expense of victims. "Your suffering is the price of someone else's freedom" is not a word of comfort to the one being trafficked. It is a word of condemnation.

The biblical narrative itself complicates this tidy solution. Genesis tells us that creation is "good," but it is not static perfection. The Hebrew notion of *shalom*—wholeness, flourishing—implies a dynamic harmony that can be disrupted. Yet the text offers no simple causal chain linking human sin to every instance of suffering. Job, that great exploration of innocent suffering, ends with God appearing in a whirlwind not to explain *why* but to show *Who*. The friends who offer explanations—"You must have sinned"—are condemned. The book's genius is its refusal to resolve the tension. It gives us not a theodicy but a lament, a permission to protest, a divine silence that is somehow more presence than absence.

#### The God Who Bleeds

If the free will defense reaches its limits, another response moves us from the courtroom to the cross. The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann, reflecting on his experience as a soldier in Hitler’s army, argued that the cross is not just how God saves us but how God *is*—a God who suffers. In the crucifixion, God does not merely sympathize with human pain from a safe distance; God enters it, becomes it, is swallowed by it. The cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a moment of theological confusion but the deepest revelation of divine love: God experiences godforsakenness.

This is not a theodicy in the traditional sense. It does not explain *why* suffering exists. Instead, it redefines what we mean by "God's goodness." The goodness of God is not a managerial efficiency that eliminates all pain. It is a solidarity that enters it. The cross says: God is not absent from your suffering; God is *in* it, beneath it, screaming with you. The crucified God is not a God who prevents the tragedy but a God who is the first victim of it, who bears the wound of the world in God's own body.

Scripture gives us this trajectory. The Psalms of lament—Psalm 88, which ends in darkness; Psalm 22, which Jesus himself quotes—are not hymns of resolution but screams of abandonment. They are canonized, preserved, *sung* in worship. This is stunning: the Bible gives us permission to accuse God, to demand answers, to refuse cheap comfort. Lamentations, that dirge over the ruins of Jerusalem, does not end with "but it all worked out." It ends with a plea: "Restore us to yourself, LORD, that we may return." The relationship is broken, and the request is for restoration, not explanation.

Jesus' life embodies this pattern. He weeps at Lazarus's tomb not as a performance but as a visceral entering into grief. He heals some but not all. He tells his disciples they will suffer, be persecuted, be killed. There is no promise of immunity. Instead, there is a promise of presence: "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20). Not "I will prevent your suffering" but "I will be in it with you." Paul's thorn in the flesh, that mysterious suffering he begs God to remove, receives not healing but a word: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). This is not a solution; it is a relationship redefined by shared vulnerability.

#### The Limits of Our Seeing

To acknowledge these responses is not to have solved the problem. The risk of any theology of suffering is that it becomes a way of managing mystery rather than dwelling in it. We must resist the temptation to let "God suffers with us" become a quieting platitude. The mother who has lost her child does not want a God who suffers too; she wants her child back. Theology must never become a way of explaining away the particularity of pain. Every instance of suffering is a unique rupture, a world ended. General answers can feel like general anesthesia—numbing when we need to feel.

Here is where we must acknowledge the limits of our understanding without using mystery as a shield against honest questioning. The biblical witness is not a systematic theodicy but a collection of voices in protest, trust, despair, and hope. Job never learns why he suffered. The writer of Ecclesiastes calls life "meaningless" under the sun. Even the resurrection of Jesus, that great promise of new creation, does not erase the scars. Thomas is invited to touch them. The woundedness is not undone; it is transformed.

What we see, then, is a God who seems to value a particular kind of world: one where love is free, where relationship is real, where the creation itself is in process, groaning toward redemption (Romans 8:22). This is not the best of all possible worlds but perhaps the best of all possible *ways* for God to be in relationship with creation—a way that includes risk, vulnerability, and the cross. The theologian's answer must always be: "I don't know why *this* suffering had to happen." But we can say, with trembling, that God has entered suffering definitively and promises to make something of it that we cannot yet see.

#### The Wound That Becomes a Way

This brings us to the pastoral heart of the matter. Intellectual responses to suffering are necessary but insufficient. They are maps, but the territory is a dark wood where maps fail. The real work is not explaining suffering but learning to live in a world marked by it. The African-American spiritual tradition, born from slavery and lynching, understood this. It did not offer explanations; it offered songs. The blues and spirituals are not theodicies but testimonies: "Nobody knows the trouble I've seen, but Jesus." The "but Jesus" is not a resolution; it is a relationship. It is the claim that in the depths, there is a companionship that does not explain but sustains.

This is why the church's response to suffering cannot be a lecture on free will or even a meditation on the cross. It must be a bowl of soup, a held hand, a weeping presence. The book of James, that most practical of epistles, says: "Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress" (1:27). The test of theology is not its logical coherence but its capacity to produce compassion. If our answers make us less present to suffering, they are not God's answers.

The problem of suffering remains. It is a wound that will not be healed until the kingdom comes in fullness. But the Christian claim is that the wound has been touched by God, that the cross is God's refusal to remain at a safe distance, that the resurrection is the promise that no suffering is wasted. It does not say that suffering is good. It says that God is good, and that God's goodness is of a kind that enters our suffering and transforms it from within.

We are left, then, not with a solution but with a person. Not with an answer but with a presence. The final word is not explanation but love—a love that bleeds, a love that rises, a love that promises to make all things new. Until then, we live in the tension: weeping with those who weep, protesting with those who protest, and holding fast to the strange, stubborn hope that the God who entered the worst of human suffering will not abandon us to it. The wound remains, but it has become a way—a way into the heart of a God whose goodness is not the absence of pain but the presence of love in the midst of it.

"Where is God?" is not first an intellectual puzzle; it is a cry from a throat raw with screaming. The problem of suffering is not a problem to be solved but a wound to be acknowledged.

And yet, it is also a profound philosophical challenge. If God is all-good, all-knowing, and all-powerful, then the existence of horrendous evil appears to be a contradiction. A God who could prevent the rape of a child but does not is either not good, not powerful, or not there. This is not a straw man erected for easy demolition; it is the stark logic of human anguish. Theologians call it the *problem of evil*, but for those in its grip, it is simply the problem of *life*. We cannot dismiss it with platitudes about "mysterious ways" without betraying those whose suffering has become their identity.

#### The Freedom of the Fallen

One of the most enduring responses to this dilemma is the free will defense, articulated most powerfully by Augustine and refined by thinkers like Alvin Plantinga. Its premise is elegant: genuine love requires genuine freedom. God desires a world where creatures can choose the good, which necessitates the possibility of choosing evil. Moral evil—cruelty, violence, oppression—is the price of freedom. God does not stand aloof as a puppet master but has created beings capable of real relationship, which means they are capable of real betrayal.

There is truth here. We intuitively rebel against the idea that we are merely programmed automatons. The Holocaust was not a natural disaster; it was a series of human choices, made by people who could have chosen otherwise. The same freedom that allows a person to cradle a dying stranger in compassion enables another to wield a machete in hatred. God has given us the terrible dignity of causality.

But this defense, for all its value, begins to fray at the edges. It explains human cruelty adequately enough, perhaps, but what of the child with leukemia? What of the tsunami that drowns thousands? Natural evil—disease, disaster, decay—cannot be laid at the feet of human freedom. Some theologians extend the free will defense to spiritual beings, blaming demonic forces or a fallen creation, but this risks becoming a speculative extension that, while attempting to preserve divine goodness, often feels like a metaphysical shell game to those experiencing suffering, as it shifts the blame to unseen forces without addressing the immediate pain. The sufferer does not care whether cancer comes from a demon or a chromosome; they care that it *comes*. And more troublingly, the free will defense can sound like a justification that protects God at the expense of victims. "Your suffering is the price of someone else's freedom" is not a word of comfort to the one being trafficked. It is a word of condemnation.

Another classical response, the soul-making theodicy associated with Irenaeus, suggests that suffering serves a pedagogical purpose: it is the furnace in which souls are forged, the resistance that builds spiritual muscle. There is biblical precedent—"suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character" (Romans 5:3-4). Yet this too can become a cruel logic when applied to particular horrors. To tell parents burying their child that this is "soul-making" is not pastoral care; it is spiritual violence. The theory may hold abstract truth, but it fails the test of love when it meets the specific, unanswerable "why" of real agony.

The biblical narrative itself complicates these tidy solutions. Genesis tells us that creation is "good," but it is not static perfection. The Hebrew notion of *shalom*—wholeness, flourishing—implies a dynamic harmony that can be disrupted. Yet the text offers no simple causal chain linking human sin to every instance of suffering. Job, that great exploration of innocent suffering, ends with God appearing in a whirlwind not to explain *why* but to show *Who*. The friends who offer explanations—"You must have sinned"—are condemned. The book's genius is its refusal to resolve the tension. It gives us not a theodicy but a lament, a permission to protest, a divine silence that is somehow more presence than absence.

#### The God Who Bleeds

If the free will defense reaches its limits, another response moves us from the courtroom to the cross. The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann, reflecting on his experience as a soldier in Hitler’s army, argued that the cross is not just how God saves us but how God *is*—a God who suffers. In the crucifixion, God does not merely sympathize with human pain from a safe distance; God enters it, becomes it, is swallowed by it. The cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a moment of theological confusion but the deepest revelation of divine love: God experiences godforsakenness.

This is not a theodicy in the traditional sense. It does not explain *why* suffering exists. Instead, it redefines what we mean by "God's goodness." The goodness of God is not a managerial efficiency that eliminates all pain. It is a solidarity that enters it. The cross says: God is not absent from your suffering; God is *in* it, beneath it, screaming with you. The crucified God is not a God who prevents the tragedy but a God who is the first victim of it, who bears the wound of the world in God's own body.

Scripture gives us this trajectory. The Psalms of lament—Psalm 88, which ends in darkness; Psalm 22, which Jesus himself quotes—are not hymns of resolution but screams of abandonment. They are canonized, preserved, *sung* in worship. This is stunning: the Bible gives us permission to accuse God, to demand answers, to refuse cheap comfort. Lamentations, that dirge over the ruins of Jerusalem, does not end with "but it all worked out." It ends with a plea: "Restore us to yourself, LORD, that we may return." The relationship is broken, and the request is for restoration, not explanation.

Jesus' life embodies this pattern. He weeps at Lazarus's tomb not as a performance but as a visceral entering into grief. He heals some but not all. He tells his disciples they will suffer, be persecuted, be killed. There is no promise of immunity. Instead, there is a promise of presence: "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20). Not "I will prevent your suffering" but "I will be in it with you." Paul's thorn in the flesh, that mysterious suffering he begs God to remove, receives not healing but a word: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). This is not a solution; it is a relationship redefined by shared vulnerability.

#### The Limits of Our Seeing

To acknowledge these responses is not to have solved the problem. The risk of any theology of suffering is that it becomes a way of managing mystery rather than dwelling in it. We must resist the temptation to let "God suffers with us" become a quieting platitude. The mother who has lost her child does not want a God who suffers too; she wants her child back. Theology must never become a way of explaining away the particularity of pain. Every instance of suffering is a unique rupture, a world ended. General answers can feel like general anesthesia—numbing when we need to feel.

Here is where we must acknowledge the limits of our understanding without using mystery as a shield against honest questioning. The biblical witness is not a systematic theodicy but a collection of voices in protest, trust, despair, and hope. Job never learns why he suffered. The writer of Ecclesiastes calls life "meaningless" under the sun. Even the resurrection of Jesus, that great promise of new creation, does not erase the scars. Thomas is invited to touch them. The woundedness is not undone; it is transformed.

What we see, then, is a God who seems to value a particular kind of world: one where love is free, where relationship is real, where the creation itself is in process, groaning toward redemption (Romans 8:22). This is not the best of all possible worlds but perhaps the best of all possible *ways* for God to be in relationship with creation—a way that includes risk, vulnerability, and the cross. The theologian's answer must always be: "I don't know why *this* suffering had to happen." But we can say, with trembling, that God has entered suffering definitively and promises to make something of it that we cannot yet see.

#### The Wound That Becomes a Way

This brings us to the pastoral heart of the matter. Intellectual responses to suffering are necessary but insufficient. They are maps, but the territory is a dark wood where maps fail. The real work is not explaining suffering but learning to live in a world marked by it. The African-American spiritual tradition, born from slavery and lynching, understood this. It did not offer explanations; it offered songs. The blues and spirituals are not theodicies but testimonies: "Nobody knows the trouble I've seen, but Jesus." The "but Jesus" is not a resolution; it is a relationship. It is the claim that in the depths, there is a companionship that does not explain but sustains.

This tradition knew something that academic theology often forgets: that the most profound truths are often expressed not in syllogisms but in shared groaning. The God of the spirituals is not a divine accountant balancing ledgers of suffering and freedom, but a suffering Savior who walks beside his people through the valley of the shadow of death. This is theology forged in the crucible of unspeakable pain, and it carries an authority that abstract speculation can never attain.

This is why the church's response to suffering cannot be a lecture on free will or even a meditation on the cross. It must be a bowl of soup, a held hand, a weeping presence. The book of James, that most practical of epistles, says: "Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress" (1:27). The test of theology is not its logical coherence but its capacity to produce compassion. If our answers make us less present to suffering, they are not God's answers.

The problem of suffering remains. It is a wound that will not be healed until the kingdom comes in fullness. But the Christian claim is that the wound has been touched by God, that the cross is God's refusal to remain at a safe distance, that the resurrection is the promise that no suffering is wasted. It does not say that suffering is good. It says that God is good, and that God's goodness is of a kind that enters our suffering and transforms it from within.

We are left, then, not with a solution but with a person. Not with an answer but with a presence. The final word is not explanation but love—a love that bleeds, a love that rises, a love that promises to make all things new. Until then, we live in the tension: weeping with those who weep, protesting with those who protest, and holding fast to the strange, stubborn hope that the God who entered the worst of human suffering will not abandon us to it. The wound remains, but it has become a way—a way into the heart of a God whose goodness is not the absence of pain but the presence of love in the midst of it.

### The Wound of the World: Suffering and the Silence of God

The question arrives not in seminary classrooms but in hospital waiting rooms, not in philosophical treatises but at gravesides. It comes from the mother who has just buried her child, from the refugee who has watched his village burn, from the woman who has lived with abuse whispered behind closed doors. "Where is God?" is not first an intellectual puzzle; it is a cry from a throat raw with screaming. The problem of suffering is not a problem to be solved but a wound to be acknowledged.

And yet, it is also a profound philosophical challenge. If God is all-good, all-knowing, and all-powerful, then the existence of horrendous evil appears to be a contradiction. A God who could prevent the rape of a child but does not is either not good, not powerful, or not there. This is not a straw man erected for easy demolition; it is the stark logic of human anguish. Many thoughtful, morally serious people have looked at this evidence and concluded that God does not exist—and their conclusion is not irrational. Theologians call it the *problem of evil*, but for those in its grip, it is simply the problem of *life*. We cannot dismiss it with platitudes about "mysterious ways" without betraying those whose suffering has become their identity.

#### The Terrible Dignity of Causality

One enduring response is the free will defense, articulated most powerfully by Augustine and refined by modern philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. Augustine's version is anchored in a metaphysical vision: evil is not a substance but a *privation*, a corruption of the good. Creation is good, but mutable beings can turn from the Good. God's permission of this turning is the price of a world where love is voluntary, not coerced. Plantinga's version is more modest and precise: it aims only to show that the existence of God and the existence of evil are *logically compatible*. Perhaps a world with free creatures who sometimes choose evil is more valuable than a world of automata who cannot choose at all. The Holocaust, then, becomes a series of human choices, made by people who could have chosen otherwise. The same freedom that allows a person to cradle a dying stranger in compassion enables another to wield a machete in hatred. God has given us the terrible dignity of causality.

There is truth here. We intuitively rebel against the idea that we are merely programmed. And yet, this defense begins to fray at the edges. It explains human cruelty adequately enough, perhaps, but what of the child with leukemia? What of the tsunami that drowns thousands? Natural evil—disease, disaster, decay—cannot be laid at the feet of human freedom. Some extend the defense to spiritual beings, blaming demonic forces or a fallen creation, but this risks becoming a metaphysical shell game. The sufferer does not care whether cancer comes from a demon or a chromosome; they care that it *comes*.

More troublingly, the free will defense can sound like a justification that protects God at the expense of victims. "Your suffering is the price of someone else's freedom" is not a word of comfort to the one being trafficked. It is a word of condemnation. The biblical narrative itself complicates this tidy solution. Genesis tells us that creation is "good"—the Hebrew *tov* meaning not static perfection but functional, purposeful design. Yet the text offers no simple causal chain linking human sin to every instance of suffering. Job, that great exploration of innocent suffering, ends with God appearing in a whirlwind not to explain *why* but to show *Who*. The friends who offer explanations—"You must have sinned"—are condemned. The book's genius is its refusal to resolve the tension. It gives us not a theodicy but a lament, a permission to protest, a divine silence that is somehow more presence than absence.

#### The Forge of the Soul

A second response, distinct from the free will defense, is the soul-making theodicy. Associated with Irenaeus and developed by modern thinkers like John Hick, it suggests that suffering serves a pedagogical purpose. This world is not a finished creation but a *soul-making* arena, a vale where character is forged through adversity. The virtues of compassion, courage, and perseverance cannot exist in a world without risk and pain. Suffering, on this view, is not merely permitted but instrumentally valuable—raw material for spiritual formation.

There is a hard truth here. We recognize that ease can corrode character, that privilege often blinds. The person who has known suffering can become more tender, more attentive to others. The apostle Paul's claim that "suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope" (Romans 5:3-4) seems to gesture in this direction.

Yet this theodicy is perhaps the most dangerous of all. It can quickly become a sanctification of suffering, a way of telling victims that their pain is *good for them*. The mother whose child dies does not need to hear that this is building her character. The child in the cancer ward is not a prop in someone else's moral education. The risk is immense: if suffering is purposeful, then we might be tempted to preserve it rather than alleviate it. The soul-making defense, like the free will defense, can become a way of protecting God's reputation at the expense of those who bleed. It forgets that while suffering *can* produce virtue, it more often produces bitterness, trauma, and despair. The Bible's own testimony is mixed on this: while Paul speaks of hope, the writer of Ecclesiastes calls life "meaningless, a chasing after the wind" (Ecclesiastes 1:14). The Psalms of lament—Psalm 88, which ends in darkness; Psalm 22, which Jesus quotes on the cross—are not hymns of moral improvement but screams of abandonment. They are canonized, preserved, *sung* in worship. This is stunning: Scripture gives us permission to accuse God, to demand answers, to refuse cheap comfort.

#### The God Who Bleeds

If these defenses reach their limits, another response moves us from the courtroom to the cross. The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann, reflecting on his experience as a soldier in Hitler's army, argued that the cross is not just how God saves us but how God *is*—a God who suffers. In the crucifixion, God does not merely sympathize with human pain from a safe distance; God enters it, becomes it, is swallowed by it. The cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a moment of theological confusion but the deepest revelation of divine love: God experiences godforsakenness.

This is not a theodicy in the traditional sense. It does not explain *why* suffering exists. Instead, it redefines what we mean by "God's goodness." The goodness of God is not a managerial efficiency that eliminates all pain. It is a solidarity that enters it. The cross says: God is not absent from your suffering; God is *in* it, beneath it, screaming with you. The crucified God is not a God who prevents tragedy but a God who is the first victim of it, who bears the wound of the world in God's own body.

Scripture gives us this trajectory. Jesus weeps at Lazarus's tomb not as a performance but as a visceral entering into grief. He heals some but not all. He tells his disciples they will suffer, be persecuted, be killed. There is no promise of immunity. Instead, there is a promise of presence: "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20). Not "I will prevent your suffering" but "I will be in it with you." Paul's thorn in the flesh, that mysterious suffering he begs God to remove, receives not healing but a word: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). This is not a solution; it is a relationship redefined by shared vulnerability.

The apostle Paul pushes this further in Romans 8, where he writes that "the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time" (Romans 8:22). But the passage does not end there. Paul continues: "In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans" (Romans 8:26). The Spirit does not observe our suffering; the Spirit *groans with us*. This is the deepest form of solidarity—not a distant God who sympathizes, but a divine presence that enters our wordless agony and carries it within the triune life.

Even this, however, must face the hardest question. The mother who has lost her child does not want a God who suffers too; she wants her child back. The cross does not retroactively justify the pain. Ivan Karamazov's refusal remains potent: no future harmony is worth the tears of a single child. To say "God suffers with you" can sound like a consolation prize when what you need is a resurrection. The theology of the cross does not erase this objection. It simply says: God agrees. God does not offer an explanation; God offers a body. The wounds in Jesus' resurrected body are not erased; they are displayed. When Thomas doubts, Jesus invites him: "Put your finger here; see my hands. But transformation is not the same as reversal. The child is still dead. The wound remains.

#### The Limits of Our Seeing

To acknowledge these responses is not to have solved the problem. The risk of any theology of suffering is that it becomes a way of managing mystery rather than dwelling in it. We must resist the temptation to let "God suffers with us" become a quieting platitude. Theology must never become a way of explaining away the particularity of pain. Every instance of suffering is a unique rupture, a world ended. General answers can feel like general anesthesia—numbing when we need to feel.

Here is where we must acknowledge the limits of our understanding without using mystery as a shield against honest questioning. The biblical witness is not a systematic theodicy but a collection of voices in protest, trust, despair, and hope. Job never learns why he suffered. The writer of Ecclesiastes calls life "meaningless" under the sun. Even the resurrection of Jesus does not erase the scars. What we see, then, is a God who seems to value a particular kind of world: one where love is free, where relationship is real, where creation itself is in process, groaning toward redemption. This is not the best of all possible worlds but perhaps the best of all possible *ways* for God to be in relationship with creation—a way that includes risk, vulnerability, and the cross. The theologian's answer must always be: "I don't know why *this* suffering had to happen." But we can say, with trembling, that God has entered suffering definitively and promises to make something of it that we cannot yet see.

This humility must extend to the church itself. For many, the wound has been inflicted not despite the church but *by* it—through abuse, spiritual manipulation, exclusion, complicity in oppression. When the institution that proclaims "God suffers with you" is the source of the suffering, the theology of solidarity becomes deeply complicated. The cross is not a shield for ecclesial failure. The church's wounds are often self-inflicted, and its victims have every right to reject its consolation. We cannot speak of divine solidarity without first confessing our own betrayals.

Nor can we ignore those who have lost faith because of suffering. The essay has spoken for them, but not to them. To those who have walked away: your leaving is not irrational. The silence you experienced may have been the silence of an empty sky, not the silence of a God who bleeds. The Christian claim is not that you must return, but that if you ever choose to, the door is held open by nail-scarred hands.

The problem of suffering remains. It is a wound that will not be healed until the kingdom comes in fullness. Intellectual responses are necessary but insufficient. Until then, we live in the tension: weeping with those who weep, protesting with those who protest, and holding fast to the strange, stubborn hope that the God who entered the worst of human suffering will not abandon us to it. The wound remains. But it has become a way—a way into the heart of a God whose goodness is not the absence of pain but the presence of love in the midst of it.

### The Wound of the World: Suffering and the Silence of God

The question arrives not in seminary classrooms but in hospital waiting rooms, not in philosophical treatises but at gravesides. It comes from the mother who has just buried her child, from the refugee who has watched his village burn, from the woman who has lived with abuse whispered behind closed doors. And yet, it is also a profound philosophical challenge. If God is all-good, all-knowing, and all-powerful, then the existence of horrendous evil appears to be a contradiction. A God who could prevent the rape of a child but does not is either not good, not powerful, or not there. This is not a straw man erected for easy demolition; it is the stark logic of human anguish. Theologians call it the *problem of evil*, but for those in its grip, it is simply the problem of *life*. We cannot dismiss it with platitudes about "mysterious ways" without betraying those whose suffering has become their identity.

#### The Freedom of the Fallen

One of the most enduring responses to this dilemma is the free will defense, articulated most powerfully by Augustine and refined by thinkers like Alvin Plantinga. Its premise is elegant: genuine love requires genuine freedom. God desires a world where creatures can choose the good, which necessitates the possibility of choosing evil. Moral evil—cruelty, violence, oppression—is the price of freedom. God does not stand aloof as a puppet master but has created beings capable of real relationship, which means they are capable of real betrayal.

There is truth here. We intuitively rebel against the idea that we are merely programmed automatons. The Holocaust was not a natural disaster; it was a series of human choices, made by people who could have chosen otherwise. The same freedom that allows a person to cradle a dying stranger in compassion enables another to wield a machete in hatred. God has given us the terrible dignity of causality.

But this defense, for all its value, begins to fray at the edges. It explains human cruelty adequately enough, perhaps, but what of the child with leukemia? What of the tsunami that drowns thousands? Natural evil—disease, disaster, decay—cannot be laid at the feet of human freedom. Some theologians extend the free will defense to spiritual beings, blaming demonic forces or a fallen creation, but this risks becoming a metaphysical shell game. The biblical image of a "groaning creation" (Romans 8:22) carries theological weight, suggesting that nature itself participates in a kind of cosmic alienation. Yet for the parent watching their child battle cancer, this remains an abstraction. The origin matters less than the reality. The sufferer does not care whether cancer comes from a demon or a chromosome; they care that it *comes*. And more troublingly, the free will defense can sound like a justification that protects God at the expense of victims. "Your suffering is the price of someone else's freedom" is not a word of comfort to the one being trafficked. It is a word of condemnation.

The biblical narrative itself complicates this tidy solution. Genesis tells us that creation is "good," but it is not static perfection. The Hebrew notion of *shalom*—wholeness, flourishing—implies a dynamic harmony that can be disrupted. Yet the text offers no simple causal chain linking human sin to every instance of suffering. Job, that great exploration of innocent suffering, ends with God appearing in a whirlwind not to explain *why* but to show *Who*. The friends who offer explanations—"You must have sinned"—are condemned. The book's genius is its refusal to resolve the tension. If the free will defense attempts to explain the *origin* of evil, and protest theodicy holds space for its scandal, a third response moves us from the courtroom to the cross. The German theologian Jürgen Moltmann, whose theology was forged in the aftermath of his conscription and imprisonment during World War II, argued that the cross is not just how God saves us but how God *is*—a God who suffers. In the crucifixion, God does not merely sympathize with human pain from a safe distance; God enters it, becomes it, is swallowed by it. The cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a moment of theological confusion but the deepest revelation of divine love: God experiences godforsakenness.

This is not a theodicy in the traditional sense. It does not explain *why* suffering exists. Instead, it redefines what we mean by "God’s goodness." The goodness of God is not a managerial efficiency that eliminates all pain. It is a solidarity that enters it. The cross says: God is not absent from your suffering; God is *in* it, beneath it, screaming with you. The crucified God is not a God who prevents the tragedy but a God who is the first victim of it, who bears the wound of the world in God’s own body.

Scripture gives us this trajectory, though it resists systematic explanation. Jesus’ life embodies this pattern. He weeps at Lazarus’s tomb not as a performance but as a visceral entering into grief. He heals some but not all. He tells his disciples they will suffer, be persecuted, be killed. There is no promise of immunity. Instead, there is a promise of presence: "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20). Not "I will prevent your suffering" but "I will be in it with you." Paul’s thorn in the flesh, that mysterious suffering he begs God to remove (whether physical, psychological, or persecution, the text leaves it deliberately vague), receives not healing but a word: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). This is not a solution; it is a relationship redefined by shared vulnerability.

Romans 8 offers perhaps the deepest biblical framework for this. Paul writes that creation was "subjected to frustration, not by its own choice, but by the will of the one who subjected it" (8:20). The groaning of creation is not a natural state but a sign that something has gone wrong, that the world is in bondage to decay. Yet this groaning is not the final word. The Spirit groans with us, "with groans that words cannot express" (8:26), and this divine groaning is the presence of God in the midst of creation’s pain. The cross is the ultimate expression of this: God does not remain outside the world’s suffering but enters into it, joining the groan.

#### The Limits of Our Seeing

To acknowledge these responses is not to have solved the problem. The risk of any theology of suffering is that it becomes a way of managing mystery rather than dwelling in it. We must resist the temptation to let "God suffers with us" become a quieting platitude. The mother who has lost her child does not want a God who suffers too; she wants her child back. Theology must never become a way of explaining away the particularity of pain. Every instance of suffering is a unique rupture, a world ended. General answers can feel like general anesthesia—numbing when we need to feel.

Here is where we must acknowledge the limits of our understanding without using mystery as a shield against honest questioning. The writer of Ecclesiastes calls life "meaningless" under the sun. Even the resurrection of Jesus, that great promise of new creation, does not erase the scars. Thomas is invited to touch them. The woundedness is not undone; it is transformed.

What we see, then, is a God who has chosen to work within a creation that is dynamic, free, and therefore risky. This is not a claim that this is the best of all possible worlds—it is a refusal of that calculus. Rather, we can say that God has committed to being present within this world’s suffering and to redeeming it from within. Whether this specific cancer, this particular tsunami, was *required* for some greater good, we cannot say and should not presume. The theologian’s answer must always be: "I don’t know why *this* suffering had to happen." But we can say, with trembling, that God has entered suffering definitively and promises to make something of it that we cannot yet see. That "something" is not a lesson learned but a world remade.

This brings us to the pastoral heart of the matter. Intellectual responses to suffering are necessary but insufficient. They are maps, but the territory is a dark wood where maps fail. The real work is not explaining suffering but learning to live in a world marked by it. The African-American spiritual tradition, born from slavery and lynching, understood this. This is why the church’s response to suffering cannot be a lecture on free will or even a meditation on the cross. It must be a bowl of soup, a held hand, a weeping presence. The problem of suffering remains. It is a wound that will not be healed until the kingdom comes in fullness. The final word is not explanation but love—a love that bleeds, a love that rises, a love that promises to make all things new. The wound remains, but it has become a way—a way into the heart of a God whose goodness is not the absence of pain but the presence of love in the midst of it, and the promise that love will have the final word.

The Problem of Suffering and the Silence of God

The most honest question a human being can ask in the face of profound suffering is not "Why does God allow this?" but "How can this possibly be compatible with a God who is both all-powerful and all-loving?" The difference is subtle but crucial. The first question presumes a tidy answer might exist, a lever we can pull or a secret we can unlock. The second simply holds up the contradiction and demands that we look at it squarely.

When a child dies slowly of bone cancer, when a tsunami erases thousands in minutes, when a woman is raped and left for dead, when mental illness drives someone to suicide, when genocide unfolds in systematic efficiency—these are not merely "difficulties" for faith. They are its potential refutation. Theologian David Bentley Hart writes bluntly that these instances of "useless" suffering, suffering that serves no discernible purpose and could be prevented without any loss of greater good, constitute a moral and logical problem that cannot be explained away. To pretend otherwise is not faith but evasion.

This is the problem of evil in its fullest force: not a philosophical puzzle to be solved but an existential scream. If God is omnipotent, he could prevent such suffering. If God is omnibenevolent, he would want to. The fact that such suffering exists suggests either that God lacks the power, lacks the love, or lacks existence altogether. Any response to this problem must begin by refusing to diminish its weight.

**The Freedom We Cannot Unmake**

One of the most enduring attempts to reconcile divine goodness with the reality of suffering is the free will defense, articulated classically by Augustine and refined by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs: a world containing creatures who freely choose to love God is more valuable than a world of automata programmed to do so. But genuine freedom entails the possibility of choosing evil. God cannot create free creatures and simultaneously guarantee they will never misuse that freedom. Suffering enters the world because human beings—and perhaps cosmic agents like demons—have freely chosen to turn from the good.

This response has genuine merit. It accounts for a great deal of moral evil: the Holocaust was not God's plan but human choice enacted on an industrial scale. The same freedom that enables a Mother Teresa to love sacrificially enables a Stalin to murder systematically. You cannot have one without the other.

Yet this defense, even at its strongest, begins to fray at the edges when we press it. First, it struggles to account for natural evil—the child's cancer, the earthquake, the parasite that blinds. One can invoke the ripple effects of a fallen world, where creation itself is corrupted by sin, but this stretches the causal chain thin. Did the tectonic plates really shift because of human rebellion? Is the child's leukemia a moral consequence? The connection feels not just speculative but cruel.

Second, and more damning from a pastoral perspective, the free will defense can sound like a justification at the moment of deepest need. To tell a grieving parent that their child's death is the price of human freedom is not comfort; it is theological arithmetic that adds insult to injury. The defense may hold logically, but it fails relationally. It addresses the problem of evil as an abstract equation while leaving the sufferer in isolation.

What the free will defense does accomplish, however, is reframing the question. It suggests that suffering is not something God directly wills but something that emerges from the risky gift of genuine existence. God creates a world where love is possible, and love requires vulnerability—not only for God, but for all creation. The cross, in this view, becomes not just a symbol of suffering but its deepest logic: God enters a world where freedom has run amok and suffers its consequences himself.

**The Cruciform Answer**

This leads to a profoundly different response, one less interested in logical defense than in divine solidarity. In this view, God's answer to suffering is not a theory but a body hanging on a tree. The crucifixion of Jesus is not a transaction that makes suffering disappear but a revelation that God has entered the darkest possibilities of human freedom and experienced them from the inside.

The Gospels do not present the cross as a neat solution. They show us a man who begs for the cup to pass, who feels abandoned, who dies screaming. The cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a proof text; it is the Bible's most honest moment. It is the moment when God himself, in human flesh, voices the protest of every sufferer. The question is not resolved; it is embodied.

The apostle Paul picks up this theme in his letter to the Philippians, where he speaks of the "fellowship of sharing in Christ's sufferings." This is not masochism but mysticism: the claim that in Christ, God has so identified with human agony that suffering becomes a place where God can be found. Not explained, but encountered. The cross does not give us a reason for suffering; it gives us a God who suffers.

This "cruciform" theodicy has deep biblical roots beyond the Gospels. The book of Job, often cited as the Bible's grappling with innocent suffering, refuses to give a tidy answer. When God finally speaks from the whirlwind, he does not explain why Job suffers. He does not reveal the cosmic wager with Satan that frames the narrative. Instead, he offers a vision of a creation too vast and wild for human comprehension. His answer is not an explanation but a relationship: "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" The question is rhetorical, but its point is not to silence Job. It is to invite him into a world where his suffering matters to God, even if it remains mysterious.

Similarly, the Psalms of lament—Psalm 88 being the most unrelenting—give voice to raw anguish without resolution. "Darkness is my closest friend," the psalmist concludes. The Bible does not rush to tie these threads into a neat bow. Instead, it preserves them as legitimate expressions of faith, not its failure. To lament is to hold God to his promises, to refuse cheap comfort.

**The Limits of What We Can Know**

Both the free will defense and the cruciform answer have limits, and intellectual honesty demands we name them. The free will defense may explain why evil is possible, but it does not explain why this particular evil happened to this particular person at this particular time. It cannot tell us why one child is cured and another is not, why one prayer is answered and another echoes into silence. It operates at the level of possibility, not providence.

The cruciform answer is deeper but also more unsettling. It offers us a God who is present in suffering, but it does not guarantee that suffering will be overcome in this life. It promises resurrection, but not always healing. It tells us that God is with us in the abyss, but the abyss remains. This is not a failure of the answer but a feature of it: it refuses to trade real pain for theological comfort.

The temptation is to retreat into mystery: "God's ways are not our ways." This is true, but when offered too quickly, it becomes a conversation-stopper, a way of protecting God from our anger and ourselves from our doubts. The Bible does not use mystery this way. Mystery in Scripture is not an opaque curtain behind which God hides his reasons; it is the overwhelming presence of a reality too large for our categories. God's ways are not our ways not because he is incomprehensibly cruel, but because his love is vaster than our capacity to understand it, and his power is exercised in ways that look like weakness.

What we cannot know, then, is not a loophole but a condition of our creatureliness. We see through a glass darkly. But the darkness is not empty; it is where God meets us. The limit of our understanding is not where faith ends but where it begins—not in certainty, but in trust.

**When Theory Meets the Hospital Room**

All of this raises the crucial pastoral question: what do we actually say to those who suffer? The answer, perhaps, is: very little. The book of Job's greatest lesson is that Job's friends are most helpful when they sit in silence. Their theological speeches, meant to defend God, only deepen Job's isolation. It is when they try to explain his suffering that they become agents of it.

The Christian response to suffering is not first an explanation but a presence. It is the church as the body of Christ, showing up with casseroles and tears, with silence and solidarity. It is the conviction that no one should suffer alone because God himself did not. The cross is not a theory that removes pain; it is a promise that pain is not the final word, and that God is present in it.

This does not mean we abandon intellectual engagement. We need robust theology to resist glib answers. We need to know that the free will defense exists, that the cruciform answer is deep, that Scripture gives us permission to protest. But we also need to know that these are tools for the classroom, not the bedside. At the bedside, what matters is not whether we can explain suffering but whether we can bear it with the sufferer.

**The Unfinished Question**

The problem of suffering remains, in the end, a problem. It is not solved; it is endured. It is not answered; it is transfigured. The Christian claim is not that suffering is good or necessary but that it has been assumed by the God who is goodness itself. The resurrection does not negate the cross; it reveals that love is stronger than death, that presence is deeper than explanation.

This leaves us with a faith that is less like a fortress of certainty and more like a practice of hope. We do not know why particular evils occur, but we know that God has entered them. We do not have a final answer to the problem of suffering, but we have a God who suffers. And perhaps, in the end, that is enough—not because it explains everything, but because it means we are not alone.

The question remains open, but the silence has been broken. Not with a syllogism, but with a scream. Not with a defense, but with a body. The God who is silent is also the God who weeps. And in that weeping, somehow, the world is held.
