It is not theodicy’s hypothetical suffering—the abstract “evil” of the philosophy seminar—but flesh, terror, and the particularity of agony. When we speak of the problem of suffering, we must begin here: not with logical formulations, but with the scream. The question is not merely how God can coexist with evil, but how a God named *Agape* can remain silent while the innocent suffer. This is the question that haunts faith, and any response that does not feel its weight is not a response at all, but an evasion.

**The Dilemma Stated**

The logical problem of evil, as formulated by J.L. Mackie and others, presents a trilemma: if God is omnipotent, omniscient, and wholly good, then evil should not exist. Either God wants to eliminate suffering and cannot (not omnipotent), can but does not want to (not wholly good), or neither can nor wants to (neither). The evidential problem sharpens the point: the sheer quantity and quality of suffering—what Marilyn McCord Adams calls “horrendous evils” that seem to defeat a person’s meaning-making capacity—makes theism improbable, if not impossible.

To be fair to the objection, one must acknowledge that this is not a temper tantrum against a minor disappointment. It is the cry of the mother at Auschwitz watching her child marched toward the gas chamber; the neurologist diagnosing a four-year-old with terminal glioblastoma; the survivor of systematic torture whose faith in humanity has been obliterated. These are not puzzles to be solved but wounds to be witnessed. Any theology that begins with a solution has already betrayed the sufferer.

**The Freedom Defense and Its Shadow**

One traditional response, developed by Augustine and refined by Alvin Plantinga, is the free will defense. Moral goodness, the argument runs, requires libertarian freedom—the capacity to choose love over hatred, fidelity over betrayal. A world containing creatures capable of moral evil is more valuable than a world of automata programmed for benevolence. God, therefore, permits evil as the necessary risk of creating moral agents. Natural evil (disease, earthquake) may be attributed to the free actions of non-human agents or the complex causal conditions required for a law-governed universe capable of supporting free creatures.

There is genuine insight here. Love that is compelled is not love; it is machinery. The possibility of Auschwitz is the dark side of the possibility of Bonhoeffer. Yet the defense buckles under the weight of horrendous evil. First, it struggles to account for the suffering of those who lack moral agency—the infant with congenital agony, the animal burned alive in a forest fire. Second, it risks implying that the value of human freedom outweighs the value of preventing particular atrocities, a calculus that seems morally repugnant when one stands beside the grave of a murdered child. As Elie Wiesel’s narrator observes in *Night*, watching a child slowly hanged by the Gestapo: “Where is God? … He is hanging here on this gallows.” The free will defense offers a reason for the possibility of evil, but it cannot look that child in the face and call it sufficient. Buddhism, for instance, takes suffering (*dukkha*) as its First Noble Truth, yet arrives at radically different conclusions: not the redemption of creation through a suffering God, but the cessation of desire that binds us to the wheel of suffering. It is the slow erosion of chronic pain, the chemical prison of clinical depression, the decade-long fading of a parent into dementia, the quiet despair of poverty that grinds away dignity without the mercy of a climactic moment. The theology that works for the Warsaw Ghetto must also work for the bedroom where someone cannot get out of bed. If our response to evil only addresses the catastrophic, we risk implying that ordinary anguish is spiritually insignificant. The God who hangs on the gallows must also be the God who sits in the waiting room, who lingers in the long years of unremarkable sorrow.

Yet we must acknowledge the limits. For the woman in active labor with a stillborn child, the free will defense is dust and ashes. For the survivor of genocide, the theology of the cross, while confessed, does not restore the lost. There is an apophatic moment in all serious theology of suffering where words must stop. I write this not from a position of safe observation. I have sat in hospital rooms where the only honest prayer was accusation. To use “mystery” as a cop-out, a way to shut down the sufferer’s question, is pastoral malpractice. We are invited to protest like Job, to weep like Jesus, and to hope like Paul, while admitting that we do not yet see how it all fits together.

It is vindicated, if at all, by the figure of the crucified Jew—Jesus of Nazareth—who promises that the last word is not suffering, but resurrection; not the grave, but the empty tomb. I offer this not as a demonstration that settles the question, but as a confession that holds the question in tension. This is not a cheap hope. It does not minimize the horror of the gallows. It offers a Presence that does not always make the scream bearable, but absorbs it into the divine life; and a promise, whispered against the evidence, that the tears are kept, counted, and one day—when the groaning finally gives birth—wiped away. Until then, we wait in the dark with Psalm 88, with Job, with the crucified God, having no answer except the presence of the One who does not look away.

When we speak of the problem of suffering, we must begin here: not with logical formulations, but with the scream. The question is not merely how God can coexist with evil, but how a God named *Agape* can remain silent while the innocent suffer. This is the question that haunts faith, and any response that does not feel its weight is not a response at all, but an evasion.

**The Dilemma Stated**

The logical problem of evil, as formulated by J.L. Mackie and others, presents a trilemma: if God is omnipotent, omniscient, and wholly good, then evil should not exist. Either God wants to eliminate suffering and cannot (not omnipotent), can but does not want to (not wholly good), or neither can nor wants to (neither). The evidential problem sharpens the point: the sheer quantity and quality of suffering—what Marilyn McCord Adams calls “horrendous evils” that seem to defeat a person’s meaning-making capacity—makes theism improbable, if not impossible.

To be fair to the objection, one must acknowledge that this is not a temper tantrum against a minor disappointment. It is the cry of the mother at Auschwitz watching her child marched toward the gas chamber; the neurologist diagnosing a four-year-old with terminal glioblastoma; the survivor of systematic torture whose faith in humanity has been obliterated. Second, it risks implying that the value of human freedom outweighs the value of preventing particular atrocities, a calculus that seems morally repugnant when one stands beside the grave of a murdered child. It explains the metaphysical structure; it does not justify the specific scream.

**The Transformation of the Question**

If the free will defense fails to justify God, perhaps justification is not what is needed. Perhaps the question itself must change. The logical problem assumes a God who stands aloof from suffering, surveying the calculus of greater goods from a safe ontological distance. But what if the premise is wrong? What if God does not stand above the suffering, observing the gallows from a distance, but enters into the godforsakenness of the gallows itself? The question then shifts from “How can God allow this?” to “Where is God in this?” This is not a non-sequitur, not a changing of the subject when the argument grows hard, but a sublation: the categories of the problem are not erased but taken up into a deeper reality. The cross does not offer us the ticket back to a paradise built on suffering—it offers us the God who tears the ticket up and enters the cell with the child.

A second response does not attempt to justify evil but rather locates God within it. This is not a theodicy in the strict sense—a justification of the ways of God to man—but a theology of the cross. Jürgen Moltmann, in *The Crucified God*, argues that the Christian God does not remain detached from suffering. Rather, in the cry of dereliction—“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—the eternal Trinity enters into the godforsakenness of suffering. God becomes the Godforsaken one.

This is not an explanation; it is a relocation. The answer, according to the New Testament, is shockingly particular: God is in the leper’s colony, touching the unclean; God is at the grave of Lazarus, weeping before he resurrects; God is in Gethsemane, sweating blood in anticipatory dread; God is on the cross, experiencing the death of the innocent. The Incarnation does not solve the logical problem of evil, but it destroys the premise that God is indifferent. Theodicy becomes theopathy—suffering with.

Before the cross, there was the Exodus: God’s name revealed to Moses as the one who has *seen* the misery of his people, who has *heard* their cry (*tsa'akah*), and who has *come down* to deliver them (Exodus 3:7-8). This is the biblical pattern: not explanation, but descent. The God of Israel is not a distant architect but one who hears cries. This motif runs through the prophetic tradition—Abraham Heschel’s “God who suffers with humanity”—and finds voice in liberation theologies that refuse to spiritualize oppression, insisting that God sides with the crucified peoples of history. The “crying God” is not merely a metaphysical concept but the one who hears the slave, the widow, the orphan, and the crucified.

Scripture bears this out not through systematic argument but through narrative and lament. The Book of Job, the Bible’s most sustained engagement with innocent suffering, refuses to offer a mechanical explanation. When God finally answers from the whirlwind, he does not explain the wager with the satan, nor does he justify Job’s boils and bereavement with reference to some greater good. Instead, he reveals himself as the wild, untamed Creator who “shuts the sea in with doors” and “gives the horse its might.” It is an answer of presence, not proposition. Job is satisfied not because he understands, but because he has seen God, and in seeing, realizes that the universe is not run by a moral accountant but by a Person who is himself the ground of meaning.

Similarly, the Psalms of lament—Psalm 88 chief among them—do not resolve suffering into spiritual lessons. “You have put me in the lowest pit,” the psalmist accuses, “darkness is my only companion.” There is no happy ending here, no “all things work together for good” closure. Yet these cries are preserved as *prayer*, as legitimate speech to God. The Bible canonizes protest, suggesting that God is big enough to absorb our rage without breaking the covenant. The suffering person is not required to smile and accept; they are invited to scream, and to find that God hears.

**The Limits of Speech and the Space for Doubt**

Yet we must acknowledge the limits. For the woman in active labor with a stillborn child, the free will defense is dust and ashes. For the survivor of genocide, the theology of the cross, while true, does not restore the lost. There is an apophatic moment in all serious theology of suffering where words must stop. Paul writes that “now we see in a mirror dimly”—*en ainigmati*, in riddles. 

For some, the cross is not enough, and the silence is too loud. Faith that survives suffering is not a moral achievement; doubt in the face of horror is not a sin. The theology of the cross must make room for those who, like the disciples on Holy Saturday, have buried God and do not expect resurrection. We must distinguish between the theoretical problem and the existential crisis. When Job’s friends arrive, they sit in silence with him for seven days, and “no one spoke a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was.” It is only when they open their mouths to defend God’s justice with theological arguments that they become “miserable comforters.” The limit of understanding is not an excuse for complacency, but a call to solidarity.

**Eschatology and the Scars of Hope**

This is not to say we should abandon the search for understanding. Theodicy is a necessary discipline, a way of honoring the rationality of faith and the moral seriousness of the question. But we must guard against eschatological escapism. The eschatological hope—Revelation’s promise that God will “wipe every tear from their eyes”—is not a compensation for suffering, as if tears could be traded for tickets to paradise. Such compensation would be unjust, a final insult to the injured. Rather, Christian hope is for *transfiguration*: the taking up of suffering into a new meaning, as in the scars of the resurrected Christ. When Jesus appears to the disciples in Luke’s Gospel, he does not present a perfected, sanitized body, but one that still bears the wounds of the nails and the spear (Luke 24:39-40). These are permanent marks of suffering taken into eternity, not erased but transformed. The tears are not wasted, not because they purchase future bliss, but because they are kept, counted, and one day—against all present evidence—addressed by the hand of the One who still bears the scars.

**Living in the Tension**

So where does this leave us? Not with a solution, but with a posture. We are left with the tension between the *already*—the cross as God’s participation in suffering—and the *not yet*—the groaning of creation awaiting redemption. We are invited to protest like Job, to weep like Jesus, and to hope like Paul, while admitting that we do not yet see how it all fits together.

The goodness of God is not vindicated by a philosophical argument that balances the ledger of pain against the value of freedom. It is vindicated, if at all, by the blood-stained figure of the crucified Jew who promises that the last word is not suffering, but resurrection; not the grave, but the empty tomb. This is not a cheap hope. It does not minimize the horror of the gallows. But it claims that the God who permits the gallows is the God who hangs there, transforming the meaning of suffering from abandonment to solidarity.

In the end, the problem of suffering is not solved; it is suffered. Faith does not offer an explanation that renders the scream unnecessary. It offers a Presence that makes the scream bearable, and a promise that the God who descended into the cry of the slaves, who wept at the tomb of his friend, who screamed in dereliction on the cross, is the same God who will come down again to wipe every tear—every single tear—from eyes that have finally seen the One who saw them all along.

**The Wound and the Whirlwind: Rethinking the Problem of Suffering**

The question is not whether God exists, but whether God can be trusted. When a child dies of leukemia, when torture chambers operate with industrial efficiency, when the tsunami erases a village in the space of a breath, the abstract puzzle of evil becomes a visceral accusation. The problem of suffering is not primarily an intellectual conundrum to be solved like a geometric proof; it is a crisis of relationship. If God is omnipotent and benevolent, then the universe’s cruelty appears to constitute a breach of divine character. The believer stands in the rubble, holding two truths that seem mutually exclusive: that God is good, and that the world is broken. To honor the question, we must resist both the cold comfort of easy answers and the paralysis of despair. We must look at the wound without looking away, and we must listen for God’s voice—not where we expect it, but where Scripture suggests it might actually be heard.

The objection itself deserves its full weight. The logical problem of evil states that the coexistence of an all-powerful, all-loving God and gratuitous suffering is contradictory. If God can prevent suffering but chooses not to, God seems negligent; if God wants to prevent suffering but cannot, God seems impotent. The evidential problem is perhaps more devastating: even if suffering is logically compatible with God’s existence, the sheer volume and distribution of pain—much of it seemingly meaningless, much of it visited upon the innocent—makes theism improbable. Natural evil (disease, disaster) compounds moral evil (violence, cruelty), and together they form a pattern that looks less like the work of a benevolent designer and more like the result of indifferent natural forces or malevolent wills. To wave this away with platitudes about “God’s plan” is not only intellectually dishonest; it is pastorally abusive. It asks the sufferer to endorse their own pain as necessary, thereby doubling the injury by demanding gratitude for the hammer blow.

One classical response, the free will defense, argues that moral evil is the price of a greater good: genuine creaturely freedom. Love, this argument suggests, requires libertarian freedom; a world of automata programmed to do good would lack the moral significance of a world where agents choose love over selfishness. God permits evil not because he desires it, but because he desires the possibility of love more than he desires the elimination of all risk. Alvin Plantinga’s refinement notes that God cannot actualize just any possible world; perhaps in every feasible world with free creatures, some evil occurs. There is something to this. We do intuit that coercion and love are opposites, and that a world without the possibility of betrayal would also lack the possibility of fidelity.

Yet the free will defense, taken alone, rings hollow in the pediatric oncology ward. It explains moral evil—why humans hurt one another—but it struggles with natural evil, the suffering that comes from biology and physics rather than choice. Moreover, it can sound like a justification that privileges abstract metaphysical goods over concrete human pain. If freedom is the reason for the Holocaust, one might reasonably ask whether the cost is too high. The defense is logically suggestive but existentially thin. It tells us that evil is possible, but not why particular evils are permitted, nor how they fit into a narrative of divine love. It is a fence around the mystery, not an entry into it.

A more radical response, and one more native to Christian Scripture, locates God’s answer not in a philosophical principle but in an event: the cross of Jesus. Here, theodicy becomes theophany. The claim is not merely that God suffers *too*, as if divine solidarity were a consolation prize, but that God enters into the godforsakenness of suffering in order to hollow out its center. On Golgotha, the cry of dereliction—“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—is not a performance. It is the Son’s experience of the absence of the Father, the rupture of the divine fellowship itself. If God is the Trinity, then the cross represents a tear in the fabric of deity. This suggests that God does not stand aloof from the problem of pain but submits to it, bearing the full weight of abandonment.

This “answer” does not explain suffering away. It does not tell us why the child died. Instead, it changes the metaphysical location of God. God is not the unmoved spectator offering explanations from the balcony; God is the crucified victim hanging in the darkness. The cross is not a theodicy in the sense of a justification that balances the ledger; it is a demonstration that God’s love is compatible with God’s silence, and that God’s power is revealed not in prevention but in redemption. The resurrection does not erase the cross; it vindicates the love that persisted through the cross. This creates a peculiar epistemological situation: we do not know why the suffering occurred, but we know that God has refused to let it be the final word. The eschatological hope—Revelation’s vision of a new heavens and new earth where tears are wiped away—does not cheapen present pain by calling it “preparation,” but it does place it within a narrative where death is swallowed up, not explained.

Yet even the cross has its limits as an intellectual solution. It tells us who God is in the midst of suffering, but it does not provide a comprehensive causal account. Here, Scripture offers a pattern rather than a proposition. The Book of Job is the canonical text on this matter, and its resolution is famously frustrating. Job demands an audience with the Divine Prosecutor; he receives instead the voice from the whirlwind. God does not explain the wager with the satan, nor justify Job’s losses. God offers a litany of cosmic mysteries: the birth of the mountain goat, the Leviathan’s scales, the storehouses of snow. The answer, such as it is, consists in the overwhelming reality of the Creator’s presence and the contingency of the creature’s knowledge. Job’s response is not comprehension but repentance in dust and ashes—not because he was wrong to protest, but because he encounters a reality that transcends his moral accounting.

This is not a cop-out if we understand it rightly. The acknowledgment of limits is not the same as the dismissal of the question. The Psalms of lament—Psalm 88 chief among them, which ends without resolution, with darkness as the poet’s only companion—give the believer permission to accuse God while remaining in the covenant. Lamentations describes the destruction of Jerusalem with unflinching horror, yet affirms that God’s mercies are new every morning *in the midst of* the wreckage, not after it is cleaned up. The biblical pattern is not stoic acceptance but passionate protest that holds onto relationship even when the relationship seems one-sided. This “protest theodicy,” articulated in modern times by theologians like Dorothee Sölle and Wendy Farley, suggests that the appropriate response to suffering is not speculative justification but prophetic indictment. God is big enough to absorb our rage.

What, then, can be said to the one who suffers? Nothing that competes with the suffering itself. Theodicy is a secondary discourse, appropriate to the study but often obscene at the bedside. The Christian vocation in the face of pain is not primarily to explain but to embody the answer of the cross: presence, solidarity, and the refusal to let the sufferer be alone. We become the body of Christ, the hands and feet that hold the dying, that feed the hungry, that weep with those who weep. This is not a substitute for intellectual honesty, but its completion. If God is love, then love is the only adequate response to the problem of evil; everything else is prologue.

We are left, finally, with a tension that is not fully resolved. The goodness of God and the reality of suffering remain in dialectical opposition. To collapse one into the other—either by declaring suffering illusory (as some forms of idealism do) or by redefining goodness as mere power (as some forms of fatalism do)—is to betray the complexity of human experience. The Christian faith asks us to hold these in suspension: to trust the character of God revealed in the crucified and risen Jesus while acknowledging that the “why” of particular horrors remains hidden in the economy of God’s wisdom, which is not our wisdom. This is not blind faith but wounded faith, a trust that has passed through the valley of the shadow and found that even there, the Shepherd is present—not with explanations, but with rod and staff, with the promise that the tears sown now will be reaped in joy, and that the God who permitted the wound will also be the God who heals it.

If God is omnipotent and benevolent, then the universe’s cruelty appears to constitute a breach of divine character. The believer stands in the rubble, holding two truths that seem mutually exclusive: that God is good, and that the world is broken. To honor the question, we must resist both the cold comfort of easy answers and the paralysis of despair. We must look at the wound without looking away, and we must listen for God’s voice—not where we expect it, but where Scripture suggests it might actually be heard.

The objection itself deserves its full weight. The logical problem of evil states that the coexistence of an all-powerful, all-loving God and gratuitous suffering is contradictory. If God can prevent suffering but chooses not to, God seems negligent; if God wants to prevent suffering but cannot, God seems impotent. The evidential problem is perhaps more devastating: even if suffering is logically compatible with God’s existence, the sheer volume and distribution of pain—much of it seemingly meaningless, much of it visited upon the innocent—makes theism improbable. 

Natural evil presents a particularly sharp challenge. Love, this argument suggests, requires libertarian freedom; a world of automata programmed to do good would lack the moral significance of a world where agents choose love over selfishness. God permits evil not because he desires it, but because he desires the possibility of love more than he desires the elimination of all risk. Alvin Plantinga’s refinement notes that God cannot actualize just any possible world; perhaps in every feasible world with free creatures, some evil occurs. There is something to this. **The Wound and the Whirlwind: Rethinking the Problem of Suffering**

The question is not whether God exists, but whether God can be trusted. When a child dies of leukemia, when torture chambers operate with industrial efficiency, when the tsunami erases a village in the space of a breath, the abstract puzzle of evil becomes a visceral accusation. The problem of suffering is not primarily an intellectual conundrum to be solved like a geometric proof; it is a crisis of relationship. If God is omnipotent and benevolent, then the universe’s cruelty appears to constitute a breach of divine character. The believer stands in the rubble, holding two truths that seem mutually exclusive: that God is good, and that the world is broken. To honor the question, we must resist both the cold comfort of easy answers and the paralysis of despair. We must look at the wound without looking away, and we must listen for God’s voice—not where we expect it, but where Scripture suggests it might actually be heard.

The objection itself deserves its full weight. The logical problem of evil states that the coexistence of an all-powerful, all-loving God and gratuitous suffering is formally contradictory. If God can prevent suffering but chooses not to, God seems negligent; if God wants to prevent suffering but cannot, God seems impotent. The evidential problem is perhaps more devastating: even if suffering is logically compatible with God’s existence, the sheer volume and distribution of pain—much of it seemingly meaningless, much of it visited upon the innocent—makes theism improbable. Natural evil (disease, disaster) compounds moral evil (violence, cruelty), and together they form a pattern that looks less like the work of a benevolent designer and more like the result of indifferent natural forces or malevolent wills. To wave this away with platitudes about “God’s plan” is not only intellectually dishonest; it is pastorally abusive. It asks the sufferer to endorse their own pain as necessary, thereby doubling the injury by demanding gratitude for the hammer blow.

One classical response, the free will defense, argues that moral evil is the price of a greater good: genuine creaturely freedom. Love, this argument suggests, requires libertarian freedom; a world of automata programmed to do good would lack the moral significance of a world where agents choose love over selfishness. God permits evil not because he desires it, but because he desires the possibility of love more than he desires the elimination of all risk. Alvin Plantinga’s refinement notes that God cannot actualize just any possible world; perhaps in every feasible world with free creatures, some evil occurs. There is something to this. We do intuit that coercion and love are opposites, and that a world without the possibility of betrayal would also lack the possibility of fidelity.

Yet the free will defense, taken alone, rings hollow in the pediatric oncology ward. It explains moral evil—why humans hurt one another—but it struggles with natural evil, the suffering that comes from biology and physics rather than choice. Moreover, it can sound like a justification that privileges abstract metaphysical goods over concrete human pain. If freedom is the reason for the Holocaust, one might reasonably ask whether the cost is too high. The defense is logically suggestive but existentially thin. It tells us that evil is possible, but not why particular evils are permitted, nor how they fit into a narrative of divine love. It is a fence around the mystery, not an entry into it.

A related tradition, the Irenaean or “soul-making” theodicy, attempts to address natural evil by arguing that suffering serves as necessary pedagogy. Through hardship, the argument runs, human souls are refined, matured, and prepared for communion with God. Suffering becomes the crucible in which virtue is formed, the chisel that sculpts moral character. While this approach takes seriously the developmental arc of human existence, it too risks becoming a justification that instrumentalizes the victim. It suggests that the child’s cancer is merely educational, that the tsunami’s victims serve as object lessons for survivors. Both the Augustinian free will defense and the Irenaean soul-making approach share a common structure: they attempt to justify particular evils by reference to greater goods. Both, in their own ways, ask the sufferer to accept their pain as part of a cosmic accounting system where the math eventually works out.

The claim is not merely that God suffers *too*, as if divine solidarity were a consolation prize, but that God enters into the godforsakenness of suffering in order to hollow out its center. On Golgotha, the cry of dereliction—“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—is not a performance. It is the Son’s experience of the absence of the Father, the rupture of the divine fellowship itself. If God is the Trinity, then the cross represents a tear in the fabric of deity. This suggests that God does not stand aloof from the problem of pain but submits to it, bearing the full weight of abandonment.

God is not the unmoved spectator offering explanations from the balcony; God is the crucified victim hanging in the darkness. This creates a peculiar epistemological situation: we do not know why the suffering occurred, but we know that God has refused to let it be the final word. When we encounter the suffering other, our vocabulary must shift from explanation to presence. The Christian vocation in the face of pain is not primarily to explain but to embody the answer of the cross: presence, solidarity, and the refusal to let the sufferer be alone. We become the body of Christ, the hands and feet that hold the dying, that feed the hungry, that weep with those who weep. We are called to be the community that refuses to let suffering isolate, that enters into the darkness rather than standing outside it with explanations. This is not blind faith but wounded faith, a trust that has passed through the valley of the shadow and found that even there, the Shepherd is present—not with explanations, but with rod and staff, with the promise that the tears sown now will be reaped in joy, and that the God who entered into the wound will also be the God who brings the final healing.

# The Wound and the Word: Rethinking the Problem of Suffering

## I. The Honest Question

The problem of suffering is not an abstract puzzle for philosophers to solve between seminars. It arrives uninvited at 3 a.m. in hospital corridors, in the hollow silence after a phone call, in the accumulated weight of ordinary griefs that never quite resolve. It is the question that refuses to stay theoretical: If God is both all-powerful and all-loving, why?

This is the logical problem of evil in its most visceral form, and it deserves more than dismissal. The ancient philosopher Epicurus framed it with surgical precision: God either wishes to prevent evil and cannot, or can and will not, or neither wishes nor can, or both wishes and can. The first two options deny divine omnipotence or benevolence; the last two seem to make God either malevolent or unnecessary. The Christian tradition has wrestled with this trilemma for millennia, and honest engagement requires acknowledging its genuine force. To suffer is to experience something that cries out for explanation, for redemption, for meaning. When that cry meets silence, faith itself trembles.

Yet the problem has a shape that pure logic cannot fully capture. Philosophers distinguish between natural evil (suffering from disease, disaster, death) and moral evil (suffering inflicted by human choice). The Holocaust survivor and Nobel laureate Elie Wiesel, writing of children consumed in Auschwitz's flames, recorded not a logical puzzle but a shattered covenant: "Never shall I forget those moments which murdered my God and my soul and turned my dreams to dust." This is the problem of suffering as lived experience—where the intellectual difficulty and the existential wound are inseparable.

## II. The Free Will Defense and Its Limits

Among the most influential philosophical responses stands the free will defense, developed with particular rigor by Alvin Plantinga. The argument proceeds thus: genuine love requires freedom; freedom requires the possibility of choosing evil; God cannot create free creatures and simultaneously guarantee they never sin. Moral evil, then, is the price of moral significance. A world with free creatures who sometimes choose badly is better than a world of deterministic automata, even if that world contains genuine horror.

There is something theologically attractive here. Scripture presents human beings as bearing the *imago Dei* precisely through our capacity for relationship, for covenant, for response. The prophets do not treat Israel's sin as mechanical failure but as broken faithfulness, genuine betrayal of genuine love. Deuteronomy 30:19 places before the people "life and death, blessings and curses," urging them to "choose life"—a choice that presupposes real alternatives. The free will defense captures this biblical intuition that love without freedom is not love.

Yet the defense faces significant limitations when pressed against the full reality of suffering. First, it addresses moral evil more naturally than natural evil. The freedom of the cancer cell, the tectonic plate, the mutating virus—these strain the analogy. Plantinga and others have extended the argument to suggest that natural evil may result from the free choices of non-human agents (demonic forces), or that natural laws consistent with moral agency necessarily produce some suffering. These extensions, while logically possible, carry an air of speculation that weakens their pastoral usefulness.

More fundamentally, the free will defense can sound, in certain formulations, like a justification of suffering rather than an explanation. When Job's friends arrive, they speak truths about divine justice that are not entirely false—yet their application to Job's particular agony constitutes a second wound. The defense must guard against becoming, in practice, a theodicy that explains away what needs to be lamented. Scripture itself offers a check here: the same tradition that affirms human freedom also contains the passionate complaint of the psalmist ("Why, O LORD, do you stand far off?"), the accusation of Habakkuk ("Why do you make me look at injustice?"), and the unanswerable silence that meets Job from the whirlwind.

## III. Soul-Making and the Cruciform God

A second major response, the soul-making theodicy associated with John Hick, shifts the frame from static perfection to dynamic transformation. Drawing on Irenaeus rather than Augustine, Hick suggests that God created an "epistemic distance" between divine reality and human experience precisely to allow for the development of genuine moral character. Suffering, on this view, is not merely permitted but instrumentally necessary for the formation of souls capable of genuine love, courage, patience, and compassion. We are created "in the image of God" but must grow into the "likeness of God" through the refining fire of experience.

This approach resonates with significant biblical themes. Romans 5:3-5 speaks of suffering producing endurance, endurance character, and character hope. James 1:2-4 instructs believers to "consider it pure joy" when facing trials, because "the testing of your faith produces perseverance." The metaphor of refinement—gold tested in fire, silver purified—appears throughout Scripture as a description of how God shapes his people. The soul-making theodicy takes seriously that we are not finished products but works in progress, and that progress often requires difficulty.

Yet this theodicy, too, must be handled with care. There is a profound difference between saying that God can redeem suffering and saying that God needs suffering to accomplish his purposes. The first is gospel; the second can become a kind of metaphysical calculus where individual agony is justified by aggregate spiritual growth. Ivan Karamazov's refusal to accept the harmony of the world at the price of one child's tears retains its moral force. Scripture itself contains the warning: "See that no one repays anyone evil for evil" (1 Thessalonians 5:15)—a command that presumes the possibility of growth without requiring evil as its instrument.

Here the cross becomes not merely one element in a theodicy but the redefinition of divine power and love itself. The Apostle Paul writes that "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:18). This is not simply that God permits suffering for greater goods, but that God enters into suffering, takes it upon himself, transforms it from within. The crucified God is not a solution to the problem of evil in the sense of an explanation that dissolves the mystery. Rather, the cross is God's answer in the sense of a personal response: I am here. I do not abandon you to it. I make it my own.

This is theologically decisive. The God who could prevent suffering but chooses instead to participate in it is not the distant watchmaker of deism, nor the manipulative architect of some theodicies. The cry of dereliction—"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—is not play-acting but genuine abandonment, the Son experiencing the full weight of divine silence so that divine silence might never be the last word. The resurrection does not erase the cross but transfigures it: the wounds remain visible in the risen body (Luke 24:39-40), now signs not of defeat but of the depth of love's penetration into human darkness.

## IV. The Limits of Understanding and the Practice of Lament

To acknowledge these theological resources is not to claim they dissolve the mystery. The book of Job, the most extended biblical treatment of innocent suffering, ends not with explanation but with encounter. God speaks from the whirlwind not to justify the divine management of the universe but to declare: "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" (Job 38:4). This is not evasion but perspective—the recognition that the creature's standpoint is necessarily limited, that the full weave of providence exceeds our capacity to trace its patterns.

Yet this limitation must not become a cop-out, a pious refusal to engage with real questions. Scripture models something more complex: sustained, even aggressive lament that never receives direct answer. The psalms of complaint (roughly one-third of the Psalter) do not resolve into easy trust. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). "Why do you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 88:14). These are preserved in Scripture not as embarrassing relics of immature faith but as normative expressions of covenant relationship. The God who invites such speech—who can bear the accusation, who does not strike the complainer dead—is different from the God of philosophical abstraction.

This suggests a posture toward suffering that is neither explanation nor resignation but participation. The Christian community is called to be, in some measure, the body of the crucified and risen Lord—bearing one another's burdens, weeping with those who weep, practicing the presence of God in the midst of absence. The church's task is not to solve the problem of evil but to be God's response to it: hands that heal, voices that comfort, presence that refuses the isolation suffering often imposes.

## V. Conclusion: Living with the Wound

The problem of suffering, honestly faced, does not admit of final theoretical resolution this side of eschatology. What the Christian tradition offers is not a solution but a witness: to a God who creates freedom and bears its cost, who permits the possibility of tragedy and enters into its reality, who promises the redemption of all things without explaining away the particular grief of each thing. This is intellectually modest—acknowledging the limits of human cognition—without being intellectually lazy. It is pastorally serious—attending to real wounds—without being sentimentally evasive.

The eschatological vision of Scripture—"He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain" (Revelation 21:4)—does not render present suffering illusory. Rather, it establishes that suffering is not ultimate, that the God who permits it has committed himself to its abolition, and that this commitment has been sealed in blood and vindicated in resurrection. To believe this is not to understand suffering but to trust the one who has suffered, to hope that the wound and the word, the cross and the empty tomb, constitute a promise that will not be broken.

In the end, the most honest response to the problem of suffering may be the one offered by the apostle Paul, writing from prison, acquainted with beatings and shipwreck and betrayal: "I consider that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us" (Romans 8:18). This is not a calculation but a conviction, born of encounter with the crucified and risen one. It is faith seeking understanding, not understanding that has mastered faith. And for those who suffer—and all of us will—it may be enough, or nearly enough, to know that the God who could explain everything has chosen instead to be with us in everything, until the morning breaks and the shadows flee away.

# The Thorn and the Thorn-Bearer: Reflections on Suffering and the Goodness of God

---

There is a moment in every serious encounter with suffering when the abstractions collapse. It comes when the phone rings at three in the morning, when the diagnosis arrives, when the casket is lowered into the ground. The theological categories we have assembled to explain pain suddenly feel like furniture in an earthquake—solid until the shaking starts. And yet we must think about these things, not because thinking can undo suffering, but because the question of God's goodness in the face of suffering is the question that will find us whether we seek it or not. It is the question the psalmist hurled at the heavens, the question that drove Job from his comfortable certainties, the question that echoes in the silence of every hospital room.

The problem, often called the logical problem of evil, can be stated simply. If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good—as the great monotheistic traditions have consistently affirmed—then why does suffering exist? An omnipotent God could prevent it. An omniscient God would know how to prevent it. A perfectly good God would will to prevent it. Yet suffering is everywhere: the child born into agony, the earthquake that swallows villages, the slow cruelty of disease, the moral monstrosity of evil acts that shatter lives. The logical structure seems airtight. Either God is not all-powerful, or not all-knowing, or not good—or, perhaps most troubling of all, God simply does not care.

I want to take this objection seriously, because it deserves seriousness. It is not a trick question. It is the cry of every person who has looked at the world's pain and asked whether anything like the Christian God can make sense of it. To dismiss it as mere intellectualism is to misunderstand both the question and those who ask it.

---

One of the most influential responses has been the free will defense, associated particularly with Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs, roughly, that God created human beings with genuine freedom—the capacity to choose rightly or wrongly, to love or to wound. A world containing free agents will necessarily be a world where some of those agents choose to harm others. The suffering in the world, on this view, is not directly caused by God but is an indirect consequence of creating beings capable of genuine moral agency. To eliminate suffering by overriding human freedom would be to eliminate the very thing that makes love and goodness possible. You cannot force someone to be good; coerced virtue is not virtue at all.

There is genuine insight here. We know that much human suffering is caused by human cruelty, greed, and indifference. Wars, abuse, exploitation—these are not natural disasters but the fruit of human choices. The free will defense names something real: we are not merely victims of circumstance; we are also perpetrators. And it preserves a crucial theological claim—that genuine love requires freedom, and that a world worth creating is a world where real choices matter.

And yet the defense feels incomplete. It accounts well for moral evil—the suffering caused by human wrongdoing—but struggles with natural evil. What of the child born with a terminal illness? What of the earthquake that kills thousands who had no choice in anything? What of the cancer that visits the righteous and the unrighteous alike? The free will defense has responses here too—perhaps natural evil is the result of a fallen creation, the consequence of cosmic rebellion—but these responses introduce their own complexities. At some point, the defender must confront the question: could God not have created a world where free beings exist but where the consequences of bad choices are less catastrophic? The defense illuminates one dimension of the problem without resolving all of it.

---

A different approach, associated with the second-century theologian Irenaeus, is sometimes called the soul-making theodicy or the "vale of soul-making." On this view, the world is not a finished product but a place of spiritual development. Suffering, while not good in itself, serves to forge character, to draw us deeper, to teach us compassion and resilience. The famous passage from Romans 8—"the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of birth until now"—suggests a world in labor, bringing forth something that does not yet exist. Pain is the fire in which souls are refined.

This theodicy has biblical resonance. The letter to the Hebrews speaks of discipline, of training, of a Father who uses trials to shape his children. The psalms of lament frequently testify that suffering drives the psalmist to deeper dependence on God. There is something true here: many of us have grown through difficulty, discovered depths we did not know we possessed, found that our suffering became the raw material for compassion toward others.

But we must be careful. This theodicy can become monstrous if pressed too far. It implies that the suffering has a purpose proportionate to the good it produces—and that calculation is morally precarious. What purpose could justify a child's agony? What refinement could make sense of the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy works best as a partial insight, not a comprehensive answer. It tells us that God can bring good from suffering—which is a word of hope—but it does not explain why that particular suffering was necessary, or why the universe was designed in such a way that suffering would be the primary tool of spiritual growth.

---

Perhaps the most distinctive Christian response is not a theodicy at all but a theopractic—the claim that God has entered into suffering himself. The cross is not merely an explanation of suffering; it is God's presence within it. In Jesus of Nazareth, the eternal God takes on flesh, experiences pain, endures betrayal, abandonment, and death. The doctrine of the incarnation means that God does not stand safely outside our anguish, offering explanations. God is in it with us.

This is deeply significant. It means that the Christian faith does not promise that suffering will be explained away. It promises something perhaps more radical: that God is not indifferent. That in the deepest darkness, God is present. The resurrection does not undo the cross; it vindicates the one who endured it. And so the Christian hope is not for a pain-free existence but for a day when God will wipe every tear from every eye—when suffering will be redeemed, not merely removed.

The biblical witness here is not triumphalist. The psalms of lament—psalms of protest, of anger, of desperate questioning—make up a substantial portion of the Psalter. Job's friends offer their explanations, and God responds not with an answer but with a question: "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" (Job 38:4). The book of Job does not explain suffering; it refuses to reduce it to a formula. And yet Job's final word is not explanation but encounter: "My ears had heard of you but now my eyes have seen you" (Job 42:5). The mystery remains, but the one who sits with us in the mystery is not himself mysterious in his love.

---

I have offered these perspectives not because any of them resolves the problem but because each names something true. The free will defense reminds us that much suffering is the fruit of human freedom—and that freedom is worth having, even at a cost. The soul-making theodicy testifies that God can bring good from darkness, that suffering can become the seed of virtue. The cross declares that God is with us in our pain, that love goes all the way down.

But I want to be honest: these are not answers that satisfy everyone, and they should not be presented as such. A mother watching her child die of cancer is not helped by being told that her suffering is contributing to her character development. The survivor of abuse is not consoled by learning about the value of free will. The theological responses we offer must be offered with trembling hands, with the awareness that words can wound even when intended to heal.

What can be said? Perhaps this: that the problem of suffering is not a problem we are meant to solve but a mystery we are meant to live within. The Christian tradition has never claimed to explain suffering; it has claimed something more audacious—that God is present in it, that it is not the last word, and that one day it will be redeemed. The cross stands at the center of this faith, and it does not explain suffering; it enters into it.

And perhaps that is enough, though it does not feel like enough. Perhaps the honest answer is that we see through a glass darkly, that we know only in part, that the full answer will come only when all things are restored. In the meantime, we are called not to explain suffering but to alleviate it, to be the hands and feet of a God who enters into our pain. The question is not finally "why do we suffer?" but "how will we respond to those who suffer?" Theodicy becomes ethics; explanation becomes compassion.

I do not know why your particular suffering is in your life. I do not know why this loss, this illness, this grief. But I know that you are not alone, and that the one who made you did not spare his own Son from suffering, and that what was true in the garden and on the cross is true now: that even in the darkest night, God is with us. That is not an answer. But it is the beginning of one.

# The Thorn and the Thorn-Bearer: Reflections on Suffering and the Goodness of God

---

There is a moment in every serious encounter with suffering when the abstractions collapse. It comes when the phone rings at three in the morning, when the diagnosis arrives, when the casket is lowered into the ground. The theological categories we have assembled to explain pain suddenly feel like furniture in an earthquake—solid until the shaking starts. And yet we must think about these things, not because thinking can undo suffering, but because the question of God's goodness in the face of suffering is the question that will find us whether we seek it or not. It is the question the psalmist hurled at the heavens, the question that drove Job from his comfortable certainties, the question that echoes in the silence of every hospital room.

The problem, often called the logical problem of evil, can be stated simply. If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good—as the great monotheistic traditions have consistently affirmed—then why does suffering exist? An omnipotent God could prevent it. An omniscient God would know how to prevent it. A perfectly good God would will to prevent it. Yet suffering is everywhere: the child born into agony, the earthquake that swallows villages, the slow cruelty of disease, the moral monstrosity of evil acts that shatter lives. The logical structure seems airtight. Either God is not all-powerful, or not all-knowing, or not good—or, perhaps most troubling of all, God simply does not care.

I want to take this objection seriously, because it deserves seriousness. It is not a trick question. It is the cry of every person who has looked at the world's pain and asked whether anything like the Christian God can make sense of it. To dismiss it as mere intellectualism is to misunderstand both the question and those who ask it.

---

One of the most influential responses has been the free will defense, associated particularly with Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs, roughly, that God created human beings with genuine freedom—the capacity to choose rightly or wrongly, to love or to wound. A world containing free agents will necessarily be a world where some of those agents choose to harm others. The suffering in the world, on this view, is not directly caused by God but is an indirect consequence of creating beings capable of genuine moral agency. To eliminate suffering by overriding human freedom would be to eliminate the very thing that makes love and goodness possible. You cannot force someone to be good; coerced virtue is not virtue at all.

There is genuine insight here. We know that much human suffering is caused by human cruelty, greed, and indifference. Wars, abuse, exploitation—these are not natural disasters but the fruit of human choices. The free will defense names something real: we are not merely victims of circumstance; we are also perpetrators. And it preserves a crucial theological claim—that genuine love requires freedom, and that a world worth creating is a world where real choices matter.

And yet the defense feels incomplete. It accounts well for moral evil—the suffering caused by human wrongdoing—but struggles with natural evil. What of the child born with a terminal illness? What of the earthquake that kills thousands who had no choice in anything? What of the cancer that visits the righteous and the unrighteous alike? The free will defense has responses here too—perhaps natural evil is the result of a fallen creation, the consequence of cosmic rebellion—but these responses introduce their own complexities. At some point, the defender must confront the question: could God not have created a world where free beings exist but where the consequences of bad choices are less catastrophic? The defense illuminates one dimension of the problem without resolving all of it.

---

A different approach, associated with the second-century theologian Irenaeus, is sometimes called the soul-making theodicy or the "vale of soul-making." On this view, the world is not a finished product but a place of spiritual development. Suffering, while not good in itself, serves to forge character, to draw us deeper, to teach us compassion and resilience. The famous passage from Romans 8—"the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of birth until now"—suggests a world in labor, bringing forth something that does not yet exist. Pain is the fire in which souls are refined.

This theodicy has biblical resonance. The letter to the Hebrews speaks of discipline, of training, of a Father who uses trials to shape his children. The psalms of lament frequently testify that suffering drives the psalmist to deeper dependence on God. There is something true here: many of us have grown through difficulty, discovered depths we did not know we possessed, found that our suffering became the raw material for compassion toward others.

But we must be careful. This theodicy can become monstrous if pressed too far. It implies that the suffering has a purpose proportionate to the good it produces—and that calculation is morally precarious. What purpose could justify a child's agony? What refinement could make sense of the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy works best as a partial insight, not a comprehensive answer. It tells us that God can bring good from suffering—which is a word of hope—but it does not explain why that particular suffering was necessary, or why the universe was designed in such a way that suffering would be the primary tool of spiritual growth.

---

And then there is the tradition of protest—the refusal to let God off the hook. The psalms of lament make up a substantial portion of the Psalter, and they do not politely ask God for patience. Psalm 13 begins, "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" This is not the quiet questioning of the curious; it is the howl of the wounded. The psalmist does not wait for an answer before bringing complaint; complaint itself is the prayer. The Hebrew prophets carried this tradition forward, demanding that God account for the suffering of the vulnerable, insisting that injustice cries out to heaven.

This "complaint faith," as theologians like Walter Brueggemann have called it, does not seek to explain suffering but to protest it—and in protesting, to maintain that God is indeed the kind of God who can be addressed, who can be challenged, who hears the cry of the afflicted. The alternative to protest is not peace but silence, not faith but resignation. And so the biblical tradition gives permission for rage, for questioning, for the kind of honesty that refuses to dress grief in the borrowed clothes of easy assurance.

---

Perhaps the most distinctive Christian response is not a theodicy at all but a theopractic—the claim that God has entered into suffering himself. The cross is not merely an explanation of suffering; it is God's presence within it. In Jesus of Nazareth, the eternal God takes on flesh, experiences pain, endures betrayal, abandonment, and death. The doctrine of the incarnation means that God does not stand safely outside our anguish, offering explanations. God is in it with us.

The traditional doctrine of divine impassibility—the claim that God cannot suffer—must be taken seriously and then set aside. If God cannot suffer, then the incarnation becomes meaningless; God remains eternally detached from our pain. But the mystery of the incarnation is precisely this: the eternal Son, "though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6-7). The kenosis—the self-emptying—is not merely the assumption of human nature but participation in human vulnerability, including the vulnerability of suffering and death. The Father abandons the Son; the Son feels the weight of separation. The answer to suffering is not a theory but a broken body and a broken relationship that God himself enters.

The Christian hope is not for a pain-free existence but for a day when God will wipe every tear from every eye—when suffering will be redeemed, not merely removed.

I want to know why God's plan required my son's blood." Her question wasn't theoretical—it was a mother's howl against the heavens. The church's job wasn't to answer her but to sit with her, to create space where her rage could exist alongside their shared hope. This is what it means to be the body of Christ in a suffering world: not to explain but to accompany, not to resolve but to remain.

---

I have offered these perspectives not because any of them resolves the problem but because each names something true. The free will defense reminds us that much suffering is the fruit of human freedom—and that freedom is worth having, even at a cost. The soul-making theodicy testifies that God can bring good from darkness, that suffering can become the seed of virtue. The tradition of protest insists that our questions are heard, that faith can hold anger and trust together. The cross declares that God is with us in our pain, that love goes all the way down.

But I want to be honest: these are not answers that satisfy everyone, and they should not be presented as such. A mother watching her child die of cancer is not helped by being told that her suffering is contributing to her character development. The survivor of abuse is not consoled by learning about the value of free will. The theological responses we offer must be offered with trembling hands, with the awareness that words can wound even when intended to heal.

What can be said? Perhaps this: that the problem of suffering is not a problem we are meant to solve but a mystery we are meant to live within. The Christian tradition has never claimed to explain suffering; it has claimed something more audacious—that God is present in it, that it is not the last word, and that one day it will be redeemed. The cross stands at the center of this faith, and it does not explain suffering; it enters into it.

We live, then, in the Saturday between Good Friday and Easter Sunday—between the reality of cross-shaped suffering and the promise of resurrection. This Saturday space is where most of life is lived, where we neither deny the reality of pain nor relinquish the hope of redemption. Our calling is not to resolve this tension but to live faithfully within it, becoming the kind of people who can hold both honest lament and genuine hope without rushing to synthesize them.

In the meantime, we are called not to explain suffering but to alleviate it, to be the hands and feet of a God who enters into our pain. The question is not finally "why do we suffer?" but "how will we respond to those who suffer?" Theodicy becomes ethics; explanation becomes compassion.

The soul-making theodicy testifies that God can bring good from darkness, that suffering can become the seed of virtue. The cross declares that God is with us in our pain, that love goes all the way down.

But I want to be honest: these are not answers that satisfy everyone, and they should not be presented as such. A mother watching her child die of cancer is not helped by being told that her suffering is contributing to her character development. The survivor of abuse is not consoled by learning about the value of free will. The theological responses we offer must be offered with trembling hands, with the awareness that words can wound even when intended to heal.

What can be said? Perhaps this: that the problem of suffering is not a problem we are meant to solve but a mystery we are meant to live within. The Christian tradition has never claimed to explain suffering; it has claimed something more audacious—that God is present in it, that it is not the last word, and that one day it will be redeemed. The cross stands at the center of this faith, and it does not explain suffering; it enters into it.

And perhaps that is enough, though it does not feel like enough. Perhaps the honest answer is that we see through a glass darkly, that we know only in part, that the full answer will come only when all things are restored. In the meantime, we are called not to explain suffering but to alleviate it, to be the hands and feet of a God who enters into our pain. The question is not finally "why do we suffer?" but "how will we respond to those who suffer?" Theodicy becomes ethics; explanation becomes compassion.

I do not know why your particular suffering is in your life. I do not know why this loss, this illness, this grief. But I know that you are not alone, and that the one who made you did not spare his own Son from suffering, and that what was true in the garden and on the cross is true now: that even in the darkest night, God is with us. That is not an answer. But it is the beginning of one.

# The Unanswered Question: Suffering and the God Who Is With Us

---

There is a moment in every serious encounter with suffering when the abstractions collapse. It comes when the phone rings at three in the morning, when the diagnosis arrives, when the casket is too small. Consider the child with Tay-Sachs disease, born seemingly healthy, who begins to lose ground at six months—losing the ability to turn over, to swallow, to see—while parents watch helplessly for years until finally, at three or four, the small body surrenders. Consider the 2011 tsunami in Japan that swept away entire families, the ocean indifferent to the grandmother holding her grandchildren, the office worker walking home. Consider the slow creep of dementia that erases a beloved parent while they still breathe. These are not abstractions. They are the texture of human existence, and they resist every theological category we assemble to explain them.

The problem, often called the logical problem of evil, can be stated simply. If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good—as the great monotheistic traditions have consistently affirmed—then why does suffering exist? An omnipotent God could prevent it. An omniscient God would know how to prevent it. A perfectly good God would will to prevent it. Yet suffering is everywhere: the child born into agony, the earthquake that swallows villages, the slow cruelty of disease, the moral monstrosity of evil acts that shatter lives. The logical structure seems airtight. Either God is not all-powerful, or not all-knowing, or not good—or, perhaps most troubling of all, God simply does not care.

But there is a deeper form of this problem that haunts the thoughtful believer. It is not merely logical but *evidential*. Even if we can conceive of a world where God and suffering coexist, the sheer scale and apparent gratuitousness of that suffering makes God's existence improbable. Not impossible, but improbable. The child with cancer. The earthquake that hits the hospital but spares the casino. The Holocaust. The daily cruelties that seem to serve no purpose whatsoever. This is the weight that presses upon faith—not that God *cannot* exist alongside suffering, but that the evidence of the world makes God's existence deeply implausible.

I want to take this objection seriously, because it deserves seriousness. It is not a trick question. It is the cry of every person who has looked at the world's pain and asked whether anything like the Christian God can make sense of it. And I want to sit with this problem longer than we usually allow, because the temptation is always to rush to answers, and sometimes the most honest thing is to name the abyss. If these three attributes cannot coexist with this world, then perhaps the most honest move is to question the attributes themselves. But that is not the only move. Let us see what resources the tradition offers—and where those resources fail.

---

One of the most influential responses has been the free will defense, associated particularly with Alvin Plantinga. The argument runs, roughly, that God created human beings with genuine *libertarian* freedom—the capacity to choose rightly or wrongly, to love or to wound, in ways that are not determined by prior causes. A world containing free agents will necessarily be a world where some of those agents choose to harm others. The suffering in the world, on this view, is not directly caused by God but is an indirect consequence of creating beings capable of genuine moral agency. To eliminate suffering by overriding human freedom would be to eliminate the very thing that makes love and goodness possible. You cannot force someone to be good; coerced virtue is not virtue at all.

Plantinga goes further. He argues that even God cannot create a world containing free agents without also permitting some of those agents to choose evil—a condition he calls "transworld depravity." If libertarian freedom is a genuine good, then its misuse is a real possibility that God must permit, not because God wills evil but because the good of free love requires the risk of its distortion.

There is genuine insight here. We know that much human suffering is caused by human cruelty, greed, and indifference. Wars, abuse, exploitation—these are not natural disasters but the fruit of human choices. The free will defense names something real: we are not merely victims of circumstance; we are also perpetrators. And it preserves a crucial theological claim—that genuine love requires freedom, and that a world worth creating is a world where real choices matter.

And yet the defense feels incomplete. It accounts well for moral evil—the suffering caused by human wrongdoing—but struggles with natural evil. What of the child born with a terminal illness? What of the earthquake that kills thousands who had no choice in anything? What of the cancer that visits the righteous and the unrighteous alike? The free will defense has responses here too—perhaps natural evil is the result of a fallen creation, the consequence of cosmic rebellion—but these responses introduce their own complexities. At some point, the defender must confront the question: could God not have created a world where free beings exist but where the consequences of bad choices are less catastrophic?

And we must also hear the critique from those who have suffered most acutely. As womanist theologian Delores Williams reminds us, talk of "soul-making" can be particularly damaging for those whose suffering under oppression has been theorized as redemptive—the slave who was told her suffering was refining her, the woman abused who was told her trials were making her stronger. The free will defense illuminates one dimension of the problem without resolving all of it.

---

A different approach, associated with the second-century theologian Irenaeus, is sometimes called the soul-making theodicy or the "vale of soul-making." But we must be careful: Irenaeus's view is not simply that suffering refines us like fire refining gold. For Irenaeus, humanity was created not perfect but *perfectible*—immature beings made in the image of God (*imago Dei*) but not yet in full likeness (*similitudo Dei*). We must grow into our calling through free response to God's invitation. The world is a pedagogical space, a place where souls are formed through the challenges necessary for moral and spiritual maturity. Suffering, on this view, is not the primary tool of refinement but rather the inevitable consequence of existing in a world where we must choose for ourselves whether to align with God's purposes.

The biblical resonance here is significant. The letter to the Hebrews speaks of discipline in a specific passage—chapter 12, verses 5-11—where the word *paideia* is better translated as "child-training" than as "punishment." God trains his children as a father trains a son, not to cause pain but to produce "a harvest of righteousness and peace" (Heb 12:11). The psalms of lament frequently testify that suffering drives the psalmist to deeper dependence on God. There is something true here: many of us have grown through difficulty, discovered depths we did not know we possessed, found that our suffering became the raw material for compassion toward others.

But we must be honest: this theodicy can become monstrous if pressed too far. It implies that the suffering has a purpose proportionate to the good it produces—and that calculation is morally precarious. What purpose could justify a child's agony? What refinement could make sense of the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy works best as a partial insight, not a comprehensive answer. It tells us that God can bring good from suffering—which is a word of hope—but it does not explain why that particular suffering was necessary, or why the universe was designed in such a way that suffering would be a tool of growth at all.

---

Perhaps the most distinctive Christian response is not a theodicy but a theology of divine solidarity—the claim that God has entered into suffering himself. The cross is not merely an explanation of suffering; it is God's presence within it. In Jesus of Nazareth, the eternal God takes on flesh, experiences pain, endures betrayal, abandonment, and death. The doctrine of the incarnation means that God does not stand safely outside our anguish, offering explanations. God is in it with us.

This is deeply significant. It means that the Christian faith does not promise that suffering will be explained away. It promises something perhaps more radical: that God is not indifferent. That in the deepest darkness, God is present. As Jürgen Moltmann put it in *The Crucified God*, the cross reveals a God who is not impassible in the traditional sense but who suffers *with* and *for* us—a God whose love is kenotic, self-emptying, going all the way down into the depths of godforsakenness. The resurrection does not undo the cross; it vindicates the one who endured it. And so the Christian hope is not for a pain-free existence but for a day when God will wipe every tear from every eye—when suffering will be redeemed, not merely removed.

The biblical witness here is not triumphalist. The psalms of lament—psalms of protest, of anger, of desperate questioning—make up a substantial portion of the Psalter. The psalmist's "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a question seeking data but a cry of abandonment. Christian faith must make room for the experience of divine hiddenness, not just divine presence. When Job's friends offer their explanations, God responds not with an answer but with a question: "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" (Job 38:4). But God's whirlwind speech doesn't refuse explanation; it reframes it. The answer is not a reason but a relationship: the Creator who governs a world too complex for human moral calculus is trustworthy because he is *good*, not because we understand. And Job's final word is not explanation but encounter: "My ears had heard of you but now my eyes have seen you" (Job 42:5). The mystery remains, but the one who sits with us in the mystery is not himself mysterious in his love.

When asked about the tower of Siloam, Jesus refuses to assign blame but says, "Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish" (Luke 13:5). The move is not explanation but eschatological redirection: suffering's urgency is moral, not metaphysical. And Romans 8 does not minimize suffering—Paul says creation is in "the pains of childbirth" and that we "groan" with the Spirit—but he anchors hope not in suffering's purpose but in God's *future* that makes present affliction "light and momentary" (2 Cor 4:17). The Spirit himself intercedes for us with "groanings too deep for words" (Rom 8:26).

---

I have offered these perspectives not because any of them resolves the problem but because each names something true. The free will defense reminds us that much suffering is the fruit of human freedom—and that freedom is worth having, even at a cost. The soul-making theodicy testifies that God can bring good from darkness, that suffering can become the seed of virtue. The theology of the cross declares that God is with us in our pain, that love goes all the way into the depths.

But I want to be honest: these are not answers that satisfy everyone, and they should not be presented as such. A mother watching her child die of cancer is not helped by being told that her suffering is contributing to her character development. The survivor of abuse is not consoled by learning about the value of free will. The theological responses we offer must be offered with trembling hands, with the awareness that words can wound even when intended to heal. And we must confess that too often the church has been a source of suffering, wielding these very answers as weapons against the vulnerable.

What can be said? Perhaps this: that the problem of suffering is not a problem we are meant to solve but a mystery we are meant to live within. The Christian tradition has never claimed to explain suffering; it has claimed something more audacious—that God is present in it, that it is not the last word, and that one day it will be redeemed. The cross stands at the center of this faith, and it does not explain suffering; it enters into it.

This shift from explanation to presence is not a failure of nerve but a theological necessity. If God is love, and love is *kenotic* (Phil 2:7), then God's answer to suffering cannot be a proposition but a self-emptying presence. Thus the question morphs: not "Why?" but "How will we embody this presence for others?" Theodicy becomes ethics; explanation becomes compassion.

I do not know why your particular suffering is in your life. I do not know why this loss, this illness, this grief. But I know that you are not alone, and that the one who made you did not spare his own Son from suffering, and that what was true in the garden and on the cross is true now: that even in the darkest night, God is with us. This is not a claim that erases your loneliness, but it is a promise that the God who may feel absent in feeling is yet present in fact—and that one day, every tear will be wiped away, and what was lost will be found, and the silence will become a song. That is not an answer that silences the question, but it is the promise that the question is not asked into a void.

The free will defense reminds us that much suffering is the fruit of human freedom—and that freedom is worth having, even at a cost. The theological responses we offer must be offered with trembling hands, with the awareness that words can wound even when intended to heal.

The question "why?" remains a legitimate question, and we who suffer are permitted—indeed, invited—to hurl it at God with all the ferocity of the psalmist who cries, "Awake, Lord! Why do you sleep?" It claims something more radical: that God will heal its wounds so completely that the former things will not come to mind—not because they were good, but because God's future goodness overwhelms them. This is not an explanation. But it is the beginning of one. And for those of us walking through the valley, it may be enough to know that we do not walk alone, that the one who made us did not spare his own Son from suffering, and that even now, in the darkest night, God is with us.
