# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a man I know who lost his daughter to cancer at age seven. He is not angry, exactly, but he is tired—tired of people telling him God has a plan, tired of being assured that his little girl is "with Jesus now," as if that console him for the absence of her laughter in his house. He does not doubt God's existence; he doubts God's goodness. And when I sit with him, I do not know what to say, because his question is the right one.

The problem of suffering is not an abstract puzzle. It is the cry of every parent who has watched a child die, every person who has suffered injustice with no remedy, every creature caught in the machinery of disease and decay. If God is both all-powerful and wholly good, why does suffering exist? This is not a question we can answer and move on. It is a question that must be lived with, honestly, by anyone who takes both faith and reality seriously.

---

## The Shape of the Problem

The classical formulation of the problem of evil runs something like this: An omnipotent God could prevent suffering. A perfectly good God would want to prevent suffering. Yet suffering exists. Either God is not omnipotent, not perfectly good, or something else is true that we have not yet considered.

This is not a straw man. It is the honest recognition that the existence of gratuitous suffering—suffering that seems to serve no redemptive purpose, suffering of the innocent, suffering that overwhelms all possible meaning—poses a genuine challenge to traditional theism. The Holocaust, the death of children, the slow cruelty of degenerative disease: these are not minor inconveniences. They are darknesses that seem incompatible with a loving God who has the power to intervene.

We must be clear: the problem is not simply that bad things happen to bad people. That, at least, seems compatible with justice. The problem is that terrible things happen to people who have done nothing to deserve it—children, the innocent, the vulnerable. This is what the philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams calls "horrendous evil," evil so great that it threatens to swallow all meaning.

---

## Free Will and Its Limits

One of the most influential responses to the problem is the free will defense, developed in various forms by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The argument is that genuine free will is a great good—one worth preserving even at significant cost. God, in creating beings with authentic freedom, could not guarantee that they would always choose rightly. To do so would require either determinism (removing genuine choice) or constant divine manipulation (making us into puppets). Either way, the good of free will would be lost.

This response has real power. It helps us understand why humans can harm one another, why wars happen, why cruelty exists. It locates the source of much suffering in human choices rather than in divine indifference. And it preserves the coherence of a God who values genuine relationship with creatures who can love in return.

But the free will defense has limits. It does not adequately explain natural evil—earthquakes, cancers, the suffering of animals. It struggles with the suffering of children, who have not exercised free will in ways that bring about their own pain. And it seems to suggest that God, having set the world in motion, simply stepped back to let the consequences unfold—a picture that may not square with the God who, in Scripture, is actively involved in the world.

---

## Soul-Making and the Purpose of Struggle

A second major response is the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick. This view suggests that the world is designed as a place of character formation—a "vale of soul-making" where creatures grow toward maturity, love, and virtue through the challenges of existence.

On this account, suffering is not merely a byproduct of free will but an instrument of growth. The difficulties we face develop patience, compassion, courage, and depth. Without struggle, we would remain shallow, undeveloped. God allows suffering not because he is indifferent but because he is crafting us through it—shaping us into the kind of beings capable of genuine love and flourishing.

There is truth here. The biblical writers certainly affirm that suffering produces character (Romans 5:3-5), that trials test and refine faith (1 Peter 1:6-7). And there is something to the observation that ease can produce softness, that some of the deepest human virtues—perseverance, empathy, courage—seem to require opposition to grow.

Yet this response also has its difficulties. It seems to suggest that the amount of suffering in the world is necessary for soul-making—a claim that is hard to defend. Could God not have created a world with enough challenge to develop virtue without also including the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy also struggles to address suffering that destroys rather than builds—suffering so extreme that it breaks people rather than strengthening them.

---

## The Cross: God in the Darkness

Perhaps the most distinctively Christian response to suffering is not an argument at all but a story—the story of God entering into suffering himself. In the incarnation, God does not remain distant from human pain but takes it upon himself. The cross is not an explanation of suffering; it is a participation in it.

This matters profoundly. It means that God is not indifferent to suffering, that he does not view it from some safe distance. He has been there. In Jesus of Nazareth, God wept, was betrayed, was tortured, and died in agony. The theodicy of the cross suggests that God does not explain suffering from outside it but meets us within it.

The Gospel accounts of Jesus' death are remarkably honest about his suffering. He cries out in abandonment (Mark 15:34). He experiences the full weight of human anguish. And in this, something is accomplished—not because suffering is good, but because love enters into the depths of human brokenness and does not leave it there. The resurrection is God's promise that suffering is not the final word, that death itself will be swallowed up in life.

This does not answer why any particular person suffers. It does not explain the cancer that takes a child. But it does something else: it promises that God is with us in the darkness, that our suffering is not outside his concern, that love is stronger than death.

---

## The Honest Struggle

The book of Job is perhaps the most honest treatment of suffering in all of literature. Job loses everything—children, wealth, health—and his friends offer explanations that sound theological but are, in fact, hollow. God's answer to Job is not an explanation but a presence. "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" God asks (Job 38:4). And yet God does not leave Job in the pit. He restores him, though not in the way Job expected.

This is significant. The biblical writers do not offer easy answers. The Psalms are full of lament, of cry, of anger at God (Psalm 88). Romans 8 does not promise that we will be spared suffering but that nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39)—a love that persists through suffering, not one that removes it.

We must be honest: there are limits to what we can understand. The Bible does not give us a theodicy that resolves every difficulty. It gives us a narrative in which God is present in the darkness, in which suffering is not ignored or explained away but met with a love that will ultimately redeem all things.

---

## A Word to the Suffering

I began with a man who lost his daughter. I end with him.

I do not have an answer that makes his pain make sense. I do not believe there is one. But I do believe that the Christian faith does not ask him to pretend that his suffering is not real, does not ask him to accept easy explanations. It asks him to bring his grief to a God who knows what it is to lose a child, to a Father who weeps with him in the darkness.

The question of suffering is the question we cannot avoid. It is the place where faith is tested, where easy answers fail, where we must simply trust that there is more to the story than we can see. This is not a cop-out. It is an acknowledgment that we are not God, that our perspective is limited, that the full answer will come only in the life to come.

But it is also a promise: that the darkness is not the end, that love will have the final word, that in the resurrection, God will wipe away every tear. Not because suffering was good, but because God is good—and his goodness is stronger than any darkness we will ever face.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a man I know who lost his daughter to cancer at age seven. He is not angry, exactly, but he is tired—tired of people telling him God has a plan, tired of being assured that his little girl is "with Jesus now," as if that could console him for the absence of her laughter in his house. He does not doubt God's existence; he doubts God's goodness. And when I sit with him, I do not know what to say, because his question is the right one.

The problem of suffering is not an abstract puzzle. It is the cry of every parent who has watched a child die, every person who has suffered injustice with no remedy, every creature caught in the machinery of disease and decay. If God is both all-powerful and wholly good, why does suffering exist? This is not a question we can answer and move on. It is a question that must be lived with, honestly, by anyone who takes both faith and reality seriously.

---

## The Shape of the Problem

The classical formulation of the problem of evil runs something like this: An omnipotent God could prevent suffering. A perfectly good God would want to prevent suffering. Yet suffering exists. Either God is not omnipotent, not perfectly good, or something else is true that we have not yet considered.

This is not a straw man. It is the honest recognition that the existence of gratuitous suffering—suffering that seems to serve no redemptive purpose, suffering of the innocent, suffering that overwhelms all possible meaning—poses a genuine challenge to traditional theism. The Holocaust, the death of children, the slow cruelty of degenerative disease: these are not minor inconveniences. They are darknesses that seem incompatible with a loving God who has the power to intervene.

We must be clear: the problem is not simply that bad things happen to bad people. That, at least, seems compatible with justice. The problem is that terrible things happen to people who have done nothing to deserve it—children, the innocent, the vulnerable. This is what the philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams calls "horrendous evil," evil so great that it threatens to swallow all meaning.

---

## Free Will and Its Limits

One of the most influential responses is the free will defense, developed in various forms by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The argument is that genuine free will is a great good—one worth preserving even at significant cost. God, in creating beings with authentic freedom, could not guarantee that they would always choose rightly. To do so would require either determinism (removing genuine choice) or constant divine manipulation (making us into puppets). Either way, the good of free will would be lost.

This response has real power. It helps us understand why humans can harm one another, why wars happen, why cruelty exists. It locates the source of much suffering in human choices rather than in divine indifference. And it preserves the coherence of a God who values genuine relationship with creatures who can love in return.

But the free will defense has limits. It does not adequately explain natural evil—earthquakes, cancers, the suffering of animals. It struggles with the suffering of children, who have not exercised free will in ways that bring about their own pain. Moreover, it underestimates how deeply our freedom has "screwed up the world," to use Marilyn McCord Adams's pointed phrase. Human sin has cascading effects that reach far beyond our individual choices—systems of oppression, environmental degradation, generational trauma. We are not merely individual agents making isolated decisions; we are embedded in webs of consequence that we did not choose but must nonetheless bear. The free will defense, for all its power, cannot fully account for this.

And it seems to suggest that God, having set the world in motion, simply stepped back to let the consequences unfold—a picture that may not square with the God who, in Scripture, is actively involved in the world, who numbers the hairs on our heads, who notices the fall of every sparrow.

---

## Soul-Making and the Purpose of Struggle

A second major response is the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick. Irenaeus spoke of the world as a "vale of soul-making"—a place where creatures, initially immature, grow through struggle toward maturity, love, and virtue. The Greek word *technē*—craft or art—may be apt here: God is crafting us through the challenges of existence, as a potter shapes clay on the wheel, as a smith tempers steel in fire.

On this account, suffering is not merely a byproduct of free will but an instrument of growth. The difficulties we face develop patience, compassion, courage, and depth. Without struggle, we would remain shallow, undeveloped. God allows suffering not because he is indifferent but because he is crafting us through it—shaping us into the kind of beings capable of genuine love and flourishing.

There is truth here. The biblical writers certainly affirm that suffering produces character (Romans 5:3-5), that trials test and refine faith (1 Peter 1:6-7). The author of Hebrews reminds readers that "the Lord disciplines those he loves" (Hebrews 12:6), and that the training of hardship, though painful, yields "a harvest of righteousness and peace" (12:11). And there is something to the observation that ease can produce softness, that some of the deepest human virtues—perseverance, empathy, courage—seem to require opposition to grow.

Yet this response also has its difficulties. It seems to suggest that the amount of suffering in the world is necessary for soul-making—a claim that is hard to defend. Could God not have created a world with enough challenge to develop virtue without also including the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy also struggles to address suffering that destroys rather than builds—suffering so extreme that it breaks people rather than strengthening them. Not all suffering is redemptive. Some of it simply devastates.

---

## The Cross: God in the Darkness

Perhaps the most distinctively Christian response to suffering is not an argument at all but a story—the story of God entering into suffering himself. In the incarnation, God does not remain distant from human pain but takes it upon himself. The cross is not an explanation of suffering; it is a participation in it.

This matters profoundly. It means that God is not indifferent to suffering, that he does not view it from some safe distance. He has been there. In Jesus of Nazareth, God wept, was betrayed, was tortured, and died in agony. The theodicy of the cross suggests that God does not explain suffering from outside it but meets us within it.

The Gospel accounts of Jesus' death are remarkably honest about his suffering. He cries out in abandonment: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34; cf. Psalm 22:1). He experiences the full weight of human anguish. And in this, something is accomplished—not because suffering is good, but because love enters into the depths of human brokenness and does not leave it there. The prophet Isaiah, writing centuries before the cross, spoke of the Suffering Servant who "was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities" (Isaiah 53:5)—a passage the early church read as prediction, as God's servant taking upon himself the suffering that should have been ours. And the writer of Hebrews makes the same point with pastoral urgency: "Because he himself suffered when he was tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted" (2:18). God does not merely observe our suffering from heaven; he descends into it.

The resurrection is God's promise that suffering is not the final word, that death itself will be swallowed up in life. But it is important to notice: the resurrection does not undo the cross. It does not take away the suffering by pretending it didn't happen. It redeems it—holds it, transforms it, carries it into eternity. This is not the same as saying suffering is good. It is saying something more mysterious: that love is stronger than suffering, that God can bring good from what was meant for evil, that the darkness does not have the final say.

This does not answer why any particular person suffers. It does not explain the cancer that takes a child. But it does something else: it promises that God is with us in the darkness, that our suffering is not outside his concern, that love is stronger than death.

---

## The Honest Struggle

The book of Job is perhaps the most honest treatment of suffering in all of literature. Job loses everything—children, wealth, health—and his friends offer explanations that sound theological but are, in fact, hollow. Job's response is not passive acceptance but protest. He demands answers of God. He complains. He refuses to pretend his suffering makes sense.

And God's answer to Job is not an explanation but a presence. "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" God asks (Job 38:4). This is not a theodicy; it is an encounter. And yet God does not leave Job in the pit. He restores him, though not in the way Job expected—and notably, the restoration comes after, not before, Job has spoken his protest.

The biblical writers do not offer easy answers. The Psalms are full of lament, of cry, of anger at God. Psalm 88 is one of the darkest poems in all of Scripture: "You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep. Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves" (88:6-7). The psalmist does not resolve his pain; he brings it to God. Romans 8 does not promise that we will be spared suffering but that nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God" (8:39)—a love that persists through suffering, not one that removes it. And even in that chapter, Paul acknowledges that "the whole creation has been groaning" (8:22), waiting for redemption.

This is what some theologians call "protest theodicy"—the recognition that it is right to protest suffering, to cry out against injustice, to refuse easy explanations. The biblical writers model this for us. They do not tell us to accept suffering quietly. They tell us to bring it to God, to wrestle with it, to refuse to let go.

We must be honest: there are limits to what we can understand. The Bible does not give us a theodicy that resolves every difficulty. It gives us a narrative in which God is present in the darkness, in which suffering is not ignored or explained away but met with a love that will ultimately redeem all things.

---

## A Word to the Suffering

I began with a man who lost his daughter. I end with him.

I do not have an answer that makes his pain make sense. I do not believe there is one. But I do believe that the Christian faith does not ask him to pretend that his suffering is not real, does not ask him to accept easy explanations. It asks him to bring his grief to a God who knows what it is to lose a child, to a Father who weeps with him in the darkness.

The question of suffering is the question we cannot avoid. It is the place where faith is tested, where easy answers fail, where we must simply trust that there is more to the story than we can see. This is not a cop-out. It is an acknowledgment that we are not God, that our perspective is limited, that the full answer will come only in the life to come.

But it is also a promise: that the darkness is not the end, that love will have the final word, that in the resurrection, God will wipe away every tear. Not because suffering was good, but because God is good—and his goodness is stronger than any darkness we will ever face.

For the man I know, and for all who suffer, that must be enough. And for now, that is not too small.

It is the moral refusal to domesticate the scream of the innocent into a theodicy that makes sense of everything. We must let the sharpest form of the objection speak before we attempt to answer it.

---

## Free Will and Its Limits

One of the most influential responses is the free will defense, developed in various forms by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The argument is that genuine free will is a great good—one worth preserving even at significant cost. God, in creating beings with authentic freedom, could not guarantee that they would always choose rightly. To do so would require either determinism (removing genuine choice) or constant divine manipulation (making us into puppets). Either way, the good of free will would be lost.

This response has real power. It helps us understand why humans can harm one another, why wars happen, why cruelty exists. It locates the source of much suffering in human choices rather than in divine indifference. And it preserves the coherence of a God who values genuine relationship with creatures who can love in return.

Whether or not this removes the logical contradiction, it leaves the evidential weight of tremendous evil untouched. The free will defense does not adequately explain natural evil—earthquakes, cancers, the suffering of animals. It struggles with the suffering of children, who have not exercised free will in ways that bring about their own pain. And it seems to suggest that God, having set the world in motion, simply stepped back to let the consequences unfold—a picture that may not square with the God who, in Scripture, is actively involved in the world.

---

## Soul-Making and the Purpose of Struggle

A second major response is the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick. This view suggests that the world is designed as a place of character formation—a "vale of soul-making" where creatures grow toward maturity, love, and virtue through the challenges of existence.

On this account, suffering is not merely a byproduct of free will but an instrument of growth. The difficulties we face develop patience, compassion, courage, and depth. Without struggle, we would remain shallow, undeveloped. God allows suffering not because he is indifferent but because he is crafting us through it—shaping us into the kind of beings capable of genuine love and flourishing.

There is truth here. The biblical writers certainly affirm that suffering produces character (Romans 5:3-5), that trials test and refine faith (1 Peter 1:6-7). And there is something to the observation that ease can produce softness, that some of the deepest human virtues—perseverance, empathy, courage—seem to require opposition to grow.

Yet this response also has its difficulties. It seems to suggest that the amount of suffering in the world is necessary for soul-making—a claim that is hard to defend. Could God not have created a world with enough challenge to develop virtue without also including the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy also struggles to address suffering that destroys rather than builds—suffering so extreme that it breaks people rather than strengthening them. And it does not adequately account for natural evil, the suffering that comes not from human freedom but from the structure of the physical world itself—from a universe whose chemistry allows both carbon-based life and cancer.

---

## Interlude: Silence

Before moving forward, we must acknowledge that between the failure of explanation and the promise of presence lies a space that must be occupied by shared silence, not further speech. The Psalmist cries, "My soul is in deep anguish. How long, Lord, how long?" (Psalm 6:3). The Nazi concentration camp survivor Etty Hillesum wrote in her diary: "You, God, cannot help us, but we must help You to help us." Sometimes the most honest thing we can do is sit in the darkness without trying to explain it away. The friends who replicate Job's comforters—speaking theology aloud to the sufferer—are rarely aware they are doing so. Sitting in silence is usually better.

---

## The Cross: God in the Darkness

Perhaps the most distinctively Christian response to suffering is not an argument at all but a story—the story of God entering into suffering himself. In the incarnation, God does not remain distant from human pain but takes it upon himself. The cross is not an explanation of suffering; it is a participation in it.

The prophet Isaiah had already pointed to this mystery four centuries before Christ: "He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). Vicarious suffering is not a late-night philosophical invention but embedded in the biblical narrative. The Servant takes upon himself the suffering that should have been ours.

This matters profoundly. It means that God is not indifferent to suffering, that he does not view it from some safe distance. He has been there. In Jesus of Nazareth, God wept, was betrayed, was tortured, and died in agony. The theodicy of the cross suggests that God does not explain suffering from outside it but meets us within it.

The Gospel accounts of Jesus' death are remarkably honest about his suffering. He cries out in abandonment (Mark 15:34). He experiences the full weight of human anguish. And in this, something is accomplished—not because suffering is good, but because love enters into the depths of human brokenness and does not leave it there.

The resurrection is God's promise that suffering is not the final word. But we must be careful not to treat it as a divine edit-and-undo button, as if the suffering simply gets erased. In the resurrection, the same body that was crucified is recognized—nail-marks and all—yet now death-proof. The Lamb's slain-ness is part of his glory (Revelation 5:6). The scars are not erased but transfigured. This means that the eschaton is not merely compensation but redemption of the past. The tears exist to be wiped; they are not retroactively removed (Revelation 21:4). God will wipe away every tear—not because suffering was good, but because his love is strong enough to take it into himself and transform it.

---

## The Honest Struggle

The book of Job is perhaps the most honest treatment of suffering in all of literature. Job loses everything—children, wealth, health—and his friends offer explanations that sound theological but are, in fact, hollow. God's answer to Job is not an explanation but a presence. "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" God asks (Job 38:4). And yet God does not leave Job in the pit. He restores him, though not in the way Job expected.

This is significant. The biblical writers do not offer easy answers. The Psalms are full of lament, of cry, of anger at God. Romans 8 does not promise that we will be spared suffering but that nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39)—a love that persists through suffering, not one that removes it. And earlier in that same chapter, Paul writes that "the whole creation has been groaning" (Romans 8:22). Scripture does not treat evil as merely anthropogenic; nature itself is in bondage, caught in the same futility as we are.

We must be honest: there are limits to what we can understand. The Bible does not give us a theodicy that resolves every difficulty. It gives us a narrative in which God is present in the darkness, in which suffering is not ignored or explained away but met with a love that will ultimately redeem all things.

---

## A Word to the Suffering

I began with a man who lost his daughter. I end with him—and with others.

I think of my grandmother, who lived with chronic pain for thirty years after a fall that never healed properly. Her suffering was not dramatic or acute; it was the slow grinding of daily ache, the way pain becomes a kind of companion you never wanted. She did not lose a child to cancer, but she knew what it was to have her body become a prison. She never found a "reason" for it. But she kept going to church, kept praying, kept lighting a candle in the quiet hours. I do not know what she believed, exactly. I know she believed in a God who saw her.

I do not have an answer that makes his pain or her pain make sense. I do not believe there is one. But I do believe that the Christian faith does not ask him to pretend that his suffering is not real, does not ask him to accept easy explanations. It asks him to bring his grief to a God who knows what it is to lose a child, to a Father who weeps with him in the darkness.

The question of suffering is the question we cannot avoid. It is the place where faith is tested, where easy answers fail, where we must simply trust that there is more to the story than we can see. This is not a cop-out. It is an acknowledgment that we are not God, that our perspective is limited, that the full answer will come only in the life to come.

But it is also a promise: that the darkness is not the end, that love will have the final word, that in the resurrection, God will wipe away every tear. Not because suffering was good, but because God is good—and his goodness is stronger than any darkness we will ever face. In the empty bedroom, in the unworn shoes by the door, in the silence that follows the question—God is there. He has not abandoned the scene of the crime. He will re-create it from inside.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a man I know who lost his daughter to cancer at age seven. He is not angry, exactly, but he is tired—tired of people telling him God has a plan, tired of being assured that his little girl is "with Jesus now," as if that could console him for the absence of her laughter in his house. He does not doubt God's existence; he doubts God's goodness. And when I sit with him, I do not know what to say, because his question is the right one.

The problem of suffering is not an abstract puzzle. It is the cry of every parent who has watched a child die, every person who has suffered injustice with no remedy, every creature caught in the machinery of disease and decay. If God is both all-powerful and wholly good, why does suffering exist? This is not a question we can answer and move on. It is a question that must be lived with, honestly, by anyone who takes both faith and reality seriously.

---

## The Shape of the Problem

The classical formulation of the problem of evil runs something like this: An omnipotent God could prevent suffering. A perfectly good God would want to prevent suffering. Yet suffering exists. Either God is not omnipotent, not perfectly good, or something else is true—something we have not yet considered.

This is not a straw man. It is the honest recognition that the existence of gratuitous suffering poses a genuine challenge to traditional theism. The philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams calls certain evils "horrendous"—so great that they threaten to swallow all meaning. The death of a child, the Holocaust, the slow cruelty of degenerative disease: these are not minor inconveniences. They are darknesses that seem incompatible with a loving God who has the power to intervene.

But the problem runs deeper than this. It is not simply that bad things happen to bad people. That, at least, seems compatible with justice. The problem is that terrible things happen to people who have done nothing to deserve it—children, the innocent, the vulnerable. And beyond even this, there is what philosophers call the *evidential* problem: the sheer scale and distribution of suffering in the world seems to exceed any explanation we might offer. There is more suffering, of more kinds, in more places, than any theodicy seems able to account for. The cumulative weight of this suffering is what makes the problem so devastating—not just a logical puzzle, but an overwhelming reality that presses against the heart of faith.

---

## Free Will and Its Limits

One of the most influential responses is the free will defense, developed in various forms by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The argument is that genuine free will is a great good—one worth preserving even at significant cost. God, in creating beings with authentic freedom, could not guarantee that they would always choose rightly. To do so would require either determinism (removing genuine choice) or constant divine manipulation (making us into puppets). Either way, the good of free will would be lost.

This response has real power. It helps us understand why humans can harm one another, why wars happen, why cruelty exists. It locates the source of much suffering in human choices rather than in divine indifference. And it preserves the coherence of a God who values genuine relationship with creatures who can love in return.

But the free will defense has significant limits. It does not adequately explain natural evil—earthquakes, cancers, the suffering of animals, the millions of years of pain that preceded human existence. It struggles with the suffering of children, who have not exercised free will in ways that bring about their own pain. And it seems to suggest that God, having set the world in motion, simply stepped back to let the consequences unfold—a picture that may not square with the God who, in Scripture, is actively involved in the world.

More fundamentally, even if free will explains *some* suffering, it seems insufficient to explain the *scale* of suffering. Could God not have created beings with free will but in circumstances where the potential for harm was more limited? The free will defense works reasonably well for explaining why humans can harm one another; it works far less well for explaining why the world is saturated with suffering that seems to have no connection to human freedom at all.

---

## Soul-Making and the Purpose of Struggle

A second major response is the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick. Irenaeus's actual view was more complex than sometimes presented: he believed the world was created "immature" and needed to grow toward its fullness. It was not that God created a perfect world and then something went wrong; rather, creation was designed from the beginning to be a place of development, with suffering built into the process of maturation. The phrase "vale of soul-making" comes from John Milton's *Paradise Lost*, but it captures something of Irenaeus's vision.

On this account, suffering is not merely a byproduct of free will but an instrument of growth. The difficulties we face develop patience, compassion, courage, and depth. Without struggle, we would remain shallow, undeveloped. God allows suffering not because he is indifferent but because he is crafting us through it—shaping us into the kind of beings capable of genuine love and flourishing.

The author of Hebrews speaks of discipline as well: "My son, do not make light of the Lord's discipline, and do not lose heart when he rebukes you" (Hebrews 12:5-11). The passage speaks of chastening that seems "painful" rather than pleasant, but it comes from a Father who loves us and wants our good. This both supports the soul-making intuition and complicates it: discipline implies a loving Father, but the suffering is still real, still difficult, still a mystery.

Yet this response also has its difficulties. It seems to suggest that the amount of suffering in the world is necessary for soul-making—a claim that is hard to defend. Could God not have created a world with enough challenge to develop virtue without also including the Holocaust, the plague, the slow death of a child? ---

I do not have an answer that makes his pain make sense. I do not believe there is one. The Christian faith does not ask him to pretend that his suffering is not real, does not ask him to accept easy explanations. It asks him to bring his grief to a God who knows what it is to lose a child, to a Father who weeps with him in the darkness.

Without struggle, we would remain shallow, undeveloped. God allows suffering not because he is indifferent but because he is crafting us through it—shaping us into the kind of beings capable of genuine love and flourishing.

There is truth here. The biblical writers certainly affirm that suffering can produce character. Paul writes in Romans 5 that *suffering for the sake of the gospel* produces perseverance, character, and hope—a specific claim about redemptive suffering within God's purposes, not a universal principle about all pain. And there is something to the observation that ease can produce softness, that some of the deepest human virtues—perseverance, empathy, courage—seem to require opposition to grow.

Yet this response also has its difficulties. It seems to suggest that the amount of suffering in the world is necessary for soul-making—a claim that is hard to defend. Could God not have created a world with enough challenge to develop virtue without also including the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy also struggles to address suffering that destroys rather than builds—suffering so extreme that it breaks people rather than strengthening them.

---

## The Cross: God in the Darkness

Perhaps the most distinctively Christian response to suffering is not an argument at all but a story—the story of God entering into suffering himself. In the incarnation, God does not remain distant from human pain but takes it upon himself. The cross is not an explanation of suffering; it is a participation in it.

This matters profoundly. It means that God is not indifferent to suffering, that he does not view it from some safe distance. He has been there. In Jesus of Nazareth, God wept, was betrayed, was tortured, and died in agony. The theodicy of the cross suggests that God does not explain suffering from outside it but meets us within it. The cross does not resolve the logical triad, but it *reframes* it: the God who permits suffering is not a distant monarch but one who enters it, bearing its cost. This doesn't explain *why* suffering exists, but it does remove the charge of divine indifference that makes the problem so acute.

The Gospel accounts of Jesus' death are remarkably honest about his suffering. He cries out in abandonment (Mark 15:34). He experiences the full weight of human anguish. And in this, something is accomplished—not because suffering is good, but because love enters into the depths of human brokenness and does not leave it there. The resurrection is God's promise that suffering is not the final word, that death itself will be swallowed up in life.

Yet Jesus' ministry was not only cross but also healing. Throughout the Gospels, Jesus actively combats suffering—curing diseases, raising the dead, driving out demons. These acts anticipate the redemption of all things, showing that suffering is not merely something God will ultimately undo but something he actively opposes now.

---

## The Honest Struggle

The book of Job is perhaps the most honest treatment of suffering in all of literature. Job loses everything—children, wealth, health—and his friends offer explanations that sound theological but are, in fact, hollow. God's answer to Job is not an explanation but a presence. "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" God asks (Job 38:4).

Yet God's answer is not simply presence—it is challenge. Job cannot comprehend the cosmos's complexity, yet he demands God account for moral order. The answer is not "trust me" but "you lack the framework to judge me"—a crucial distinction that preserves divine mystery without minimizing Job's pain. And yet God does not leave Job in the pit. He restores him, though not in the way Job expected.

This is significant. The biblical writers do not offer easy answers. The Psalms are full of lament, of cry, of anger at God (Psalm 88). Romans 8 does not promise that we will be spared suffering but that nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39)—a love that persists through suffering, not one that removes it.

The Bible not only permits but *canonizes* anger at God. Psalm 88 ends without resolution: "Darkness is my closest friend." Lamentations refuses to look past the ruin. For the man who lost his daughter, his grief may never find "closure"—and faith does not require it. The promise is not that pain will be explained, but that it will be *borne*, both by him and by the God who weeps with him. Some wounds remain open until the resurrection, and that is not faithlessness but honesty.

---

## A Word to the Suffering

I began with a man who lost his daughter. I end with him.

I do not have an answer that makes his pain make sense. I do not believe there is one. But I do believe that the Christian faith does not ask him to pretend that his suffering is not real, does not ask him to accept easy explanations. It asks him to bring his grief to a God who knows what it is to lose a child, to a Father who weeps with him in the darkness.

The question of suffering is the question we cannot avoid. It is the place where faith is tested, where easy answers fail, where we must simply trust that there is more to the story than we can see. This is not a deferral but a recognition that some truths exceed our epistemic grasp—yet we trust the character of the God revealed in Christ.

But it is also a promise: that the darkness is not the end, that love will have the final word, that in the resurrection, God will wipe away every tear. Not because suffering was good, but because God is good—and his goodness is stronger than any darkness we will ever face.

# The Weight of the Question: Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a man I know who lost his daughter to cancer at age seven. He is not angry, exactly, but he is tired—tired of people telling him God has a plan, tired of being assured that his little girl is "with Jesus now," as if that could console him for the absence of her laughter in his house. He does not doubt God's existence; he doubts God's goodness. And when I sit with him, I do not know what to say, because his question is the right one.

The problem of suffering is not an abstract puzzle. It is the cry of every parent who has watched a child die, every person who has suffered injustice with no remedy, every creature caught in the machinery of disease and decay. If God is both all-powerful and wholly good, why does suffering exist? This is not a question we can answer and move on. It is a question that must be lived with, honestly, by anyone who takes both faith and reality seriously.

---

## The Shape of the Problem

The classical formulation of the problem of evil runs something like this: An omnipotent God could prevent suffering. A perfectly good God would want to prevent suffering. Yet suffering exists. Either God is not omnipotent, not perfectly good, or something else is true that we have not yet considered.

This is not a straw man. It is the honest recognition that the existence of gratuitous suffering—suffering that seems to serve no redemptive purpose, suffering of the innocent, suffering that overwhelms all possible meaning—poses a genuine challenge to traditional theism. The Holocaust, the death of children, the slow cruelty of degenerative disease: these are not minor inconveniences. They are darknesses that seem incompatible with a loving God who has the power to intervene.

We must be clear: the problem is not simply that bad things happen to bad people. That, at least, seems compatible with justice. The problem is that terrible things happen to people who have done nothing to deserve it—children, the innocent, the vulnerable. This is what the philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams calls "horrendous evil," evil so great that it threatens to swallow all meaning.

---

## Free Will and Its Limits

One of the most influential responses is the free will defense, developed in various forms by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The argument is that genuine free will is a great good—one worth preserving even at significant cost. God, in creating beings with authentic freedom, could not guarantee that they would always choose rightly. To do so would require either determinism (removing genuine choice) or constant divine manipulation (making us into puppets). Either way, the good of free will would be lost.

This response has real power. It helps us understand why humans can harm one another, why wars happen, why cruelty exists. It locates the source of much suffering in human choices rather than in divine indifference. And it preserves the coherence of a God who values genuine relationship with creatures who can love in return.

But the free will defense has limits. It does not adequately explain natural evil—earthquakes, cancers, the suffering of animals. It struggles with the suffering of children, who have not exercised free will in ways that bring about their own pain. And it seems to suggest that God, having set the world in motion, simply stepped back to let the consequences unfold—a picture that may not square with the God who, in Scripture, is actively involved in the world.

---

## Soul-Making and Its Dangers

A second major response is the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick. This view suggests that the world is designed as a place of character formation—a "vale of soul-making" where creatures grow toward maturity, love, and virtue through the challenges of existence.

On this account, suffering is not merely a byproduct of free will but an instrument of growth. The difficulties we face develop patience, compassion, courage, and depth. Without struggle, we would remain shallow, undeveloped. God allows suffering not because he is indifferent but because he is crafting us through it—shaping us into the kind of beings capable of genuine love and flourishing.

There is truth here. Writing to communities experiencing persecution, Paul and Peter do not explain why suffering exists in the abstract, but testify to what God can produce *within* it: perseverance, character, hope. Romans 5:3-5 does not promise that suffering will be proportioned to our growth; it witnesses that God is not absent from the crucible. These are pastoral testimonies, not philosophical principles extracted from their context.

Yet this response also has its difficulties. It seems to suggest that the amount of suffering in the world is necessary for soul-making—a claim that is hard to defend. Could God not have created a world with enough challenge to develop virtue without also including the Holocaust? The soul-making theodicy struggles to address suffering that destroys rather than builds—suffering so extreme that it breaks people rather than strengthening them.

And we must be honest: to speak of "soul-making" in the presence of the grieving father would be obscene. His daughter's death was not a pedagogical tool. If soul-making is true, it is true only as a description of how God meets us in surviving suffering, never as a justification for why the suffering was necessary.

---

## When Explanations Become Violence

Here we must also recognize that theological explanations can themselves become a form of violence. There is a tradition—represented by thinkers like Abraham Joshua Heschel, Dorothee Sölle, and voices in the Black theological tradition—that refuses the very project of theodicy. On this view, to explain suffering is to excuse it, to build intellectual frameworks that render the sufferer complicit in their own destruction.

This protest theodicy does not offer a better answer; it refuses to offer any answer at all. It stands with Job's friends and refuses to be comforted—not because comfort is impossible, but because the comforters are liars. When we tell the grieving father that his daughter is "with Jesus," we may be offering what feels like hope, but we are also telling him that the universe is fundamentally just, that her death made sense, that God needed her to die to accomplish something. This is not pastoral. It is a kind of theological violence.

The cross does not validate this violence. Here, suffering is not justified by its useful products; it is entered, shared, and ultimately judged. If there is a theodicy of the cross, it is a theodicy that refuses theodicy—that refuses to explain suffering intellectually while entering it relationally.

---

## The Cross: God in the Darkness

Perhaps the most distinctively Christian response to suffering is not an argument at all but a story—the story of God entering into suffering himself. In the incarnation, God does not remain distant from human pain but takes it upon himself. The cross is not an explanation of suffering; it is a participation in it.

This matters profoundly. It means that God is not indifferent to suffering, that he does not view it from some safe distance. He has been there. In Jesus of Nazareth, God wept, was betrayed, was tortured, and died in agony. The theodicy of the cross suggests that God does not explain suffering from outside it but meets us within it.

The Gospel accounts of Jesus' death are remarkably honest about his suffering. He cries out in abandonment (Mark 15:34). He experiences the full weight of human anguish. And in this, something is accomplished—not because suffering is good, but because love enters into the depths of human brokenness and does not leave it there. The resurrection is God's promise that suffering is not the final word, that death itself will be swallowed up in life.

This does not answer why any particular person suffers. It does not explain the cancer that takes a child. But it does something else: it promises that God is with us in the darkness, that our suffering is not outside his concern, that love is stronger than death.

---

## The Honest Struggle

The book of Job is perhaps the most honest treatment of suffering in all of literature. Job loses everything—children, wealth, health—and his friends offer explanations that sound theological but are, in fact, hollow. God's answer to Job is not an explanation but a presence—and it is also a radical decentering. "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" God asks (Job 38:4). This is not merely comfort; it is a challenge that humbles Job into silence, that strips away the pretense that Job deserves to understand.

And yet God does not leave Job in the pit. He restores him, though not in the way Job expected. The God of the whirlwind is also the God who draws near. This is significant. The biblical writers do not offer easy answers. The Psalms are full of lament, of cry, of anger at God (Psalm 88—the only psalm without a resolution). Romans 8 does not promise that we will be spared suffering but that nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39)—a love that persists through suffering, not one that removes it.

---

## A Word to the Suffering

I began with a man who lost his daughter. I end with him.

I do not have an answer that makes his pain make sense. I do not believe there is one. But I do believe that the Christian faith does not ask him to pretend that his suffering is not real, does not ask him to accept easy explanations. It asks him to bring his grief to a God who knows what it is to lose a child, to a Father who weeps with him in the darkness.

The question of suffering is the question we cannot avoid. It is the place where faith is tested, where easy answers fail, where we must simply trust that there is more to the story than we can see. We are not given the view from above, only the view from within the cross—where God himself seems to cry out in abandonment. To trust in the darkness is not to accept that we lack clearance for God's secret files, but to believe that the One who shares our incomprehension is still, somehow, trustworthy.

But this is not a cop-out. It is an acknowledgment that we are creatures, not Creator, that our perspective is limited, that the full answer will come only in the life to come. And it is a promise: that the darkness is not the end, that love will have the final word, that in the resurrection, God will wipe away every tear.

The resurrection does not explain why she died, does not weave her suffering into a necessary pattern. It promises, instead, that her death—like Christ's—is not the final word about God's relationship to her. The tears are not wiped away because they were unreal, but because they are finally, fully heard. Not because suffering was good, but because God is good—and his goodness is stronger than any darkness we will ever face.

# Wrestling in the Dark: The Problem of Suffering and the Goodness of God

There is a moment, known to anyone who has sat with a dying friend, held a child in pain, or stared at the wreckage of a life shattered by cruelty, when the question forces itself through every theological abstraction: Where is God? And if God is good—if God is love—how can this be?

This is not an academic question. It is the most human question, and it deserves more than technical answers. But neither does it deserve to be avoided. The problem of evil and suffering has haunted religious thought for millennia, and for good reason: it strikes at the very heart of what we believe about God. If God is omnipotent, God could prevent suffering. If God is omniscient, God knows about it. If God is omnibenevolent, God wants to prevent it. Yet suffering exists in abundance. This is the logical puzzle that has driven some toward atheism and others toward increasingly elaborate theological defenses. Neither response is foolish. Both emerge from honest engagement with the world as we experience it.

---

The problem admits no easy resolution, and those who claim otherwise have usually not thought about it deeply enough. The suffering we witness takes many forms: the suffering caused by human cruelty—war, abuse, exploitation—where genuine moral agency lies behind the pain. And the suffering that seems to have no moral source at all: earthquakes, cancers, the slow death of a child from disease no one chose. The first we call *moral evil*; the second, *natural evil*. Both weigh heavily on the conscience of faith.

What makes the problem so persistent is that these two categories blur in practice. A hurricane kills not because anyone willed it but because the world operates according to physical laws that sometimes devastate human life. A pandemic spreads through no one's conscious intent yet devastates communities. Even the suffering caused by human evil compounds across generations in ways no individual chose. The web of causation is tangled beyond easy sorting, and any theodicy—any attempt to justify God's goodness in the face of suffering—must grapple with this complexity.

---

One of the most influential responses is the *free will defense*, which argues that genuine love requires genuine freedom. If God were to prevent every harmful action by overriding human choice, we would be little more than puppets, and love would be impossible. Love, by its nature, must be chosen—and choice entails the possibility of choosing wrongly. This defense has significant force. It explains why God does not simply eliminate evil by divine fiat: such intervention would destroy the conditions for authentic relationship. We are not called to be loved by God as automatons but as persons capable of reciprocal love.

Yet the free will defense has well-known limits. It illuminates moral evil—the suffering caused by human choices—but struggles with natural evil. What freedom produced the earthquake? What choices led to the cancer cell? To be sure, we have complicated the natural world through environmental damage, and some natural disasters have human fingerprints. But the deeper problem remains: if God could have created a world with different physical laws—laws that did not permit tsunamis or hurricanes—why didn't God? The free will defense, powerful as it is, does not answer every form of suffering.

---

A second influential approach is the *soul-making theodicy*, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed by thinkers like John Hick. This view holds that the world is designed not as a paradise but as a crucible—a place where human beings are gradually formed into the image of God. Suffering, on this account, serves a purpose: it develops virtues that could never be grown in comfort. Courage is forged in the face of danger. Patience is learned through waiting. Compassion arises only when we have known need. Without the challenges of the world, we would remain spiritually infantile, lacking the character that makes us truly good.

There is something deeply biblical about this insight. The Exodus wilderness was not a mistake but a place of formation; the Israelites were shaped there into a people capable of covenant faithfulness. Paul writes of creation "groaning" in anticipation of redemption, as though the whole material order is in labor, producing something that cannot come about without pain. The New Testament consistently presents the Christian life as involving suffering—not as a bug but as a feature. We are "being transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory" (2 Corinthians 3:18), and that transformation often comes through hardship.

Yet this theodicy also strains against intuition. The scale of suffering seems disproportionate to any conceivable spiritual benefit. A child dies of leukemia at age four—what "soul-making" occurred in those brief, painful years? The reply that God's timescales differ from ours may be true, but it can feel like a concession wrung out by desperation. The soul-making theodicy offers a framework, but it does not fully answer the grief of those who suffer.

---

Perhaps the most honest biblical response is not a theodicy at all but a *protest theodicy*—an acknowledgment that faith does not mean the absence of outrage. The Bible is far more comfortable with wrestling than many Christian traditions allow. Job, the blameless man, confronts God with accusations of injustice and receives, in the end, not an explanation but an encounter. God does not justify the suffering; God shows up in the whirlwind and asks Job to contemplate the mysteries of creation. The Psalms are filled with laments—cries of abandonment, accusations of divine absence, demands for justice. "How long, O Lord?" rings out again and again, and it is never rebuked as impious.

Jesus himself, in the garden of Gethsemane, does not explain suffering; he cries out in anguish, sweating drops of blood, asking if there is any other way. The cross is not a philosophical solution to the problem of evil. It is God's *presence* in the midst of it—not triumphalist justification but identification. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34). The one who is wholly divine experiences the full weight of human suffering, and in that experience, something is transformed. God does not stand apart from suffering, offering explanations; God enters into it, and from within that entry, resurrection becomes possible.

This is perhaps the deepest Christian witness: not that suffering has a reason we can grasp, but that God does not leave us alone in it. The cross is the scandal of theodicy—God absorbing the worst that humanity can do and more, entering the darkness fully rather than explaining it from a distance.

---

I do not write these words as one who has solved the problem. I write as one who has sat with the dying, who has known grief, who has asked the questions that will not stay quiet. There are depths of suffering that no theodicy can touch—the suffering of innocents, the suffering that seems utterly wasted, the suffering that breaks people rather than building them. To speak of "purpose" in such moments can feel like a kind of violence.

And yet faith, at its best, does not pretend to have answers where answers do not exist. It holds open a space for questioning, for lament, for anger—without abandoning the fundamental trust that the universe has a creator who is not indifferent. The God of the Bible is not a silent cosmic architect but a God who wrestles with creation, who suffers with it, who weeps over it. The resurrection is not the reversal of suffering but the promise that suffering's final word is not death.

We see through a glass darkly (1 Corinthians 13:12). The limits of our understanding are real, and to acknowledge them is not cowardice but honesty. But the darkness is not total. There is enough light to walk by—enough to trust that the story is not meaningless, even when we cannot read it. Enough to love in the midst of pain, to hope against hope, to believe that even suffering itself will be redeemed.

What else can we do but continue the wrestling? The question of suffering is, finally, the question of whether love is worth believing in. And that is a question we answer not with arguments but with how we live in a world that breaks our hearts.

# Bearing the Weight of Suffering: A Meditation on God's Goodness

There is a kind of suffering that resists philosophy. It arrives not as an abstract puzzle but as a phone call in the night, a diagnosis, a casket lowered into the earth. The problem of evil is not merely a logical dilemma to be solved; it is a wound that each of us, in our own way, must learn to carry. What I want to do in these reflections is not to dissolve this problem—thereby insulting the intelligence of those who suffer—but to sit with it honestly, to trace the contours of a mystery that has occupied some of the finest minds in human history, and to ask whether faith might offer not an answer but a way of enduring.

The problem, in its starkest form, is this: If God is wholly good and wholly powerful, why is there suffering? Why do children die of starvation? Why do earthquakes bury thousands? Why does cruelty flourish and innocence bleed? These are not rhetorical questions. They are the questions that drive people from faith, and they are the questions that keep those who believe awake at night. The philosopher David Hume put the point with devastating clarity: either God wishes to prevent evil but cannot, in which case God is not omnipotent; or God can prevent evil but does not wish to, in which case God is not wholly good; or God neither can nor wishes to prevent evil, in which case God is neither good nor powerful. The logic seems airtight, and it deserves better than evasion.

---

One of the most influential responses to this problem has been the free will defence. The idea is deceptively simple: God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, had to create beings capable of genuine choice. Love that is coerced is not love; it is manipulation. And so God gave humanity freedom—the freedom to choose good or evil, to build or destroy. The suffering that fills our world, on this account, is largely the fruit of human freedom: our capacity for cruelty, our neglect of the vulnerable, our endless wars and betrayals. God does not will suffering; God wills creatures who can love, and love requires the possibility of its opposite.

This is not a trivial answer. It has real power. It explains, at least partially, why a good God might permit certain kinds of suffering—those that flow from human freedom. And it preserves both God's goodness and God's power: God can intervene but chooses, for the sake of something greater, not to override our freedom.

But the free will defence has its limits. It does not explain what are sometimes called "natural evils"—earthquakes, hurricanes, cancers, the suffering of animals. These do not seem to be the result of human sin. A child born with a terrible disease did not choose to suffer; the tectonic plates did not choose to shift. To say that these evils are permitted because God wanted to create a world with regular laws, laws that make free will possible, is to make a point of sorts—but it feels like a point that slides past the ache in our chests. There is also the harder question: even if free will explains much, does it explain *so much*? The magnitude and distribution of suffering seems disproportionate to any good that might come from human freedom. Is the Holocaust, really, the price of love?

These objections do not refute the free will defence, but they show that it cannot be the whole story. It is a piece of the puzzle, not the puzzle itself.

---

Another response, older and in some ways more ambitious, is what is often called the soul-making theodicy. Associated with the early church father Irenaeus, this view holds that the world was created not in a state of completion but in a state of becoming. Humanity was made imperfect, with the capacity for growth, and the purpose of existence is to be gradually transformed into the image of God—through choice, through struggle, through the very trials that test and form us. Suffering, on this account, is not merely a problem to be solved but a means through which character is forged. The poet George MacDonald put it this way: "It is not the crown that makes the king, but the being made a king." Pain refines; difficulty educates; the pressure of adversity reveals and creates depths that comfort could never produce.

There is truth here that resonates with human experience. We know, in our own lives, that some of our deepest growth has come through loss, through failure, through the dark nights that forced us to find resources we did not know we had. The philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams has argued, with striking honesty, that some suffering can be "red incorporable"—that is, capable of being taken up into a larger narrative of meaning and woven into a life that, in the end, is glorious.

And yet. This theodicy, too, has its fractures. It seems to imply that the amount of suffering in the world is roughly proportionate to the amount of growth it can produce—which is plainly false. The suffering of a child dying in agony from a rare disease does not appear to be generating soul-making in any recognizable sense. There is a moral asymmetry between the suffering of the one and the benefit of the many that troubles this view. And it risks becoming a kind of spiritual utilitarianism, weighing costs and benefits, as if God were running some vast cosmic cost-benefit analysis. The mother holding her dying child is not likely to find much comfort in being told that her child's suffering is "making souls."

---

What I have been describing so far are intellectual frameworks, ways of thinking about the problem. But perhaps the deepest response to suffering is not a framework at all but a story—one that does not explain suffering from the outside but enters into it from within. I mean the story of the cross.

The Christian faith does not offer a theodicy that stands at a distance from suffering. It offers a God who enters suffering, who takes it upon himself, who refuses to remain distant from the pain of his creatures. This is the staggering claim of the Incarnation: the eternal Son of God became flesh, lived among us, and died the death of a criminal. The cross is not a demonstration that God has solved the problem of suffering; it is God in the very midst of the problem, bearing its full weight. In the cry of Jesus on the hill—"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—we hear not a theological explanation but the sound of God himself suffering. The question is not answered; it is absorbed.

This is, I think, the most that can be said: that God is with us in our suffering, that God does not observe our pain from some remove but enters it, that the cross is the guarantee that no suffering is meaningless or forgotten. The resurrection is the promise that suffering is not the final word—that death will be defeated, that tears will be wiped away, that the wounded world will be made new. But we do not yet live in that new creation. We live in the "already but not yet," in the tension between the promise and its fulfillment.

---

I want to be honest: these responses do not satisfy entirely, and I do not think they are meant to. The problem of suffering is a mystery that exceeds our grasp, and any answer that claims to dissolve it completely has, I suspect, not understood the question. But there is a difference between an evasion and an acknowledgment of mystery. To say that we cannot fully understand why suffering exists is not to say that nothing can be said—it is to say that what can be said must be said with humility, with brokenness, with an awareness that we see through a glass darkly.

The Bible itself does not give easy answers. The book of Job is especially instructive: Job demands an explanation, and God responds not with a theodicy but with a question—"Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?"—which is to say, you cannot understand this from where you stand. And yet God does not leave Job in his suffering; God meets him in the whirlwind, and Job's response is not "Now I understand" but "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen you." That is a different kind of knowledge—not intellectual mastery but relational encounter. It is enough to sustain faith without resolving the tension.

---

I want to end where we began: with the real weight of suffering, which is not a puzzle to be solved but a mystery to be lived. I think of those who are suffering as they read these words—the grief that will not lift, the pain that will not ease, the questions that will not quiet. I do not have an answer for you. But I have this: that you are not alone, that the God who made you is a God who suffers, that the cross is the proof that no pain is wasted and no tear is forgotten. That is not a solution. It is a presence. And perhaps, in the end, it is enough.

One of the most influential responses to this problem has been the free will defence. The idea is deceptively simple: God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, had to create beings capable of genuine choice. Love that is coerced is not love; it is manipulation. And so God gave humanity freedom—the freedom to choose good or evil, to build or destroy. The suffering that fills our world, on this account, is largely the fruit of human freedom: our capacity for cruelty, our neglect of the vulnerable, our endless wars and betrayals. God does not will suffering; God wills creatures who can love, and love requires the possibility of its opposite.

This is not a trivial answer. It has real power. It explains, at least partially, why a good God might permit certain kinds of suffering—those that flow from human freedom. And it preserves both God's goodness and God's power: God can intervene but chooses, for the sake of something greater, not to override our freedom.

But the free will defence has its limits. It does not explain what are sometimes called "natural evils"—earthquakes, hurricanes, cancers, the suffering of animals. These do not seem to be the result of human sin. A child born with a terrible disease did not choose to suffer; the tectonic plates did not choose to shift. To say that these evils are permitted because God wanted to create a world with regular laws, laws that make free will possible, is to make a point of sorts—but it feels like a point that slides past the ache in our chests. There is also the harder question: even if free will explains much, does it explain *so much*? The magnitude and distribution of suffering seems disproportionate to any good that might come from human freedom. Is the Holocaust, really, the price of love?

These objections do not refute the free will defence, but they show that it cannot be the whole story. It is a piece of the puzzle, not the puzzle itself.

---

Another response, older and in some ways more ambitious, is what is often called the soul-making theodicy. Associated with the early church father Irenaeus, this view holds that the world was created not in a state of completion but in a state of becoming. There is a moral asymmetry between the suffering of the one and the benefit of the many that troubles this view. And it risks becoming a kind of spiritual utilitarianism, weighing costs and benefits, as if God were running some vast cosmic cost-benefit analysis. ---

What I have been describing so far are intellectual frameworks, ways of thinking about the problem. And in that tension, the cross is the guarantee that no suffering is meaningless or forgotten—that even the pain we cannot understand is held, is carried, is held in the very heart of God.

---

I want to be honest: these responses do not satisfy entirely, and I do not think they are meant to. The problem of suffering is a mystery that exceeds our grasp, and any answer that claims to dissolve it completely has, I suspect, not understood the question. But there is a difference between an evasion and an acknowledgment of mystery. To say that we cannot fully understand why suffering exists is not to say that nothing can be said—it is to say that what can be said must be said with humility, with brokenness, with an awareness that we see through a glass darkly.

And yet. There is a word that remains. It is not an explanation; it is a person. It is the God who did not remain distant but drew near. It is the Christ who did not escape suffering but entered it fully. It is the Spirit who "helps us in our weakness. But I can give you this: the God who made you is a God who knows suffering from the inside. The tears you cry, the cries you cannot put into words, the ache that will not ease—these are not hidden from him. They are carried in the wounds of Christ. And one day, in a world made new, every wound will be healed, every tear will be wiped away, and love will be finally and fully what it was always meant to be. That is not a solution. It is a hope. But I have this: that you are not alone, that the God who made you is a God who suffers, that the cross is the proof that no pain is wasted and no tear is forgotten. That is not a solution. It is a presence. And perhaps, in the end, it is enough.
