To say that these evils are permitted because God wanted to create a world with regular laws, laws that make free will possible, is to make a point of sorts—but it feels like a point that slides past the ache in our chests. There is also the harder question: even if free will explains much, does it explain *so much*? The magnitude and distribution of suffering seems disproportionate to any good that might come from human freedom. Is the Holocaust, really, the price of love?

These objections do not refute the free will defence, but they show that it cannot be the whole story. It is a piece of the puzzle, not the puzzle itself.

---

Another response, older and in some ways more ambitious, is what is often called the soul-making theodicy. Associated with the early church father Irenaeus, this view holds that the world was created not in a state of completion but in a state of becoming—a perspective that has deep roots in Eastern Orthodox theology and echoes throughout the Christian mystical tradition. Humanity was made imperfect, with the capacity for growth, and the purpose of existence is to be gradually transformed into the image of God—through choice, through struggle, through the very trials that test and form us. This idea is not merely philosophical speculation; it has deep biblical resonance. The apostle Paul writes that "suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope" (Romans 5:3-4). James encourages his readers to "consider it pure joy" when they face trials, "because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance" (James 1:2-3). Suffering, on this account, is not merely an obstacle to be overcome but a means through which character is forged. The poet George MacDonald put it this way: "It is not the crown that makes the king, but the being made a king." Pain refines; difficulty educates; the pressure of adversity reveals and creates depths that comfort could never produce.

There is truth here that resonates with human experience. We know, in our own lives, that some of our deepest growth has come through loss, through failure, through the dark nights that forced us to find resources we did not know we had. The philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams has argued, with striking honesty, that some suffering can be "red incorporable"—that is, capable of being taken up into a larger narrative of meaning and woven into a life that, in the end, is glorious.

And yet. This theodicy, too, has its fractures. It seems to imply that the amount of suffering in the world is roughly proportionate to the amount of growth it can produce—which is plainly false. The suffering of a child dying in agony from a rare disease does not appear to be generating soul-making in any recognizable sense. There is a moral asymmetry between the suffering of the one and the benefit of the many that troubles this view. And it risks becoming a kind of spiritual utilitarianism, weighing costs and benefits, as if God were running some vast cosmic cost-benefit analysis. The mother holding her dying child is not likely to find much comfort in being told that her child's suffering is "making souls."

---

What I have been describing so far are intellectual frameworks, ways of thinking about the problem. But perhaps the deepest response to suffering is not a framework at all but a story—one that does not explain suffering from the outside but enters into it from within. I mean the story of the cross.

The Christian faith does not offer a theodicy that stands at a distance from suffering. It offers a God who enters suffering, who takes it upon himself, who refuses to remain distant from the pain of his creatures. This is the staggering claim of the Incarnation: the eternal Son of God became flesh, lived among us, and died the death of a criminal. In the person of Jesus Christ, God himself experiences the full weight of human pain—not as a distant observer but as a participant in the drama of suffering. The cross is not a demonstration that God has solved the problem of suffering; it is God in the very midst of the problem, bearing its full weight. In the cry of Jesus on the hill—"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—we hear not a theological explanation but the sound of God himself suffering. The question is not answered; it is absorbed.

This is, I think, the most that can be said: that God is with us in our suffering, that God does not observe our pain from some remove but enters it, that the cross is the guarantee that no suffering is meaningless or forgotten. The resurrection is the promise that suffering is not the final word—that death will be defeated, that tears will be wiped away, that the wounded world will be made new. But we do not yet live in that new creation. We live in the "already but not yet," in the tension between the promise and its fulfillment.

---

I want to be honest: these responses do not satisfy entirely, and I do not think they are meant to. The problem of suffering is a mystery that exceeds our grasp, and any answer that claims to dissolve it completely has, I suspect, not understood the question. We must also acknowledge that the limits of our understanding are not merely a matter of our finite minds struggling to grasp infinite realities—there is also the irreducible mystery of God's own nature. God's ways are not our ways (Isaiah 55:8); God is transcendent, beyond our full comprehension. We see through a glass darkly, and even our clearest theological visions are partial, glimpsed in fragments. To say that we cannot fully understand why suffering exists is not to say that nothing can be said—it is to say that what can be said must be said with humility, with brokenness, with an awareness that we see through a glass darkly.

That is a different kind of knowledge—not intellectual mastery but relational encounter. It is enough to sustain faith without resolving the tension.

---

I want to end where we began: with the real weight of suffering, which is not a puzzle to be solved but a mystery to be lived. I think of those who are suffering as they read these words—the grief that will not lift, the pain that will not ease, the questions that will not quiet. I do not have an answer for you. But I have this: that you are not alone, that the God who made you is a God who suffers, that the cross is the proof that no pain is wasted and no tear is forgotten. That is not a solution. It is a presence. And perhaps, in the end, it is enough.

# Bearing the Weight of Suffering: A Meditation on God's Goodness

There is a kind of suffering that resists philosophy. It arrives not as an abstract puzzle but as a phone call in the night, a diagnosis, a casket lowered into the earth. The problem of evil is not merely a logical dilemma to be solved; it is a wound that each of us, in our own way, must learn to carry. What I want to do in these reflections is not to dissolve this problem—thereby insulting the intelligence of those who suffer—but to sit with it honestly, to trace the contours of a mystery that has occupied some of the finest minds in human history, and to ask whether faith might offer not an answer but a way of enduring.

The problem, in its starkest form, is this: If God is wholly good and wholly powerful, why is there suffering? Why do children die of starvation? Why do earthquakes bury thousands? Why does cruelty flourish and innocence bleed? These are not rhetorical questions. They are the questions that drive people from faith, and they are the questions that keep those who believe awake at night. The philosopher David Hume put the point with devastating clarity: either God wishes to prevent evil but cannot, in which case God is not omnipotent; or God can prevent evil but does not wish to, in which case God is not wholly good; or God neither can nor wishes to prevent evil, in which case God is neither good nor powerful. The logic seems airtight, and it deserves better than evasion.

---

One of the most influential responses to this problem has been the free will defence. The idea is deceptively simple: God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, had to create beings capable of genuine choice. Love that is coerced is not love; it is manipulation. And so God gave humanity freedom—the freedom to choose good or evil, to build or destroy. The suffering that fills our world, on this account, is largely the fruit of human freedom: our capacity for cruelty, our neglect of the vulnerable, our endless wars and betrayals. God does not will suffering; God wills creatures who can love, and love requires the possibility of its opposite.

This is not a trivial answer. It has real power. It explains, at least partially, why a good God might permit certain kinds of suffering—those that flow from human freedom. And it preserves both God's goodness and God's power: God can intervene but chooses, for the sake of something greater, not to override our freedom.

But the free will defence has its limits, and it is worth sitting with those limits honestly. First, there is the problem of what philosophers call "natural evil"—earthquakes, hurricanes, cancers, the suffering of animals. These do not seem to be the result of human sin. A child born with a terrible disease did not choose to suffer; the tectonic plates did not shift because someone willed it. To say that these evils are permitted because God wanted to create a world with regular laws, laws that make free will possible, is to make a point of sorts—but it feels like a point that slides past the ache in our chests.

There is also the harder question of magnitude. Even if free will explains much, does it explain *so much*? The Holocaust was not an act of nature; it was a monstrous human choice. But does that make it easier to understand? Six million Jews murdered because of human freedom—is that really the price of love? The suffering of a child dying of hunger in a world of plenty—is that simply the cost of the kind of love God wanted to create? These objections do not refute the free will defence entirely, but they show that it cannot be the whole story. It is a piece of the puzzle, not the puzzle itself.

---

Another response, older and in some ways more ambitious, is what is often called the soul-making theodicy. Associated with the early church father Irenaeus, this view holds that the world was created not in a state of completion but in a state of becoming. Humanity was made imperfect, with the capacity for growth, and the purpose of existence is to be gradually transformed into the image of God—through choice, through struggle, through the very trials that test and form us. Suffering, on this account, is not merely a problem to be solved but a means through which character is forged. The poet George MacDonald put it this way: "It is not the crown that makes the king, but the being made a king." Pain refines; difficulty educates; the pressure of adversity reveals and creates depths that comfort could never produce.

There is truth here that resonates with human experience. We know, in our own lives, that some of our deepest growth has come through loss, through failure, through the dark nights that forced us to find resources we did not know we had.

But this theodicy, too, has its fractures. It seems to imply that the amount of suffering in the world is roughly proportionate to the amount of growth it can produce—which is plainly false. The suffering of a child dying in agony from a rare disease does not appear to be generating soul-making in any recognizable sense. There is a moral asymmetry between the suffering of the one and the benefit of the many that troubles this view.

The philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams has offered an important refinement here. She argues that for what she calls "horrendous evils"—suffering so terrible that it threatens to destroy a person's entire life—standard soul-making explanations are not enough. The answer is not simply that suffering produces growth, but that God takes our suffering into himself and transforms it. This insight brings us closer to the heart of the Christian response.

---

Before turning to that response, however, I want to acknowledge another biblical strand that is often overlooked: the tradition of protest. The Psalms of Lament do not quietly accept suffering; they rage against it, question it, demand answers. "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" cries the psalmist in Psalm 13. There is no resolution, no happy ending within the psalm itself. The writer does not arrive at peace; he remains in anguish.

This tradition matters. It suggests that faithful wrestling with suffering is itself a form of faith—not passive acceptance but honest argument with God. Abraham bargained with God over Sodom. Moses complained that God had sent him to Pharaoh only to make things worse. The biblical God, it turns out, can handle our anger, our confusion, our protest. The psalms of lament are not failures of faith; they are exercises of it.

What I have been describing so far are intellectual frameworks, ways of thinking about the problem. I mean the story of the cross.

And nothing—"neither death nor life, nor angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation"—can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.

This is the "already but not yet" in which we live. The cross has won the victory, but we do not yet experience its fullness. The resurrection has begun the new creation, but the old creation still groans. We live in the tension between what God has done and what God will do. The cross is the answer—but it is an answer we wait to receive.

---

The problem of suffering is a mystery that exceeds our grasp, and any answer that claims to dissolve it completely has, I suspect, not understood the question. To say that we cannot fully understand why suffering exists is not to say that nothing can be said—it is to say that what can be said must be said with humility, with brokenness, with an awareness that we see through a glass darkly.

The Bible itself does not give easy answers. The book of Job is especially instructive: Job demands an explanation, and God responds not with a theodicy but with a question—"Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?"—which is to say, you cannot understand this from where you stand. And yet God does not leave Job in his suffering; God meets him in the whirlwind, and Job's response is not "Now I understand" but "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen you." That is a different kind of knowledge—not intellectual mastery but relational encounter. It is enough to sustain faith without resolving the tension.

---

I want to end where we began: with the real weight of suffering, which is not a puzzle to be solved but a mystery to be lived. I think of those who are suffering as they read these words—the grief that will not lift, the pain that will not ease, the questions that will not quiet. I do not have an answer for you.

But I have this: that you are not alone. The God who made you is a God who suffers. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus did not explanations his way through the night; he sweat blood and asked if there was any other way. On the cross, he felt the full horror of abandonment. The cross is the proof that no suffering is meaningless and no tear is forgotten. This is not a solution to the problem of pain. It is a presence in the midst of it.

And there is a difference—a pastoral difference, a real difference—between a suffering that is alone and a suffering in which one is accompanied. God does not promise to take the pain away. But God promises to be with us in it. And that changes the loneliness of the suffering, even if it does not change the suffering itself. In the end, perhaps that is enough: not an answer, but a presence. Not a theodicy, but a Companion.

There is a moral asymmetry between the suffering of the one and the benefit of the many that troubles this view. And it risks becoming a kind of spiritual utilitarianism, weighing costs and benefits, as if God were running some vast cosmic cost-benefit analysis. ---

But perhaps the deepest response to suffering is not a framework at all but a story—one that does not explain suffering from the outside but enters into it from within. And before I tell that story, I want to acknowledge that some suffering may resist even the best theological frameworks. The prophet Abraham Heschel wrote that God is "moved by suffering." The theologian Dorothee Sölle spoke of a "suffering that makes room for protest." The theologian Kenneth Surin argued that some evils may be "gratuitous"—so extreme that no theodicy can render them intelligible, even to God. This is not a position that allows for easy resolution, and I include it here because it is honest. The book of Job is honest about this. Job does not receive a theodicy; he receives a whirlwind. And his response is not "Now I understand" but "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen you." That is a different kind of knowledge—not intellectual mastery but relational encounter.

Job, it is worth remembering, wants his day in court. He is not asking for a vision of cosmic grandeur; he is demanding justice. He wants God to weigh in on the scales and find him righteous despite his suffering. And God's answer, strangely, is not a defence but a relationship. "Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?" God asks—and the question is not meant to diminish Job's pain but to re-establish the terms of their conversation. It is not a data-download; it is a recalling of Job to the covenant. The legal/forensic texture of Job's complaint matters: the sufferer is not a problem to be managed but a person to be met.

The Psalms give us language for this. Psalm 22 opens with words of absolute abandonment: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" It moves through anguish into praise: "All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD." This trajectory—from abandonment to vindication—is not a quick fix. It holds the darkness and the light in the same breath. And Lamentations, that unflinching book of communal grief, gives us words like these: "My soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is." The writer does not pretend to understand. But the very act of writing—of giving language to anguish—is itself an act of faith. The church has always sung its lament, knowing that protest and praise are not opposites but companions.

---

Now I come to what I believe is the deepest response the Christian faith offers: the story of the cross.

The Christian faith does not offer a theodicy that stands at a distance from suffering. It offers a God who enters suffering, who takes it upon himself, who refuses to remain distant from the pain of his creatures. This is the staggering claim of the Incarnation: the eternal Son of God became flesh, lived among us, and died the death of a criminal. The cross is not a demonstration that God has solved the problem of suffering; it is God in the very midst of the problem, bearing its full weight. In the cry of Jesus on the hill—"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—we hear not a theological explanation but the sound of God himself suffering. The question is not answered; it is absorbed.

By "meaning," I do not mean a silver-lining explanation, some cosmic rationale that makes the pain explicable. I mean something more надежний: the promise that every suffering is held inside God's memory and future, never lost to oblivion. This is not a solution; it is a presence. God promises to carry every suffering into meaning—not because we can see how, but because God is faithful, and the resurrection is the proof that no wound is final.

The resurrection is the promise that suffering is not the final word—that death will be defeated, that tears will be wiped away, that the wounded world will be made new. But we do not yet live in that new creation. We live in the "already but not yet," in the tension between the promise and its fulfillment.

---

I want to end with something concrete. In my parish, we place a black cloth on the altar during Holy Week. Before the service, people pin to it the names of those they have lost—the dead, the dying, the disappeared, the disillusioned. The cloth grows heavier each day, weighted down with paper notes and photographs. And on Easter morning, we lift that cloth away, and the altar is bare, and the word that rings out is "Alleluia." It is not a solution. It is a practice. It is a way of saying that we will carry what God already carries, and that we will not carry it alone.

# Bearing the Weight of Suffering: A Meditation on God's Goodness

There is a kind of suffering that resists philosophy. It arrives not as an abstract puzzle but as a phone call in the night, a diagnosis, a casket lowered into the earth. The problem of evil is not merely a logical dilemma to be solved; it is a wound that each of us, in our own way, must learn to carry. What I want to do in these reflections is not to dissolve this problem—thereby insulting the intelligence of those who suffer—but to sit with it honestly, to trace the contours of a mystery that has occupied some of the finest minds in human history, and to ask whether faith might offer not an answer but a way of enduring.

The problem, in its starkest form, is this: If God is wholly good and wholly powerful, why is there suffering? Why do children die of starvation? Why do earthquakes bury thousands? Why does cruelty flourish and innocence bleed? These are not rhetorical questions. They are the questions that drive people from faith, and they are the questions that keep those who believe awake at night. The philosopher David Hume put the point with devastating clarity: either God wishes to prevent evil but cannot, in which case God is not omnipotent; or God can prevent evil but does not wish to, in which case God is not wholly good; or God neither can nor wishes to prevent evil, in which case God is neither good nor powerful. The logic seems airtight, and it deserves better than evasion.

But there is a form of this problem that runs deeper than logic. It is not merely that suffering seems *possible* in a world created by a good and powerful God—it is that the *scale* and *distribution* of suffering appears wildly disproportionate to any conceivable purpose. The child who dies in agony from cancer; the earthquake that levels a city of innocents; the Holocaust, that abomination carried out by human hands but permitted by divine silence. Here the problem is not merely that suffering exists, but that it exists in quantities and patterns that seem to mock any theodicy, however sophisticated. This is what philosophers call the *evidential* problem of evil: not a logical contradiction, but a weight of evidence that makes belief in a good and powerful God feel increasingly untenable. It is this problem—more than any abstract trilemma—that breaks people's faith. It deserves to be named honestly.

---

One of the most influential responses to this problem has been the free will defence. The idea is deceptively simple: God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, had to create beings capable of genuine choice. Love that is coerced is not love; it is manipulation. And so God gave humanity freedom—the freedom to choose good or evil, to build or destroy. The suffering that fills our world, on this account, is largely the fruit of human freedom: our capacity for cruelty, our neglect of the vulnerable, our endless wars and betrayals. God does not will suffering; God wills creatures who can love, and love requires the possibility of its opposite.

This is not a trivial answer. It has real power. It explains, at least partially, why a good God might permit certain kinds of suffering—those that flow from human freedom. And it preserves both God's goodness and God's power: God can intervene but chooses, for the sake of something greater, not to override our freedom. The philosopher Alvin Plantinga has shown, with considerable sophistication, that even an omnipotent God cannot create a world containing free creatures who never choose evil—a logical impossibility, not a failure of divine will.

But the free will defence has its limits. It does not explain what are sometimes called "natural evils"—earthquakes, hurricanes, cancers, the suffering of animals. These do not seem to be the result of human sin. A child born with a terrible disease did not choose to suffer; the tectonic plates did not choose to shift. To say that these evils are permitted because God wanted to create a world with regular laws, laws that make free will possible, is to make a point of sorts—but it feels like a point that slides past the ache in our chests. And there is the harder question: even if free will explains much, does it explain *so much*? The magnitude and distribution of suffering seems disproportionate to any good that might come from human freedom. Is the Holocaust, really, the price of love? These objections do not refute the free will defence, but they show that it cannot be the whole story. It is a piece of the puzzle, not the puzzle itself.

---

Another response, older and in some ways more ambitious, is what is often called the soul-making theodicy. Associated with the early church father Irenaeus, this view holds that the world was created not in a state of completion but in a state of becoming. Humanity was made imperfect, with the capacity for growth, and the purpose of existence is to be gradually transformed into the image of God—through choice, through struggle, through the very trials that test and form us. Suffering, on this account, is not merely a problem to be solved but a means through which character is forged. The poet George MacDonald put it this way: "It is not the crown that makes the king, but the being made a king." Pain refines; difficulty educates; the pressure of adversity reveals and creates depths that comfort could never produce.

There is truth here that resonates with human experience. We know, in our own lives, that some of our deepest growth has come through loss, through failure, through the dark nights that forced us to find resources we did not know we had. The philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams has argued, with striking honesty, that some suffering can be "red incorporable"—that is, capable of being taken up into a larger narrative of meaning and woven into a life that, in the end, is glorious. She does not pretend this is easy. She acknowledges that some horrors seem beyond redemption—and yet she holds that nothing is beyond God's redemptive power.

And yet. This theodicy, too, has its fractures. It seems to imply that the amount of suffering in the world is roughly proportionate to the amount of growth it can produce—which is plainly false. The suffering of a child dying in agony from a rare disease does not appear to be generating soul-making in any recognizable sense. There is a moral asymmetry between the suffering of the one and the benefit of the many that troubles this view. And it risks becoming a kind of spiritual utilitarianism, weighing costs and benefits, as if God were running some vast cosmic cost-benefit analysis. The mother holding her dying child is not likely to find much comfort in being told that her child's suffering is "making souls."

---

What I have been describing so far are intellectual frameworks, ways of thinking about the problem. But perhaps the deepest response to suffering is not a framework at all but a story—one that does not explain suffering from the outside but enters into it from within. I mean the story of the cross.

The Christian faith does not offer a theodicy that stands at a distance from suffering. It offers a God who enters suffering, who takes it upon himself, who refuses to remain distant from the pain of his creatures. This is the staggering claim of the Incarnation: the eternal Son of God became flesh, lived among us, and died the death of a criminal. In the cry of Jesus on the hill—"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—we hear not a theological explanation but the sound of God himself suffering. The question is not answered; it is absorbed.

But what does the cross *mean* for the problem of suffering? Several things, I think. First, it is a **substitution**: Christ takes upon himself the suffering that should be ours, bearing the weight of sin and its consequences in his own body. Second, it is a **recapitulation**: in Christ, God enters the human condition in its fullness, including its brokenness, and thereby redeems it from within. Third, and perhaps most profoundly, it is a **victory**: the cross is not the end but the means by which God defeats the powers that cause suffering—sin, death, evil itself. This is the ancient theme of Christus Victor, the ransom paid not merely to appease an angry God but to liberate those held captive by the powers of darkness. The resurrection is the vindication of this victory: death has been defeated, and the suffering creation is being made new.

This is, I think, the most that can be said: that God is with us in our suffering, that God does not observe our pain from some remove but enters it, that the cross is the guarantee that no suffering is meaningless or forgotten. We do not yet live in that new creation. We live in the "already but not yet," in the tension between the promise and its fulfillment. But the promise is real, and it is grounded not in abstract logic but in the empty tomb.

---

I want to be honest: these responses do not satisfy entirely, and I do not think they are meant to. The problem of suffering is a mystery that exceeds our grasp, and any answer that claims to dissolve it completely has, I suspect, not understood the question. But there is a difference between an evasion and an acknowledgment of mystery. To say that we cannot fully understand why suffering exists is not to say that nothing can be said—it is to say that what can be said must be said with humility, with brokenness, with an awareness that we see through a glass darkly.

The Bible itself does not give easy answers. The book of Job is especially instructive: Job demands an explanation, and God responds not with a theodicy but with a question—"Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?"—which is to say, you cannot understand this from where you stand. And yet God does not leave Job in his suffering; God meets him in the whirlwind, and Job's response is not "Now I understand" but "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen you." That is a different kind of knowledge—not intellectual mastery but relational encounter. It is enough to sustain faith without resolving the tension.

The Psalms of lament point in the same direction. The psalmist cries out in anguish, complains to God, demands answers—and is not rebuked for doubt but invited into deeper communion. Romans 8 speaks of the whole creation groaning, waiting for redemption, and of the Spirit interceding for us with groanings too deep for words. This is not a theology of explanation but of solidarity. The God who made all things is in the process of redeeming all things—and that process includes suffering, is even shaped by it, even now.

---

I want to end where we began: with the real weight of suffering, which is not a puzzle to be solved but a mystery to be lived. I think of those who are suffering as they read these words—the grief that will not lift, the pain that will not ease, the questions that will not quiet. I do not have an answer for you. But I have this: that you are not alone, that the God who made you is a God who suffers, that the cross is the proof that no pain is wasted and no tear is forgotten. The resurrection is the promise that suffering is not the final word—that death will be defeated, that the wounded world will be made new, that every tear will be wiped away. This is not a solution. It is a presence. And it is enough—not because suffering is easy, but because in the midst of it, we are held.

The question is not answered with words; it is absorbed into the flesh of God, who bears it without explaining it away.

This is, I think, the most that can be said: that God is with us in our suffering, that God does not observe our pain from some remove but enters it, that the cross is the guarantee that no suffering is meaningless or forgotten. The resurrection is the promise that suffering is not the final word—that death will be defeated, that tears will be wiped away, that the wounded world will be made new.

But we do not yet live in that new creation. We live in the tension between promise and fulfillment, what Paul calls the "already but not yet." In Romans 8, Paul writes that creation "groans" and we "groan" with it, "subjected to futility," waiting for redemption. We peer into this mystery as through frosted glass—aware of shapes and shadows, but the full picture eludes us. Yet the one who calls us forward has been where we are. He knows. He remembers. He carries.

---

I want to be honest: these responses do not satisfy entirely, and I do not think they are meant to. The problem of suffering is a mystery that exceeds our grasp, and any answer that claims to dissolve it completely has, I suspect, not understood the question. But there is a difference between an evasion and an acknowledgment of mystery. To say that we cannot fully understand why suffering exists is not to say that nothing can be said—it is to say that what can be said must be said with humility, with brokenness, with an awareness that we see only partial understanding.

The Bible itself does not give easy answers. The book of Job is especially instructive: Job demands an explanation, and God responds not with a theodicy but with a question—"Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?"—which is to say, you cannot understand this from where you stand. And yet God does not leave Job in his suffering; God meets him in the whirlwind, and Job's response is not "Now I understand" but "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen you." That is a different kind of knowledge—not intellectual mastery but relational encounter. It is enough to sustain faith without resolving the tension.

---

I want to end where we began: with the real weight of suffering, which is not a puzzle to be solved but a mystery to be lived. I think of those who are suffering as they read these words—the grief that will not lift, the pain that will not ease, the questions that will not quiet. I do not have an answer for you. But I have this: that you are not alone, that the God who made you is a God who suffers, that the cross is the proof that no pain is wasted and no tear is forgotten. That is not a solution. It is a presence. And in the end, it is not "perhaps" enough—it is the only thing that has ever been enough.

# Bearing the Weight of Suffering: A Meditation on God's Goodness

There is a kind of suffering that resists philosophy. It arrives not as an abstract puzzle but as a phone call in the night, a diagnosis, a casket lowered into the earth—the mother in the pediatric oncology ward who has not slept in weeks, the survivor of a mudslide who no longer recognizes her own village, the man who wakes each morning into a depression that no medication touches. The problem of evil is not merely a logical dilemma to be solved; it is a wound that each of us, in our own way, must learn to carry. What I want to do in these reflections is not to dissolve this problem—thereby insulting the intelligence of those who suffer—but to sit with it honestly, to trace the contours of a mystery that has occupied some of the finest minds in human history, and to ask whether faith might offer not an answer but a way of enduring.

The problem, in its starkest form, is this: If God is wholly good and wholly powerful, why is there suffering? Why do children die of starvation? Why do earthquakes bury thousands? Why does cruelty flourish and innocence bleed? These are not rhetorical questions. They are the questions that drive people from faith, and they are the questions that keep those who believe awake at night. The philosopher David Hume put the point with devastating clarity: either God wishes to prevent evil but cannot, in which case God is not omnipotent; or God can prevent evil but does not wish to, in which case God is not wholly good; or God neither can nor wishes to prevent evil, in which case God is neither good nor powerful. The logic seems airtight, and it deserves better than evasion.

---

One of the most influential responses to this problem has been the free will defence. The idea is deceptively simple: God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, had to create beings capable of genuine choice. Love that is coerced is not love; it is manipulation. And so God gave humanity freedom—the freedom to choose good or evil, to build or destroy. The suffering that fills our world, on this account, is largely the fruit of human freedom: our capacity for cruelty, our neglect of the vulnerable, our endless wars and betrayals. God does not will suffering; God wills creatures who can love, and love requires the possibility of its opposite.

This is not a trivial answer. It has real power. It explains, at least partially, why a good God might permit certain kinds of suffering—those that flow from human freedom. And it preserves both God's goodness and God's power: God can intervene but chooses, for the sake of something greater, not to override our freedom.

But the free will defence, important as it is, must be distinguished from a full theodicy. A defence offers a possible reason why God might permit evil; a theodicy claims to identify the actual reason. The free will defence does the former, not the latter. Moreover, it does not explain what are sometimes called "natural evils"—earthquakes, hurricanes, cancers, the suffering of animals. These do not seem to be the result of human sin. A child born with a terrible disease did not choose to suffer; the tectonic plates did not choose to shift. Some theologians have suggested that natural evil is connected to human freedom through our stewardship of creation—that a world groaning under ecological damage reflects humanity's failure to tend the garden—but this remains contested. To say that these evils are permitted because God wanted to create a world with regular laws, laws that make free will possible, is to make a point of sorts—but it feels like a point that slides past the ache in our chests. There is also the harder question: even if free will explains much, does it explain *so much*? The magnitude and distribution of suffering seems disproportionate to any good that might come from human freedom. Is the Holocaust, really, the price of love?

These objections do not refute the free will defence, but they show that it cannot be the whole story. It is a piece of the puzzle, not the puzzle itself.

---

Another response, older and in some ways more ambitious, is what is often called the soul-making theodicy. Associated with the early church father Irenaeus, this view holds that the world was created not in a state of completion but in a state of becoming. Humanity was made imperfect, with the capacity for growth, and the purpose of existence is to be gradually transformed into the image of God—through choice, through struggle, through the very trials that test and form us. Suffering, on this account, is not merely a problem to be solved but a means through which character is forged. The poet George MacDonald put it this way: "It is not the crown that makes the king, but the being made a king." Pain refines; difficulty educates; the pressure of adversity reveals and creates depths that comfort could never produce.

There is truth here that resonates with human experience. We know, in our own lives, that some of our deepest growth has come through loss, through failure, through the dark nights that forced us to find resources we did not know we had. The philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams has argued, with striking honesty, that some suffering can be "red incorporable"—that is, capable of being taken up into a larger narrative of meaning and woven into a life that, in the end, is glorious.

And yet. This theodicy, too, has its fractures. It seems to imply that the amount of suffering in the world is roughly proportionate to the amount of growth it can produce—which is plainly false. The suffering of a child dying in agony from a rare disease does not appear to be generating soul-making in any recognizable sense. There is a moral asymmetry between the suffering of the one and the benefit of the many that troubles this view. And it risks becoming a kind of spiritual utilitarianism, weighing costs and benefits, as if God were running some vast cosmic cost-benefit analysis. The mother holding her dying child is not likely to find much comfort in being told that her child's suffering is "making souls."

There is also a darker reality that this theodicy struggles to address: some suffering does not forge character but destroys it. Some pain does not refine but shatters—addiction that remakes the brain in its image, trauma that severs the capacity for trust, suffering so overwhelming that no meaning can be extracted from it. The soul-making theodicy, for all its insight, cannot speak adequately to what might be called "destructive suffering"—the pain that yields nothing, the anguish that is simply waste. And yet, as I will suggest, even this suffering is not outside the reach of the God who enters into it.

---

But before turning to that, I want to acknowledge another dimension of the problem—one that is often missing from philosophical discussions but that the biblical tradition takes with the utmost seriousness. I mean the tradition of protest, of lament, of arguing with God.

The Psalms of Lament—the cries of the righteous sufferer that make up nearly a third of the Psalter—do not offer explanations. They scream. "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). "Why do you hide your face?" (Psalm 88:14). These are not prayers of quiet resignation; they are lawsuits, accusations, demands. The book of Job is often read as a story about the limits of human understanding, and so it is—but it is also a story about the legitimacy of protest. Job refuses to accept his suffering as deserved. He argues with his friends, he argues with God, and in the end God does not rebuke Job for his arguments but for the comforters who tried to explain away his pain. "You have not spoken of me what is right," God says to Job's friends, "as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7-8). There is a holiness to protest itself. Faithfulness sometimes looks like wrestling rather than acceptance.

This tradition of holy anger runs through the entire biblical narrative. Abraham bargains with God over Sodom. Moses demands to know why God has sent him to Pharaoh. The prophet Habakkuk complains that God seems indifferent to injustice—and receives an answer that is less a solution than a promise: "The righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). And in our own century, Elie Wiesel, survivor of the Holocaust, refused to forgive God for the camps, writing in *Night* that "the Kantian idea" had become impossible for him—not because he lost his mind, but because he kept it. This is protest theodicy: the refusal to accept suffering quietly, the insistence that God hear the cry of the afflicted. The Bible gives us language not just to endure suffering but to rage against it. And perhaps that rage, too, is a form of faith—the faith that suffering is wrong, that it should not be, that even if God permits it, God is not indifferent to its weight.

---

What I have been describing so far are intellectual frameworks, ways of thinking about the problem. But perhaps the deepest response to suffering is not a framework at all but a story—one that does not explain suffering from the outside but enters into it from within. I mean the story of the cross.

The Christian faith does not offer a theodicy that stands at a distance from suffering. It offers a God who enters suffering, who takes it upon himself, who refuses to remain distant from the pain of his creatures. This is the staggering claim of the Incarnation: the eternal Son of God became flesh, lived among us, and died the death of a criminal. The cross is not a demonstration that God has solved the problem of suffering; it is God in the very midst of the problem, bearing its full weight. In the cry of Jesus on the hill—"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—we hear not a theological explanation but the sound of God himself suffering. The question is not answered; it is absorbed.

This is, I think, the most that can be said: that God is with us in our suffering, that God does not observe our pain from some remove but enters it, that the cross is the guarantee that no suffering is meaningless or forgotten. The resurrection is the promise that suffering is not the final word—that death will be defeated, that tears will be wiped away, that the wounded world will be made new. But we do not yet live in that new creation. We live in the "already but not yet," in the tension between the promise and its fulfillment.

I should be clear: the cross does not solve the logical problem of evil. It does not explain why suffering exists. It is not a theoretical theodicy but a practical one—not an answer to the question "why?" but a response to the question "how?" How shall we endure? How shall we live in the face of pain? The cross offers not an explanation but a presence. It does not tell us that suffering is for our good but tells us that God suffers with us, that we are not alone, that even the cry of dereliction is heard.

And this presence extends to the darkest places—to suffering that breaks and unmakes, to pain that yields no growth, to the anguish that seems utterly wasted. If the cross is God entering suffering, it is God entering even these sorrows, holding the suffering that cannot be综合利用, the grief that cannot be turned to gain. There is no suffering so destructive, so final, so lost, that God's solidarity does not reach it. This is not a promise that all suffering will make sense; it is a promise that no suffering is outside the circle of God's love.

---

I want to be honest: these responses do not satisfy entirely, and I do not think they are meant to. The problem of suffering is a mystery that exceeds our grasp, and any answer that claims to dissolve it completely has, I suspect, not understood the question. But there is a difference between an evasion and an acknowledgment of mystery. To say that we cannot fully understand why suffering exists is not to say that nothing can be said—it is to say that what can be said must be said with humility, with brokenness, with an awareness that we see through a glass darkly.

The Bible itself does not give easy answers. The book of Job is especially instructive: Job demands an explanation, and God responds not with a theodicy but with a question—"Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?"—which is to say, you cannot understand this from where you stand. And yet God does not leave Job in his suffering; God meets him in the whirlwind, and Job's response is not "Now I understand" but "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen you" (Job 42:5). That is a different kind of knowledge—not intellectual mastery but relational encounter. It is enough to sustain faith without resolving the tension. And the text adds one more thing: God restores Job's fortunes. The answer is not explanation but presence, and beyond that, restoration. We are held in mystery, but we are not held in nothing.

---

I want to end where we began: with the real weight of suffering, which is not a puzzle to be solved but a mystery to be lived. I think of those who are suffering as they read these words—the grief that will not lift, the pain that will not ease, the questions that will not quiet. I do not have an answer for you. But I have this: that you are not alone, that the God who made you is a God who suffers, that the cross is the proof that no pain is wasted and no tear is forgotten. You may rage. You may lament. You may refuse to accept what has happened to you as somehow good. The Psalter gives you language for that refusal. Job gives you permission to argue. And the cross gives you a God who enters the darkness with you, who does not explain but holds, who does not answer but remains. That is not a solution. It is a presence. And perhaps, in the end, it is enough.

48wzy5i0un2jcnZI3Fh1M.text:
There is a question that presses upon anyone who takes both faith and experience seriously: How can a God who is truly good and truly powerful allow the world to be saturated with suffering? This is not an abstract puzzle to be dispatched in a seminar room. It is the cry that rises from hospitals in the small hours, from parents bending over coffins too small, from the silence of those who have endured losses that language cannot hold. The question is old, but it does not age. And it deserves more than the easy answers we sometimes offer.

The problem, stated charitably, runs something like this: If God is all-powerful, God could prevent suffering. If God is all-good, God would want to prevent suffering. Yet suffering exists in abundance. Either God is not all-powerful, or God is not all-good, or—perhaps most troubling—God exists but is indifferent to human pain. The tension is not merely logical; it is existential. It strikes at the heart of whether the universe is fundamentally friendly or hostile, whether our lives have meaning beyond what we ourselves invent.

It is right to name this as a genuine problem, not a pseudo-question to be dissolved by linguistic trickery. Those who have suffered deeply—and those who have sat with them—know that easy answers ring hollow. The problem of evil is one of the most serious intellectual challenges that faith has ever faced, and it has driven thoughtful people away from belief altogether. To engage with it honestly, we must not minimize its force.

---

One of the most influential responses has been the free will defense, developed in various forms by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The idea is that God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, had to grant them genuine freedom—including the freedom to harm others and themselves. A world of free agents will inevitably contain cruelty, violence, betrayal, and all the moral evils that humans inflict upon one another. God could have created robots who never chose wrongly, but such beings could not have loved. Love, by its nature, must be free.

This response carries real weight. It helps us see that a world filled with meaning and moral depth cannot be a world in which God simply coerces goodness. The capacity for genuine relationship—with God and with others—requires the possibility of saying no. And when we look at the history of human cruelty, much of it flows from human choices: wars chosen, abuses committed, injustices sustained. We are not innocent victims of a cosmic machinery; we are agents who harm one another.

Yet the free will defense has limits that honest reflection must acknowledge. It explains moral evil—evil caused by human choices—but it struggles with what philosophers call natural evil: earthquakes, diseases, hurricanes, the suffering of children and animals. A child born with a terminal illness did not choose anything; the fault, if there is one, lies in the design of nature itself. Either God could have created a world without such natural evils and chose not to, or God could not have—and if the former, the question returns in full force. The free will defense also raises the uncomfortable question of whether the immense scale of human suffering is truly necessary for the goods of freedom and love. Could God not have created free beings who, on balance, harm far less than they do?

---

A second major response is what is often called the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick. The idea is that the world, as we experience it, is not the final product of God's creation but a "vale of soul-making"—a place where finite, developing beings can grow toward genuine goodness, wisdom, and love. Suffering, on this view, serves a purpose: it builds character, deepens compassion, reveals the fragility of worldly attachments, and draws us toward dependence on God.

There is something genuinely true here. Many of us can look back at our own lives and recognize that suffering—loss, failure, pain—produced growth that ease and comfort could never have generated. The virtues forged in difficulty seem more sturdy than those acquired in serenity. And the biblical witness does seem to suggest that the Christian hope is not a return to Eden but a participation in the divine nature, a process of becoming more fully what God intends us to be.

But this response, too, presses against the limits of what we can plausibly maintain. The scale and nature of suffering in our world seem wildly disproportionate to any soul-making purpose. A child who dies in agony from a disease that even adults find unbearable—is this really necessary for her soul-making? The earthquakes that kill tens of thousands, the plagues that sweep through populations, the daily cruelties of a fallen world: do these truly serve a purpose of growth that could not be achieved in some less brutal fashion? The soul-making theodicy risks becoming a theodicy of optimization, as if God were balancing ledger sheets of suffering against spiritual growth. And it raises a troubling further question: What of those who do not grow, who are broken by suffering, whose souls are crushed rather than refined? The theodicy, if pressed too far, begins to feel like a counsel of survivors.

---

It is at this point that the Christian tradition turns, not primarily to an explanation, but to an event: the cross of Jesus Christ. This is not a deductive argument but something deeper—a claim that God has not remained distant from human suffering but has entered into it. In the incarnation, God takes on flesh and, in that flesh, experiences the full weight of human pain: betrayal, abandonment, physical torture, the feeling of God-forsakenness. The cry of Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not an aberration in the life of Jesus; it is the heart of the matter.

This matters because it rules out certain conceptions of God that might otherwise seem attractive. It is not that God is impassible, locked in serene indifference above the fray. Nor is God simply the great architect who designed the universe and then stepped back. In Christ, God gets involved—and gets involved precisely in the most painful way. The cross does not explain why suffering exists in the abstract, but it does something perhaps more important: it assures those who suffer that they are not alone, that their suffering is taken up into something redemptive, that even the darkest experiences of abandonment are held within the embrace of divine love.

The theologian Jürgen Moltmann, who wrote extensively about the cross in the wake of his own experiences during and after World War II, insisted that the resurrection of Christ is the promise that no suffering is final, that the power of love is stronger than death. This is not a neat answer to the problem of evil—it is, rather, a refusal to let evil have the last word. The Christian hope is not that suffering makes sense but that suffering will be redeemed.

---

The Bible itself, particularly the Psalms and the book of Job, models a different way of approaching the question of suffering. The Psalms are full of laments—cries of pain, protest, even anger directed at God. "Why are you so far from helping me?" the psalmist cries. "I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint." This is not the language of neat theodicy; it is the language of real people bringing their real suffering into the presence of a God who can handle their honesty. And in Job, when the protagonist demands answers from God, what he receives is not a philosophical explanation but an encounter: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding." The divine response is not a defense but an invitation into mystery—a reminder that the ways of God are not the ways of humans, that there is more to the story than we can see from within our limited perspective.

Yet Job's encounter is not empty. God does speak, and Job does receive. And Romans 8, that magnificent chapter of hope, acknowledges that "the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of creation," but insists that we are not alone in our groaning—the Spirit intercedes for us with sighs too deep for words, and nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. This is not a solution to the problem; it is a holding of the problem in a context of trust.

---

What, then, can we say? We can say that the problem of suffering is real, that it resists easy answers, and that those who offer glib explanations have not taken the weight of it seriously enough. We can say that the Christian faith does not exempt us from the difficulty but rather meets us in the midst of it—that the cross of Christ is God's answer not to the logic of evil but to the experience of it, a promise of presence and a pledge of redemption. We can say that the goods of freedom and love and character are real, that suffering can serve purposes of growth, and that God can bring good out of even the worst evil—but we must also say that we do not see the whole picture, that our explanations are partial and provisional, that there is a mystery we cannot penetrate.

And we can say this: that faith is not the absence of the question but the willingness to live within it, to hold both the cry of protest and the whisper of hope, to trust that the God who made the world and entered its suffering has not abandoned it and will not abandon us. The problem of suffering remains. But it is met, in the end, not by a proof but by a person—by the one who suffered for us, with us, and beyond us, and who promises that weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning.

The capacity for genuine relationship—with God and with others—requires the possibility of saying no. And when we look at the history of human cruelty, much of it flows from human choices: wars chosen, abuses committed, injustices sustained. It explains moral evil—evil caused by human choices—but it struggles devastatingly with what philosophers call natural evil: earthquakes, tsunamis, diseases, hurricanes, the suffering of children and animals. A child born with a terminal illness did not choose anything. A fawn trapped in a forest fire made no decision that led to its suffering. The fault, if there is one, lies in the design of nature itself—the brutal biology of predators and prey, the tectonic instability of the earth, the cellular mutations that produce cancer. This is not the language of neat theodicy; it is the language of real people bringing their real suffering into the presence of a God who can handle their honesty.

We can say that the Christian faith does not exempt us from the difficulty but rather meets us in the midst of it—that the cross of Christ is God's answer not to the logic of evil but to the experience of it, a promise of presence and a pledge of redemption. The problem of suffering remains. But it is met, in the end, not by a proof but by a person—by the one who suffered for us, with us, and beyond us, and who promises that weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning.

# The Problem of Suffering: A Revised Essay

There is a question that presses upon anyone who takes both faith and experience seriously: How can a God who is truly good and truly powerful allow the world to be saturated with suffering? This is not an abstract puzzle to be dispatched in a seminar room. It is the cry that rises from hospitals in the small hours, from parents bending over coffins too small, from the silence of those who have endured losses that language cannot hold. The question is old, but it does not age. And it deserves more than the easy answers we sometimes offer.

The problem, stated charitably, runs something like this: If God is all-powerful, God could prevent suffering. If God is all-good, God would want to prevent suffering. Yet suffering exists in abundance. Either God is not all-powerful, or God is not all-good, or—perhaps most troubling—God exists but is indifferent to human pain. The tension is not merely logical; it is existential. It strikes at the heart of whether the universe is fundamentally friendly or hostile, whether our lives have meaning beyond what we ourselves invent.

It is right to name this as a genuine problem, not a pseudo-question to be dissolved by linguistic trickery. Those who have suffered deeply—and those who have sat with them—know that easy answers ring hollow. The problem of evil is one of the most serious intellectual challenges that faith has ever faced, and it has driven thoughtful people away from belief altogether. To engage with it honestly, we must not minimize its force.

---

One of the most influential responses has been the free will defense, developed in various forms by philosophers like Alvin Plantinga. The idea is that God, in creating beings capable of genuine love, had to grant them genuine freedom—including the freedom to harm others and themselves. A world of free agents will inevitably contain cruelty, violence, betrayal, and all the moral evils that humans inflict upon one another. God could have created robots who never chose wrongly, but such beings could not have loved. Love, by its nature, must be free.

This response carries real weight. It helps us see that a world filled with meaning and moral depth cannot be a world in which God simply coerces goodness. The capacity for genuine relationship—with God and with others—requires the possibility of saying no. And when we look at the history of human cruelty, much of it flows from human choices: wars chosen, abuses committed, injustices sustained. We are not innocent victims of a cosmic machinery; we are agents who harm one another.

Yet the free will defense has limits that honest reflection must acknowledge. It explains moral evil—evil caused by human choices—but it struggles with what philosophers call natural evil: earthquakes, diseases, hurricanes, the suffering of children and animals. A child born with a terminal illness did not choose anything; the fault, if there is one, lies in the design of nature itself. The defense also raises the uncomfortable question of whether the immense scale of human suffering is truly necessary for the goods of freedom and love. Could God not have created free beings who, on balance, harm far less than they do? Perhaps more fundamentally: did God have to create a world where the mere *potential* for freedom necessarily resulted in *this much* realized evil? ---

A second major response is what is often called the soul-making theodicy, associated with the early church father Irenaeus and developed in modern times by philosophers like John Hick. The idea is that the world, as we experience it, is not the final product of God's creation but a "vale of soul-making"—a place where finite, developing beings can grow toward genuine goodness, wisdom, and love. Suffering, on this view, serves a purpose: it builds character, deepens compassion, reveals the fragility of worldly attachments, and draws us toward dependence on God.

There is something genuinely true here. Many of us can look back at our own lives and recognize that suffering—loss, failure, pain—produced growth that ease and comfort could never have generated. The virtues forged in difficulty seem more sturdy than those acquired in serenity. A child who dies in agony from a disease that even adults find unbearable—is this really necessary for her soul-making? The earthquakes that kill tens of thousands, the plagues that sweep through populations, the daily cruelties of a fallen world: do these truly serve a purpose of growth that could not be achieved in some less brutal fashion? The soul-making theodicy risks becoming a theodicy of optimization, as if God were balancing ledger sheets of suffering against spiritual growth. The cry of Psalm 22, placed on the lips of Jesus in the Gospel narratives—"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—is not an aberration in the life of Jesus; it is the heart of the matter.

This matters because it rules out certain conceptions of God that might otherwise seem attractive. It is not that God is impassible, locked in serene indifference above the fray. Nor is God simply the great architect who designed the universe and then stepped back. In Christ, God gets involved—and gets involved precisely in the most painful way.

The theologian Jürgen Moltmann, who wrote extensively about the cross in the wake of his own experiences during and after World War II, insisted on something more radical still. For Moltmann, the cross is not merely God entering into suffering generally; it is God experiencing the godforsakenness of the cross—the actual suffering of the absence of God, a rupture in the divine life itself. The Father turns away from the Son; the Son bears the full weight of abandonment. This is more than solidarity; it is a participation in suffering so complete that it transforms our understanding of who God is.

The cross does not explain why suffering exists in the abstract, but it does something perhaps more important: it assures those who suffer that they are not alone, that their suffering is taken up into something redemptive, that even the darkest experiences of abandonment are held within the embrace of divine love. And this presence is not merely spiritual—it is embodied in the community that breaks bread, visits the prisoner, binds wounds, and refuses to look away.

---

A third response, often overlooked in systematic treatments, is what scholars call protest theodicy—the refusal to justify suffering, the insistence that God stands with the sufferer against the injustice of suffering rather than explaining it. The Jewish tradition has a word for this: *chutzpah*, the audacity to cry out against Heaven even while remaining in relationship with it. Thinkers like Abraham Joshua Heschel and Dorothee Sölle have insisted that some responses to suffering are not failures of faith but its deepest expression—the cry of those who believe too much in God's goodness to accept its violation quietly.

The Psalms themselves model this. They are full of laments—cries of pain, protest, even anger directed at God. "Why are you so far from helping me?" the psalmist cries. "I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint." This is not the language of neat theodicy; it is the language of real people bringing their real suffering into the presence of a God who can handle their honesty.

And in Job, when the protagonist demands answers from God, what he receives is not a philosophical explanation but an encounter: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding." Some readers find this divine response troubling—an exercise of divine power that silences the victim rather than vindicating him. Yet even this troubling aspect reminds us that explanations from on high may not satisfy those who suffer on the ground, that the text itself models the limits of theological explanation, including its own. Job does receive an answer, but it is the answer of presence, not information.

And Romans 8, that magnificent chapter of hope, acknowledges that "the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of *childbirth*"—the metaphor is crucial, gestational, pointing toward a purpose and a hope, not random suffering. Paul insists that we are not alone in our groaning—the Spirit intercedes for us with sighs too deep for words, and nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. This is not a solution to the problem; it is a holding of the problem in a context of trust.

---

What, then, can we say? We can say that the problem of suffering is real, that it resists easy answers, and that those who offer glib explanations have not taken the weight of it seriously enough. We can say that the Christian faith does not exempt us from the difficulty but rather meets us in the midst of it—that the cross of Christ is God's answer not to the logic of evil but to the experience of it, a promise of presence and a pledge of redemption. We can say that the goods of freedom and love and character are real, that suffering can serve purposes of growth, and that God can bring good out of even the worst evil—but we must also say that we do not see the whole picture, that our explanations are partial and provisional, that there is a mystery we cannot penetrate.

The problem remains unsolved. But it is met, in the end, not by a proof but by a presence—the one who weeps with us in the night, and promises, against all evidence, that morning will come. We cannot see how the pieces fit. But we are invited to trust the one who holds them.

# Bearing the Unbearable: Suffering, Silence, and the Goodness of God

There is a moment—often unexpected, often in the small hours of the night—when the question ceases to be abstract and becomes unbearable. A child's diagnosis. A marriage ending. A loneliness that no presence can penetrate. In those moments, the problem of evil is not a philosophical puzzle; it is a wound that will not close.

I want to begin by acknowledging what should be obvious: this essay will not solve the problem of suffering. No essay can. What I hope to offer is something more modest and perhaps more useful: a wrestling with the questions, an honest accounting of the resources the Christian tradition offers, and an acknowledgment of what remains opaque. If you are currently in the valley of deep grief, you may find little comfort here. But perhaps you will find that you are not alone in your questions.

---

## The Shape of the Problem

The classical formulation of the problem of evil is deceptively simple. It runs something like this: If God is omnipotent—able to prevent all suffering— and omnibenevolent—wholly good and desirous of our well-being—then why does suffering exist? The contradiction seems inescapable. Either God lacks the power to stop suffering, in which case God is not omnipotent; or God lacks the desire to stop it, in which case God is not wholly good; or, most troubling of all, God simply does not care.

This is not a straw man. It is a profound challenge that has occupied some of the finest minds in the Christian tradition, and it deserves a serious answer. The atheist philosopher David Hume put it forcefully: "Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? Then he is impotent. Is he able, but not willing? Then he is malevolent. Is he both able and willing? Whence then evil?"

We must not soften this question. It is the most formidable objection to theism, and those who dismiss it lightly have not understood its force.

---

## Free Will and the Space Between

One of the most influential responses is what we might call the *free will defence*. The argument runs that genuine love requires freedom. A world in which God mechanically prevented all harm would be a world of puppets, not persons. Love, by its very nature, must be chosen—and choosing love entails the possibility of choosing otherwise. The suffering we inflict on one another, the cruelty and indifference that scar human life, flows from this freedom. We are not passive victims of a cosmic accident; we are agents capable of great nobility and great atrocity.

There is something undeniably true here. Much of the suffering in the world is caused by human choices—war, oppression, neglect, betrayal. The free will defence names a real feature of our condition. When we witness the aftermath of violence, we recognize that *people* did this, not merely nature.

Yet this response has well-known limits. It struggles to account for natural evil—the earthquake, the cancer, the child born into a world of pain through no one's fault. It is cold comfort to the parent whose infant suffers from a congenital disease. "God gave us free will," they might reasonably say, "but my baby never chose anything." The free will defence illuminates one category of suffering but does not resolve all of it.

---

## Soul-Making and the Purposeful Valley

A second response, developed by the early church father Irenaeus and refined in more recent theology, is the *soul-making theodicy*. This view suggests that the world, as it is, is not a finished product but a place of becoming. We are not created complete; we are shaped through the trials of life into the people God intends us to be. Suffering, in this account, is not merely a byproduct of free will but an instrument of growth.

The apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, articulates something like this: "We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28). He does not say all things *are* good, but that they *work together* for good. The process is not pleasant—it involves "groaning" and "suffering" (Romans 8:22-23). Yet Paul holds that this transformation into the image of Christ is worth the cost.

There is genuine wisdom here. Many of us know, in retrospect, how suffering forged qualities in us that ease could never have produced—patience, compassion, depth. The person we became after loss is not the person we would have become without it.

But this response also has limits. It can feel like a subtle form of victim-blaming, suggesting that those who suffer are simply not yet spiritually mature enough to see the purpose. It can become a way of avoiding the harder questions: What of the child who dies before any "soul-making" can occur? What of suffering that seems to produce not wisdom but bitterness? The soul-making theodicy offers a framework, but it does not unlock every door.

---

## The God Who Suffers

Perhaps the most profound response is not a defence at all but a *reorientation*. It begins not with philosophy but with the cross.

The Christian faith does not offer a God who observes suffering from a distance, calculating how best to use it for some greater purpose. It offers a God who enters into suffering. In Jesus Christ, God takes on flesh and walks the way of grief, abandonment, and death. The resurrection does not erase the cross; it vindicates the one who died on it. But the suffering remains real. It is not an illusion or a necessary stepping stone. It is the place where God meets us.

This is the heart of the matter: the Christian God is not *explained* by suffering but *defined* by response to it. The question is not merely "Why do we suffer?" but "What has God done in the midst of it?"

The biblical witness is clear on this point. The Psalms are full of lament—cries of anger, confusion, and despair that do not resolve into easy answers (Psalm 22, Psalm 88). Job demands an accounting from God, and what he receives is not an explanation but an encounter. God's answer to Job is not a lecture on the purposes of suffering but a self-revelation: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" (Job 38:4). The effect is not to explain pain but to place it within a larger story in which God is present.

The cross tells us that God does not remain untouched by our anguish. God *participates* in it. This is the distinctive claim of Christian theodicy: that the answer to suffering is not a theodicy at all but a Person.

---

## What We Cannot Know

I have offered you two major frameworks—the free will defence and the soul-making theodicy—alongside the irreducible mystery of the cross. But I must be honest: these responses do not answer every question. There is much that remains in shadow.

We cannot reconcile the death of a child with any neat theology of purpose. We cannot explain why one person is born into comfort and another into misery. The scales of justice in this world are profoundly unequal, and the Christian faith does not pretend otherwise.

What we can say is this: the question "Where is God in my suffering?" has an answer, but it is not a proposition. It is a person—broken, present, and risen. The resurrection does not promise that we will understand our suffering, only that we will not be abandoned to it.

To those who are in the depths right now, I offer no easy comfort. The words ofScripture that once brought peace may now ring hollow. That too is part of the journey. The tradition of lament gives us permission to bring our anger, our confusion, and our grief to God—not as a problem to be solved but as a relationship to be lived.

We see through a glass darkly. We do not see clearly. But we are seen, and we are known, and we are held. That is not an answer. But perhaps, in the end, it is enough.
